signals.title: Paimon: pypaimon-written TIMESTAMP-partitioned tables are unreadable (partition directory spelling mismatch, raw STD_EXCEPTION)
signals.text: **Describe what's wrong** A Paimon table with a `TIMESTAMP` partition key written by pypaimon (the Python implementation of Paimon, version 2.0.0) is unreadable by ClickHouse: every read fails with `Code: 1001. DB::Exception: std::__1::filesystem::filesystem_error ... No such file or directory`, because ClickHouse and pypaimon spell the partition directory name differently. pypaimon writes the partition directory as `t=2026-01-01 12:00:00.123000` (literal space between date and time, unescaped colons, microsecond digits regardless of the declared precision). ClickHouse, following the Java Paimon spelling (the same one used by the `paimon_timestamp_partition` fixtures added in #113401, e.g. `ts=1960-03-04T05%3A06%3A07.000000891`), reconstructs the path as `t=2026-01-01T12%3A00%3A00.123` (`T` separator, `%3A`-escaped colons, precision-scaled fraction digits) and looks for a directory that does not exist. Two aspects seem worth fixing or deciding on the ClickHouse side, even though the spelling divergence itself arguably originates in pypaimon: 1. Whether the reader should tolerate the alternative spelling (pypaimon-written timestamp-partitioned tables are presumably readable by pypaimon itself — it reads its own table back fine — so the two implementations disagree about the on-disk contract, and tables written by the Python toolchain are silently incompatible with ClickHouse). 2. The failure surfaces as `STD_EXCEPTION` (code 1001) leaking a raw `std::filesystem` error, rather than a catchable, actionable message naming the table/partition mismatch. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master, version 26.8.1.1516. **How to reproduce** Write a timestamp-partitioned table with pypaimon (`pip install pypaimon pyarrow`): ```python import datetime as dt import pyarrow as pa from pypaimon import CatalogFactory, Schema cat = CatalogFactory.create({"warehouse": "/tmp/paimon_ts_wh"}) cat.create_database("db", False) schema = pa.schema([("t", pa.timestamp("ms")), ("k", pa.int64()), ("v", pa.int64())]) cat.create_table("db.ts", Schema.from_pyarrow_schema(schema, partition_keys=["t"]), False) tbl = cat.get_table("db.ts") wb = tbl.new_batch_write_builder() w, c = wb.new_write(), wb.new_commit() w.write_arrow(pa.table({ "t": pa.array([dt.datetime(2026, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0, 123000), dt.datetime(2026, 1, 2, 13, 30, 0, 456000)], pa.timestamp("ms")), "k": pa.array([1, 2], pa.int64()), "v": pa.array([10, 20], pa.int64())})) c.commit(w.prepare_commit()) ``` The directory pypaimon creates is: ``` $ ls /tmp/paimon_ts_wh/db.db/ts/ manifest schema snapshot 't=2026-01-01 12:00:00.123000' 't=2026-01-02 13:30:00.456000' ``` Read it with ClickHouse: ``` $ clickhouse local -q "SELECT * FROM paimonLocal('/tmp/paimon_ts_wh/db.db/ts') ORDER BY k" Code: 1001. DB::Exception: std::__1::filesystem::filesystem_error: filesystem error: Got unexpected error while getting file metadata: No such file or directory ["/tmp/paimon_ts_wh/db.db/ts/t=2026-01-01T12%3A00%3A00.123/bucket-0/data-....parquet"]. (STD_EXCEPTION) ``` The path in the error shows the spelling ClickHouse reconstructed from the manifest `BinaryRow` partition value; the directory on disk uses pypaimon's spelling. **Expected behavior** Either the table reads back its two rows (if the pypaimon spelling is considered acceptable input), or a catchable error explains that the partition directory referenced by the manifest was not found — not a raw `std::filesystem` exception. **Additional context** pypaimon reads its own table back correctly, so the data itself is intact; only the partition-path reconstruction disagrees. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113401 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115042 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113337 Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: Server crash (SIGSEGV) in gRPC response compression (`zlib_compress` / `deflateEnd`)
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115036 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108074 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114054 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114045 ### Describe what's wrong The server received `SIGSEGV` inside gRPC's response compression path while executing `SELECT 0 FROM numbers(1000000)` over gRPC with `transport_compression`, in the `amd_cfi` build of the `WeeklyCFI` workflow (PR validation run of #115036). This is a plain segmentation fault (`Address: 0x50. Access: read. Address not mapped to object.`), not a CFI trap (CFI violations trap with `SIGILL`): ``` 2. free_default 3. deflateEnd 4. zlib_compress(grpc_slice_buffer*, grpc_slice_buffer*, int) (.llvm.6130045630295956944) 5. grpc_msg_compress(grpc_compression_algorithm, grpc_slice_buffer*, grpc_slice_buffer*) 6. grpc_core::ChannelCompression::CompressMessage(...) ... 13. grpc_call_start_batch 14. grpc::internal::CallOpSet<...>::ContinueFillOpsAfterInterception() 15. DB::(anonymous namespace)::Responder<(DB::(anonymous namespace)::CallType)0>::writeAndFinish(...) 16. DB::(anonymous namespace)::Call::sendResult() 17. DB::(anonymous namespace)::Call::run() ``` The crash made `test_grpc_protocol/test.py::test_transport_compression` fail and cascaded into `test_opentelemetry_context_propagation` and `test_restart` (dead server). All three passed on retry, so the crash is probabilistic, and this stack has exactly one confirmed occurrence so far — whether the build profile (`amd_cfi` is the only integration-test build with ThinLTO) matters is unknown. `test_transport_compression` has failed occasionally in other builds (`amd_asan`, `amd_msan`, `amd_tsan`, `amd_binary`, `amd_llvm_coverage`) in other PRs, but with different signatures (server unreachable at test start, cluster startup/teardown problems), so those are not confirmed instances of this crash. Possibly relevant: the deflate subsystem is under active churn — #108074 (use libdeflate for gzip/zlib/deflate, merged 2026-07-14) is being reverted in #114054 (closes #114045), that revert touches `tests/integration/test_grpc_protocol/test.py` and `src/Server/grpc_protos/clickhouse_grpc.proto`, and on 2026-08-16 — the same day as this crash — `test_transport_compression` also failed in #114054's Bugfix validation on both architectures. #108074 predates four green `WeeklyCFI` runs that exercised this test, so it is not a clean attribution either. ### How to reproduce * Commit: 6d53f1de970dcf1f88b4e208cdd03091cd098272 (PR head merge of #115036, version 26.8.1.1) * Build: `amd_cfi` (`-DENABLE_THINLTO=1 -DENABLE_CFI=1 -DSPLIT_DEBUG_SYMBOLS=ON -DBUILD_STRIPPED_BINARY=1`, RelWithDebInfo) * Test: `tests/integration/test_grpc_protocol/test.py::test_transport_compression` (probabilistic; one occurrence in one run so far) CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115036&sha=30c47a7d9420ba1e86365979016e7765cbc080da&name_0=WeeklyCFI&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28amd_cfi%2C%202%2F4%29 No fiddle link: the crash needs a gRPC client with transport compression against the server, which fiddle cannot exercise.

signals.title: Empty `symbols` and `lines` in `system.trace_log` in the `amd_cfi` build profile
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115036 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100419 ### Describe what's wrong In the `amd_cfi` build (ThinLTO + CFI + `SPLIT_DEBUG_SYMBOLS` + `BUILD_STRIPPED_BINARY` — ClickHouse's only CI test build with ThinLTO), query profiler symbolization is completely broken: every row of `system.trace_log` has all-empty `symbols` and all-empty `lines`, while `build_id` still resolves. Both symbolization tests fail deterministically (49/49 and 52/52 reruns, with and without randomized settings): * `03150_trace_log_add_build_id` — `countIf(arrayExists(x -> x != '', symbols)) > 1` returns `0` (symbol names come from the binary's own symbol table) * `03150_trace_log_source_lines` — the equivalent check on `lines` returns `0` (source lines come from DWARF) The tests pass in every regular (non-ThinLTO) CI build. This is a longstanding property of the `amd_cfi` profile, not a recent regression: the tests have failed under it since at least 2026-07-13 (validation runs of #100419, including after `-DSPLIT_DEBUG_SYMBOLS=ON` was added there) and have never passed under it. Which ingredient is responsible (ThinLTO, the CFI flags, or the stripped/split-debug packaging) is not yet isolated; the commit message of `ed28e41bf7` in #100419 claims `amd_release` (ThinLTO without CFI) passes the test, which would point at the CFI flags, but that claim is unverified in CI. If ThinLTO alone turns out to be sufficient, official release builds would be affected too, and no CI job other than `WeeklyCFI` would see it. ### How to reproduce * Commit: 6d53f1de970dcf1f88b4e208cdd03091cd098272 (PR head merge of #115036, version 26.8.1.1) * Build: `amd_cfi` (`-DENABLE_THINLTO=1 -DENABLE_CFI=1 -DSPLIT_DEBUG_SYMBOLS=ON -DBUILD_STRIPPED_BINARY=1`, RelWithDebInfo) * Run `03150_trace_log_add_build_id` or `03150_trace_log_source_lines` CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115036&sha=30c47a7d9420ba1e86365979016e7765cbc080da&name_0=WeeklyCFI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_cfi%2C%20parallel%29 No fiddle link: reproducing needs a ThinLTO+CFI build, which fiddle does not provide.

signals.title: Wrong result: optimize_trivial_count_query makes count(arrayJoin(arr)) return the table's row count instead of the number of array elements
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe what's wrong - With the default `optimize_trivial_count_query = 1`, `SELECT count(arrayJoin(arr)) FROM t` returns the number of rows in the table instead of the number of array elements. - arrayJoin is a row-multiplying operator, so the aggregate must observe the post-expansion stream. The trivial-count optimization replaces the entire table read with a stored row counter and never evaluates count's argument, so the ARRAY JOIN expansion is silently dropped. No error, no warning. - The optimization rests on the premise "the number of rows the aggregate sees equals the number of rows stored in the table." That holds for `count()`, `count(1)` and `count(non_nullable_col)`, but arrayJoin breaks it, and nothing in the guard list checks for it. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce - https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/a93a2cb4-e0f1-450b-a97e-0acef509da3b ``` ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬──────────┐ │ Query │ Result │ Correct? │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(arrayJoin(A)) │ 2 │ ✗ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(arrayJoin(A)) SETTINGS optimize_trivial_count_query = 0 │ 5 │ ✓ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(*) FROM (SELECT arrayJoin(A) ...) │ 5 │ ✓ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ sum(length(A)) │ 5 │ ✓ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴──────────┘ ``` ### Expected behavior - The `count(arrayJoin(A))` should return the total number of array elements across all rows, equivalent to sum(length(A)). ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signals.title: Azure managed-identity token failure surfaces as STD_EXCEPTION (code 1001) instead of a catchable authentication error
signals.text: **Describe what's wrong** When Azure Blob Storage authentication goes through `ManagedIdentityCredential` (the default `getAuthMethod` fallback when a disk carries no `account_key` / `connection_string` / `use_workload_identity`) and the identity endpoint rejects the token request, the query fails with `Code: 1001` (`STD_EXCEPTION`) — the Azure SDK's `Azure::Core::Credentials::AuthenticationException` propagates to the client untranslated instead of being classified as an authentication error. ``` Code: 1001. DB::Exception: Azure::Core::Credentials::AuthenticationException: GetToken(): error response: 401 Unauthorized {}. (STD_EXCEPTION) ``` The equivalent GCS flow translates the same failure shape properly: `PocoHTTPClientGCPOAuth::requestBearerToken` throws `AUTHENTICATION_FAILED` (code 516) on a non-OK token response. The Azure identity path should do the same — code 1001 is the raw-`std::exception` class, so clients and error monitoring cannot distinguish a misconfigured/denied managed identity from an internal error, and `system.errors` attributes it to `STD_EXCEPTION`. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduced on master 26.8.1.1554 (official build). Deterministic: 20/20 runs. **How to reproduce** Run a token endpoint that rejects requests (the App Service managed-identity protocol, stdlib only): ```python # mi_reject.py from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def log_message(self, *_): pass def do_GET(self): self.send_response(401) self.send_header("Content-Length", "2") self.send_header("Connection", "close") self.end_headers() self.wfile.write(b"{}") HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 9399), H).serve_forever() ``` Then point the managed-identity App Service env at it and create a table on a credential-less dynamic Azure disk (no real storage account is needed — the failure happens at token mint, before any storage request): ```bash python3 mi_reject.py & IDENTITY_ENDPOINT="http://127.0.0.1:9399/mi" IDENTITY_HEADER="x" \ clickhouse local --query " CREATE TABLE t (k Int64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS disk = disk(type = 'azure_blob_storage', endpoint = 'https://127.0.0.1:1/acct/cont/pfx/', skip_access_check = 0)" ``` **Expected behavior** A catchable authentication error (e.g. `AUTHENTICATION_FAILED`, code 516, like the GCS OAuth flow), not the `STD_EXCEPTION` class. **Additional context** The same untranslated-`AuthenticationException` propagation likely affects the other Azure identity flows (`WorkloadIdentityCredential`, service principal), since none of the call sites wrap `GetToken` failures. Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: BACKUP to S3 Express fails with InvalidPart: CompleteMultipartUpload omits the per-part checksums that checksummed multipart uploads require
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong `BACKUP ... TO S3(...)` with an S3 Express One Zone destination fails for every backup that contains a file larger than `s3_max_single_part_upload_size` (default 32 MiB) — the multipart upload of that file can never be completed. Mechanism: express mode is activated by `isS3ExpressEndpoint` (a substring match on the endpoint, `src/IO/S3/Client.cpp`), and it makes every upload request checksummed: `CreateMultipartUpload` is sent with `x-amz-checksum-algorithm: CRC32` and every `UploadPart` carries `x-amz-checksum-crc32` (`RequestChecksumRequired` in `src/IO/S3/Requests.h`). The S3 API requires that completing a multipart upload created with a checksum algorithm include each part's checksum in the `CompleteMultipartUpload` request. The INSERT write path handles this: `WriteBufferFromS3` computes each part's checksum and attaches it to the completed parts (`multipart_checksums` in `src/IO/WriteBufferFromS3.cpp`). But `copyS3File` / `copyDataToS3File` — the path backups use (`src/Backups/BackupIO_S3.cpp`) — builds the completed parts from `ETag` and `PartNumber` only (`multipart_upload.AddParts(part.WithETag(multipart_tags[i]).WithPartNumber(...))` in `src/IO/S3/copyS3File.cpp`), so the completion is rejected. The native server-side copy path (`UploadPartCopy`) in the same file has the same gap. Two side effects worth noting: an S3 disk on an Express bucket works (writes go through `WriteBufferFromS3`), while `BACKUP` of the same server to the same bucket cannot complete; and `isTransientCompleteMultipartUploadError` classifies the rejection as transient, so the doomed `CompleteMultipartUpload` is pointlessly retried several times before the backup fails. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — current master: `src/IO/S3/copyS3File.cpp` has no per-part checksum handling. Reproduced on a recent 26.8 development build. ### How to reproduce Express request shaping is activated purely by the endpoint substring, and MinIO enforces the same checksummed-multipart completion contract as AWS, so this reproduces without a real Express bucket: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, filler String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toString(sipHash64(number)) FROM numbers(800000); -- endpoint containing "s3express" -> express request shaping; the lowered -- thresholds only shrink the data needed to trigger a multipart upload SET s3_max_single_part_upload_size = 4194304, s3_min_upload_part_size = 5242880; BACKUP TABLE t TO S3('http://s3express.localhost:9000/clickfawkes/bk', '<key>', '<secret>'); ``` with `s3express.localhost` pointing at a plain MinIO (`*.localhost` resolves to loopback on systemd machines). The backup fails with `InvalidPart` on every run; the byte-identical backup through the same MinIO under a non-express hostname succeeds and round-trips via `RESTORE`. A wire capture of the failing run shows: `CreateMultipartUpload` carries `x-amz-checksum-algorithm: CRC32`, every `UploadPart` carries `x-amz-checksum-crc32`, and the `CompleteMultipartUpload` body contains only `ETag`/`PartNumber` elements per part: ```xml <CompleteMultipartUpload xmlns="http://s3.amazonaws.com/doc/2006-03-01/"> <Part> <ETag>"63cc2deb63afc264fbe535396204dede"</ETag> <PartNumber>1</PartNumber> </Part> ... </CompleteMultipartUpload> ``` I have not run this against a real S3 Express One Zone bucket; there the same completion is rejected by the same documented API rule (a multipart upload created with a checksum algorithm must be completed with each part's checksum), and the default 32 MiB threshold means any real backup hits it. ### Expected behavior The backup completes. `CompleteMultipartUpload` includes each part's `ChecksumCRC32` whenever the upload was created with a checksum algorithm. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` <Error> copyDataToS3File: While performing multipart upload of object bk_express/data/default/t/all_1_1_0/data.bin in bucket clickfawkes: Code: 499. DB::Exception: Message: Unable to parse ExceptionName: InvalidPart Message: One or more of the specified parts could not be found. The part may not have been uploaded, or the specified entity tag may not match the part's entity tag., Key: bk_express/data/default/t/all_1_1_0/data.bin, Bucket: clickfawkes, Tags: "410d419fd94fdfa2e222d6437eae7023" "5ea9a0982b745fdba59f4214468efeb8" ... (S3_ERROR) ``` ### Additional context The open PR #107318 (`s3_upload_checksum_algorithm` setting) generalizes the express-only checksum code and adds exactly the missing per-part checksum bookkeeping to `copyS3File`, so it appears to fix this as a side effect — but there seems to be no issue tracking the S3 Express backup breakage itself, and that PR is motivated by a different case (FIPS/Object Lock).

signals.title: ASOF JOIN returns a different tied row depending on join_algorithm and on the number of rows on the right side
signals.text: ### Describe the unexpected behaviour When the right side of an `ASOF JOIN` has more than one row with the same value in the ASOF column, which of those rows comes back depends on the join algorithm. It also depends on how many rows are on the right side, which is the part that surprised me. `full_sorting_merge` consistently returns the last of the tied rows. `hash` returns different ones depending on row count. With 252 rows on the right it returns `B`, with 259 it returns `A`. Nothing else differs between those two runs. I think the cause is in `src/Interpreters/RowRefs.cpp`. Entries are radix sorted when there are more than 256 of them, and go through `::sort` otherwise: ```cpp if (likely(entries.size() > 256)) { ... RadixSort<RadixSortTraits>::executeLSDWithTrySort(entries.data(), entries.size(), is_descending); ... } ... ::sort(entries.begin(), entries.end(), GreaterEntryOperator()); ``` `::sort` is pdqsort, which is not stable, so below the threshold the relative order of equal keys is arbitrary. Above it the radix sort is stable and keeps insertion order. The 256 boundary in the code is exactly where the result flips. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Reproduced on `master` built locally, `SELECT version()` reports 26.8.1.1. I have not checked older releases. ### How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE r (id UInt32, t UInt32, v String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (id, t, v); INSERT INTO r SELECT 1, 1, 'filler' FROM numbers(250); INSERT INTO r VALUES (1, 10, 'A'), (1, 10, 'B'); OPTIMIZE TABLE r FINAL; CREATE TABLE l (id UInt32, t UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (id, t); INSERT INTO l VALUES (1, 20); SELECT r.v FROM l ASOF JOIN r ON l.id = r.id AND l.t >= r.t SETTINGS join_algorithm = 'hash'; ``` Both rows at `t = 10` are valid matches for the left row at `t = 20`, so the join has to pick one. Results: | rows on right | `join_algorithm = 'hash'` | `join_algorithm = 'full_sorting_merge'` | | --- | --- | --- | | 252 (`numbers(250)`) | `B` | `B` | | 259 (`numbers(257)`) | `A` | `B` | Change only the argument to `numbers()` between the two runs. ### Expected behavior I am not sure what the right answer is, which is why I am opening an issue instead of sending a patch. The docs for `ASOF JOIN` do not currently say anything about duplicate values in the ASOF column, so there is nothing to check the behaviour against. Two options I can see: - pick a tie break rule, first or last matching row, and make both algorithms follow it - leave it unspecified but state that in the documentation Either is fine by me. What bothers me is that the same query on the same data can start returning a different row once the table grows past a few hundred rows, with no settings changed and nothing in the output to indicate it. If you are joining trades to quotes and two quotes share a timestamp, the query stops being reproducible and there is no signal that anything happened. ### Additional context Tested on a single part after `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL`, one join key, `UInt32` timestamps. I have not checked multi part tables, multiple join keys, or `DateTime64`, so the behaviour there may differ.

signals.title: Automatic parallel replicas on TPC-H: evaluation and fixes
signals.text: Record of an evaluation of `automatic_parallel_replicas_mode` (AutoPR) against TPC-H and the defects it exposed. ## Setup Three-replica staging cluster, remote storage. 44 queries: an adapted/optimized TPC-H set (`a01`–`a22`, rewritten to use `IN` subqueries, aggregation pushdown and similar) and the official set (`o01`–`o22`), at sf=100 and sf=1, with statistics defined on all 8 tables and `use_statistics=1`. Three modes per query — single-node, plain parallel replicas, AutoPR — three warm-ups then four measured runs, median per cell. Headline metric is the geomean of per-query ratios against single-node; the median is useless here because AutoPR declines on most queries by design. ## Result sf=100, after the fixes below: | | geomean vs single-node | improved ≥10% | regressed ≥10% | |---|---|---|---| | AutoPR | **−9.6%** | 9 / 44 | **1 / 44** | | plain parallel replicas | −9.7% | 16 / 44 | 4 / 44 | Changed queries: | query | single-node | plain PR | AutoPR | plain PR | AutoPR | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | `a01` | 2658 | 1072 | 1145 | −60% | **−57%** | | `a19` | 1954 | 850 | 862 | −56% | **−56%** | | `o19` | 2575 | 1146 | 1176 | −55% | **−54%** | | `o01` | 2390 | 1118 | 1154 | −53% | **−52%** | | `a06` | 193 | 114 | 108 | −41% | **−44%** | | `o06` | 194 | 120 | 128 | −38% | **−34%** | | `a17` | 1390 | 976 | 978 | −30% | **−30%** | | `a13` | 1324 | 940 | 976 | −29% | **−26%** | | `o12` | 534 | 388 | 400 | −27% | **−25%** | | `a16` | 289 | 988 | 290 | **+242%** | +0% | | `o16` | 308 | 464 | 327 | **+51%** | +6% | | `a20` | 367 | 404 | 350 | +10% | −5% | | `a10` | 1788 | 1374 | 1725 | −23% | −4% | | `o11` | 479 | 379 | 472 | −21% | −1% | | `o09` | 3892 | 3398 | 3832 | −13% | −2% | | `a11` | 280 | 247 | 288 | −12% | +3% | | `o15` | 276 | 244 | 302 | −12% | +9% | | `o14` | 165 | 147 | 164 | −11% | −1% | | `a15` | 272 | 244 | 287 | −10% | +6% | | `o03` | 3025 | 3302 | 3192 | +9% | +6% | | `a07` | 1720 | 1718 | 1824 | −0% | +6% | | `a14` | 236 | 236 | 250 | +0% | +6% | | `a02` | 568 | 738 | 690 | +30% | **+21%** | Progression as fixes landed (geomean, all 44): −8.2% → −10.0% → −9.6%. At sf=1 AutoPR is +11.4% and declines 39 of 43 queries — correctly, since plain PR is +11.1% there. The residual is the probe plan build, a fixed cost on queries running in 13–318 ms. Still open: - **`query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges` is inert under parallel replicas** (details below). q16 is +228% for plain PR; AutoPR declines it, so AutoPR numbers are unaffected. - **AutoPR never accepts with `parallel_replicas_plan_based=1`** — 0 replicas engaged on all 44 queries, geomean +1.1% (pure probe overhead) against AutoPR's −10.2%. Plain PR + plan-based is a different trade rather than a regression (−9.6% vs −8.7%): it wins where query-tree mode is flat (`o07` −47%, `o08` −49%, `o09` −46%, `a02` −3% vs +27%) and loses where query-tree mode wins (`a17`, `a19`). - Shipping `IN` sets to replicas as temporary tables was prototyped and dropped: it fixes `a02` (+28% → +3%) but costs the same elsewhere (`a03` +2% → +35%, `a12` +2% → +36%), geomean ≈ 0. ## Fixed 1. **Selectivity estimation builds the `IN` set it is measuring.** The estimator executed `IN (subquery)` during planning purely to measure it. → [#114389](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114389) 2. **Compact-part input-bytes estimate assumes LZ4.** `estimateCompressedColumnSize` sampled with LZ4 regardless of the column's codec, overshooting ZSTD compact parts 1.5–3.5×. → [#114535](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114535) 3. **The probe re-runs the query's `IN` subqueries.** Index analysis over the probe's reads builds the set on the spot (`KeyCondition::tryPrepareSetIndexForIn`), re-executing subqueries the single-node plan had already run. → [#114231](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114231) 4. **Index analysis transplanted to one read only.** The replicas plan is built without index analysis and only the matched read gets the single-node result; other reads scan everything. q03 selected 94,718 marks against plain PR's 60,963. q22 +96% → +14%, q12 +13% → −13%, q14 +23% → −15%. → [#115153](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115153) 5. **The probe materializes `GLOBAL IN` / `GLOBAL JOIN` subqueries by executing them.** Building the discardable probe runs the `GLOBAL` rewrite, which executes each subquery. q15 materialized the `revenue0` view twice — 8444 marks against single-node's 5670. q15 +33% → +3% (adapted), +46% → +2% (official). → [115154](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115154) 6. **Cancelling waits out an unannounced replica's planning.** `cancelBefore` drains the packet in flight before cancelling; for a replica that has not announced, that packet is `MergeTreeAllRangesAnnouncement`, sent only after the replica has built its own plan. So the initiator blocks for that replica's whole planning phase to receive a message it no longer needs. Sending `Cancel` costs 0.04 ms and the replica acts 0.3 ms later — none of the cost is the wire. q22 +53% → +1%, q20 +96% → +17%, q04 +46% → −1%; each slowdown equalled its read-request time (318 / 353 / 604 ms). → [#114862](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114862) ## Structural limits (not defects) - **The parallelized table is chosen by position, not size.** `findTableForParallelReplicas` picks the leftmost usable table: on q03 (`FROM orders, (subquery over lineitem)`) that coordinates `orders` while the expensive `lineitem` scan stays on the initiator. Coordinated share is 1834 of 23,815 marks on q22, 1200 of 27,236 on q02. - **Only one read step is coordinated** (`TODO(nickitat)` in `considerEnablingParallelReplicas.cpp`). - **Not all queries are supported to begin with**: ``` ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ outcome │ queries │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ reached the cost model │ 27 / 44 │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ BAIL: cannot find matching node │ 9 / 44 — a05 a07 a10 a13 a15 a21 o08 o09 o13 │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ no decision reached (PR not applicable) │ 8 / 44 — a14 o02 o04 o15 o17 o20 o21 o22 │ └─────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` As for the missing wins (achieved by PRs but not AutoPR): ``` ┌───────┬──────┬──────┬────────┬──────┬──────┬──────────────────────┐ │ query │ def │ PR │ AutoPR │ PR% │ APR% │ why AutoPR missed it │ ├───────┼──────┼──────┼────────┼──────┼──────┼──────────────────────┤ │ a10 │ 1788 │ 1374 │ 1725 │ −23% │ −4% │ no match │ ├───────┼──────┼──────┼────────┼──────┼──────┼──────────────────────┤ │ o09 │ 3892 │ 3398 │ 3832 │ −13% │ −2% │ no match │ ├───────┼──────┼──────┼────────┼──────┼──────┼──────────────────────┤ │ a15 │ 272 │ 244 │ 287 │ −10% │ +6% │ no match │ ├───────┼──────┼──────┼────────┼──────┼──────┼──────────────────────┤ │ o11 │ 479 │ 379 │ 472 │ −21% │ −1% │ model │ ├───────┼──────┼──────┼────────┼──────┼──────┼──────────────────────┤ │ a11 │ 280 │ 247 │ 288 │ −12% │ +3% │ model │ ├───────┼──────┼──────┼────────┼──────┼──────┼──────────────────────┤ │ o14 │ 165 │ 147 │ 164 │ −11% │ −1% │ model │ ├───────┼──────┼──────┼────────┼──────┼──────┼──────────────────────┤ │ o15 │ 276 │ 244 │ 302 │ −12% │ +9% │ no decision reached │ └───────┴──────┴──────┴────────┴──────┴──────┴──────────────────────┘ signals.title: Support shipping window (partitioned) sorts with plan-based parallel replicas
signals.text: Plan-based parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_plan_based`) lifts the split marker through `SortingStep`: the sort is cloned into the fragment shipped to the replicas and the initiator keeps a `MergingSorted` step above the union, so each replica sorts its own rows and the initiator only merges. A window function's pre-sort is also a `SortingStep`, but a special one: it is built with the partitioning constructor (`Planner::addWindowSteps`), so `partition_by_description` is set. Its contract is *one stream per `PARTITION BY` group*, not one sorted stream - `SortingStep::fullSort` scatters by the partition keys and deliberately skips the final merge, and `WindowStep` then runs one `WindowTransform` per stream. That contract cannot be expressed by the `MergingSorted` step the pass puts on the initiator, so such a sort is currently rejected in `sortingCanBeShipped` (`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp`) and window queries keep the split below the sort, the same as with classic parallel replicas. Shipping it collapsed both the sort and the window to a single stream. With `max_threads = 4` and a three-replica cluster: ```sql SELECT p, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY a) FROM t_win; ``` `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 0` (sort stays on the initiator): ``` (Window) Resize 4 → 4 WindowTransform × 4 (Sorting) MergeSortingTransform × 4 LimitsCheckingTransform × 4 PartialSortingTransform × 4 Resize × 4 3 → 1 ScatterByPartitionTransform × 3 1 → 4 ``` `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 1` with the sort shipped: ``` (Window) Resize 1 → 4 WindowTransform (Sorting) MergingSortedTransform 3 → 1 ``` Results stayed correct, because `full_sort_description` is `PARTITION BY` followed by `ORDER BY`, so a single globally merged stream still holds each partition contiguously and in order. What is lost is the per-partition parallelism of both the sort and the window. Two ways to support shipping it: 1. Clone the sort into the fragment *without* `partition_by_description`. Each replica then returns one stream sorted by `full_sort_description` and the initiator's merge produces a valid input for a single `WindowTransform`. The sorting work is distributed; the window itself still runs on one stream (`query_plan_enable_multithreading_after_window_functions` restores parallelism after it). 2. Preserve the per-partition scope on the initiator - re-scatter above the merge, or rebuild the parent as a partitioned sort. Closer to the current pipeline, but the replica-side scatter produces mutually unordered streams, so the merge contract has to be reworked. Note that read-in-order gives no reason to prefer shipping today: `optimizeReadInOrder` early-returns on a partitioned sort unless `query_plan_reuse_storage_ordering_for_window_functions` is enabled, and that setting defaults to `false`. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114315

signals.title: azureBlobStorage INSERT surfaces connection failure as raw Azure::Storage::StorageException (code 1001, STD_EXCEPTION) — s3 throws catchable S3_ERROR on the same shape
signals.text: **Describe what's wrong** When an `azureBlobStorage` INSERT cannot reach the storage endpoint (connection refused), the query fails with `Code: 1001` (`STD_EXCEPTION`) — the Azure SDK's `Azure::Storage::StorageException` propagates to the client untranslated instead of being classified as a storage/network error. ``` Code: 1001. DB::Exception: Azure::Storage::StorageException: 500 Poco::Exception. Code: 1000, e.code() = 111, Connection refused,. (STD_EXCEPTION) ``` The `s3` table function translates the identical failure shape properly — connection refused surfaces as a catchable `S3_ERROR`: ``` Code: 499. DB::Exception: Failed to check existence of key p.parquet in bucket bucket: Poco::Exception. Code: 1000, e.code() = 111, Connection refused (version 26.8.1.1554 (official build)). HTTP response code: 18446744073709551615, error type: NETWORK_CONNECTION. (S3_ERROR) ``` The azure READ path also classifies it (the schema-inference wrapper returns `CANNOT_EXTRACT_TABLE_STRUCTURE`, code 636) — only the write path lets the raw SDK exception through. Code 1001 is the raw-`std::exception` class, so clients and error monitoring cannot distinguish an unreachable endpoint from an internal error, and `system.errors` attributes it to `STD_EXCEPTION`. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduced on master 26.8.1.1554 (official build). Deterministic: 20/20 runs. **How to reproduce** No storage account or emulator is needed — any connection-refused endpoint shows it (port 1 below): ```bash clickhouse local --query " INSERT INTO FUNCTION azureBlobStorage( 'DefaultEndpointsProtocol=http;AccountName=devstoreaccount1;AccountKey=Eby8vdM02xNOcqFlqUwJPLlmEtlCDXJ1OUzFT50uSRZ6IFsuFq2UVErCz4I6tq/K1SZFPTOtr/KBHBeksoGMGw==;BlobEndpoint=http://127.0.0.1:1/devstoreaccount1;', 'cont', 'p.parquet', 'Parquet', 'k Int64') SELECT 1" ``` (The account key is Azurite's public well-known development key; it is not a secret.) **Expected behavior** A catchable storage/network error (the `s3` write path's `S3_ERROR` treatment of the same failure — or `AZURE_BLOB_STORAGE_ERROR`), not the `STD_EXCEPTION` class. **Additional context** Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115127 — the same untranslated-Azure-SDK-exception theme on the credential-mint path (`Azure::Core::Credentials::AuthenticationException`); this report is the storage-operation flavor, which fails on a different call site. Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: Expression in SELECT evaluated on rows filtered out by WHERE when JOIN runtime filter fuses with Prewhere Actions (regression 26.1 → 26.2)
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe what's wrong Since 26.2, a SELECT expression that is only valid for rows matching a WHERE predicate can throw because the SELECT expression and its WHERE guard are fused into sibling nodes in a single Prewhere Actions step. The SELECT expression is evaluated on rows that the WHERE clause should have already eliminated. This is a regression introduced by #95838, which postpones PREWHERE optimization until after JOIN runtime filter construction, causing the runtime filter, WHERE predicates, and SELECT expressions to all be folded into the same ActionsDAG step. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Reproducer: https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/bfadcea1-3c93-4960-9d16-71db35056613 ``` CREATE TABLE t (a UInt8, s String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'x'); SELECT toUInt64(s) AS k FROM t INNER JOIN (SELECT toUInt64(1) AS wh) AS r2 ON toUInt64(s) = r2.wh WHERE a = 1 AND s LIKE '1%'; ``` Does not reproduce on 26.1. Reproducer on 26.2 can be mitigated by disabling the optimization: `SETTINGS enable_join_runtime_filters = 0` ### Expected behavior Queries should always follow the "filter before project" concept in the SQL standard ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Received exception from server (version 26.2.1): Code: 6. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:9000. DB::Exception: Cannot parse string 'x' as UInt64: syntax error at begin of string. Note: there are toUInt64OrZero and toUInt64OrNull functions, which returns zero/NULL instead of throwing exception: while executing 'FUNCTION toUInt64(s : 0) -> toUInt64(__table1.s) UInt64 : 4': While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder). (CANNOT_PARSE_TEXT) (query: SELECT toUInt64(s) AS k FROM t INNER JOIN (SELECT toUInt64(1) AS wh) AS r2 ON toUInt64(s) = r2.wh WHERE a = 1 AND s LIKE '1%';) ``` ### Related issues and pull requests Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/95838 ### Additional context #95838 (26.2) postponed PREWHERE optimisation to run after JOIN runtime filter construction so that runtime filters can also be pushed to PREWHERE. The side effect is that the runtime filter, the WHERE conditions, and the SELECT expressions are fused into a single Actions step as siblings at the table scan level: ``` FUNCTION like(s, '1%') -- WHERE guard FUNCTION toUInt64(s) -- SELECT expression — should only run on rows surviving the guard ``` Because they are siblings, toUInt64(s) runs on every row before the LIKE filter eliminates them.

signals.title: Stress tests fail to restart the server after `04323_text_index_marks_empty_part`: startup rejects a corrupted marks file that `ATTACH TABLE` tolerates
signals.text: Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114091 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115036 ### Describe what's wrong Stress test jobs fail with `Cannot start clickhouse-server` when the run kills the server while `04323_text_index_marks_empty_part` is in its corruption window. The test deliberately appends one byte to `skp_idx_idx.mrk4` (24 → 25 bytes) and removes `checksums.txt` of the empty part, then re-attaches, queries and drops the table. If the server is killed between the corruption and the final `DROP`, the corrupted table stays on disk and the post-stress restart fails: ``` DB::Exception: Load job 'load table test_3.t_text_idx_empty' failed: Code: 246. DB::Exception: Bad size of marks file '/var/lib/clickhouse/store/.../all_1_10_4/skp_idx_idx.mrk4': 25, must be: 24: Cannot attach table `test_3`.`t_text_idx_empty` ... (CORRUPTED_DATA) ``` Four occurrences since 2026-08-14, all the same signature: PRs #113347, #100391, #76184 (`Stress test (amd_tsan)`/`(arm_tsan)`) and #115036 (`Stress test (arm_release)`, [report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115036&sha=9156269951fd4455486a9ea61e5e9ac1e12e2ba1&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_release%29)). The window was widened by #114091 (merged 2026-08-10), which pinned the empty part with `remove_empty_parts = 0` — before that, the cleanup thread usually removed the corrupted empty part before a restart could trip over it, which is consistent with the failures starting on 2026-08-14. Two ways to read it: 1. Server inconsistency: the running server *tolerates* this state — the test itself does `ATTACH TABLE`, `SYSTEM PREWARM MARK CACHE` and `SELECT` on the corrupted part successfully — but the startup metadata load rejects the very same on-disk state and fails the whole table load. Startup being stricter than `ATTACH` means any kill inside the window bricks the table until manual intervention. 2. Test hygiene: a `no-stress` tag is not supported by design ("stress tests must be able to run every test"), so the test must be kill-safe, and with `remove_empty_parts = 0` it is not — there is no point in its corruption window where a kill leaves a startup-loadable state. ### How to reproduce * Run `04323_text_index_marks_empty_part`, kill the server after the `printf '\x00' >> .../skp_idx_idx.mrk4` / `rm checksums.txt` step (before the final `DROP TABLE`), and start the server again — table load fails with `CORRUPTED_DATA` while the same state was attachable before the kill. * In CI: any stress job that kills the server inside that window. No fiddle link: requires killing and restarting the server around on-disk state, which fiddle cannot do.

signals.title: mergeTreeIndex table function ignores the source table's row policy
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **A user restricted by a SELECT row policy can read the primary-key (and minmax-index) column values of the rows the policy hides, by calling `mergeTreeIndex(db, table)` instead of selecting from the table.** - **Root cause:** [`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp:413`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp#L413) - the access check is grant-only; there is no row-policy lookup for `source_table->getStorageID()` before the primary-key values are exposed. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `StorageMergeTreeIndex::readImpl` ([`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp:413`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp#L413)) checks only `AccessType::SELECT` on the source table and then streams primary-key granule values straight out of the parts. It never calls `Context::getRowPolicyFilter`, unlike its two siblings: `StorageMergeTreeTextIndex::readImpl` ([`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeTextIndex.cpp:446`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeTextIndex.cpp#L446)) and, as of this PR, `StorageFromMergeTreeProjection::read` ([`src/Storages/MergeTree/StorageFromMergeTreeProjection.cpp:51`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/MergeTree/StorageFromMergeTreeProjection.cpp#L51)). **Affected locations:** - [`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp:413`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeIndex.cpp#L413) — readImpl: grant-only access check, no row-policy lookup before streaming primary-key values - [`src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeTextIndex.cpp:446`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/StorageMergeTreeTextIndex.cpp#L446) — sibling that DOES enforce the row policy - the shape the fix should follow - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/StorageFromMergeTreeProjection.cpp:51`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/9c7ecedbfc68c/src/Storages/MergeTree/StorageFromMergeTreeProjection.cpp#L51) — the sibling this PR fixes **Impact:** Row-policy bypass. Any user holding plain SELECT on a table (the normal case for a row-policy-restricted user) can enumerate primary-key column values for every row, including rows the policy hides. With `index_granularity = 1` every row's key is exposed; at the default granularity every 8192nd row's key is. `with_minmax = true` additionally exposes per-part min/max of the key columns across hidden rows. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `9c7ecedbfc68c`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Test: a row policy on the source table must not be bypassed by the mergeTreeIndex table function. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_mt_index_rp; DROP ROW POLICY IF EXISTS rp_mt_index ON t_mt_index_rp; CREATE TABLE t_mt_index_rp (id UInt64, department String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (department, id) SETTINGS index_granularity = 1; INSERT INTO t_mt_index_rp VALUES (1, 'engineering'), (2, 'finance'), (3, 'engineering'), (4, 'hr'); CREATE ROW POLICY rp_mt_index ON t_mt_index_rp FOR SELECT USING department = 'engineering' TO ALL; SELECT '-- base table honours the policy'; SELECT id, department FROM t_mt_index_rp ORDER BY id; SELECT '-- mergeTreeIndex must not expose primary key values of policy-hidden rows'; SELECT DISTINCT department FROM mergeTreeIndex(currentDatabase(), 't_mt_index_rp') ORDER BY department; -- { serverError ACCESS_DENIED } DROP ROW POLICY rp_mt_index ON t_mt_index_rp; DROP TABLE t_mt_index_rp; ``` ### Expected behavior ``` -- base table honours the policy 1 engineering 3 engineering -- mergeTreeIndex must not expose primary key values of policy-hidden rows ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` -- base table honours the policy 1 engineering 3 engineering -- mergeTreeIndex must not expose primary key values of policy-hidden rows engineering finance hr ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Mirror `StorageMergeTreeTextIndex::readImpl`: in `StorageMergeTreeIndex::readImpl`, after the `checkAccess`, fetch `context->getRowPolicyFilter(source_storage_id.getDatabaseName(), source_storage_id.getTableName(), RowPolicyFilterType::SELECT_FILTER)` and throw `ACCESS_DENIED` when it is set and not always-true (the index dump is per-granule, so the policy cannot be applied per row). </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - `mergeTreeAnalyzeIndexes` and `mergeTreeCodecBlockCounts` were audited and expose no column values (part names, granule ranges, byte/codec counts only), so they are out of scope - but the granule ranges they report do reveal row counts of a policy-restricted table. Found during automated review of [PR #112329](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112329). Severity P1 · Finding `h_pr112329_001` </details> cc @yariks5s @KochetovNicolai (from #112329)

signals.title: optimize_read_in_order may consume too much memory
signals.text: Consider following query pipeline: ``` ┌─explain───────────────────────────────────────┐ │ (Expression) │ │ ExpressionTransform │ │ (Limit) │ │ Limit │ │ (Aggregating) │ │ FinalizeAggregatedTransform │ │ AggregatingInOrderTransform │ │ (Expression) │ │ ExpressionTransform │ │ (ReadFromMergeTree) │ │ ExpressionTransform │ │ MergingSortedTransform 1803 → 1 │ │ ExpressionTransform × 1803 │ │ MergeTreeInOrder × 1803 0 → 1 │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` Assume we're reading 3 columns, each `MergeTreeInOrder` will have 3 `CompressedReadBuffer`. Let's say we set table compressed block size to 8MB, then each `CompressedReadBuffer` must allocate at least 8MB to hold uncompressed data. So we need at least 1803 x 3 x 8M = 42GB to execute this query pipeline. If not using `optimize_read_in_order` we can just set `max_threads` to limit number of streams. But when using `optimize_read_in_order`, always have num streams == num parts. I think we can improve the `optimize_read_in_order` case by trying to destroy the merge tree reader once a `MergeTreeInOrder` done its job. What I'm observing now is when a `MergeTreeInOrder` has done reading from part, it doesn't destroy the reader, so the `CompressedReadBuffer` object remains, occupies some memory while doing nothing. @KochetovNicolai what do you think about this issue? <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #106215 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1592` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Add `user_files_policy` server setting for custom disks in user_files directory
signals.text: Add a new `user_files_policy` server configuration parameter, similar to `tmp_policy`, that allows user files to reside on custom storage volumes, including S3-backed disks. When configured, the policy's volume (which must have exactly one volume) provides the disks for user file storage. All file operations (`file()` table function, `StorageFile`, dictionaries, `DatabaseFilesystem`, etc.) now route through the `IDisk` interface when a volume is configured, enabling S3 and other remote storage backends. Key changes: - `user_files_policy` setting in `ServerSettings` with XML config example - `Context` stores `VolumePtr` and exposes `getUserFilesVolume`, `getUserFilesPaths`, `setUserFilesPolicy` - `StorageFile` supports disk-based glob matching via `listFilesWithRegexpMatchingOnDisk`, disk-based reads via `disk->readFile`, and disk-based writes via `disk->writeFile` - `FunctionFile` reads through disk I/O when volume is configured - All 13 callers of `getUserFilesPath` updated for multi-path validation - Helper overloads `pathStartsWith(path, vector)` and `fileOrSymlinkPathStartsWith(path, vector)` added - Integration test with local multi-disk and S3 (`s3_plain`) scenarios ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `user_files_policy` server setting to store `user_files` on a custom disk, including S3-backed disks. signals.title: Add assertions in IColumn::mutate to verify deep unique ownership of sub-columns
signals.text: Investigation for https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/99920 This is a draft PR with diagnostic assertions to help find a COW violation bug where columns stored in `HashJoin` have their `allocatedBytes()` change because internal sub-columns are modified by someone who treats immutable columns as mutable. ## What was found The bug manifests as `data->allocated_size != debug_allocated_size` exception in debug builds. Investigation narrowed it down to: 1. **Removing the single-chunk optimization** in `Squashing.cpp:70-72` fixes the bug — this optimization passes chunks through without `IColumn::mutate`, so columns remain shared with Memory engine blocks 2. The **modification happens between** `addBlockToJoin` calls — during pipeline processing of the next chunk 3. The mutation is a **reallocation** (reserve/grow), not a data write — `protect()` (mprotect) doesn't catch it 4. The assertions in this PR (`IColumn::mutate` deep ownership check) **do NOT fire** — meaning the mutation happens outside the `IColumn::mutate` path entirely. Someone treats an immutable column as mutable without going through `mutate`. ## Reproducer The test `04049_fix_hashjoin_shared_column_allocated_size` reproduces the exception in debug builds. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100185&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/100185](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F100185+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add `borrow_from_cache` object storage and `memory` metadata types
signals.text: Add a new object storage type `borrow_from_cache` that allocates space in a named filesystem cache using ephemeral `FileSegment`s. Each stored object is backed by a cache segment held alive via `FileSegmentsHolder`; when released, the cache reclaims the space. Add a new metadata type `memory` that keeps all file-to-blob mappings and directory structure entirely in memory with no persistence. On server restart all data is lost, which is acceptable for the intended use case of temporary tables. Configuration example: ``` disk(type=object_storage, object_storage_type='borrow_from_cache', metadata_type='memory', cache_name='some_cache') ``` ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A new object storage type and metadata type suitable for temporary tables. Add a new object storage type `borrow_from_cache` that allocates space in a named filesystem cache and holds it from eviction. Add a new metadata storage type `memory` that keeps the mapping in memory. For example, this could allow creating temporary tables with custom engines in the Cloud without using S3. Closes #75551. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100371&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/100371](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F100371+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Disable read-in-order when primary key selectivity is poor
signals.text: When the WHERE clause cannot use the primary key effectively (e.g., `LIKE '%...'`), the `optimize_read_in_order` optimization kills parallelism: each part is read by a single stream instead of many. This can make `ORDER BY` queries 4x slower than the same query without `ORDER BY`. Example on a 2.5B row table with `ORDER BY path` and `WHERE path LIKE '%stderr.log'`: - Without ORDER BY: ~9.5s - With ORDER BY (read-in-order): ~40s - With `optimize_read_in_order = 0`: ~9.6s The fix adds a runtime check in `ReadFromMergeTree::spreadMarkRanges`: if the primary key index selected more than a configurable fraction of all granules and there is no LIMIT, we fall back to parallel reading with per-stream `PartialSortingTransform` + `MergeSortingTransform`, so the output is still sorted as the `SortingStep` above expects. New setting `read_in_order_max_primary_key_ratio` controls the threshold. The default is 1.0, which preserves the previous behavior (never disable read-in-order based on primary key selectivity): the heuristic is opt-in until the default threshold is tuned against the performance report. Set it below 1.0 (e.g. 0.5) to enable the guard. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add a new setting `read_in_order_max_primary_key_ratio` that can disable the read-in-order optimization when the primary key selectivity is poor (more than the given fraction of granules selected), falling back to parallel reading with sorting. This avoids severe parallelism loss for queries like `SELECT ... WHERE path LIKE '%...' ORDER BY path`. The default 1.0 preserves the previous behavior; set a lower value (e.g. 0.5) to enable the heuristic. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) New setting `read_in_order_max_primary_key_ratio` (Float, default 1.0): maximum ratio of selected to total primary key granules for `optimize_read_in_order` to stay enabled. When the ratio exceeds this value, read-in-order is disabled in favor of parallel reading with per-stream sorting. The default 1.0 preserves the old behavior. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100377&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/100377](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F100377+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add leader election for non-replicated MergeTree on shared storage
signals.text: Add leader election for non-replicated MergeTree tables on shared object storage (currently `S3`; `Azure` is implemented but not yet enabled, pending test coverage), enabling active/standby failover without external coordination (no Keeper). Uses conditional writes (`If-Match` / `If-None-Match`) on object storage to maintain a lease file with JSON content `{"version":1,"leader_id":"...","timestamp":...}`. The leader renews its lease periodically; followers monitor and claim leadership when the lease expires. New MergeTree settings: - `leader_election` (Bool, default false) — enable leader election - `leader_election_heartbeat_interval` (Seconds, default 10) — lease renewal interval - `leader_election_session_timeout` (Seconds, default 30) — lease expiry threshold; must be at least 3x the heartbeat interval When not the leader, inserts, merges, mutations, and DDL are blocked; background data processing is skipped. Participating nodes should keep their clocks synchronized (NTP) to within `leader_election_session_timeout`; the conditional-write protocol always prevents split-brain, but excessive clock skew can cause leadership churn. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/91613 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `leader_election` setting for non-replicated MergeTree tables on shared object storage, enabling active/standby failover using conditional writes without external coordination. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Three new MergeTree-level settings are added: - `leader_election` (Bool) — When enabled on a non-replicated MergeTree table stored on an `S3` object storage disk (`Azure` is implemented but rejected at table creation until it has test coverage), multiple ClickHouse instances sharing the same data path will elect a single leader. Only the leader performs writes, merges, and mutations. Followers act as read-only replicas and automatically claim leadership when the current leader's lease expires. - `leader_election_heartbeat_interval` (Seconds, default 10) — How often the leader renews its lease and followers check for an expired lease. - `leader_election_session_timeout` (Seconds, default 30) — How long a lease remains valid without renewal. Must be at least 3x `leader_election_heartbeat_interval`. Example: ```sql CREATE TABLE shared_table (x UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x SETTINGS leader_election = true, leader_election_heartbeat_interval = 10, leader_election_session_timeout = 30; ``` <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **High Risk** > High risk because it introduces new leader-election coordination and modifies core `MergeTree` write/DDL/drop and catalog cleanup paths; bugs could cause write unavailability or accidental deletion/incorrect visibility on shared storage. > > **Overview** > Adds a **Beta** `leader_election` mode for non-replicated `MergeTree` tables on shared S3/Azure, using a conditional-write lease file to ensure only one instance performs inserts/merges/mutations while followers remain read-only and can take over on failure. > > Introduces new MergeTree settings (`leader_election`, `leader_election_heartbeat_interval`, `leader_election_session_timeout`) with validation, new `MergeTreeLeaderElection*` metrics/events, and follower part-refresh + leader takeover sync to load new parts and advance block counters before enabling writes. > > Hardens destructive operations for shared-storage tables: blocks most `ALTER`/partition-mutation operations and `RENAME` under leader election, gates background processing on leadership, and updates drop/cleanup logic (`dropSkipsDataDirectoryCleanup`, `DatabaseCatalog`/`StorageTableProxy` fail-closed behavior) to avoid recursive deletion or hangs when tables are shared or cannot be materialized. Adds documentation and integration/stateless tests covering failover, metrics, validation, and rejection cases. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 78c1252915ba512bebf94a147932158e1bacecf0. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. signals.title: Implement FIFO admission queue with per-waiter wakeup for ProcessList
signals.text: ## Summary This PR adds a FIFO admission queue to `ProcessList` as an alternative to the existing `condvar`-based admission (`have_space` → `notify_all`) and the `QuerySlot` resource scheduler. When `enable_query_admission_queue` is enabled, queries that exceed `max_concurrent_queries` enter a per-waiter FIFO queue instead of thundering-herd `notify_all` wakeups or immediate rejection. Each waiter gets its own `std::condition_variable`, so exactly one query is woken when a slot becomes available — O(1) wakeup with strict FIFO ordering. The queue includes a periodic alive-check that detects disconnected clients via `MSG_DONTWAIT | MSG_PEEK` on the socket, preventing slot leaks from abandoned connections. As a secondary optimization, `ThreadPool::worker` replaces `sched_yield` spin in the `Preparing→Running` handshake with `std::atomic::wait/notify_one`, eliminating a context-switch amplification loop that degraded throughput under high concurrency. ### Why not just use `CREATE RESOURCE ... (QUERY)` / `CREATE WORKLOAD`? The resource scheduler's query slot mechanism achieves similar throughput and latency, but requires DDL setup (`CREATE RESOURCE`, `CREATE WORKLOAD`). This PR simply extends the existing `max_concurrent_queries` + `queue_max_wait_ms` behavior — one server setting to enable, no DDL needed. It also adds client disconnect detection and observable metrics (`QueryAdmissionQueueLength`, `QueryAdmissionQueueWaitMicroseconds`) out of the box. **Changes:** - New server settings `enable_query_admission_queue` (default false) and `admission_queue_alive_check_interval_ms` (default 5000, clamped to [500, 10000]) - FIFO admission queue in `ProcessList::insert` using `std::deque<AdmissionWaiter>` with per-waiter `std::condition_variable` and `notify_one` - `QueryStatus::holds_admission_slot` tracks whether a query holds an admission slot, released in `executeQuery` (same timing as `QuerySlot`) or `~ProcessListEntry` - `releaseAdmissionSlotLocked(Lock &)` follows ClickHouse's lock-proof pattern (like `MergeTreeData::Transaction::commit(DataPartsLock &)`) - Socket alive-check callback (`SocketAliveCheck.h`) registered per protocol handler (TCP, HTTP, MySQL, PostgreSQL, gRPC, Arrow Flight) - New metric `QueryAdmissionQueueLength` and profile event `QueryAdmissionQueueWaitMicroseconds` - `ThreadPool::worker` uses `std::atomic::wait/notify_one` instead of `sched_yield` for thread startup handshake - Condition variable `have_space` renamed to `query_finished` to reflect its actual semantics (not admission-specific) - Uses `LockAndOverCommitTrackerBlocker` in `QueryStatus::releaseAdmissionSlot` to prevent deadlock with `OvercommitTracker` - 7 integration tests covering: basic admission, `REPLACE RUNNING QUERY`, no slot leak on timeout, client disconnect detection, wait-time profile event, `max_execution_time` fallback, and no-timeout-when-both-zero ## Benchmark Results Tested on a 96-core machine with k6 HTTP load testing, 5 scenarios, 3 rounds each with rotation for fairness. All three variants (FIFO, QuerySlot, Legacy) use the same binary — only server config differs. **Throughput (total iterations in 20s, avg of 3 rounds):** | Scenario | FIFO | QuerySlot | Legacy | vs QS | vs Legacy | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 150 concurrent, 100 slots | 53020 | 52792 | 52124 | +0.4% | +1.7% | | 200 concurrent, 100 slots | 53140 | 52901 | 51770 | +0.5% | +2.6% | | 500 concurrent, 100 slots | 53173 | 53032 | 50542 | +0.3% | +5.2% | | 500 concurrent, 10 slots | 112285 | 112290 | 68088 | -0.0% | +64.9% | | 200 concurrent mixed, 100 slots | 38043 | 37999 | 37406 | +0.1% | +1.7% | **p95 Latency (avg of 3 rounds):** | Scenario | FIFO | QuerySlot | Legacy | vs QS | vs Legacy | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 150 concurrent, 100 slots | 67.0ms | 67.2ms | 107.0ms | -0.3% | -37.4% | | 200 concurrent, 100 slots | 85.5ms | 85.6ms | 174.7ms | -0.2% | -51.1% | | 500 concurrent, 100 slots | 200.1ms | 200.5ms | 552.3ms | -0.2% | -63.8% | | 500 concurrent, 10 slots | 94.6ms | 95.1ms | 434.8ms | -0.5% | -78.2% | | 200 concurrent mixed, 100 slots | 222.8ms | 222.6ms | 285.9ms | +0.1% | -22.1% | **Tail spread (p95 - median, avg of 3 rounds):** | Scenario | FIFO | QuerySlot | Legacy | |---|---:|---:|---:| | 150 concurrent, 100 slots | 11.1ms | 11.0ms | 57.5ms | | 200 concurrent, 100 slots | 10.8ms | 10.6ms | 113.8ms | | 500 concurrent, 100 slots | 11.2ms | 11.1ms | 409.5ms | | 500 concurrent, 10 slots | 5.8ms | 6.3ms | 331.9ms | | 200 concurrent mixed, 100 slots | 157.1ms | 156.5ms | 207.0ms | FIFO matches `QuerySlot` throughput and latency across all scenarios while being significantly simpler to configure. Both dramatically outperform Legacy under contention — up to 65% higher throughput and 78% lower p95 latency at extreme bottleneck (500 concurrent connections, 10 slots). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add FIFO admission queue for `ProcessList` with per-waiter wakeup, configurable via `enable_query_admission_queue` server setting. Provides strict FIFO ordering, automatic client disconnect detection, and eliminates thundering-herd wakeups under high concurrency. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) New server settings: - `enable_query_admission_queue` (Bool, default `false`): When enabled, queries exceeding `max_concurrent_queries` wait in a FIFO queue instead of being rejected. Requires `queue_max_wait_ms > 0` on the query side. - `admission_queue_alive_check_interval_ms` (UInt64, default `5000`): Interval in milliseconds for checking if queued clients are still connected. Clamped to [500, 10000]. New metric: `QueryAdmissionQueueLength` — current number of queries waiting in the admission queue. New profile event: `QueryAdmissionQueueWaitMicroseconds` — time spent waiting in the admission queue. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Changes core query admission/concurrency paths in `ProcessList` and adds early-release/disconnect checks across multiple protocol handlers, which could affect fairness, timeouts, or query lifecycle under load. Mitigated by being gated behind a new server setting and covered by new integration tests. > > **Overview** > Adds an optional **FIFO query admission queue** for `max_concurrent_queries` (gated by new server setting `enable_query_admission_queue`) so excess queries wait in a per-waiter queue with `notify_one` wakeups instead of the legacy broadcast `condvar` path. > > Introduces disconnect-aware waiting via a new per-query `Context` callback (`setConnectionAliveCheck`) with a tunable server setting `admission_queue_alive_check_interval_ms`, plus new observability (`CurrentMetrics::QueryAdmissionQueueLength` and `ProfileEvents::QueryAdmissionQueueWaitMicroseconds`) and early admission-slot release in `executeQuery`. > > Separately replaces a ThreadPool startup busy-yield with `std::atomic::wait/notify_one`, and adds integration tests/config to validate FIFO ordering, timeouts/fallback behavior, replace-running-query interaction, disconnect cleanup, and metric/event reporting. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit fc0a34660161b24c95747aa28dbd3d111492870c. signals.title: Add arrayPermutations, arrayPartialPermutations, and arrayCombinations
signals.text: Closes #43175 ### Changelog category: - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added new array combinatorics functions: `arrayPermutations`, `arrayPartialPermutations`, and `arrayCombinations`. These functions generate permutations and combinations by element indexes (so equal values may produce duplicate rows), validate argument `k`, and enforce result-size limits via `function_range_max_elements_in_block`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written in code Motivation: - Add built-in SQL functions for common combinatorics tasks on arrays without using external logic. Parameters: - `arrayPermutations(arr)`: - `arr`: source array, returns all full permutations. - `arrayPartialPermutations(arr, k)`: - `arr`: source array. - `k`: selection length, must be non-negative and not exceed array length. - `arrayCombinations(arr, k)`: - `arr`: source array. - `k`: combination length, must be non-negative and not exceed array length. - Result size is limited by `function_range_max_elements_in_block`. Example use: - `SELECT arrayPermutations([1, 2, 3]);` - `SELECT arrayPartialPermutations([1, 2, 3], 2);` - `SELECT arrayCombinations([1, 2, 3], 2);`

signals.title: Add argMaxMany(N) and argMinMany(N) aggregate functions
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added `argMaxMany(N)(arg, val)` and `argMinMany(N)(arg, val)` aggregate functions that return an `Array` of the N `arg` values corresponding to the N largest (or smallest) `val` values, sorted by `val`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) `argMaxMany(N)(arg, val)` — returns an array of the N `arg` values corresponding to the N largest `val` values, sorted by `val` descending. `argMinMany(N)(arg, val)` is the symmetric counterpart returning the N smallest. **Motivation:** Extends the `argMax`/`argMin`/`argAndMax`/`argAndMin` family (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57568). The existing `argMax` returns only the single top result. `argMaxMany(N)` lets you retrieve the top-N in one aggregation pass instead of using a subquery with `ORDER BY … LIMIT N`. Example: ```sql -- Top-2 slowest files by compile time SELECT argMaxMany(2)(file, dur) FROM build_time_trace WHERE name = 'ExecuteCompiler' -- Returns: ['src/Functions/CastOverloadResolver.cpp', 'src/Interpreters/ActionsDAG.cpp'] ``` **Parameters:** `N` — positive integer, the maximum number of elements to return. **Null handling:** Null `val` values are skipped (consistent with `argMax`/`argMin`). When fewer than N rows are present all rows are returned. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Adds new core aggregate functions with custom state management, heap logic, and serialization, which could affect performance/memory usage and introduce edge-case bugs (nulls, ordering, merges) despite being additive. > > **Overview** > Introduces new aggregate functions `argMaxMany(N)(arg, val)` and `argMinMany(N)(arg, val)` that return the top/bottom-N `arg` values by `val` as an `Array`, skipping `NULL` `val` values and sorting results by `val`. > > Implements a shared heap-based aggregation state with parameter validation (positive `N`, upper bound, and comparable non-`Dynamic`/non-`Variant` `val` types), registers the functions in the aggregate factory, and adds stateless SQL tests plus new/updated docs (including **See also** cross-links for the argMin/argMax family). > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 89e8b73650c9e5e438f0a17bd8a3b8dc6d1caa4b. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signals.title: Auto-escape XML special characters in from_env config substitutions
signals.text: ### What this PR does When direct config values loaded via `from_env` contain XML special characters (`&`, `<`, `>`), the `ConfigProcessor` failed with `SAXParseException` because the raw value was concatenated directly into an XML string. Direct values are now escaped before being embedded into the XML DOM, so an environment variable can hold any XML-1.0-legal value — including one that looks like an XML fragment (taken as literal text) and one that contains the `]]>` sequence the XML grammar forbids in character data. Existing `<include from_env="..."/>` substitutions continue to interpret their value as an XML subtree. The contents of a ZooKeeper node referenced via `from_zk` may be a whole subtree. A value beginning with `<` is parsed as an XML fragment (both for a structural `<include>` and for a leaf substitution), which is kept for backward compatibility because earlier versions always interpreted a `from_zk` value as XML. An explicit `<include from_zk="..." yaml="true"/>` parses a non-`<` value as a YAML subtree. Without `yaml="true"`, the value remains literal text, so `<include>` is also the generic "replace this element with the node contents" form and may carry a leaf value such as a secret. Whitespace surrounding that `<include>` becomes part of the leaf value, so direct leaf substitutions such as `<password from_zk="..."/>` or `<some_setting from_zk="..."/>` are recommended when exact bytes matter. Those direct leaf substitutions keep a non-`<` value as literal text using its exact original bytes, so existing *plain-text* scalar substitutions and secrets keep working unchanged on upgrade. There is one deliberate behavior change on upgrade: a leaf value that was XML-entity-encoded to satisfy the old parser (which reparsed every `from_zk` value as XML and rejected a raw `&`, `<` or `>` as not well-formed) is now kept as its exact original bytes. A value stored as `a&b` used to decode to `a&b`, but now resolves to the literal `a&b`; such values must be stored raw (`a&b`) instead. This is documented in `docs/concepts/features/configuration/server-config/configuration-files.mdx` and covered by an integration regression. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78835 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry: Fixed direct config substitutions via `from_env` failing when XML-1.0-legal values contain XML special characters like `&`, `<`, `>`, or the `]]>` sequence; existing `<include from_env="..."/>` XML-subtree substitutions are unchanged. An explicit `<include from_zk="..." yaml="true"/>` substitution can read a YAML subtree wherever the generic `<include>` form is used, including inside a leaf element, so it must not be used for a literal secret or setting. Without the explicit `yaml="true"` attribute, a non-`<` value is literal text, but direct non-`<` leaf `from_zk` substitutions are recommended for exact-byte secrets/settings, because surrounding whitespace of an `<include>` becomes part of a leaf value. Values beginning with `<` continue to be interpreted as XML fragments for backward compatibility. Upgrade note: a non-`<` leaf `from_zk` value that was previously XML-entity-encoded (for example `a&b`) now resolves to its exact literal bytes and must be stored raw (`a&b`) instead. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101773&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101773](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101773+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Ask for continuation in single-line mode when query is incomplete
signals.text: ### What this PR does In single-line interactive mode, pressing Enter on an incomplete query (one where the parser reaches the end of input still expecting more tokens) no longer sends it and shows a syntax error. Instead, a newline is inserted into the same edit buffer, exactly like pressing Alt+Enter, so the whole query stays under a single prompt and the arrow keys can navigate and edit across all of its lines. A trailing `;` still forces submission (for example, to deliberately submit an incomplete query and see its syntax error). This replaces the earlier approach that printed a separate `:-] ` continuation prompt and read additional lines, which prevented cross-line editing and could split pasted queries. The completeness check is now passed to `ReplxxLineReader` as a callback and consulted from the `commit_action` bound to Enter. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/64886 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): In single-line interactive mode, `clickhouse-client` now keeps an incomplete query under a single prompt and lets you continue it on the next line (like pressing Alt+Enter) instead of sending it immediately. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (not required for this change)

signals.text: Adds the `groupBloomFilter` aggregate function and the `bloomFilterContains` scalar function for memory-efficient probabilistic set-membership testing. This can be used to detect new values, perform approximate deduplication checks, and compare large datasets without materializing exact sets. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/11700 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add the `groupBloomFilter` aggregate function for building Bloom filter states and the `bloomFilterContains` scalar function for testing whether values are probably present. The functions support configurable expected element counts, false-positive rates, and seeds, and work with the `-State` and `-MergeState` combinators and `AggregatingMergeTree`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Documentation is added in `docs/en/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/groupbloomfilter.md` and `docs/en/sql-reference/functions/bloom-filter-functions.md`.
