signals.title: Auto-retry infra failures on fork PRs
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113052 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The fork-approval gate consumes `run_attempt` 1, concluding `action_required` with zero jobs, so a fork PR's first attempt that runs anything is attempt 2. `retry_infra_failures.yml` selected candidates two ways that both assume attempt 1 is the real run, so an infra-killed fork run was invisible to the hourly auto-retry. I hit this through the CI database slowdown that #113052 fixed: on 2026-08-01 it killed `Config Workflow` on about 65 PRs across authors, and the fork ones still sit with a never-executed test matrix. **Attempt.** The filter widens to `.attempt <= 2`, then a candidate at attempt 2 is accepted only if attempt 1 concluded `action_required`, so a genuine retry stays excluded and same-repo runs are unaffected. Keying on `head_repository.fork` instead over-selects: 5 of 115 sampled fork runs at attempt 2 had already been retried rather than gate-deferred. **Window.** The 6 hour cutoff compared `createdAt`, which GitHub pins to the gated attempt, while `startedAt` advances to the attempt that ran. Over 400 failed runs, 87 are skewed by over a minute (p90 6.94h, max 22.98h) and 13 exceed the cutoff. The field alone is insufficient: the listing is ordered by `createdAt`, so those runs sit deep in it, and at `--limit 50` the swap rescues no further gated run, at `--limit 200` it rescues one and loses none. Validated by running the selector's own query, old and new, against the live listing: the fixed one selects a strict superset, each newly visible run individually confirmed approval-gated with jobs on attempt 2. Attempt 3 stays excluded by `<= 2`, so reruns remain bounded and `MAX_RERUNS` is unchanged. Newly visible runs still face the unchanged infra heuristic, so this restores visibility, not reruns. The hourly cron is only observable after merge. This prevents recurrence; it does not unstick runs already past the cutoff.

signals.title: Cache text-index pattern bailouts
signals.text: Broad `LIKE` and `ILIKE` text-index queries can exceed `text_index_like_max_postings_to_read` while scanning each part's dictionary and safely fall back to evaluating the original predicate. Repeated queries currently repeat that expensive dictionary scan even though the same part, pattern set, and threshold produce the same bailout. Cache the bailout decision in the existing text-index tokens cache, keyed by the immutable part/index identity, complete pattern-query set, and posting-list threshold. Cache hits call the existing `TextIndexAnalyzer::bypassPatternQueries` path, so they only bypass an optimization and cannot incorrectly prune data. The cache is controlled by the default-on `use_text_index_pattern_bypass_cache` setting and cleared by the existing `SYSTEM CLEAR TEXT INDEX TOKENS CACHE` statement. `TextIndexDiscardPatternScan` continues to count actual scan bailouts, while the new `TextIndexPatternBypassCacheHits` event counts cached bypasses. Tests cover correctness against an index-disabled scan, first and repeated executions, cache disabling and clearing, changed thresholds, different patterns and pattern sets, and both `LIKE` and `ILIKE`. In a 64-part benchmark, repeated queries reduced dictionary reads from 3,200 to zero and improved throughput by approximately 6% for `LIKE` and 10.5% for `ILIKE`. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112742 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Cache text-index pattern dictionary-scan bailouts to avoid repeated dictionary reads for broad `LIKE` and `ILIKE` queries. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113572&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113572](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113572+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Docs: add `NOSIGN` to public `s3` documentation queries
signals.text: Update anonymous public S3 documentation examples to pass `NOSIGN` explicitly following the ClickHouse 26.7 server credential behavior change. This prevents public reads from attempting to use server-managed credentials. The audit also found and repairs two stale public paths: the LAION guide now uses the surviving 10-million-row shard, and the S3 brace-expansion example references the four files that currently exist. Authenticated, requester-pays, write, placeholder, and Foursquare examples are intentionally outside this PR. Related: https://linear.app/clickhouse/issue/DOC-945/update-public-s3-docs-examples-to-use-nosign ### Changelog category (leave one): - Documentation (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Updated public S3 documentation examples to use `NOSIGN` and repaired stale public dataset paths.

signals.title: Add experimental Wallaby floating-point compression codec
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110613 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the experimental `Wallaby` lossless compression codec for `Float32` and `Float64` columns: it adaptively picks the cheapest of constant, decimal (Frame-of-Reference or zigzag-delta bit-packing, with PFOR-style patching and ULP-adjustment lanes), or XOR encoding per 1024-value block. Gated behind the `allow_experimental_codecs` setting. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Motivation.** This follows the evaluation of the `Chimp` codec proposal (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467) and of the newer floating-point compression literature: `ALP` (SIGMOD 2024), `Elf` (VLDB 2023), `Camel` (SIGMOD 2025), `Kangaroo` (SIGMOD 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3802076, in production in Alibaba Lindorm since 2024), and the independent evaluation "Beyond Compression" (PVLDB 18(11), 2025). No single family dominates: integerization (`ALP`) wins on decimal-mappable data and decompression speed; the XOR family wins on non-decimal and mixed-precision data; run-length collapse wins on repetitive IoT data. `Wallaby` picks per 1024-value block, and its delta-packing of integerized values exploits time-series smoothness that neither `ALP` (plain Frame-of-Reference) nor the XOR codecs use. **Patent note.** The mantissa-erasure preprocessing shared by `Elf`, `Elf+`, `SElf*` and `Kangaroo` (erasing low mantissa bits derived from the decimal-place count and exponent) is covered by patent US 12,289,120 B2 (Chongqing University, granted 2025-04-29), including the decompression side. `Wallaby` deliberately does not implement it. All building blocks used here are prior art or openly licensed: `Gorilla` XOR (2015), windowed references with an explicit index (Chimp128, VLDB 2022), integerization with FOR bit-packing (`ALP`, MIT-licensed reference, already in ClickHouse as the shared `FFOR` helper), and delta/zigzag/run-length encoding. The encoder-side reference search is three O(1) hash probes, not Kangaroo's LZ-history algorithm; the on-disk format is original. **Decimal-scale chooser.** The decimal scale (`alpha`, now signed) is chosen per vector by measurement, not by a fixed rule: candidates are generated from four sources (the scales of 32 sampled values, with the sample grown up to 256 exactly when a stronger pruning bound would pay for itself; the trailing-decimal-zero structure of the quantized reference, which enumerates scales at which subsets of the vector become exact; the minimal scales of exception values, which discovers a high-precision minority the sample missed; and the exact scales behind tolerant votes, for when a voted scale fails on the rest of the vector), each candidate is evaluated against the full vector, and the smallest measured payload wins. Exceptions are bounded only by a size-based budget — a candidate is abandoned exactly when its exceptions alone already make it larger than the best encoding known for this vector, or when the running width of its packed lanes provably cannot come in under it. Pruning uses only provable bounds (counted sampled failures and failure carry-over from wider scales — never width extrapolation, which can prune true winners), so the chooser never skips a scale that could win. The scale that won the previous vector is evaluated first, and homogeneous vectors stay at a single full pass. **Lane capping, ULP-adjustment lanes, signed scales** (added after reading the pcodec, `ALP`, and FastLanes internals). The packed lane width can be capped below the widest value, exiling outliers into the existing exception list — PFOR-style patching, chosen in closed form from a width histogram for Frame-of-Reference and by an exact chain walk for the delta lanes. Values that integerize only up to a small distance are absorbed by a second bit-packed lane set of zigzag ULP adjustments instead of 10-byte raw exceptions (the idea behind pcodec's `FloatMult`): decimals disturbed by lossy arithmetic — a `Float32` round trip, a unit conversion — no longer force the vector to XOR. The scale is signed as in `ALP`'s `(e, f)` factorization: a negative scale divides by a power of ten, so integers ending in decimal zeros (cents, millisecond timestamps holding whole seconds) pack their cofactors, including magnitudes beyond the `Int64` domain. The XOR window search additionally probes the previous value's lookback distance, which interleaved series keep hitting. Per vector, the candidates compete on the cheaper of the exception list and the adjustment lanes, and only the winner takes one capping pass. These mechanisms are what moved sensors `temperature` −7 %, sensors `pressure` −3 %, weather `tempMax` −2.7 %, and the synthetic `smooth gauge` −11 % against the previous revision of the tables below. **Synthetic benchmarks** (this machine, `clickhouse local`, 10M `Float64` values per dataset, `max_threads = 1`, compressed size after `OPTIMIZE FINAL`; insert is the best of 3 runs, `SELECT` is `sum(x)`, mean of 5 runs; `PCO` is the pcodec Rust crate linked as a codec by #110613, compiled into the same binary, at its default level 8; smallest size and fastest insert / select per row in bold — times are in seconds, lower is better; dataset-specific, not a general claim. The `Chimp` numbers in the previous revision of this description were measured against an older encoder revision and are omitted; the qualitative picture for `Chimp` — robust on non-decimal data, slow to decompress — is unchanged): | Dataset | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | FPC | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | sine+2dp noise — size | 33.5 MB | 81.9 MB | 68.7 MB | 22.7 MB | **11.4 MB** | 15.2 MB | | — insert / select, s | 0.45 / 0.098 | 0.93 / 0.092 | 0.80 / 0.079 | 0.32 / **0.019** | 1.01 / 0.079 | **0.31** / 0.024 | | random walk 3dp — size | 32.6 MB | 66.0 MB | 64.1 MB | **0.12** / 0.023 | 0.23 / 0.091 | 0.15 / 0.081 | 0.27 / **0.022** | 0.79 / **0.022** | 0.50 / **0.022** | **Real datasets** (from the [sample datasets](https://clickhouse.com/docs/get-started/sample-datasets): [ClickBench hits](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench), 100M rows — it has no `Float` columns, so representative numeric columns are cast to `Float32`/`Float64`, which is exactly the "floats that are really integers" shape common in practice; [mgbench](https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/example-datasets/brown-benchmark) `logs1` machine metrics, 22M rows, `Nullable(Float32)` as in the reference schema; [environmental sensors](https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/example-datasets/environmental-sensors) 2019-06 BME280, 31.2M rows, `Float32`; [NOAA weather](https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/example-datasets/noaa), 100M rows, tenths stored as `Float32` with 1 decimal). All columns are pre-sorted by the reference schema's `ORDER BY`; compressed size of the column after `OPTIMIZE FINAL`, one binary for all codecs. Best floating-point codec in bold; `ZSTD(3)` shown as the generic-compression baseline: | Column | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | 44.5 MB | 86.1 MB | 88.9 MB | **66.8 MB** | 71.1 MB | | mgbench `cpu_user` | 32.0 MB | 75.5 MB | 79.0 MB | **53.8 MB** | 58.0 MB | | mgbench `mem_free` | 48.4 MB | 73.9 MB | 82.5 MB | **53.7 MB** | 65.5 MB | | sensors `temperature` | 74.4 MB | 132.3 MB | 59.6 MB | 64.9 MB | **55.2 MB** | | sensors `humidity` | 80.2 MB | 125.4 MB | 55.7 MB | 82.8 MB | **55.5 MB** | | sensors `pressure` | 99.1 MB | 131.9 MB | 98.1 MB | **79.7 MB** | 95.1 MB | | weather `tempMax` | 29.8 MB | 102.3 MB | 33.9 MB | **24.5 MB** | 29.3 MB | | weather `precipitation` | 56.4 MB | 144.5 MB | 131.9 MB | **33.3 MB** | 72.2 MB | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 235.6 MB | 244.4 MB | 215.9 MB | **128.1 MB** | 215.9 MB | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | 37.9 MB | 52.5 MB | 141.7 MB | **43.1 MB** | 46.6 MB | | hits `UserID` (F64) | 149.7 MB | 152.4 MB | 684.2 MB | **120.3 MB** | 155.2 MB | Compression / decompression time on the same runs, in seconds — lower is better, best per row in bold (insert best-of-3 / `sum(x)` mean-of-5, `max_threads = 1`; the select column includes the scan-and-sum overhead): | Column | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | 0.43 / 0.12 | **0.24** / 0.15 | 0.35 / **0.06** | 0.95 / 0.10 | 2.00 / 0.19 | | mgbench `cpu_user` | 0.39 / 0.10 | **0.22** / 0.14 | 0.33 / **0.05** | 0.79 / 0.10 | 1.66 / 0.16 | | mgbench `mem_free` | 0.37 / 0.13 | **0.24** / 0.15 | 0.26 / **0.05** | 1.05 / 0.10 | 1.46 / 0.16 | | sensors `temperature` | 0.80 / 0.18 | 0.32 / 0.21 | **0.30** / **0.06** | 1.72 / 0.16 | 1.71 / **0.06** | | sensors `humidity` | 0.76 / 0.18 | 0.34 / 0.21 | **0.30** / **0.05** | 1.51 / 0.12 | 1.91 / 0.06 | | sensors `pressure` | 0.42 / 0.15 | 0.33 / 0.21 | **0.31** / **0.06** | 1.65 / 0.11 | 2.49 / 0.07 | | weather `tempMax` | 0.76 / 0.17 | **0.54** / 0.27 | 0.57 / **0.10** | 1.31 / 0.20 | 1.00 / **0.10** | | weather `precipitation` | 1.16 / 0.33 | **0.70** / 0.45 | 1.14 / **0.13** | 3.02 / 0.53 | 2.98 / 0.40 | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 3.31 / 1.09 | **1.02** / 0.57 | 2.59 / **0.16** | 6.59 / 0.47 | 3.19 / 0.18 | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | 0.94 / 0.28 | **0.60** / 0.34 | 0.91 / **0.12** | 2.32 / 0.34 | 1.70 / 0.31 | | hits `UserID` (F64) | 1.57 / 0.42 | **0.85** / 0.45 | 2.16 / **0.24** | 3.42 / 0.44 | 3.33 / 0.50 | **Encoder cost.** Compared with the previous revision of this table, compression is 1.2–2.8x slower while decompression is unchanged or slightly faster (`smooth gauge` decodes 44 % faster now that a decimal mode wins it instead of XOR). Benchmarking the intermediate revision that contains only the provable-bound chooser rework attributes the cost: on the mgbench and sensors `temperature` columns that rework alone accounts for 60–80 % of the slowdown (`load_one` 0.81 → 1.74 s of the final 2.00 s), while on sensors `pressure` and hits `EventTime` the wider candidate space that the new mechanisms open dominates (1.43 → 2.49 s and 2.15 → 3.19 s). The trade was made knowingly: the size wins above come from the same revisions, and the encoder keeps a running lane-width floor that abandons hopeless scans mid-vector and a double-buffered winner so no scale is quantized twice. **Comparison with PCodec.** `PCO` is the strongest competitor overall. On ratio it is the smallest floating-point codec on 9 of the 11 columns, and the standalone `pco` CLI compressing each column as one chunk does better still (e.g. mgbench `load_one` 36.7 MB, weather `precipitation` 32.2 MB): per-64-KiB-block operation costs pcodec 20-45 % of its ratio, since every block re-learns its tANS tables and delta state. On compression speed the two are now roughly at parity — `Wallaby` up to 2x faster on the hits columns and weather `tempMax`, `PCO` up to 2x faster on the mgbench and sensor columns. On decompression `PCO` is 1.5–2.7x slower than `Wallaby` on the columns where a `Wallaby` decimal mode wins (sensors, weather `tempMax`, hits `EventTime`) and *faster* on the XOR-mode columns (mgbench, hits `UserID`) — the serial XOR bitstream is the slowest of `Wallaby`'s decode paths, while pcodec's decode cost is uniform. Against `ALP`, `Wallaby` is smaller on all 11 columns — dramatically so where `ALP`'s Frame-of-Reference degenerates (hits `UserID` 155 MB vs 684 MB, hits `ResolutionWidth` 47 MB vs 142 MB, weather `precipitation` 72 MB vs 132 MB). A correction to earlier revisions of this description: in-engine `PCO` was previously reported as 10-70x slower. That measurement came from a local build affected by a build-system bug that compiles all vendored Rust code with `opt-level = 0` unless `-DSANITIZE=` is passed explicitly (a `contrib/corrosion-cmake` condition mistakes `SANITIZE=OFF` for an enabled sanitizer; CI is unaffected because it always passes the flag). The numbers above are from a corrected build; a separate fix for the build system is being prepared. **Where `Wallaby` is not the winner.** On columns dominated by entropy redundancy rather than numeric structure — the three mgbench columns, weather `precipitation`, hits `ResolutionWidth`/`UserID` — plain `ZSTD` and/or `PCO` produce smaller data. Chaining helps exactly there, because the XOR/EQUAL residues are more entropy-codable than raw floats: | Column | `ZSTD(3)` | `ALP, ZSTD` | `Wallaby, ZSTD` | |---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | **44.5 MB** | 56.0 MB | 49.0 MB | | mgbench `cpu_user` | **32.0 MB** | 46.1 MB | 35.6 MB | | mgbench `mem_free` | 48.4 MB | 54.4 MB | **42.4 MB** | | sensors `temperature` | 74.4 MB | 58.2 MB | **54.2 MB** | | sensors `humidity` | 80.2 MB | 55.1 MB | **55.0 MB** | | sensors `pressure` | 99.1 MB | 97.8 MB | **90.1 MB** | | weather `tempMax` | 29.8 MB | 29.2 MB | **27.6 MB** | | weather `precipitation` | 56.4 MB | **54.6 MB** | 65.7 MB | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 235.6 MB | **212.8 MB** | 213.0 MB | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | **37.9 MB** | 57.8 MB | 43.2 MB | | hits `UserID` (F64) | **149.7 MB** | 192.5 MB | 154.5 MB | `CODEC(Wallaby, ZSTD)` is the best of the three on 5 of the 11 columns — on the sensor columns and weather `tempMax` now by a clear margin where the previous revision tied `ALP, ZSTD` — and within 0.1 % on `EventTime`. The interesting exception is `precipitation`, where `ALP, ZSTD` wins because `ALP`'s plain Frame-of-Reference lanes on zero-dominated data are almost pure zero bytes, which `ZSTD` collapses better than `Wallaby`'s already-compact XOR runs. Side observation from benchmarking (independent of this PR): for `Nullable` columns the null-map substream appears to be stored uncompressed (+1 byte per row for every codec, including `LZ4`/`ZSTD`) — visible as a constant +22 MB / +31.2 MB across all codecs on the mgbench / sensors columns. Worth a separate look. Correctness: bit-exact round trip is verified by the encoder for every value with a per-value raw-exception fallback (`NaN` payloads, infinities, denormals, signed zeros, arbitrary bit patterns are all preserved; verified on random bit patterns and on all real datasets by multiset checksums in tests; the sensors dataset contributes 9298 genuine `NaN` values). The decoder validates all lengths and bounds, so corrupt input causes an exception, not undefined behavior; a decompression fuzzer target is included. An adversarial review of the current revision additionally round-tripped ~15M hostile values (per-block scale flips, `NaN` payloads, subnormals, domain edges) bit-exactly on both float widths. Note on the `NativeFormat` spec: the spec enumerates the column codec method bytes accepted on the `decompress=1` input path, so this PR adds the `0xa0` (`Wallaby`) entry with an experimental-status note, matching the existing `SZ3`/`Quantized`/`ZXC` entries. #### CI Settings (Only check the boxes if you know what you are doing): - [ ] Allow: All Required Checks - [ ] Allow: Stateless tests - [ ] Allow: Stateful tests - [ ] Allow: Integration Tests - [ ] Allow: Performance tests - [ ] Allow: All Builds - [ ] Allow: batch 1, 2 for multi-batch jobs - [ ] Allow: batch 3, 4, 5, 6 for multi-batch jobs --- - [ ] Exclude: Style check - [ ] Exclude: Fast test - [ ] Exclude: All with ASAN - [ ] Exclude: All with TSAN, MSAN, UBSAN, Coverage - [ ] Exclude: All with aarch64, release, debug --- - [ ] Do not test - [ ] Woolen Wolfdog - [ ] Upload binaries for special builds - [ ] Disable merge-commit - [ ] Disable CI cache --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113575&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113575](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113575+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)]

signals.title: Fix GCD codec behavior on signed values
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78190 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed GCD codec handling of signed fixed-width values with negative numbers. Previously it computed the divisor from signed values directly, which could miss the common divisor and significantly reduce compression efficiency for signed integer and decimal columns. It now computes the divisor from magnitudes for signed types while preserving existing behavior for unsigned types and decompression. ### Description GCD pre-processing was using signed values directly when discovering the common divisor. For signed fixed-width storage types, negative values could therefore spoil divisor discovery and make CODEC(GCD) compress much worse than expected, even though the data still had a large common divisor in magnitude. The fix makes CompressionCodecGCD compute the divisor on unsigned magnitudes for signed types, and threads signedness from the column type into codec instantiation so Int* and signed Decimal* columns use the correct path. This also handles the signed-minimum edge case safely by avoiding signed negation overflow. Unsigned behavior is unchanged. The type-agnostic fallback is kept deliberately unchanged: unlike T64, GCD still does not throw when type information is unavailable and falls back to the 1-byte unsigned path. That preserves correctness for cases such as default_compression_codec or CODEC(Default) resolution without a concrete column type, but signed data on that path may still compress less efficiently because signedness is unknown. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113798&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113798](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113798+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add JOIN observability columns to system.query_log
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111352 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111748 ## Motivation `system.query_log` says almost nothing about what the JOINs in a query actually did. Answering questions like "which queries ran a `CROSS` join we didn't expect", "which joins fell back to `grace_hash` and spilled to disk", or "which algorithm was really chosen when `join_algorithm = 'auto'`" currently requires re-running `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` (impossible post-mortem) or scraping `ProfileEvents` query by query. ## Changes Four columns are added to `system.query_log`, with the matching fields in `QueryLogElement`: - `used_number_of_joins` (`UInt64`) — the number of physical joins executed by the query. It is collected from the query pipeline, so it reflects the joins that really ran after all optimizations, not the number of `JOIN` clauses in the query text. - `used_join_algorithms` (`Array(LowCardinality(String))`) — the algorithms that were actually used, e.g. `hash`, `parallel_hash`, `grace_hash`, `direct`, `full_sorting_merge`, `partial_merge`. The `join_algorithm` setting only lists the allowed algorithms; the choice among them happens at runtime, and an algorithm can even be replaced mid-execution (a `hash` join switching to `grace_hash` under memory pressure). - `used_join_kinds` (`Array(LowCardinality(String))`) — Kind of the joins present in the query. - `used_join_strictness` (`Array(LowCardinality(String))`) — Strictness of the joins present in the query. - `join_spilled_to_disk` (`UInt8`) — whether any of the joins spilled to disk. This PR currently adds the schema only. The fields are declared but nothing populates them yet, so the columns read as `0` and `[]`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added four columns to `system.query_log` describing the JOINs a query executed: `used_number_of_joins` (the number of physical joins in the executed pipeline), `used_join_algorithms` (the algorithms actually used at runtime, which can differ from the `join_algorithm` setting), `used_join_kinds` (`INNER`, `LEFT`, `CROSS`, `ASOF` and so on), and `join_spilled_to_disk` (whether any join wrote temporary data to disk). This makes it possible to find problematic JOIN patterns across a fleet without reproducing each query.

signals.title: Check the query cancellation while filling `system.parts` and its siblings
signals.text: The tables based on `StorageSystemPartsBase` (`system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`) build the whole result eagerly in `initializePipeline`, so a cancelled or timed out query kept building rows over every storage and part until the very end. In a stress test with ThreadFuzzer this took minutes and tripped the hung check: a `SELECT` over `system.parts_columns` (with a filter matching every active part on the server) stayed in the process list for 252 seconds with `is_cancelled = 1` and `max_execution_time = 10`. Check the query status per storage and per part, following the pattern of `system.zookeeper` and `system.remote_data_paths`. The check also covers the storage-discovery prepass in `StoragesInfoStream` (the eager enumeration of all databases and tables), the analogous prepass in `StoragesDroppedInfoStream` (so `system.dropped_tables_parts` is interruptible as well), the skip loop in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::next`, and the per-storage part enumeration itself: the `MergeTreeData` helpers (`getDataPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllDataPartsVector`, `getProjectionPartsVectorForInternalUsage`, `getAllProjectionPartsVector`) take an optional `need_stop` callback that is checked periodically while the parts snapshot is being built. The two column-oriented tables additionally check the query status inside their column-enumeration loops and their metadata prepass, so a very wide table does not create a long uninterruptible stretch inside a single storage. The return value of `checkTimeLimit` is honored, so with `timeout_overflow_mode = 'break'` the eager build stops at the soft deadline and returns the rows collected so far. The table-lock acquisition in `StoragesInfoStreamBase::tryLockTable` is interruptible as well: instead of a single wait inside `RWLockImpl::getLock` for the whole `lock_acquire_timeout`, the lock is acquired in 100 ms slices with a query-status poll between the attempts (the total timeout and the `DEADLOCK_AVOIDED` semantics are preserved), so a killed or soft-timed-out query does not sit in the lock wait while a concurrent DDL query holds the drop lock. The test `04869_system_parts_lock_wait_cancellation` pins this with a share lock held by a long `SELECT` and a `DROP TABLE` in an `Ordinary` database queued behind it. The test uses the new `slowdown_system_parts_enumeration` failpoint, which only affects the specially named test tables (so concurrently running tests are unaffected). It sleeps 500 ms on every enumerated part, so building the full result for a 20-part table takes at least 10 seconds, and it sleeps 1 second per `COLUMNS_CANCELLATION_CHECK_PERIOD` (128) enumerated columns of a part, so building the full `system.parts_columns` / `system.projection_parts_columns` result over a single part with 1,025 columns (and a projection over all of them) takes at least 8 seconds. The test asserts that queries with a 1 second deadline in the `break` mode finish well under that (the elapsed time is taken from `system.query_log`, because the startup of `clickhouse-client` alone takes seconds in the debug and sanitizer builds), which is only possible by stopping at the per-part and per-column cancellation checkpoints. Timed assertions are needed because a plain row-count assertion cannot distinguish a build with the fix from one without: in the `break` mode the executor drops the eagerly built result after the deadline in both cases. The test also asserts partial row counts under a pre-expired deadline for all five tables, including `system.dropped_tables_parts` over a deterministic dropped-table fixture. The pre-expired-deadline checks also run under the failpoint, so the fewer-rows assertion is deterministic even on a machine fast enough to build the whole result in under a millisecond. For tables with the `_snap` name marker, the failpoint additionally slows down the parts-snapshot walks inside `MergeTreeData` (500 ms per enumerated part) and makes them poll the stop callback on every element, and for tables with the `_meta` name marker it slows down the column-metadata prepass of the column-oriented tables (1 second per 128 enumerated metadata columns), so the timed checks also prove that the snapshot materialization and the prepass are interruptible: all six of these checks fail against a binary with the `need_stop` polls and the prepass checkpoints disabled. Caught by `Stress test (arm_asan_ubsan, s3)`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113722&sha=ceedb772f6aa36e221d25ce48f9af71f032a7b08&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113722 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Queries over `system.parts`, `system.parts_columns`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.projection_parts_columns`, and `system.dropped_tables_parts` now react to cancellation and `max_execution_time` while the result is being built.

signals.title: Make background merges and mutations observe cancellation in the S3 retry loop
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed background merges and mutations ignoring cancellation while reading from an unreachable S3 endpoint. Such a merge or mutation kept retrying to its retry budget, so `KILL MUTATION`, `SYSTEM STOP MERGES`, `SYSTEM STOP TTL MERGES` and shutdown had no effect on it, and a following `DROP TABLE` waited for it, blocking further `DROP`/`DETACH` on that database. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58479 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/66656 A mutation whose `IN` subquery reads an unreachable S3 endpoint ignored `KILL MUTATION` and kept retrying to its budget. The following `DROP TABLE` blocked in `MergeTreeBackgroundExecutor::removeTasksCorrespondingToStorage` with `DROP`/`DETACH DATABASE` queued behind it, which a stress-test hung check reported as a possible deadlock. A merge reading through an S3 disk hangs the same way under `SYSTEM STOP MERGES` or shutdown. Root cause: the S3 layer already checks cancellation before sleeping between retries (`Client::RetryStrategy::ShouldRetry`, `Client::HeadObject`, the redirect loop), but those checks were dead for background work. They resolve through `ThreadStatus::isQueryCanceled`, whose predicate the `ThreadGroup` constructor routes through the query context's process-list element, which nothing on the merge or mutate path ever sets, so it answered constant `false`. Cancellation is recorded in `MergeListElement::is_cancelled` and in the merges blocker instead, which the IO layer cannot see, and `PipelineExecutor::cancel` cannot preempt a processor already inside `work()`. The fix installs that blocker-or-entry-flag predicate on the merge or mutation thread group, so the existing cancellation points become live. Both the boolean and the throwing predicate are set, since their consumers are disjoint, and a detected cancellation is latched, mirroring the merge path, so a blocker released while the read is between attempts cannot resurrect it. `ReadBufferFromS3::processException` now reports a cancelled read as cancelled rather than rethrowing the stale S3 error. A projection sub-merge is left to its parent's predicate: it re-enters `mergePartsToTemporaryPart` from inside a running merge whose group is already attached, and an attach copies shared data once. `SYSTEM STOP TTL MERGES` mirrors both of `MergeTask`'s own TTL conditions, an assigned TTL merge or a regular merge that settled on removing expired values, but not one whose removal that blocker had disabled before the merge started, which completes correctly without removal. A test arm pins each of the three. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113939&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113939](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113939+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not kill a mutation whose transaction is past its commit point
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a server abort (`LOGICAL_ERROR: Cannot find mutation`) when `KILL MUTATION` raced the `COMMIT` of the transaction that had started the mutation. `KILL MUTATION` now reports `cant_cancel` for a mutation whose transaction has already passed its commit point, instead of destroying state the commit still needs. ### Description `StorageMergeTree::killMutation` erased the `current_mutations_by_version` entry and removed `mutation_*.txt` **before** resolving the owning transaction, calling `TransactionLog::rollbackTransaction` only afterwards. Past the commit point that rollback is a no-op: `rollback` CASes `csn` `UnknownCSN -> RolledBackCSN`, which fails once `beforeCommit` stored `CommittingCSN`, so `rollbackTransaction` early-returns. The erase, however, is permanent. The committing thread then reached `afterCommit` -> `setMutationCSN`, could not find the entry, and threw `LOGICAL_ERROR "Cannot find mutation"` from a `noexcept` function, aborting the server. The fix resolves the transaction first and claims the cancellation through `rollback`'s `csn` CAS before destroying anything. That CAS contends with `beforeCommit`'s `UnknownCSN -> CommittingCSN` CAS on the same atomic, so exactly one wins and the decision is atomic with respect to the commit point. When the commit wins, `killMutation` returns `CancelCannotBeSent` (`cant_cancel`) and changes nothing. Merely reading the CSN would not be enough: the commit does not take `currently_processing_in_background_mutex`, so read-then-erase is a TOCTOU that reproduces the same abort. Refusing loses no work, because `beforeCommit` waits for every mutation of the transaction before its CAS, and it matches how `executeRollback` and `KILL TRANSACTION` already treat a committing transaction. The non-transactional path is unchanged, and `setMutationCSN` is deliberately untouched: an early return there would silently drop a committed mutation's CSN. Reaching this requires `allow_experimental_transactions`, enabled by `tests/config` for every stateless and stress job. Validation: the new stateless test drives the race deterministically with three new pauseable failpoints; it aborts the server without the fix and passes with it. 50/50 randomized and 50/50 plain runs pass, and a scope over every `KILL MUTATION` test plus the transaction-isolation families shows no verdict change against the unmodified build. `afterCommit` remains `noexcept` with no internal guard, so any other future throw there is still fatal; that is the #45736 family, for a separate change. No related open issue found.

signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/metadata
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Adds Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` support for `TimeSeries` tables.** ### Description This adds the Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` endpoint backed by the `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table. ### Why this matters - **Prometheus-compatible tools** use `/api/v1/metadata` to discover **metric types, help text, and units**. - Without this endpoint, clients need separate configuration or lose this metadata when using ClickHouse as a Prometheus-compatible endpoint. - This keeps the `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table as the **source of truth** for that metadata. Supported parameters: - `metric` filters the response to one metric family. - `limit` limits the number of metric families. - `limit_per_metric` limits the metadata objects returned for each family. Other details: - Metadata objects are unique. Entries returned for each family are sorted. - `limit=0` returns no metric families. - Zero and negative `limit_per_metric` values mean no per-family limit. - Positive `limit_per_metric` values bound the number of unique metadata objects returned for each family. The selected subset is not specified. - `FINAL` is used whenever the Metrics target supports it, including wrapped targets. - Metadata parameters stay endpoint-local and are not treated as ClickHouse settings. - The generated query uses the normal query pipeline and is recorded in `query_log`. - Access to the configured `TimeSeries` table and related table functions is checked. - The endpoint works with dedicated handlers and the combined `/api/v1` handler. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - unique metadata across multiple parts. - stable results after `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL`. - JSON escaping for quotes, backslashes, newlines, tabs, and Unicode. - metric filtering and both limit parameters. - invalid limit values. - high-cardinality metadata with per-family limits. - primary-key filtering. - wrapped `FINAL` targets. - aliases and `prefer_column_name_to_alias`. - query logging. - endpoint and table-function access control. - unknown endpoint handling. - GET/HEAD and unsupported-method handling. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Documentation was added to the Prometheus protocols page. It covers the handler configuration and supported parameters. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114038&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114038](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114038+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add a full-featured AI agent to the client (the `?` command)
signals.text: Turns the primitive `??` "generate one SQL query" helper in the client into a full interactive AI agent, available with a single `?` (`??` is kept as an alias). The agent works over a live connection: it is given the context of the recent queries in the session (with results truncated to the first and last lines to save tokens, plus error messages) and can use tools to read the query history from `system.user_query_log`, inspect the schema (`SHOW`/`DESCRIBE`/`SHOW CREATE`), consult the embedded documentation (`system.documentation`, the same source as the `help` command), run read-only queries without confirmation under a sandbox (`readonly = 1`, a 30-second and a 10 GiB limit, no table functions reaching outside of the server's tables; if the session forbids applying these limits, the query fails instead of running without them), and run any other query after asking the user for confirmation. Queries it runs are echoed and executed on the user's connection and displayed exactly as if the user had typed them; it prints its thoughts and tool calls as it works, and the conversation keeps its context across `?` invocations within a session. When no client-side AI provider is configured (neither the `ai` section of the client configuration nor the `OPENAI_API_KEY`/`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variables), the agent falls back to the server-side `aiGenerate` function of the connected server (or of `clickhouse-local`) when it has default credentials configured for it (`ai_function_text_default_credentials`), so it works with no client-side setup when the administrator has already enabled AI functions. Implementation lives in `src/Client/AI/`: the agent loop (`AIAgent`), two model backends (`AIAgentTransport`: native tool-calling via `ai-sdk-cpp`, and a text tool-call protocol on top of `aiGenerate`), the tools (`AIAgentTools`), the read-only statement allowlist (`AIQueryValidation`), and the recent-query context buffer (`QueryContextBuffer`). Unit tests cover the tool-call protocol parsing, the read-only validation, and the context buffer; the end-to-end loop (both backends and the confirmation gate) was validated by driving `clickhouse-local` against a mock OpenAI endpoint. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The embedded AI assistant of `clickhouse-client` and `clickhouse-local` is now a full agent, invoked with a single `?`. It sees the recent queries and their results, explores the schema and the documentation, runs read-only queries on its own (and other queries with confirmation) displayed as if you typed them, and can use the server-side `aiGenerate` function when no client-side AI provider is configured. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114043&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114043](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114043+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Revert "Use libdeflate for gzip/zlib/deflate compression and decompression"
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114045 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108074 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Revert #108074 (use libdeflate for gzip/zlib/deflate): its streaming decompressor suspends only at DEFLATE block boundaries, so decompressing an HTTP request body whose single DEFLATE block spans the whole stream (the shape zlib-ng produces at level 1, which is the default in the official .NET SDK) was `O(n^2)` in the compressed block size and buffered the whole block in memory. A 22 MB gzip body that 26.6 ingested in 0.3 s took 15 s on 26.7. This returns the gzip/zlib/deflate paths to zlib-ng, restoring 26.6 behavior. The `gzip`/`deflate` compression levels `10-12` that 26.7 introduced stay accepted and are clamped to `9`, the maximum level supported by `zlib`, so configurations written against 26.7 keep working. ### Details This is a plain `git revert` of the merge commit of #108074, with the following manual adjustments: - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04230_iceberg_optimize_metadata_not_initialized_104711.sh` and `04240_iceberg_supports_parallel_insert_mv_104891.sh` keep their current (post-#108074) form: they now corrupt Iceberg metadata files directly instead of relying on `output_format_compression_level=11` being rejected, which works regardless of the compression backend. - The relocated doc `docs/reference/statements/select/into-outfile.mdx` documents the compression level range as `1-12` for `gzip`/`deflate` with the clamp, since the old `docs/en` tree no longer exists for the revert to apply to. The text for `http_zlib_compression_level` is changed in the `DECLARE` docstring in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`, because `docs/reference/settings/session-settings/http.mdx` is inside an `AUTOGENERATED` region and hand-editing it fails the `No direct edits to generated or read-only docs` check. **Backward compatibility.** 26.7 shipped `libdeflate` and, with it, `gzip`/`deflate` compression levels `10-12` on every output surface that routes through `CompressionMethod`: `INTO OUTFILE ... LEVEL`, `output_format_compression_level`, `http_zlib_compression_level` and the gRPC `output_compression_level`. A plain revert would narrow the accepted range back to `1-9`, so existing queries and settings profiles would start failing with `Invalid compression level` or `deflateInit2 failed: stream error`. To avoid that, `getCompressionLevelRange` keeps returning `1-12` for `gzip`/`zlib` and `createWriteCompressedWrapper` clamps levels above `9` to zlib's maximum. Levels above `12` are still rejected, as in 26.7. Two tests are restored in a backend-agnostic form instead of being deleted with the feature: - `04842_parquet_gzip_compression_level` round-trips a mixed-compressibility dataset through Parquet with `output_format_parquet_compression_method='gzip'` at levels `1, 3, 6, 9, 12`, keeping non-default-level coverage of `output_format_compression_level` for Parquet. - `04843_outfile_compression_level_range` covers the accepted `INTO OUTFILE ... LEVEL` range for `gzip`/`deflate`, the clamp of `10-12`, and the rejection of `13`. Additionally, gzip-compressed Parquet pages are now decompressed with a one-shot `inflate` loop (`decompressGzip` in `src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/Reader.cpp`) instead of the streaming `ZlibInflatingReadBuffer`. The streaming path could not tell a clean end of the gzip stream from a damaged one, because `zlib` validates the trailer (`CRC32` and `ISIZE`) only on the read after the one that filled the output exactly, while the reader stops as soon as it has `uncompressed_page_size` bytes — so a corrupted trailer was accepted silently. The one-shot loop requires `Z_STREAM_END`, while ignoring bytes left in the page after the last member, since `compressed_page_size` is the number of bytes the page owns and a writer may pad it. Two more tests cover this: - `04848_parquet_gzip_corrupted_trailer` corrupts a page's gzip `CRC32` in place and requires the read to be rejected, with and without page checksum verification. - `04892_parquet_gzip_padded_page` pads a gzip dictionary page and requires the file to keep reading back identically. A follow-up PR will re-introduce libdeflate with the streaming decompressor fixed to suspend at symbol granularity (linear time, bounded memory).

signals.title: Fix quadratic gzip/zlib streaming decompression of single-block streams
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114045 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108074 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114054 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/libdeflate/pull/6 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `O(n^2)` decompression of gzip/zlib/deflate streams whose single DEFLATE block spans the whole stream, the shape zlib-ng produces at compression level 1 (the default of the official .NET SDK): a 24 MiB gzip HTTP body that took 11 s to ingest in 26.7 now takes 0.12 s, identical to a multi-block body, with memory bounded by the buffer size instead of the block size. ### Details The root cause: the streaming decompressor added to `contrib/libdeflate` kept its resume checkpoint only at DEFLATE block boundaries. On input exhaustion or output-buffer overflow it rolled back to the start of the current block, so for a stream that is one giant block, every socket refill re-decoded the block from its beginning — quadratic time — and the whole block's output had to be buffered before any byte was exposed — unbounded memory. The work happens in `copyDataImpl` while assembling the query, before the query starts, so it was invisible in `system.processes` and `query_duration_ms`. The fix (https://github.com/ClickHouse/libdeflate/pull/6, vendored by this PR in `contrib/libdeflate`) re-takes the checkpoint at every symbol boundary in the generic decode loop, plus two new decompressor fields (`in_block`, `block_is_final`) that let a resumed call jump straight back into symbol decoding — the litlen/offset decode tables already persist in the decompressor between calls. The fastloop is untouched: suspensions can only trigger from the generic loop, which always runs between the fastloop and input exhaustion. A suspension now loses at most one partially decoded symbol, so decompression is linear-time with bounded memory regardless of block structure. `LibdeflateInflatingReadBuffer` needed no logic changes, only comment updates: its "grow the output buffer" path is now reachable only when a single match (≤ 258 bytes) or stored block (≤ 64 KiB) exceeds the free output region. Verification: - Standalone harness: 5000+ randomized round-trips (zlib streams at all levels with random flush points; crafted static- and dynamic-Huffman single-block streams with matches reaching the full 32 KiB window; input chunking down to 1 byte; random output regions), zlib inflate as decode oracle, one-shot decoder as cross-check, and a progress assertion on every suspension. - End-to-end with the issue's reproducer shape (24 MiB single-block gzip body, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, local release build): **11.25 s before → 0.12 s after**, now identical to a multi-block body of the same content (0.12 s). Verified the vendored zlib-ng really emits this shape: at level 1 it produces 1 block for a 4 MiB input (stock zlib: 80 blocks). - No throughput regression on normal multi-block streams: 685 → 697 MB/s on a 256 MB zlib-level-6 stream. New tests: - `LibdeflateSingleBlock.StreamingConsumesInputWithinBlock` pins the linearity contract (a suspension inside a Huffman block leaves at most a few bytes unconsumed). Against the pre-fix library it fails immediately, with 35 MB left unconsumed on a 32 MiB single-block stream. - `LibdeflateInflateTest.RoundTripFromZlibNgLevelOneLarge` decodes a large stream produced by the vendored zlib-ng at level 1 — the real-encoder shape of the issue. - `LibdeflateInflateTest.SingleDeflateBlockSpanningWholeMember` decodes crafted single-block gzip/zlib members through `LibdeflateInflatingReadBuffer`. - `04836_http_gzip_single_deflate_block` ingests a crafted single-block gzip body over HTTP with chunked transfer encoding, end to end. Because the pre-fix decoder is correct, just quadratic, the assertion is on time: the body is one 36 MB block and the request is capped at 15 s. Ingest time for a single-block body of a given size, release build, `master`'s `contrib/libdeflate` vs this branch's: 10 MB - 1.8 s vs 0.05 s; 20 MB - 6.9 s; 40 MB - 27.3 s vs 0.20 s; 48 MB - 39.1 s vs 0.25 s. So the limit sits 2.6x below the pre-fix time and 60x above the fixed one, and the clean quadratic growth means the pre-fix margin does not depend on the machine speed. The payload is 120 lines of 400 KB so that line parsing and the `MergeTree` write do not dominate. Note: `Bugfix validation (unit tests)` reports `ERROR` (inconclusive, non-blocking) here for a structural reason: the fix itself lives in `contrib/libdeflate`, and the job cannot populate its merge-base "before" worktree at the merge-base submodule revision, so it refuses to build a before-binary that would validate the wrong submodule code. The functional test above is what validates the fix. Note: this PR and the revert #114054 are alternatives on master — if the revert merges first, this branch will be updated to re-apply the integration together with the fix; if this merges first, the revert can be closed (the 26.7 backport of the revert can proceed independently). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114059&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114059](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114059+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Convert stateless tests that modify the server's data on disk to integration tests
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113978 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114056 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114057 Stateless tests are not allowed to modify the server's data on disk at all (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113978#pullrequestreview-4891978370): the stateless suite runs against arbitrary server configurations — object storage, shared merge tree, encrypted disks — where the local part layout either does not exist or does not mean what the test assumes, and modifying it corrupts shared state. This PR converts all stateless tests that do such manipulation into integration tests, grouped by scenario, and adds a style check that rejects new ones: **Extended existing modules:** - `test_broken_projections` ← `02254_projection_broken_part`, `04511_check_table_broken_projection_columns` - `test_broken_tmp_txn_version_startup` ← `04104_transaction_version_metadata_dummy_tid_load`, `04492_attach_as_replicated_clears_tmp_txn_version`, `04493_attach_part_clears_tmp_txn_version`, `04507_packed_part_stale_txn_version_guard` - `test_lost_part` ← `02369_lost_part_intersecting_merges`, `02370_lost_part_intersecting_merges`, `04215_replicated_missing_covered_part_on_start` **New modules:** - `test_corrupted_part_files` (files inside part directories damaged/removed; loading, fetching, and `CHECK TABLE` reactions) ← `02253_empty_part_checksums`, `02255_broken_parts_chain_on_start`, `02444_async_broken_outdated_part_loading`, `04151_unique_key_sst_rebuild_on_load`, `04235_corrupted_columns_substreams_detection`, `04323_text_index_marks_empty_part`, `04506_packed_part_fetch_checksum` - `test_mutations_with_tampered_parts` (mutations over parts with old-version emulation or corrupted index files) ← `04401_dynamic_mutation_old_part_no_substreams_file`, `04412_mutation_old_part_basic_map_partial`, `04426_mutate_repair_corrupted_missing_idx_checksums`, `04427_mutate_some_columns_drop_index_corrupted_idx`, `04428_mutate_corrupted_text_index_multistream`, `04431_mutate_corrupted_index_sibling_owns_file` - `test_attach_tampered_detached_parts` (detached part directories manipulated before `ATTACH` / `DROP DETACHED`) ← `04063_drop_detached_part_with_try_n_suffix`, `04246_materialize_index_force_recalc` (the canned `part_25.8.tar.gz` moves into the module), `04402_mutate_all_columns_preserve_legacy_idx_minmax`, `04403_mutate_preserve_legacy_idx_packed_minmax`, `04404_mutate_rebuild_legacy_idx_minmax`, `04425_mutate_mixed_legacy_idx_minmax` - `test_backups_from_disk` (backups placed or tampered with directly on the `backups` disk) ← `04054_backup_restore_validate_entry_paths`, `04495_backup_metadata_version_overflow`, `02864_restore_table_with_broken_part`, `03001_restore_from_old_backup_with_matview_inner_table_metadata`, `03214_backup_and_clear_old_temporary_directories`, `03231_old_backup_without_access_entities_dependents`. The canned backup zips move from `tests/queries/0_stateless/backups/` into the module, and `helpers/install_predefined_backup.sh` is replaced by a module helper. - `test_server_metadata_files` (direct manipulation of on-disk table metadata `.sql` and the `flags/` directory) ← `03001_matview_columns_after_modify_query`, `04329_create_or_replace_force_drop_flag`, `04545_attach_projection_part_offset_setting_disabled` The conversions are faithful: every `.reference` output became an exact assertion, the originals' explanatory comments are preserved, and `DETACH`/`ATTACH` stayed `DETACH`/`ATTACH` except where the original explicitly emulated a server restart (`02255`, `04215` — "on start" scenarios now use a real server restart). Notable finds along the way: - `02444_async_broken_outdated_part_loading` contained a quoting bug since its introduction: `rm -f "$path/*.bin"` never expanded the glob, so the "broken" outdated part was never actually broken. The converted test applies the corruption for real, and the assertions still hold. - `02255_broken_parts_chain_on_start` dropped a nonexistent table (`projection_broken_parts_1`) in cleanup instead of its own tables. Verified locally against a fresh master binary: all new tests pass under the integration runner, and the tampered-parts modules were additionally cross-checked against a pre-fix binary where the bug-detecting assertions fire as intended. The style check (`server_data_manipulation_in_stateless_tests` in `ci/jobs/check_style.py`, folded in from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114056) flags stateless `.sh` tests that fetch a server-side filesystem path from a system table (`system.parts`, `system.detached_parts`, `system.projection_parts`, `system.tables`, `system.disks`, `system.server_settings` with `name = 'path'`) and also run file-modifying shell commands (`rm`/`cp`/`mv`/`dd`/`truncate`/`ln`/`chmod`/`touch`/`mkdir`/`tar`, `sed -i`, output redirection into a variable-derived path, `clickhouse-disks write`/`remove`/...). With all offenders converted here, the exclusion list holds only one documented false positive (`04326_disks_app_read_checksums`, which writes an `mktemp` scratch file under `CLICKHOUSE_TMP`) and `04630_merge_over_stale_packed_tmp_dir`, whose conversion is pending in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114057. Verified: the check is clean on this branch and catches each converted test if its stateless original is restored. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114070&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114070](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114070+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix vector search with `arrayJoin` below the sort and with a row policy
signals.text: Fixes for the vector search `ORDER BY <distance> LIMIT` optimization. **`arrayJoin` below the sort.** `arrayJoin` changes the number of rows - an empty array drops its base row - so the rewrite must not shortlist base rows before it runs. `optimizeTopK` rejects `arrayJoin` for this reason (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/82279), but the vector search optimization did not, so the rows that a later base row would have contributed were never produced: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt32, tags Array(UInt32), vec Array(Float32), INDEX idx vec TYPE vector_similarity('hnsw', 'cosineDistance', 2)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id SETTINGS index_granularity = 4; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, if(number < 16, [], [number]), [toFloat32(number), toFloat32(number + 1)] FROM numbers(64); SELECT arrayJoin(tags) FROM t ORDER BY cosineDistance(vec, [0., 1.]) LIMIT 1; -- returned nothing; with `use_skip_indexes = 0` it returns 16 ``` **A row policy is an additional filter.** A row policy restricts rows inside the reader just like a `WHERE` or a `PREWHERE`, but it did not participate in `additional_filters_present`, so a query filtered only by a policy was treated as unfiltered: the `vector_search_filter_strategy = 'prefilter'` bailout was skipped, so an explicit request for exact search was ignored, and the index fetched only `LIMIT` neighbours without the `vector_search_index_fetch_multiplier` compensation, which the policy can then discard. **Filters that read the vector column broke the non-rescoring rewrite** (found during review). The rewrite drops the physical vector column from the read list and replaces it with the virtual `_distance` column, so any filter that still needs the column was left without its input and the query failed with `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` (an exception, pre-existing on master). The rewrite is now skipped - the same treatment as the vector column in `SELECT` - when the column is read by: - a row policy (including a policy carried in the deferred filter under `FINAL` with `apply_row_policy_after_final`), - a plain `WHERE` filter below the sort, e.g. `WHERE length(vec) > 0` (reachable with default settings, because the implicit `PREWHERE` optimization is disabled for vector-search candidates). The quantized-codes rewrite (`useVectorSearchWithQuantizedCodes`) is not affected by these problems: it splices the shortlist above the whole `Expression`/`Filter` chain, so the expansion and the filters run below it, and its reader-side filters prefilter the approximate ranking. This was checked with the same queries. `FINAL` with an explicit `PREWHERE` is covered by a separate regression test. `FINAL` can defer a `PREWHERE` until after the merge, but the deferral copies the filter and clears `query_info.prewhere_info` only when the pipeline is built, i.e. past every query plan optimization, so the existing `getPrewhereInfo` bailout still fires and the physical vector column survives for the deferred filter. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/82279 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110188 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed vector search returning too few rows for a query with `arrayJoin` below `ORDER BY <distance> LIMIT`. A row policy now counts as an additional filter for vector search, so `vector_search_filter_strategy = 'prefilter'` is honored and the index fetch multiplier is applied for a query filtered by a row policy. Fixed `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` for a non-rescoring vector search query when a `WHERE` filter or a row policy reads the vector column. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Fix mixed-case PromQL aggregation operators
signals.text: ### Description PromQL keywords are case-insensitive, and the grammar already accepts mixed-case aggregation operators. However, the parser kept the original spelling in the query tree, so expressions such as `SuM(up)` reached lowercase-only lowering dispatch and failed as unsupported. This change normalizes aggregation operator names when building the query tree. The normalization is limited to aggregation expressions, so metric names such as bare `SUM` and case-sensitive function names keep their original spelling. Parser coverage includes mixed-case `sum`, mixed-case `topk` with grouping, and preservation of the bare `SUM` metric name. ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL aggregation operators now accept mixed letter casing, matching Prometheus.** <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1569` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix `bloom_filter` index skipping granules for a `FixedString` constant
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112693 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `hasAny`, `hasAll`, `has`, `indexOf`, `mapContainsKey`, `mapContainsValue` and `mapContains` returning too few rows, or failing with `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE`, when a `bloom_filter` index is queried with a `FixedString` constant. The index hashed the padded form of the constant while the function compares the unpadded one, so a matching granule was skipped. ### Description A `bloom_filter` skip index silently returns too few rows when the constant is a `FixedString`, and in four cases raises `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE` on a query that succeeds without the index: ```sql CREATE TABLE k (id UInt64, v Array(String), INDEX idx v TYPE bloom_filter GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id SETTINGS index_granularity = 1; INSERT INTO k VALUES (0,['V0']),(1,['V0\0']),(2,['X']); SELECT count() FROM k WHERE hasAny(v, [toFixedString('V0',3)]); -- 0, wrong SELECT count() FROM k WHERE hasAny(v, [toFixedString('V0',3)]) SETTINGS use_skip_indexes=0; -- 1 ``` Root cause: the array-search functions coerce the constant with CAST before comparing it to the elements (`hasAny`/`hasAll`, and `has`/`indexOf` over a `FixedString` element, cast both sides to the least supertype; `has`/`indexOf` over a `LowCardinality` element cast the constant straight to the dictionary type), and a CAST of `FixedString` to `String` strips the trailing zero padding. The index instead converted the constant with `convertFieldToType`, which keeps the padding, so it hashed a value the function never compares and pruned granules that match. The error cases are the same cause: an oversized `Field` passed through unchanged and reached a column `insert` during index analysis. The fix replicates the coercion at the `Field` level, which is exact because the string casts involved are fully predictable: strip the padding of a `FixedString` constant, re-pad it to the width of the element type (the stored form of every element the function can match), and decline the index when the constant has no stored representation, so a runtime `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE` stays reachable instead of becoming a silent empty result. The direct cast to a dictionary type rejects an over-wide `FixedString` constant before stripping, while the supertype cast strips first - that one ordering difference is the only divergence between the two coercions, so it is a `bool` rather than a second code path. `has`/`indexOf` over a plain `String` element compare the constant's raw padded bytes (`executeString`) and keep the old conversion, as does `has(<constant array>, <indexed scalar>)`, whose runtime compares `Field`s directly. #### `Map` predicates `mapContainsKey`, `mapContainsValue`, `mapContains` and `has` over a `Map` are adapters of the same `arrayIndex.h` machinery, so a `bloom_filter` index on `mapKeys`/`mapValues` needs the same coercion - and it needs to pick the mode from the `Map` type rather than from the index header, because the `mapKeys`/`mapValues` index expression strips `LowCardinality` from the key/value type while the `mapContains*` adapters run over the keys/values subcolumn, which keeps it. Reading the mode from the stripped header alone would still prune a matching granule on `Map(LowCardinality(String), ...)`, which is broken on `master` today independently of the constant's width. `has` over a `Map` is the one exception, and it goes the other way: `FunctionArrayIndex::executeMap` rewrites the map to an array of its keys and calls `recursiveRemoveLowCardinality` on both arguments before `executeArrayImpl`, so it compares the raw padded bytes exactly like `has` over an `Array(String)`, unlike `mapContainsKey` on the same column. Its element type is therefore stripped of `LowCardinality` before the mode is read. The direct array spellings `has(mapKeys(m), ...)` / `indexOf(mapValues(m), ...)` need no special handling: `mapKeys`/`mapValues` return a full `Array` with `LowCardinality` stripped from the type, so the index header type is already the type the runtime compares against. This supersedes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112693 with a smaller implementation of the same semantics (one `Field`-level helper instead of a two-mode column-cast round-trip through `getLeastSupertype` plus a batched clone of `createColumnFromConstantArray`). The array test - 115 assertions over the full element-type/function/constant-width matrix, including granule-pruning and `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE` reachability assertions - is taken unchanged from that pull request and passes byte-identically, so the two implementations are behaviorally equivalent on the covered surface. Three further tests cover the `Map` predicates, the direct `mapKeys`/`mapValues` array spellings, and `has` over a `Map` with `LowCardinality` keys; each compares the indexed answer against an unindexed oracle.

signals.title: Honour lock_acquire_timeout for the lightweight update lock in Keeper
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112380 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed lightweight `UPDATE` on `ReplicatedMergeTree` being rejected with `TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED` after a few seconds under concurrent updates, long before the configured `lock_acquire_timeout` elapsed. The Keeper lock acquisition loop was bounded by a fixed number of tries instead of by the timeout, so raising `lock_acquire_timeout` had no effect. ### Description A valid lightweight `UPDATE` was rejected with ``` Code: 159. Failed to get lock with 100 tries for lightwegiht update in auto mode. (TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED) ``` after about 3 seconds, with `lock_acquire_timeout` at 120 seconds and the cluster granting locks normally. `update_parallel_mode` defaults to `auto`, so this is the default path. Root cause: `getLockForAutoMode` watched the parent directory `.../lightweight_updates/in_progress`, whose child set changes on every concurrent update, and `Poco::Event` returns at once when already signalled: across 15228 waits requesting 120000 ms the longest was 0.086 s, so the loop spun to `max_tries = 100`. `getLockForSyncMode` had the same shape, at ~6 s. Elapsed time against `lock_acquire_timeout` is now the only failure condition, and the wait is on the conflicting update's own node: - Remaining time is a `Stopwatch` subtraction in the millisecond domain: the setting has no upper constraint and a `steady_clock` deadline overflows above ~9223372036 s. - `ZBADVERSION` from the parent-version CAS, which any unrelated update invalidates, has no node to wait on, so it backs off 50 ms instead of retrying at once, counted by a new `PatchesAcquireLockBadVersionRetries` profile event. - The wait is split into 3 s slices polling query cancellation, plus one poll on leaving the loop so a cancellation arriving in the last slice is not reported as the lock timing out. All four paths share this helper, including the plain `MergeTree` ones that waited in a single `try_lock_for`/`wait_for`: with a held lock and `max_execution_time = 2`, each now ends on its own limit. The first attempt stays unconditional, so an uncontended update still succeeds at `lock_acquire_timeout = 0`. Behaviour change: a query that failed after a few seconds may now wait up to `lock_acquire_timeout`, as the setting documents. Acquisition is still unfair (the `EphemeralSequential` node is created but not used for ordering); fair queueing needs a predecessor-watch protocol and a mixed-version story, out of scope. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Debug build, single node with embedded Keeper. 15 concurrent same-column updaters split into three arms by `lock_acquire_timeout`, in one concurrency window. Time-to-failure must track the timeout. | arm | `lock_acquire_timeout` | before | after | |---|---|---|---| | A | 120 s (default) | 13/237 rejected at 3.03/3.23/3.62 s | 0/205 rejected | | B | 600 s | 11/233 rejected at 3.03/3.26/3.48 s | 0/219 rejected | | C | 3 s | 19/242 rejected at 3.14/3.25/3.51 s | 11/269 rejected at 3.08/3.08/3.10 s | Before, every arm failed at the same ~3.2 s regardless of its timeout; after, only the 3 s arm fails, at its own. Same for `update_parallel_mode = 'sync'` (~6.2 s before). Each mechanism was checked against a build with only that mechanism removed, Build IDs asserted: - parent-directory watch restored: 19 lock tries against 2, passing the table above identically, i.e. the deadline alone turns a premature failure into a busy spin. - `ZBADVERSION` backoff removed: worst-case tries for one query 221/228/176 across three repeats, against 115/116/115 with it (measured directly, not asserted by the test). - unchunked wait: a waiter with `max_execution_time = 2` runs 17.2 s uninterrupted, against stopping at 3.03 s. With only the loop-exit poll removed, all four `lock_acquire_timeout = 2.5` arms report the lock timeout at ~2.52 s instead of their own 2 s limit. - watch re-registered per slice: a waiter parked across six slices registers 7 watches on the node, against 1. `03100_lwu_57_lock_acquire_timeout` covers the timeout arms, a large timeout, churn bounding the try count, a lost parent-version CAS, cancellation on both engines and in the single-slice case, and watch registration by one parked waiter. It fails on unpatched master. Every arm is fixed by construction rather than timed: holders and the CAS victim park at failpoints, so the watch arm's span is 12331-12345 ms against a 9000 ms bound over six randomized runs, and the CAS arm pins its one retry. Parked time falls inside `PatchesAcquireLockMicroseconds`, so that arm does not assert the backoff duration. `03100_lwu_35_lock_profile_events` still passes. </details>

signals.title: Fix JIT-compiled min and max on DateTime64 comparing timestamps as unsigned
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113942 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/101203 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `min` and `max` on `DateTime64` columns returning wrong results once the aggregate is JIT compiled and the data contains timestamps before 1970. `is_signed` was not specialised for `DateTime64` and `Time64`, which derive from `Decimal64`, so the generated code compared tick counts as unsigned integers and a pre-1970 timestamp won `max` and lost `min`. ### Description Closes: #113942 `min(dt)`/`max(dt)` over a `DateTime64` column silently return the wrong row once the aggregate is JIT compiled (after `min_count_to_compile_aggregate_expression`, default 3) and the group mixes pre-1970 and post-1970 values. Both columns are wrong: the negative tick count reads as a huge unsigned value, so it wins `max` and loses `min`. Root cause: `is_signed` is explicitly specialised for `Decimal32/64/128/256` in `base/base/Decimal_fwd.h`, but `DateTime64` and `Time64` are *derived classes* of `Decimal64`, not aliases, and a base's explicit specialisation does not apply to a derived class. So `is_signed_v<DateTime64>` fell back to `std::is_signed_v` of a class type, i.e. `false`, and `SingleValueDataFixed<T>::compileMinMax`/`compileMinMaxMerge` emitted `icmp ult`/`ugt`. This completes #101203, which introduced the `is_signed_v` use and fixed only the `Decimal*` half. The fix constrains the specialisation on the existing `DB::is_decimal` concept instead of enumerating types, so it follows the single place that defines which types are decimals and a future decimal type cannot silently regress. One source line changes. Validation: a new stateless test covers scales 0/3/9, the `Nullable` and `-If` combinators and the state-merge path, and fails on a build with the trait reverted. Every other `is_signed_v` user was checked to be unreachable for these two types, so the only behaviour change is the intended one. `Time64` has the same trait gap, but on the *aggregate* path it is unreachable: it is absent from `FOR_SINGLE_VALUE_NUMERIC_TYPES`, so its `min`/`max` uses the non-compilable generic state and is already correct. The specialisation covers it because it is genuinely signed, and it removes the trap where adding `Time64` to that list would reintroduce this bug. Residual, out of scope: compiled scalar expressions use a separate predicate, `typeIsSigned` in `src/DataTypes/Native.cpp`, which is missing `Time`, so `if(cond, Time, Time64)` returns a zero-extended `Time`. Pre-existing, identical on master, fixed in a separate PR. cc @Manerone
