the select column includes the scan-and-sum overhead): | Column | ZSTD(3) | Gorilla | ALP | PCO | **Wallaby** | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | 0.43 / 0.12 | **0.24** / 0.15 | 0.35 / **0.06** | 0.95 / 0.10 | 2.00 / 0.19 | | mgbench `cpu_user` | 0.39 / 0.10 | **0.22** / 0.14 | 0.33 / **0.05** | 0.79 / 0.10 | 1.66 / 0.16 | | mgbench `mem_free` | 0.37 / 0.13 | **0.24** / 0.15 | 0.26 / **0.05** | 1.05 / 0.10 | 1.46 / 0.16 | | sensors `temperature` | 0.80 / 0.18 | 0.32 / 0.21 | **0.30** / **0.06** | 1.72 / 0.16 | 1.71 / **0.06** | | sensors `humidity` | 0.76 / 0.18 | 0.34 / 0.21 | **0.30** / **0.05** | 1.51 / 0.12 | 1.91 / 0.06 | | sensors `pressure` | 0.42 / 0.15 | 0.33 / 0.21 | **0.31** / **0.06** | 1.65 / 0.11 | 2.49 / 0.07 | | weather `tempMax` | 0.76 / 0.17 | **0.54** / 0.27 | 0.57 / **0.10** | 1.31 / 0.20 | 1.00 / **0.10** | | weather `precipitation` | 1.16 / 0.33 | **0.70** / 0.45 | 1.14 / **0.13** | 3.02 / 0.53 | 2.98 / 0.40 | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 3.31 / 1.09 | **1.02** / 0.57 | 2.59 / **0.16** | 6.59 / 0.47 | 3.19 / 0.18 | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | 0.94 / 0.28 | **0.60** / 0.34 | 0.91 / **0.12** | 2.32 / 0.34 | 1.70 / 0.31 | | hits `UserID` (F64) | 1.57 / 0.42 | **0.85** / 0.45 | 2.16 / **0.24** | 3.42 / 0.44 | 3.33 / 0.50 | **Encoder cost.** Compared with the previous revision of this table, compression is 1.2–2.8x slower while decompression is unchanged or slightly faster (`smooth gauge` decodes 44 % faster now that a decimal mode wins it instead of XOR). Benchmarking the intermediate revision that contains only the provable-bound chooser rework attributes the cost: on the mgbench and sensors `temperature` columns that rework alone accounts for 60–80 % of the slowdown (`load_one` 0.81 → 1.74 s of the final 2.00 s), while on sensors `pressure` and hits `EventTime` the wider candidate space that the new mechanisms open dominates (1.43 → 2.49 s and 2.15 → 3.19 s). The trade was made knowingly: the size wins above come from the same revisions, and the encoder keeps a running lane-width floor that abandons hopeless scans mid-vector and a double-buffered winner so no scale is quantized twice. **Comparison with PCodec.** `PCO` is the strongest competitor overall. On ratio it is the smallest floating-point codec on 9 of the 11 columns, and the standalone `pco` CLI compressing each column as one chunk does better still (e.g. mgbench `load_one` 36.7 MB, weather `precipitation` 32.2 MB): per-64-KiB-block operation costs pcodec 20-45 % of its ratio, since every block re-learns its tANS tables and delta state. On compression speed the two are now roughly at parity — `Wallaby` up to 2x faster on the hits columns and weather `tempMax`, `PCO` up to 2x faster on the mgbench and sensor columns. On decompression `PCO` is 1.5–2.7x slower than `Wallaby` on the columns where a `Wallaby` decimal mode wins (sensors, weather `tempMax`, hits `EventTime`) and *faster* on the XOR-mode columns (mgbench, hits `UserID`) — the serial XOR bitstream is the slowest of `Wallaby`'s decode paths, while pcodec's decode cost is uniform. Against `ALP`, `Wallaby` is smaller on all 11 columns — dramatically so where `ALP`'s Frame-of-Reference degenerates (hits `UserID` 155 MB vs 684 MB, hits `ResolutionWidth` 47 MB vs 142 MB, weather `precipitation` 72 MB vs 132 MB). A correction to earlier revisions of this description: in-engine `PCO` was previously reported as 10-70x slower. That measurement came from a local build affected by a build-system bug that compiles all vendored Rust code with `opt-level = 0` unless `-DSANITIZE=` is passed explicitly (a `contrib/corrosion-cmake` condition mistakes `SANITIZE=OFF` for an enabled sanitizer; CI is unaffected because it always passes the flag). The numbers above are from a corrected build; a separate fix for the build system is being prepared. **Where `Wallaby` is not the winner.** On columns dominated by entropy redundancy rather than numeric structure — the three mgbench columns, weather `precipitation`, hits `ResolutionWidth`/`UserID` — plain `ZSTD` and/or `PCO` produce smaller data. Chaining helps exactly there, because the XOR/EQUAL residues are more entropy-codable than raw floats: | Column | `ZSTD(3)` | `ALP, ZSTD` | `Wallaby, ZSTD` | |---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | **44.5 MB** | 56.0 MB | 49.0 MB | | mgbench `cpu_user` | **32.0 MB** | 46.1 MB | 35.6 MB | | mgbench `mem_free` | 48.4 MB | 54.4 MB | **42.4 MB** | | sensors `temperature` | 74.4 MB | 58.2 MB | **54.2 MB** | | sensors `humidity` | 80.2 MB | 55.1 MB | **55.0 MB** | | sensors `pressure` | 99.1 MB | 97.8 MB | **90.1 MB** | | weather `tempMax` | 29.8 MB | 29.2 MB | **27.6 MB** | | weather `precipitation` | 56.4 MB | **54.6 MB** | 65.7 MB | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 235.6 MB | **212.8 MB** | 213.0 MB | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | **37.9 MB** | 57.8 MB | 43.2 MB | | hits `UserID` (F64) | **149.7 MB** | 192.5 MB | 154.5 MB | `CODEC(Wallaby, ZSTD)` is the best of the three on 5 of the 11 columns — on the sensor columns and weather `tempMax` now by a clear margin where the previous revision tied `ALP, ZSTD` — and within 0.1 % on `EventTime`. The interesting exception is `precipitation`, where `ALP, ZSTD` wins because `ALP`'s plain Frame-of-Reference lanes on zero-dominated data are almost pure zero bytes, which `ZSTD` collapses better than `Wallaby`'s already-compact XOR runs. Side observation from benchmarking (independent of this PR): for `Nullable` columns the null-map substream appears to be stored uncompressed (+1 byte per row for every codec, including `LZ4`/`ZSTD`) — visible as a constant +22 MB / +31.2 MB across all codecs on the mgbench / sensors columns. Worth a separate look. Correctness: bit-exact round trip is verified by the encoder for every value with a per-value raw-exception fallback (`NaN` payloads, infinities, denormals, signed zeros, arbitrary bit patterns are all preserved; verified on random bit patterns and on all real datasets by multiset checksums in tests; the sensors dataset contributes 9298 genuine `NaN` values). The decoder validates all lengths and bounds, so corrupt input causes an exception, not undefined behavior; a decompression fuzzer target is included. An adversarial review of the current revision additionally round-tripped ~15M hostile values (per-block scale flips, `NaN` payloads, subnormals, domain edges) bit-exactly on both float widths. Note on the `NativeFormat` spec: the spec enumerates the column codec method bytes accepted on the `decompress=1` input path, so this PR adds the `0xa0` (`Wallaby`) entry with an experimental-status note, matching the existing `SZ3`/`Quantized`/`ZXC` entries. #### CI Settings (Only check the boxes if you know what you are doing): - [ ] Allow: All Required Checks - [ ] Allow: Stateless tests - [ ] Allow: Stateful tests - [ ] Allow: Integration Tests - [ ] Allow: Performance tests - [ ] Allow: All Builds - [ ] Allow: batch 1, 2 for multi-batch jobs - [ ] Allow: batch 3, 4, 5, 6 for multi-batch jobs --- - [ ] Exclude: Style check - [ ] Exclude: Fast test - [ ] Exclude: All with ASAN - [ ] Exclude: All with TSAN, MSAN, UBSAN, Coverage - [ ] Exclude: All with aarch64, release, debug --- - [ ] Do not test - [ ] Woolen Wolfdog - [ ] Upload binaries for special builds - [ ] Disable merge-commit - [ ] Disable CI cache --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113575&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113575](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113575+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)]

signal.title: Fix JIT-compiled min and max on DateTime64 comparing timestamps as unsigned
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113942 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/101203 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `min` and `max` on `DateTime64` columns returning wrong results once the aggregate is JIT compiled and the data contains timestamps before 1970. `is_signed` was not specialised for `DateTime64` and `Time64`, which derive from `Decimal64`, so the generated code compared tick counts as unsigned integers and a pre-1970 timestamp won `max` and lost `min`. ### Description Closes: #113942 `min(dt)`/`max(dt)` over a `DateTime64` column silently return the wrong row once the aggregate is JIT compiled (after `min_count_to_compile_aggregate_expression`, default 3) and the group mixes pre-1970 and post-1970 values. Both columns are wrong: the negative tick count reads as a huge unsigned value, so it wins `max` and loses `min`. Root cause: `is_signed` is explicitly specialised for `Decimal32/64/128/256` in `base/base/Decimal_fwd.h`, but `DateTime64` and `Time64` are *derived classes* of `Decimal64`, not aliases, and a base's explicit specialisation does not apply to a derived class. So `is_signed_v<DateTime64>` fell back to `std::is_signed_v` of a class type, i.e. `false`, and `SingleValueDataFixed<T>::compileMinMax`/`compileMinMaxMerge` emitted `icmp ult`/`ugt`. This completes #101203, which introduced the `is_signed_v` use and fixed only the `Decimal*` half. The fix constrains the specialisation on the existing `DB::is_decimal` concept instead of enumerating types, so it follows the single place that defines which types are decimals and a future decimal type cannot silently regress. One source line changes. Validation: a new stateless test covers scales 0/3/9, the `Nullable` and `-If` combinators and the state-merge path, and fails on a build with the trait reverted. Every other `is_signed_v` user was checked to be unreachable for these two types, so the only behaviour change is the intended one. `Time64` has the same trait gap, but on the *aggregate* path it is unreachable: it is absent from `FOR_SINGLE_VALUE_NUMERIC_TYPES`, so its `min`/`max` uses the non-compilable generic state and is already correct. The specialisation covers it because it is genuinely signed, and it removes the trap where adding `Time64` to that list would reintroduce this bug. Residual, out of scope: compiled scalar expressions use a separate predicate, `typeIsSigned` in `src/DataTypes/Native.cpp`, which is missing `Time`, so `if(cond, Time, Time64)` returns a zero-extended `Time`. Pre-existing, identical on master, fixed in a separate PR. cc @Manerone

signal.title: Fix data race and use-after-free on DataLakeConfiguration::current_metadata
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113265 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a data race and a use-after-free on the metadata of a DeltaLake or Iceberg table. Two concurrent queries that read `total_rows` or `total_bytes` from `system.tables` for the same table could have one query replace the table's metadata while the other was still reading it, which could crash the server. Closes #113265. ### Description Two concurrent `SELECT ... FROM system.tables` scans over the same DeltaLake or Iceberg table race on `DataLakeConfiguration::current_metadata`. The field was a plain `std::unique_ptr` with no synchronization, while the configuration is shared: `StorageObjectStorage::totalRows` and `totalBytes` both call the mutating `configuration->update()` and then read the metadata back. TSAN reported the pointer race, but the consequence is worse. The read path was `assertInitialized()` followed by a separate `current_metadata->totalRows(...)` statement, while `update()` destroys the old metadata, so a reader can pass the null check and then call through the freed pointer. A local TSAN repro shows both the race and a heap-use-after-free freed by `~DeltaLakeMetadataDeltaKernel` on that line, and it kills the server. `current_metadata` becomes a `std::shared_ptr` guarded by a mutex, and every reader takes a copy of the pointer under the lock and calls through that copy. Holding a strong reference for the whole call is what closes the use-after-free: guarding only the null check would narrow the window without removing it. Writers build the new metadata outside the lock and publish under it, and the displaced object is destroyed after the lock is released, because `~IcebergMetadata` waits for its background prefetch task. Seven of the eight touched source files are there only because `getExternalMetadata` had to stop returning a raw pointer, so its six consumers keep the metadata alive while they use it. `StorageSystemIcebergFiles` needs that: it parks the pointer across `generate()` calls. The metadata subclasses are unchanged, and all 12 template instantiations are covered because the fix is in the template body. `TSA_GUARDED_BY` under `-Weverything -Werror` makes any remaining unguarded access a build error. Validation: a TSAN repro of 4 concurrent unrestricted `system.tables` scans reports the race 29 times before the fix and 0 after, at identical query counts (48 scans each), and the server survives only with the fix.

signal.title: Fix wrong results of the partial aggregation strategy in distributed query plans
signal.text: The partial+merge aggregation strategy of `make_distributed_plan` rewrites a final aggregation into a partial `AggregatingStep` plus a memory-efficient `MergingAggregatedStep`. The memory-efficient merge consumes each input as a stream of two-level buckets in ascending order, but the rewrite kept `should_produce_results_in_order_of_bucket_number = false` on the partial step, so its multi-stream output was combined into the single exchange stream in arbitrary order. When a bucket arrived after the merge had already emitted it, the merge emitted it a second time: duplicated `GROUP BY` keys with split aggregate states (for ClickBench Q08, a wrong `COUNT(DISTINCT UserID)`). The fix, one commit each: - Make the row count estimation look through `LogicalExchangeStep`. The `#if CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD` guard around it was needed when the exchange steps existed only in the private repo; since they are in the public repo, the guard only made every aggregation over a distributed read fall back to the Shuffle strategy in non-cloud builds (and masked this bug there). - Validate the bucket delivery order in `GroupingAggregatedTransform`: an unannounced late bucket now fails with a `LOGICAL_ERROR` exception instead of silently duplicating groups. - Wait for delayed buckets in `GroupingAggregatedTransform` when the consumer needs the output in bucket order, and release the announcements of finished inputs. Covered by a gtest. - Build the partial step with `should_produce_results_in_order_of_bucket_number = true` when the merge is memory-efficient (`AggregatingStep::cloneAsPartial`). The partial aggregation then produces a single bucket-ordered stream per worker, the same contract the classic distributed path establishes on shards. Covered by a stateless test that reproduces the duplicated keys on the code without the fix (about 80% of single runs, 8 repetitions, 50k rows, ~0.5s). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix duplicated `GROUP BY` keys in the partial aggregation strategy of `make_distributed_plan`, and allow this strategy for aggregations over a distributed read. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114523&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114523](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114523+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Do not pop hints on a line displayed programmatically
signal.text: When a query is displayed at once rather than typed — recalled from the history with Up/Down/Ctrl-P/Ctrl-N, found by the incremental (Ctrl-T) or fuzzy (Ctrl-R) history search, pasted, brought back from the external editor, or preloaded — the as-you-type hints no longer appear at its end. With hints visible, the next Up/Down press would navigate the hints instead of the history, so navigating the history quickly was impossible. The hints are shown again as soon as the line is edited. The suppression is armed before the navigation action because replxx repaints (and regenerates the hints) inside `history_move` itself, and the displayed text is additionally pinned afterwards because replxx may throttle that repaint and replay it after the key handler returns (its "rapid refresh" of e.g. a held-down Up key). Verified with a new pty regression test (`04909_client_hints_history_navigation`, 4 cases), which fails on the previous binary in all three suppression cases; the existing `04402_clickhouse_client_autocomplete_inline_hints` (11 cases) and the hint-related expect tests still pass. signal.title: Fix PostgreSQL-protocol authentication for users that also have an ssh_key
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/76839 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix authentication over the PostgreSQL wire protocol for users with several authentication methods: a user that also had an `ssh_key` method (or any other method that stores no password) was rejected with `Invalid user or password` even when the correct password for its `scram_sha256_password` method was supplied, and a wrong SCRAM salt was sent to the client when the SCRAM method was not the last one (e.g. for a user with `scram_sha256_password` followed by `sha256_password`). A user with multiple authentication methods, one of which is `ssh_key`, could not authenticate over the PostgreSQL protocol at all (in either order of the methods), while the same user authenticated fine over the native, MySQL, and HTTP protocols. Reproduced on 26.7.3.19 and current master. Anyone who adds a public SSH key to their user (e.g. for the SSH endpoint) silently loses PostgreSQL access with a misleading "wrong password" error. Two defects, both fixed (each order of methods hits at least one of them): 1. `checkScramSHA256Authentication` did not check the type of the authentication method it verifies the client proof against, and `IAccessStorage::authenticateImpl` calls it for every method of the user. For methods that store no password hash (e.g. `ssh_key`), the empty hash was passed to `hmacSHA256` as the HMAC key; `EVP_MAC_init` fails for a null key, so the check threw `OPENSSL_ERROR` (`Authentication failed: Code: 454. DB::Exception: EVP_MAC_init failed`) instead of returning false, aborting the whole authentication instead of trying the next method of the user. Now it returns false for non-SCRAM methods, the same way `checkMySQLAuthentication` handles non-MySQL-compatible methods. 2. `ScrambleSHA256Auth::authenticate` in the PostgreSQL handler sent the salt of the *last* authentication method of the user instead of the salt of the SCRAM method, so the client derived a salted password that could never match the stored verifier: an empty salt when `ssh_key` was last, or an unrelated random salt when e.g. `sha256_password` was. Now it sends the salt of the first `scram_sha256_password` method. Verified before/after with `psql` against a local server; added an integration test covering both method orders, the `scram_sha256_password` + `sha256_password` combination, and wrong-password rejection. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115084&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115084](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115084+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Report RabbitMQ container recreation attempts made by the startup retry
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114415 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114434 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description #114415 made the RabbitMQ readiness waiter recreate a container that fails to start and try again, turning a 21-case module abort into a passing run. When the second attempt succeeds, every channel that could record the first failure closes at once: artifact collection is gated on a failing suite (`if failed_suits:`), the report log strips setup logs from passed tests (`--report-log-exclude-logs-on-passed-tests`), and `job.log` never carried harness logging. The recovered failure survives only as an anomalous duration on the module's first test: +123.5 s against a p99 of 13.4 s over 7774 runs of that test and lane. So a retry-absorbed run discards exactly the diagnostics #114415 added to show where a hang is stuck. Now: - the waiter copies the failed attempt's `rabbit.log` out of the instance directory before recreating the container (that directory is removed on teardown) and emits a stable `RABBITMQ_RECREATE` token. The copy is named per process, cluster, waiter call and attempt, because S3 upload keys use the basename alone; - at job end the script counts those tokens across the per-worker pytest logs, puts the count in `Result.info` and attaches the preserved logs, whatever the outcome. The failure-gated paths are left alone. A recreation is not itself a verdict, so only `info` and `files` are touched: status and labels stay as the test results set them, and the count is appended after the job's own `Failures: N/M` summary rather than replacing it. Forcing a retry on a healthy host passes, and the count reaches `result_*.json` with the 107,336 B broker log attached. The same run with the reporting removed attaches nothing; a run that never retried writes no count; a forced-red run keeps its `Failures: 1/1`. `test_system_stop.py` is 21 passed. Both sides are unit-tested, each arm checked against a mutation of the code it pins. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114947&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114947](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114947+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Stop SeaweedFS deleting live object folders in stateless CI
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113828 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113828 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Since 2026-08-12, `s3 storage` stateless jobs intermittently failed an ordinary INSERT with `Code: 499 ... Immediately after upload: Object ... suddenly disappeared (S3_ERROR)`. Root cause is upstream and now fixed. SeaweedFS's filer listed a folder's children on a non-recursive delete, returned early if it found any, then swept the children unconditionally, so an object committed between the listing and the sweep lost its entry after S3 had already answered 200. From a failing master run: ``` 16:18:17.675651 EmptyFolderCleaner: deleting empty folder /buckets/test/test/jys 16:18:17.676290 PUT of the object SUCCEEDS, 282 bytes 16:18:17.678805 verifying HEAD -> 404 16:18:17.681060 WriteBufferFromS3: Nothing to abort (so ClickHouse did not remove it) ``` I reported it as seaweedfs/seaweedfs#10779; it is fixed by seaweedfs/seaweedfs#10782 (sweep only on the recursive path) and seaweedfs/seaweedfs#10783 (restore a folder that received an entry while it was deleted). Both are ancestors of the 4.42 tag, so this takes 4.42 and drops the cleanup-delay workaround the PR originally carried. Both pin sites move together, as the Dockerfile comment requires. Validated by running the shipped setup script's own sequence against 4.42 and 4.41, identical except the binary: gateway up, bucket create, filer write probe, `filer.copy`, then PUT, immediate HEAD, GET, ListObjectsV2 and DELETE over S3 all pass on both, so the bump is not a regression on the CI path (134 upstream commits, several in `s3api`). Example: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=e9f46105394805fb1a160303c4f40b52ad053522&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20parallel%2C%202%2F3%29

signal.title: Fix Arrow Flight Basic authentication for clients sending unpadded Base64
signal.text: The Arrow Flight server rejected clients that send the `authorization: Basic <credentials>` header with the Base64-encoded credentials not padded with `=`. The Go Flight client does exactly that — for example, the ADBC Flight SQL driver with the plain `username`/`password` options performs the `AuthenticateBasicToken` handshake this way, so connecting to ClickHouse failed with a meaningless error: ``` UNKNOWN: [FlightSQL] Unexpected error in RPC handling (Unknown; AuthenticateBasicToken). Vendor code: 2 ``` The cause: `Poco::Base64Decoder` requires padding by default and throws `Poco::DataFormatException`, which escaped `AuthMiddlewareFactory::StartCall` (it only caught `DB::Exception`) into gRPC, which converted it to the generic `UNKNOWN` status above. The fix: - Decode the credentials with the `BASE64_NO_PADDING` option, which accepts both padded and unpadded input, so Go-based Flight clients (including ADBC) can authenticate. - Convert a failed Base64 decode into a proper `AUTHENTICATION_FAILED` exception, reported to the client as an `Unauthenticated` Flight error with a clear message. - Catch the remaining exception types in `StartCall` so no exception can escape into gRPC and produce the meaningless `Unexpected error in RPC handling` status. Verified end-to-end with `adbc_driver_flightsql` 1.12.0: connecting with plain `username`/`password` and running a query now works, while padded Basic credentials, Bearer tokens, and wrong-password errors behave as before. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Arrow Flight server: accept `Basic` authentication credentials encoded in Base64 without padding, as sent by Go-based Flight clients such as the ADBC Flight SQL driver, and return a proper authentication error instead of a generic `Unexpected error in RPC handling` when the `authorization` header is malformed. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115085&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115085](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115085+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Support `Merge` tables with plan-based parallel replicas
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/67770 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972 Lets a `Merge` table be read with parallel replicas, implemented on top of the plan-based parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_plan_based`). `ReadFromMerge` is opaque to the parallel-replicas plan transformation: it unites the pipelines of its per-table subplans instead of their plans, so the underlying `MergeTree` reads do not exist yet while the plan is transformed. An eligible `ReadFromMerge` is therefore expanded into a plan-level `UnionStep` over those child reads, right before the reads to distribute are collected. A `Merge` then has exactly the shape the transformation already distributes - a union of `MergeTree` reads - so the reads are coordinated across the replicas, and the steps above the `Merge` (aggregation, joins) are distributed as well, without any `Merge`-specific code in the coordinator, in the serialization or in the local plan. The expansion is off by default, gated by the new setting `parallel_replicas_allow_merge_tables`, and takes effect only together with `parallel_replicas_plan_based`. A `Merge` is read by a single replica when one of its children is not a plain `MergeTree` read, when the read is `FINAL`, or when no table matches its regexp. This is an alternative to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972, which implements the same feature on the legacy (query-tree-based) path. There, the query text is reshipped and every replica re-analyzes it, which needs a fail-close handshake (`parallel_replicas_designated_table`, `_freshness_checked_tables`, `_merge_child_tables`) to guard against the set of underlying tables differing across replicas or changing between planning and reading. The plan-based path ships a serialized plan fragment with the tables already resolved, so none of that is needed. Tests: three new stateless tests - the core feature and its negative cases (`04907`), the query shapes a `Merge` can be read with, including the `merge` table function, a filter on the `_table` virtual column and reading in order with a limit (`04908`), and `Merge` tables inside JOINs on either side of the join (`04909`). Each of them checks the results against non-parallel execution and asserts through the plan how the query was distributed. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A `Merge` table can now be read with parallel replicas: the reads from the underlying `MergeTree` tables are coordinated across the replicas, and the aggregations and joins above them are distributed too. Enabled by the new setting `parallel_replicas_allow_merge_tables`, which takes effect together with `parallel_replicas_plan_based`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115001&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115001](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115001+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup` for single-column complex keys wrapped in `tuple`
signal.text: Since 25.12, the analyzer pass `InverseDictionaryLookupPass` (setting `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup`, enabled by default) rewrites `dictGet(dict, attr, key_expr) <op> const` into a comparison of the key expression against dictionary keys: either constants folded from `dictGetKeys` (`key_expr = const`, `key_expr IN [consts]`, or `0`), or the subquery form `key_expr IN (SELECT <key columns> FROM dictionary(dict) WHERE attr <op> const)`. The key expression is reused verbatim as the left-hand side, while all rewrite shapes produce bare key values on the right-hand side. A complex-key dictionary with a single key column accepts (and much existing SQL uses) the `tuple()`-wrapped call form `dictGet(..., tuple(k))` — for it, the rewrite pits a one-element `Tuple` against a scalar, and a query that works on every release before 25.12 fails with `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT`. Multi-column keys are unaffected: `(k1, k2) IN (SELECT k1, k2 ...)` is the standard SQL form and the types line up. ## How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE dict_source (k UUID, k2 String, attr String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; INSERT INTO dict_source VALUES ('11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111', 'a', 'paywall'), ('22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222', 'b', 'onboarding'); CREATE DICTIONARY single_key_dict (k UUID, attr String DEFAULT '') PRIMARY KEY k SOURCE(CLICKHOUSE(TABLE 'dict_source')) LIFETIME(0) LAYOUT(COMPLEX_KEY_HASHED()); CREATE TABLE data (k UUID, k2 String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; INSERT INTO data VALUES ('11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111', 'a'), ('33333333-3333-3333-3333-333333333333', 'c'); -- Must return 1, but fails since 25.12: SELECT count() FROM data WHERE dictGet('single_key_dict', 'attr', tuple(k)) = 'paywall'; ``` On master the query fails in the constant-fold path: ``` Code: 43. DB::Exception: Illegal types of arguments (`Tuple(UUID)`, `UUID`) of function `equals`. (ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT) ``` On 26.3 (before the `dictGetKeys` constant fold existed) the same query fails in the subquery path with `Illegal type Tuple(UUID) of argument of function toUUID`. The workaround on affected releases is `SETTINGS optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup = 0`, which returns the correct result. The bare-key form `dictGet(..., k)` and multi-column keys work on all versions. ## The fix Normalize the key expression once, before both rewrite paths, when the dictionary key is composite with exactly one key column and the key expression resolves to a one-element tuple (including a `Nullable` one, e.g. produced by `if(cond, tuple(k), NULL)`): - a syntactic `tuple(k)` call is replaced by its argument; - any other tuple-typed expression (e.g. a column of type `Tuple(UUID)`) is wrapped in `tupleElement(expr, 1)`, which propagates `NULL` with the same semantics `dictGet` has for `NULL` keys. The rewrite still fires for these queries — the new test asserts the rewritten plans via `EXPLAIN SYNTAX run_query_tree_passes=1` for all three constant-fold shapes and both subquery shapes. Simple-key dictionaries are deliberately not unwrapped: `dictGet(simple_dict, attr, tuple(id))` is rejected (`Illegal type Tuple(UInt64) of argument of function toUInt64`) even with the optimization disabled, so normalizing there would make otherwise-invalid queries succeed only while the optimization is on. A `Tuple`-typed dictionary key column cannot conflict with the unwrapping because dictionaries reject `Tuple` attribute types (`Unknown type Tuple(UUID) for dictionary attribute`). ## Implicit key type conversion Review pointed out a second gap in the same rewrite: `dictGet` implicitly converts the key expression to the key column type (`IDictionary::convertKeyColumns`, which uses `castColumnAccurate` — see also `02176_dict_get_has_implicit_key_cast`), so e.g. a `String` key expression is a valid lookup key for a `UUID` key column. The rewritten comparison converts via a common supertype instead, so any single-column key whose type has no common supertype with the key column type failed with `NO_COMMON_TYPE` — with the tuple wrapper, bare on a complex-key dictionary, and on simple-key dictionaries alike (the latter two forms were broken this way before this PR as well). The conversion contract includes the throwing behavior: `castColumnAccurate` throws on values the key column type cannot represent (with a `UInt8` key column, `dictGet(..., toInt16(x))` throws on `x = -1` or `x = 300`), while a comparison evaluated in a common supertype would silently return false for them. So the key expression is left untouched only when the key column type is itself the least supertype of the two types — a provably total widening, e.g. a narrow integer column against a wide key type, which keeps the expression usable for index analysis and keeps `04276_function_dict_get_keys_edge_cases` byte-identical (this is the same criterion `canReplaceWithDictGetKeys` already uses for the attribute side). Any other single-column mismatch is wrapped in `accurateCast` to the key column type, which matches `castColumnAccurate` semantics exactly, including throwing the same `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` on lossy values. The criterion is total for integer-to-float pairs as well: `getLeastSupertype` refuses e.g. `Int64` with `Float64` (not enough mantissa bits), so an integer expression stays on the no-cast path only when the float key type represents every its value exactly. A `Nullable` expression that needs such a conversion makes `dictGet` itself throw regardless of the optimization (at `NULL` rows the nested column holds default values, and e.g. an empty string does not parse as `UUID`), so the rewrite is skipped there and the query keeps its unoptimized behavior. One pre-existing behavior is kept and pinned by the test: when the attribute value matches no keys, the predicate constant-folds to `0` without evaluating the key expression, so a conversion error that the unoptimized `dictGet` would throw for unconvertible rows disappears together with the lookup — the same already happens for bare mistyped key expressions on master, like for any constant fold that eliminates evaluation. Review also caught a related pre-existing defect in the single-match constant fold, fixed here since the tuple normalization newly routes the wrapped spelling into it (it used to throw instead): when the attribute value belongs to the NULL-keyed row of a dictionary with a `Nullable` key column, the fold produced `key_expr = NULL`, which is NULL for every row, while `dictGet` misses the NULL row for non-NULL keys and the predicate must be false there (observable under `NOT`, `isNull`, or in a projection; a bare `Nullable` key expression like `toNullable(id)` hits the same fold on master). A single NULL key now keeps the `IN [NULL]` form, which is false for non-NULL keys and NULL for NULL keys — matching `dictGet`, which returns NULL for a NULL key expression and does not match the NULL-keyed row through it. Known pre-existing gap, intentionally out of scope: multi-column composite keys with a mistyped component (e.g. `dictGet(dict, attr, tuple(toString(id), id_key))` over a `(UInt64, String)` key) hit the same `NO_COMMON_TYPE` failure. Fixing that requires rebuilding the tuple with per-element casts and is better done as a follow-up than inside this backport-targeted fix. The new test `04891_optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup_single_key_tuple` covers the failing forms (syntactic tuple, tuple-typed column, `Nullable` tuple, implicitly-converted `String` keys — wrapped, bare, and simple-key, and lossy `Int16`-over-`UInt8` keys both in-range and throwing out-of-range), the bare-key, numeric-widening and two-column-key controls, a constant on either side of the comparison, the equal-error behavior for `Nullable` keys that need conversion, the zero-match constant-fold behavior, and result equality with the optimization on and off. All existing `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup` tests pass unchanged. ## Backport This is a regression in an official stable release (25.12) affecting all later releases, including 26.3 LTS. Please consider labeling for backport to 26.3 (`v26.3-must-backport`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` and `NO_COMMON_TYPE` errors when `optimize_inverse_dictionary_lookup` rewrites `dictGet` comparisons: for complex-key dictionaries with a single key column called with a `tuple()`-wrapped (possibly `Nullable`) key expression, and for single-column keys whose expression relies on `dictGet`'s implicit key type conversion (e.g. a `String` expression for a `UUID` key). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114865&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114865](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114865+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix the fuzzer dictionary coverage check aborting under a UTF-8 locale
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111025 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: #111025 `NightlyFuzzers` / `libFuzzer tests` has died inside `generate_dictionary` on every scheduled run since 2026-07-31, the first night this check reached master (6 as of 2026-08-05, each an `ERROR` with no leaf results). It aborts before any fuzzer runs, so nightly fuzzing produced no coverage while both builds stayed green: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=09da4d1ba6dbeb378fce8001f0da90ae344c5736&name_0=NightlyFuzzers&name_1=libFuzzer%20tests The check in `tests/fuzz/update_dict.sh` pinned `LC_ALL=C` on both `sort` children but not on `comm`. The container's ambient locale is `en_US.UTF-8` (`ci/docker/test-base/Dockerfile:160`), and the quoted multi-word keywords order differently under the two collations (`"ADD INDEX"` before `"ADD"` under C, after it under `en_US.utf8`), so `comm` diagnosed the C-sorted input as unsorted and exited 1. Under `set -euo pipefail` that aborted the command substitution before the verdict was evaluated: hence the `comm: ... not in sorted order` warnings and never the script's own token list. The dictionary itself was generated correctly. Review surfaced a second defect in the same check: `set -e` does not observe the exit status of a command inside a process substitution, so a failing `sort` went unnoticed. An unreadable `all.dict` sorted to nothing, `comm` reported an empty diff and the check passed, disarming the gate; an unreadable `source.dict` made every token look missing. So the check now pins `LC_ALL=C` on `comm`, materializes both sorted dictionaries into files, and captures `comm`'s status explicitly. `generate_source_dict.sh:80` already used `LC_ALL=C comm`: a missed call site. Validated against the real dictionaries under ambient `LC_ALL=en_US.utf8`: the check passes, still names a deleted token, and `all.dict` stays byte-identical, so the gate is restored rather than silenced. `libFuzzer tests` runs only in `NightlyFuzzers`, so this PR's own CI cannot exercise the script. `ci/tests/test_fuzzer_dict_coverage_check_locale.py` guards it directly under a UTF-8 collating locale, with arms for the abort and both sort failures. `CI Tests` digests the script, so editing it reruns the guard.

signal.title: Fix quadratic gzip/zlib streaming decompression of single-block streams
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114045 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108074 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114054 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/libdeflate/pull/6 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `O(n^2)` decompression of gzip/zlib/deflate streams whose single DEFLATE block spans the whole stream, the shape zlib-ng produces at compression level 1 (the default of the official .NET SDK): a 24 MiB gzip HTTP body that took 11 s to ingest in 26.7 now takes 0.12 s, identical to a multi-block body, with memory bounded by the buffer size instead of the block size. ### Details The root cause: the streaming decompressor added to `contrib/libdeflate` kept its resume checkpoint only at DEFLATE block boundaries. On input exhaustion or output-buffer overflow it rolled back to the start of the current block, so for a stream that is one giant block, every socket refill re-decoded the block from its beginning — quadratic time — and the whole block's output had to be buffered before any byte was exposed — unbounded memory. The work happens in `copyDataImpl` while assembling the query, before the query starts, so it was invisible in `system.processes` and `query_duration_ms`. The fix (https://github.com/ClickHouse/libdeflate/pull/6, vendored by this PR in `contrib/libdeflate`) re-takes the checkpoint at every symbol boundary in the generic decode loop, plus two new decompressor fields (`in_block`, `block_is_final`) that let a resumed call jump straight back into symbol decoding — the litlen/offset decode tables already persist in the decompressor between calls. The fastloop is untouched: suspensions can only trigger from the generic loop, which always runs between the fastloop and input exhaustion. A suspension now loses at most one partially decoded symbol, so decompression is linear-time with bounded memory regardless of block structure. `LibdeflateInflatingReadBuffer` needed no logic changes, only comment updates: its "grow the output buffer" path is now reachable only when a single match (≤ 258 bytes) or stored block (≤ 64 KiB) exceeds the free output region. Verification: - Standalone harness: 5000+ randomized round-trips (zlib streams at all levels with random flush points; crafted static- and dynamic-Huffman single-block streams with matches reaching the full 32 KiB window; input chunking down to 1 byte; random output regions), zlib inflate as decode oracle, one-shot decoder as cross-check, and a progress assertion on every suspension. - End-to-end with the issue's reproducer shape (24 MiB single-block gzip body, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, local release build): **11.25 s before → 0.12 s after**, now identical to a multi-block body of the same content (0.12 s). Verified the vendored zlib-ng really emits this shape: at level 1 it produces 1 block for a 4 MiB input (stock zlib: 80 blocks). - No throughput regression on normal multi-block streams: 685 → 697 MB/s on a 256 MB zlib-level-6 stream. New tests: - `LibdeflateSingleBlock.StreamingConsumesInputWithinBlock` pins the linearity contract (a suspension inside a Huffman block leaves at most a few bytes unconsumed). Against the pre-fix library it fails immediately, with 35 MB left unconsumed on a 32 MiB single-block stream. - `LibdeflateInflateTest.RoundTripFromZlibNgLevelOneLarge` decodes a large stream produced by the vendored zlib-ng at level 1 — the real-encoder shape of the issue. - `LibdeflateInflateTest.SingleDeflateBlockSpanningWholeMember` decodes crafted single-block gzip/zlib members through `LibdeflateInflatingReadBuffer`. - `04836_http_gzip_single_deflate_block` ingests a crafted single-block gzip body over HTTP with chunked transfer encoding, end to end. Because the pre-fix decoder is correct, just quadratic, the assertion is on time: the body is one 36 MB block and the request is capped at 15 s. Ingest time for a single-block body of a given size, release build, `master`'s `contrib/libdeflate` vs this branch's: 10 MB - 1.8 s vs 0.05 s; 20 MB - 6.9 s; 40 MB - 27.3 s vs 0.20 s; 48 MB - 39.1 s vs 0.25 s. So the limit sits 2.6x below the pre-fix time and 60x above the fixed one, and the clean quadratic growth means the pre-fix margin does not depend on the machine speed. The payload is 120 lines of 400 KB so that line parsing and the `MergeTree` write do not dominate. Note: `Bugfix validation (unit tests)` reports `ERROR` (inconclusive, non-blocking) here for a structural reason: the fix itself lives in `contrib/libdeflate`, and the job cannot populate its merge-base "before" worktree at the merge-base submodule revision, so it refuses to build a before-binary that would validate the wrong submodule code. The functional test above is what validates the fix. Note: this PR and the revert #114054 are alternatives on master — if the revert merges first, this branch will be updated to re-apply the integration together with the fix; if this merges first, the revert can be closed (the 26.7 backport of the revert can proceed independently). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114059&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114059](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114059+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add the `default_session_user` server setting
signal.text: Adds a way to configure which user is assumed when a client connects without specifying a user name, instead of the hardcoded `default`. - A new server setting, `default_session_user` (default `default`), is applied when the user name is empty: an HTTP request without the `user` parameter and `X-ClickHouse-User` header (including Basic credentials with an empty username and a key without a user), a native protocol `Hello` packet with an empty user name (previously rejected, now accepted), MySQL and PostgreSQL handshakes with an empty user name, a gRPC query without `user_name`, an Arrow Flight call without an `authorization` header (or with Basic credentials with an empty user name), and the web terminal auth message without a user field. Setting the value to an empty string prohibits connections without a user name. HTTP handlers with a fixed user (the `user` key inside `handler` of an `http_handlers` rule, or the `user` key of a `prometheus` protocol) authenticate as their configured user and ignore the setting, including the empty reject mode. - Composable protocol endpoints (the `protocols` section) can override the setting per endpoint with a `default_session_user` key, so different listening ports can serve different anonymous users. The key is looked up from the endpoint's module through `impl` references, and the endpoint is restarted on config reload when the value changes. - Interserver connections never use the default session user: they identify themselves with a special marker instead of a user name and are authenticated by the cluster secret and the initial user. Configuring `default_session_user` on an `interserver` composable protocol is rejected as a configuration error. The `NativeProtocol.md` specification and the composable protocols documentation are updated accordingly. Covered by the new integration test `test_default_session_user` (all protocols including gRPC and Arrow Flight, per-endpoint overrides, the explicit reject mode, fixed-user handlers on an endpoint with the reject mode, and a two-node cluster with a secret verifying that remote queries still run as the initiating user). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `default_session_user` server setting: the user to authenticate as when a client connects without specifying a user name (previously hardcoded to `default`; the native, MySQL, and PostgreSQL protocols now accept an empty user name instead of rejecting it, and Arrow Flight honors the setting instead of its own hardcoded `default`). Composable protocol endpoints in the `protocols` section can override it per endpoint with a `default_session_user` key, so different listening ports can serve different anonymous users. Setting it to an empty string prohibits connections without a user name. Interserver connections never use the default session user. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110179&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110179](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110179+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Apply read in order with ORDER BY for plan-based parallel replicas
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114723 Plan-based parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_plan_based`) splits the plan at the reading step into a `UNION` of a local read and a fragment shipped to the replicas. The split marker was lifted through `Expression`/`Filter`/`Aggregating`/`Union`/`Join`, but not through `SortingStep`, so for a plain `ORDER BY` the sort stayed on the initiator above the union and neither the local half nor the shipped fragment contained a `Sorting` above the read. `ReadFromMergeTree::requestReadingInOrder` was therefore never called on either side and both announced `CoordinationMode::Default`: results were correct, but the read-in-order optimization was lost compared to classic parallel replicas, which uses `ReadPoolParallelReplicasInOrder` for the same query. The split now lifts through `SortingStep` the same way it already does through `AggregatingStep`: a full sort is cloned into the fragment and the initiator keeps a `MergingSorted` sort above the union. Each side then re-derives read-in-order from the same sort description and they agree on `WithOrder` / `ReverseOrder` - `ReverseOrder` was not reachable under plan-based parallel replicas before. Since `SortingStep::serialize` drops the limit, a top-N is restated as an explicit `LimitStep` inside the fragment, as `tryMakeDistributedSorting` already does; it is skipped when an enclosing `LIMIT` has `alwaysReadTillEnd`, so `exact_rows_before_limit` stays exact. This also fixes a pre-existing failure on the same path: `tryOptimizeTopK` injects an internal `__topKFilter` function that is not registered in `FunctionFactory`. It was suppressed for `make_distributed_plan` but not for plan-based parallel replicas, so `SELECT ... ORDER BY <non-primary-key> LIMIT n` failed on the replica with `Unknown function __topKFilter`. A read that carries Top-K is now excluded from the shipped fragment (`mergeTreeReadCanBeShipped`), so such a query stays local and keeps its Top-K filtering instead of being distributed. Suppressing Top-K up front instead was rejected: enabling `parallel_replicas_plan_based` does not by itself mean the plan gets shipped, so that would silently lose Top-K for queries that end up running locally anyway. Verified locally against a three-replica cluster: `ReadType: InOrder` / `InReverseOrder` and `ReadPoolParallelReplicasInOrder` are reached, the coordinator logs `WithOrder` and `ReverseOrder`, and results stay identical to non-parallel execution for `ORDER BY` with `LIMIT`, deep `OFFSET`, filters, `WITH TIES`, `LIMIT BY`, `exact_rows_before_limit` and a full-sorting merge join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Apply the read-in-order optimization to `ORDER BY` queries when `parallel_replicas_plan_based` is enabled: the sort is now shipped to the replicas and merged on the initiator, so each replica reads in the sorting key order. Also fixes `Unknown function __topKFilter` for `ORDER BY` on a non-primary-key column with this setting enabled. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114315&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114315](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114315+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Hash the type-derived parameter in the ALP, FPC and GCD codecs
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113940 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113798 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `ALP`, `FPC` and `GCD` omitting their type-derived parameter from the codec hash. In a Compact part the writer shares one compressed stream per distinct codec hash, so two columns of different value width under the same codec collided and shared one codec object carrying the wrong width. This rejected valid inserts with `CANNOT_COMPRESS` when the widths disagreed, and otherwise compressed one of the columns worse than it should have. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113940 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113798 `MergeTreeDataPartWriterCompact::addStreams` keys compressed-stream reuse on `codec->getHash()` with no key-equality fallback, so a hash collision is an object-identity collision. Three codecs resolve a parameter from the column type, keep it out of the codec description AST, and hash only that AST, so two columns of different width shared one codec object and the loser of the race got the other's width: - `ALP` and `FPC` derive `float_width`. With `Float64` declared first the shared codec carries `float_width = 8`, a `Float32` granule is not a multiple of 8, and `ALP` throws `Code: 270 ... data size 404 is not aligned to 8 (CANNOT_COMPRESS)`. A mixed-width `Tuple(Float64, Float32) CODEC(ALP)` reaches the same throw, since the codec is resolved per substream. `FPC` ceil-divides instead of throwing, so its half is ratio-only: measured +10.0%. - `GCD` derives `gcd_bytes_size`, so the divisor width depended on declaration order and the ratio suffered. Data round-trips either way, because the width is in the GCD block header. Added on review request so the class stays revertable as one change; #113798 fixes the same `updateHash` for its own `is_signed_type` and goes forward independently. The fix adds the missing field to each hash, matching `SZ3`, `DoubleDelta`, `Gorilla`, `T64` and `Delta`, which already hash their type-derived width. Wide parts were never affected: one stream per column. Two consequences worth noting. Codec hashes also gate `can_substitute_codec_arguments`, a whole-codec flag, so `Tuple(Float32, Float64) CODEC(FPC, LZ4)` now shows as `CODEC(FPC, LZ4)` rather than `CODEC(FPC(12), LZ4)`; `Delta` and `Gorilla` already behave this way, same-width tuples still resolve, and a bare `CODEC(FPC)` still means level 12. No format change: each codec records the parameter in its own block header, so existing parts stay readable both ways. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Debug build, base `f9dd35fa7f57bbd8ec97be53c15acd82848a98f1`. ALP/FPC (build id `a0327326e75c88c307e5efda56857c3df38552c7`): | Check | Before | After | |---|---|---| | `INSERT`, default table, f64 then f32, 101 rows | `Code: 270 ... 404 is not aligned to 8` | 101 rows, Compact part | | `Tuple(Float64, Float32) CODEC(ALP)`, default table | `Code: 270 ... 12012 is not aligned to 8` | 1001 rows, values round-trip | | ALP mixed vs two single-column tables | 234896 vs 228332, order dependent | 228332 == 228332 | | FPC mixed vs two single-column tables | 238887 vs 217185 | 217185 == 217185 | GCD (build id `bb612f0c6681bdde02436c553770393ff66f63fe`, pre-fix control `0a3b06892a5a9cafc8bc2c68a19d5fe9dff3f312`): | Check | Before | After | |---|---|---| | `UInt16` + `UInt64` mixed vs two single-column tables | 80815 vs 80830 | 80830 == 80830 | | declaration order invariance (`u16, u64` vs `u64, u16`) | 160544 vs 160540 | identical | | round-trip on the mixed table | 20000/20000 | 20000/20000 | | same tables as Wide parts (control, no stream sharing) | already equal | already equal | `04861_codec_hash_type_derived_params` (renamed, since it no longer covers only float width) fails on the parent commit and passes with the fix; the two new GCD assertions were verified to redden independently, 5/5 runs failing before and 10/10 passing after under randomized settings, and 4-way self-parallel runs pass. A control build patching only `ALP` left the `FPC` numbers at exactly 238887, confirming the `FPC` measurement is not leaking from the `ALP` change. </details>

signal.title: Do not postpone a hardlink-only mutation because the part is large
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112106 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `ALTER TABLE ... DROP INDEX` and `DROP PROJECTION` being postponed forever with `Exceed max source part size` on a part larger than the free space. Such a mutation hardlinks the files it does not touch and unlinks the dropped ones, so it needs space for a little metadata rather than for a copy of the part, and the free-space requirement is now computed accordingly. Previously an index could not be dropped to reclaim space precisely when the space was needed. Closes #112106. ### Description Mutation selection compared the free-space budget against the whole size of the source part, whatever the mutation was going to do to it. That size is what a full rewrite needs, but a `DROP INDEX` on a Wide part in full storage takes the partial route: it hardlinks every file it does not touch and unlinks the dropped ones. So a part bigger than the budget was postponed forever, and dropping an index to free space became impossible exactly when the space was needed: ``` command: (DROP INDEX fts_ngram__event) parts_postpone_reasons: {'all_1_37840_11_36968':'Exceed max source part size'} ``` A mutation is now classified as hardlink-only when it provably takes the partial route and writes none of that route's data-copying outputs, and then gets the smallest reservation the storage grants on the source part's own disk instead of one covering the whole part. Guard and reservation are both corrected, on both engines: they reduce to the same inequality, so exempting only the guard would turn a diagnosable postpone into `NOT_ENOUGH_SPACE` thrown out of selection. The classification is re-validated in the executing task wherever its inputs become final, always before any file is created, so a misclassification returns the part to its previous behaviour with the reason in `system.mutations` and never fills the disk. Outside the class only the statistics handling below changes. **Testing.** Two stateless tests pin the budget to one byte with the existing failpoints, so no disk manipulation is needed, and assert that the reported case and a `DROP PROJECTION` complete while eight negative controls stay postponed and a ninth, whose copy mode is flipped mid-flight, is refused and then completes on retry. An integration test on real size-limited tmpfs disks covers what the failpoints cannot: that the reservation is small and names the right disk after the source part moves. <details> <summary>Classification, scoping, tests</summary> **The class.** Wide part in full storage with no unrecorded dynamic substreams, only `DROP INDEX` or `DROP PROJECTION` and not their `CLEAR` forms, no pending rename outside the command list, no patch parts, not copying instead of hardlinking, no packed skip-index archive to rebuild. Any doubt means not exempt. Replicated side: decided at assignment and again at execution, reservation taken at queue selection, and never diverted into a fetch, which would reserve the sender's whole part. **Statistics are left alone whenever the mutation neither rewrites any column nor can change which ones the part holds**, as `DROP INDEX` and `DROP PROJECTION` cannot: `statistics.packed` is hardlinked with its inherited checksums instead of being re-serialized to identical content. `DROP STATISTICS`, `DROP COLUMN`, `RENAME COLUMN`, `MODIFY COLUMN`, `MATERIALIZE COLUMN`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and any recalculation write them as before. This is scoped to *any* partial-route mutation rather than to the exempt ones: keying it on the exemption would make it depend on this replica's config and live queue state, so two replicas executing one log entry could write parts differing byte for byte, and the differing one is then forced to fetch the whole result part - the outcome this change exists to avoid. **`DROP STATISTICS` is not exempt** although it is interpreter-free like `DROP INDEX`: it changes the set, so the archive is written anew at a size the small reservation does not cover. **Tests.** Controls that must stay postponed: `DELETE` on both engines, a Compact part, a Wide+Packed part, `always_use_copy_instead_of_hardlinks`, `CLEAR INDEX`, `DROP STATISTICS`, the pool throttle. Oracles: a route oracle from `system.part_log`, two threshold-free write-footprint comparisons, a two-replica case with both fetch-preference thresholds at zero, and a paused entry whose copy mode or source-part disk changes underneath it. </details>

signal.title: Fix GCD codec behavior on signed values
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78190 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed GCD codec handling of signed fixed-width values with negative numbers. Previously it computed the divisor from signed values directly, which could miss the common divisor and significantly reduce compression efficiency for signed integer and decimal columns. It now computes the divisor from magnitudes for signed types while preserving existing behavior for unsigned types and decompression. ### Description GCD pre-processing was using signed values directly when discovering the common divisor. For signed fixed-width storage types, negative values could therefore spoil divisor discovery and make CODEC(GCD) compress much worse than expected, even though the data still had a large common divisor in magnitude. The fix makes CompressionCodecGCD compute the divisor on unsigned magnitudes for signed types, and threads signedness from the column type into codec instantiation so Int* and signed Decimal* columns use the correct path. This also handles the signed-minimum edge case safely by avoiding signed negation overflow. Unsigned behavior is unchanged. The type-agnostic fallback is kept deliberately unchanged: unlike T64, GCD still does not throw when type information is unavailable and falls back to the 1-byte unsigned path. That preserves correctness for cases such as default_compression_codec or CODEC(Default) resolution without a concrete column type, but signed data on that path may still compress less efficiently because signedness is unknown. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113798&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113798](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113798+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Cache text-index pattern bailouts
signal.text: Broad `LIKE` and `ILIKE` text-index queries can exceed `text_index_like_max_postings_to_read` while scanning each part's dictionary and safely fall back to evaluating the original predicate. Repeated queries currently repeat that expensive dictionary scan even though the same part, pattern set, and threshold produce the same bailout. Cache the bailout decision in the existing text-index tokens cache, keyed by the immutable part/index identity, complete pattern-query set, and posting-list threshold. Cache hits call the existing `TextIndexAnalyzer::bypassPatternQueries` path, so they only bypass an optimization and cannot incorrectly prune data. The cache is controlled by the default-on `use_text_index_pattern_bypass_cache` setting and cleared by the existing `SYSTEM CLEAR TEXT INDEX TOKENS CACHE` statement. `TextIndexDiscardPatternScan` continues to count actual scan bailouts, while the new `TextIndexPatternBypassCacheHits` event counts cached bypasses. Tests cover correctness against an index-disabled scan, first and repeated executions, cache disabling and clearing, changed thresholds, different patterns and pattern sets, and both `LIKE` and `ILIKE`. In a 64-part benchmark, repeated queries reduced dictionary reads from 3,200 to zero and improved throughput by approximately 6% for `LIKE` and 10.5% for `ILIKE`. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112742 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Cache text-index pattern dictionary-scan bailouts to avoid repeated dictionary reads for broad `LIKE` and `ILIKE` queries. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113572&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113572](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113572+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix loading suggestions in the embedded client (SSH interface and Web terminal)
signal.text: The embedded client (the SSH interface and the Web terminal) did not load autocompletion words, so TAB completion and as-you-type hints did not work there. The suggestions were loaded through a separate `LocalConnection` created from a bare context, whose constructor creates a new `Session` and authenticates as the `default` user with an empty password. Inside a real server this is wrong twice: - On any server where `default` has a password or does not exist, the authentication fails, so no completions from `system.completions` are ever loaded — and the error message is written to the server's stderr, invisible to the user. - On servers where `default` can log in with an empty password, the words were loaded with the grants of `default` instead of the logged-in user, leaking names of databases, tables and columns the user is not allowed to see (`system.completions` filters by the querying user's access rights). Now the embedded client loads suggestions synchronously through its main, already-authenticated connection. It is idle at that point, and the embedded client always waits for suggestions to load before showing the prompt anyway. Errors are reported to the user's terminal instead of the server's stderr. Added integration tests for both interfaces: an interactive SSH PTY session and a `/webterminal` WebSocket session, each checking that a table the user can see is TAB-completed while a table the user has no grants on is not. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix autocompletion (hints and TAB completion from `system.completions`) in the embedded client used by the SSH interface and the Web terminal: suggestions were loaded through a separate connection that authenticated as the `default` user with an empty password, which failed on servers where `default` has a password, and otherwise leaked names of entities the logged-in user has no access to. Suggestions are now loaded through the session's own connection. - [ ] Documentation entry for user-facing changes <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115086&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115086](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115086+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Push down volume-reducing functions in query plan
signal.text: Adds a query plan optimization that pushes volume-reducing functions (`length`, `lengthUTF8`, `empty`, `notEmpty`) below the `Sorting` and `Filter` steps, so those steps carry the fixed-size result instead of the original `String` / `FixedString` argument. The rewrite is done with `ActionsDAG::split`: the function nodes form the first part, which becomes a new step below the child, and the second part becomes the parent step's `ActionsDAG` and reads the results as inputs. It only fires when the wide argument column really stops flowing through the child step — the column is removed from the child's output, and unless the child reads it itself it is not even produced below the child. `tryExecuteFunctionsAfterSorting` and `trySplitFilter` keep the pushed functions where they are, so the optimizations do not move the same nodes in opposite directions. For the shape from the issue below, `SELECT avg(length(s)) FROM test WHERE notEmpty(s)`, the filter still needs `s` to evaluate its condition, but `length(s)` is now computed before the filter, so the wide column is not copied for the surviving rows. Enabled by default; can be turned off with `query_plan_push_down_volume_reducing_functions = 0`. An earlier attempt at the same optimization was https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86139 by @talmawash, credited as a co-author. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/82378 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86139 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a query plan optimization that pushes volume-reducing functions (`length`, `lengthUTF8`, `empty`, `notEmpty`) below the `Sorting` and `Filter` steps, replacing the wide `String` / `FixedString` argument with the fixed-size result, so it is neither buffered by a sort nor copied by a filter. Controlled by the new setting `query_plan_push_down_volume_reducing_functions`, enabled by default. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106199&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/106199](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F106199+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
