signal.title: Perform the `Too many parts` check once per INSERT query
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109000 `MergeTreeSink::onStart` and `ReplicatedMergeTreeSink::onStart` perform the `parts_to_throw_insert` / `parts_to_delay_insert` check, and `onStart` is the only place where an `INSERT` may be rejected with `TOO_MANY_PARTS` - rejecting a query that has already written a part is not acceptable, as the comment right above the call says. Since #109000 a plain `INSERT` writes through up to `max_insert_threads` sinks running in parallel, and every one of them runs `onStart` (`ExceptionKeepingTransform::prepare` returns `Ready` for the `Start` stage of every sink, whether or not it ever receives a chunk). The `onStart` calls of the different sinks are not ordered with respect to each other's writes: a sink that the executor schedules late runs its check *after* another sink of the same query has already committed a part, counts that part, and rejects the query in the middle of it. The `INSERT` fails with `TOO_MANY_PARTS` even though the table was below the threshold when the query started - and even when the table was empty and the only part counted is the one the query wrote itself. Note that #109000 exposed the flaw rather than introduced it. The parallel sink fan-out itself (`sink_stream_size = max_insert_threads` in `InsertDependenciesBuilder`) has been in place for the `INSERT SELECT` path since `031a9d5a528`, and the default of `max_insert_threads` changed from `1` to `0` (auto, the number of CPU cores) in 26.8 - so an `INSERT SELECT` into a MergeTree table could already be rejected by a stream that counted a part the query had written itself. Before #109000 the plain-`INSERT` pipeline passed a hardcoded `/*max_insert_threads*/ 1` to the builder and always had a single sink, which is why the flaky tests below - all of them plain `INSERT ... VALUES` - only started failing when that changed. The check is now shared by all the sinks of one query: the first sink to reach `onStart` runs it and the others wait until it is finished, so it runs exactly once and strictly before any of the sinks writes anything. This restores the behaviour that the single-sink pipeline had. Only the rejection is shared: the `parts_to_delay_insert` backpressure is applied by every sink before each of its blocks, including the first one, so a parallel `INSERT` keeps the same per-block throttling as a single-sink one (a sink that receives no data does not delay). The gates live in a small per-query registry (`InsertStartGates`) keyed by the physical destination table id. `InsertDependenciesBuilder` creates the registry and takes each sink's gate from it next to `setRuntimeData` / `setHasDependentMaterializedViews`, so the sinks of all the streams that write into the same table share one gate - including the branches of different materialized views converging on the same target table. An `Alias` destination forwards the write through a nested `INSERT` per parallel branch and the real check runs inside those nested inserts, so `AliasSink` receives the registry and threads it into the nested `InterpreterInsertQuery`, whose builder inherits it instead of creating its own. `Distributed` and `Buffer` destinations are always kept single-stream by #109000, so their own pre-write checks are unaffected - but their in-query nested `INSERT`s into the underlying tables are not. The *local* writes of a `Distributed` destination run through nested `INSERT`s into the underlying table: one per incoming block on the `writeToLocal` path (the direct local write of a background-send insert with `prefer_localhost_replica`) and one per local replica job on the foreground path. Each of them used to create its own gates, so the second block of a multi-block `INSERT` counted the part the first block had already committed on the local target and failed the query mid-way; `DistributedSink` also receives the registry and threads it into both nested `INSERT` paths (the new test `04826_insert_distributed_local_too_many_parts_gate` covers a two-block insert into a local target with `parts_to_throw_insert = 1` on both paths). The `parallel_distributed_insert_select` rewrite of an `INSERT ... SELECT` between two `Distributed` tables writes the local shards the same way - one nested `InterpreterInsertQuery` per destination shard this server belongs to - and a server can be local for several destination shards of one cluster, so those sibling nested `INSERT`s write into the same underlying table and now share one registry as well (the new test `04847_insert_parallel_distributed_insert_select_local_shards` covers a two-local-shard cluster with `parts_to_throw_insert = 1` on the target, plus the non-parallel quorum variant of the same topology). The direct writes of a `Buffer` destination run through nested `INSERT`s into its destination table as well: one per block that bypasses the buffer by exceeding the max thresholds, and one per flush the buffer runs by threshold from within the query - so a later direct write of a multi-block `INSERT` used to count the part an earlier one had committed on the destination; `BufferSink` also receives the registry and threads it through `flushBuffer` / `writeBlockToDestination` into those nested `INSERT`s, while the background flush keeps creating fresh gates per flush as before (the new test `04827_insert_buffer_direct_write_too_many_parts_gate` covers both paths with `parts_to_throw_insert = 1` on the destination). A `TimeSeries` destination forwards the write through nested `INSERT`s into its inner target tables, so `TimeSeriesSink` also receives the registry and threads it into them, sharing the check across sibling branches converging on the same `TimeSeries` table. Those nested pipelines are now created in `onStart` rather than in the sink's constructor: the registry reaches the sink only after `StorageTimeSeries::write` has returned it, so building them in the constructor handed them an empty registry and the sharing held only by the accident of every sink of the query being constructed before any of them writes anything. A `WindowView` forwards every chunk of every branch into a fresh sink of its inner table, so `PushingToWindowViewSink` also receives the registry and threads it into `StorageWindowView::writeIntoWindowView`, which sets the query's gate of the inner table on the sinks it creates - sharing the check across the branches and across the successive chunks of one branch. This path cannot be covered by a test yet: a window view currently cannot receive inserted data at all - the view dependency of the source table is never registered and a direct `INSERT` into a window view fails with `std::out_of_range` - both since before this change (they reproduce on 26.7), see https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113493. A related single-in-flight-part contract exists one level up: a non-parallel quorum insert (`insert_quorum >= 2` or `'auto'`, with `insert_quorum_parallel = 0`) permits a single in-flight quorum part per table, which is why its `max_insert_threads` fan-out is kept single-stream. But the single sink stream is still duplicated into one branch per dependent materialized view, and with `parallel_view_processing = 1` those branches ran concurrently - two views converging on one `ReplicatedMergeTree` target raced two in-flight quorum parts of one `INSERT` against each other, so a sibling branch could fail with `UNSATISFIED_QUORUM_FOR_PREVIOUS_WRITE` or conflict on the `/quorum/status` node. The serialization such an insert needs is derived from the collected sink graph, not from the settings alone (`InsertDependenciesBuilder::computeQuorumStreamRequirements`): only writes reaching a `ReplicatedMergeTree` table are quorum writes, and only two of them racing on the same table conflict. The `INSERT SELECT` fan-out - which had no quorum guard at all - is kept single-stream only when a branch of the write may produce a quorum part: a reachable `ReplicatedMergeTree` target, or a forwarding storage (an `Alias`, a `Distributed`, a `Buffer`, a `WindowView`, a `TimeSeries`) that hides its physical destination, in which case the probe fails closed. An insert whose write graph never reaches a replicated table keeps its `max_insert_threads` fan-out even under a global quorum profile. Only the branches reachable in the executable graph are counted: a view branch pruned from the graph - e.g. a view whose dropped target table is ignored by `ignore_materialized_views_with_dropped_target_table` - never creates a sink, so it does not force the serialization (the new test `04825_insert_quorum_ignored_broken_view_fanout` covers a broken ignored view attached to a plain `MergeTree` destination). The dependent views of such an insert are pushed sequentially only when two branches converge on the same replicated table (a sequential branch blocks in `commitPart` until the quorum of its part is satisfied, so the next branch starts with the quorum node already gone) or when a hidden write target makes such a convergence impossible to rule out - branches writing to distinct replicated tables keep running concurrently, since they do not share a `/quorum/status` node. An `Alias` destination hides its target's views behind the nested `INSERT` its sink runs, and that nested `INSERT` observes the same settings and derives the same requirements. The new test `04828_insert_timeseries_too_many_parts_gate` exercises non-parallel quorum inserts through two views converging on one `TimeSeries` table whose data table is replicated - the shape that raced `UNSATISFIED_QUORUM_FOR_PREVIOUS_WRITE` before `TimeSeries` was included in the hidden-target probes. The new test `04817_insert_quorum_sequential_dependent_views` covers the `INSERT SELECT` fan-out deterministically via `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` and exercises quorum inserts through two materialized views converging on one replicated target with `parallel_view_processing = 1`; the new test `04823_insert_quorum_graph_derived_serialization` covers the fan-out kept for a plain `MergeTree` destination, the fan-out dropped when a dependent materialized view targets a replicated table, and quorum inserts through two views writing to two distinct replicated tables. `parallel_view_processing = 0` gets the same treatment on the `INSERT SELECT` path: `buildInsertPipeline` already kept a plain `INSERT` single-stream when the destination is a forwarding storage that hides its target's dependent-view graph behind the nested `INSERT` its sinks run (`serial_hidden_views`), but `addInsertToSelectPipeline` still passed the raw `max_insert_threads` to the builder - which sees no views for such a destination - so an `INSERT SELECT` into an `Alias` fanned out into several `AliasSink`s whose hidden materialized views ran concurrently across sibling branches despite the setting. The guard is now mirrored there; an `Alias` in front of a target with dependent views is the only topology whose fan-out survived to that point, since `Distributed`, `Buffer` and `TimeSeries` destinations are already collapsed to one stream by the builder's `supportsParallelInsert` check. The new test `04869_insert_select_alias_hidden_views_serial` covers the single stream with a hidden dependent view, and the fan-out kept both without dependent views and with `parallel_view_processing = 1`. This is the cause of a family of flaky tests that started failing on `master` on 2026-08-01, right after #109000 was merged, each of them rejecting an `INSERT` that counts the part it has written itself: | test | failing query | reported parts | | --- | --- | --- | | `02458_relax_too_many_parts` | `INSERT INTO test VALUES (6, 'a')` | 3 with `parts_to_throw_insert = 3` | | `02280_add_query_level_settings` | `INSERT INTO table_for_alter VALUES (1, '1')` into an empty table | 1 with `parts_to_throw_insert = 1` | | `00980_merge_alter_settings` | `INSERT INTO table_for_alter VALUES (1, '1')` into an empty table | 1 with `parts_to_throw_insert = 1` | | `02015_async_inserts_5` | `INSERT INTO async_inserts VALUES` | 1 with `parts_to_throw_insert = 1` | The server log of the `02458_relax_too_many_parts` failure below shows the mechanism directly: 26 sinks are created for the query, its part `all_5_5_0` is renamed into place at `01:46:59.792095`, and the query is rejected with `Too many parts (3 ...)` at `01:46:59.798713` - six milliseconds after it committed the part it is being counted for. Report of that failure (`MergeQueueCI`, `Fast test`): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=gh-readonly-queue/master/pr-112777-508dbed54a148ce6ae2dabe8ff91f4c7842bb1a0&sha=c71ec1f59e4b52ffe87c96e12743488cec72a7e0&name_0=MergeQueueCI&name_1=Fast%20test Corresponding pull request: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112777 The new test `04692_insert_too_many_parts_check_once_per_query` covers both halves: an `INSERT` with a large `max_insert_threads` that brings a table from one part up to `parts_to_throw_insert = 2` has to be accepted, and `ProfileEvents['DelayedInserts']` of a single-row `INSERT` has to match the number of blocks the query actually writes (one; two when the query writes through two materialized views converging on the same target table) rather than the number of streams it writes through - also when it writes through an `Alias`. `TimeSeries` is also classified as a forwarding storage in the deduplication-safety probes (`storageDeduplicatesBlocksOnInsert`, `storageRebuildsDeduplicationIdsOnInsert`, `forwardedInsertReachesDependentView`, `forwardedInsertHidesDependentView`, `forwardedInsertHidesDependentViewForwardingToSeparateContext`), since `TimeSeriesSink` forwards a plain block into its nested `INSERT`s and drops the outer chunk's `DeduplicationInfo`. This is fail-close classification only, not a reachable fix: `StorageTimeSeries` does not override `IStorage::supportsParallelInsert`, so an insert whose graph reaches a `TimeSeries` table is already single-stream and the probes cannot change the outcome - and writes arriving through `TimeSeriesSink` turn out not to deduplicate on the inner tables at all, so no rows are lost when two views converge on one `TimeSeries` table. The clauses keep the classification correct if `StorageTimeSeries` ever starts supporting parallel inserts. The new test `04846_insert_mv_timeseries_dedup_parallel_views` pins the no-row-loss half end to end: two identical materialized views converging on one `TimeSeries` table with a deduplicating data table (`non_replicated_deduplication_window`) under `parallel_view_processing = 1` land both branches in full - nothing is deduplicated between the sibling branches of one query. #### Relation to #114016 While this pull request was open, #114016 landed on `master` with a narrower fix for the same root cause: it evaluates the check on the query thread in the `MergeTreeSink` / `ReplicatedMergeTreeSink` constructor and rethrows it from `onStart`. Merging `master` resolves that in favour of the shared gate, which subsumes it - a sink whose `onStart` runs late skips the check instead of re-running it - and additionally covers the sinks that are created *during* execution, which the constructor placement cannot: the nested `INSERT`s of `Alias`, `Distributed`, `Buffer`, `WindowView` and `TimeSeries`. Everything else from #114016 is kept, including the `merge_tree_sink_on_start_random_sleep` failpoint and its test `04826_parallel_insert_sinks_too_many_parts_self_race`, which the shared gate also makes pass. signal.title: Hand the connection to the built-in web UI pages over `postMessage`
signal.text: The built-in web UI pages — `/play`, `/docs`, `/dashboard`, `/schema`, `/merges`, `/jemalloc`, `/processors-profile`, `/binary` — take their connection from their own query string, which cannot carry a password: a URL ends up in browser history, `Referer` headers, server access logs and proxy logs. Only `/webterminal` could be handed credentials by the page embedding it, in a `postMessage` message. Every page now speaks that same exchange: ``` page -> host {type: 'clickhouse-hello'} host -> page {type: 'clickhouse-credentials', url, user, password} ``` The page announces itself as soon as it can apply a connection, and the host answers. The page has to speak first because a host that opened it with `window.open` cannot observe when a cross-origin document became ready, and an embedded page would otherwise race its host's `load` handler. Having adopted a connection, each page redoes what it had already loaded with the previous one, so the handover also works when it arrives after the page started querying: `/play` re-probes the credentials, `/docs` rebuilds its cross-link name cache and re-runs the displayed search, `/dashboard` and `/processors-profile` chain their reload behind the load already in flight (two concurrent loads would otherwise duplicate charts, or let a stale failure overwrite a good listing), `/schema` and `/jemalloc` reload, and `/binary` drops its cached tiles and redraws. ## Opening `/docs` from `/play` The Documentation icon in the `/play` sidebar is the first user of the handover. A plain click opens `/docs` through `window.open` — the anchor's `rel=noopener` would sever the handle — and hands the whole connection over, so the documentation search runs against the same server as the same user without the password appearing in a URL. A middle or modifier click keeps the browser's native new-tab handling, which carries `?user=` only, since such a window has no link back to `/play`. ## Security A reply is accepted only from the one window that opened or embeds the page, and only from an exact origin: the page's own, `https://console.clickhouse.cloud`, `https://console.clickhouse-staging.com` or `https://clickhouse.com`. The list is exact rather than a domain suffix on purpose — every ClickHouse Cloud service endpoint is a `*.clickhouse.cloud` host that serves content of its owner's choosing, and a trusted host can aim a page at a server of its own through `url`, which the user may then type credentials into believing it is still their own service. `webterminal.html` gated its own exchange on such a suffix and now uses the same exact list. `url` is optional and defaults to the server the page already points at, but the credentials are replaced wholesale: a message that names only a server cannot attach credentials it did not carry to it, which is what keeps a password filled in by the browser's password manager for this page's origin from following a `url` elsewhere. Outbound, credentials are always sent with an exact target origin, never `'*'`; the readiness announcement carries no secrets, only the fact that the page exists, which its host knows already. Verified in Chromium against a mock endpoint: the `/play` → `/docs` handover, the handover into an iframe for all eight pages, rejection of a handover from an untrusted origin and from a same-origin window that is not the page's host, the wholesale credential replacement, and the exactness of the origin list for all nine pages (`https://myserviceendpoint.clickhouse.cloud`, `https://evil.clickhouse.com`, `http://console.clickhouse.cloud` and `https://console.clickhouse.cloud.evil.com` are all rejected). The committed test asserts that every served page implements both halves of the exchange and that its origin list stayed exact. The protocol is documented in `docs/concepts/features/interfaces/web-ui-embedding.mdx`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The built-in web UI pages (`/play`, `/docs`, `/dashboard`, `/schema`, `/merges`, `/jemalloc`, `/processors-profile`, `/binary`) can now be handed their connection — server URL, user and password — in a `postMessage` message by the page that opened or embedded them, instead of taking it from their own query string, where a password would be recorded in browser history, referrer headers and access logs. `/play` uses this when opening `/docs`, so the documentation search connects to the same server as the same user. A page accepts a connection only from the window that opened or embeds it, and only from an exact list of trusted origins. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115067&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115067](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115067+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix data race on DataTypeAggregateFunction version during Native serialization
signal.text: Related: found by the `arm_tsan` and `azure, amd_tsan` Stress tests (STID 3977-4818, ThreadSanitizer data race). No existing issue. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/94859 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog. ### Description A single `DataTypeAggregateFunction` instance is shared across query result blocks: it lives once in the table's column description and is aliased by shallow column copies. `NativeWriter`/`NativeReader` called `setVersionToAggregateFunctions`, which walked to the leaf type and wrote its `mutable version` field in place. Two concurrent `Native` serializations of the same aggregate-function-typed column then raced on that field, and the version written for one old connection stayed on the shared type, so every later query read the states at that version - for `sumMap` over `Decimal32` that returns wrong values. Reports: * https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109496&sha=62eeb400eafe86cedff9b5a4e9a36aa722633cda&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 * https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=b59441bd06c2fcb6b103a30874528cc398afc723&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28azure%2C%20amd_tsan%29 **That fix has since landed on `master`** through #94859 and #112052: `setVersionToAggregateFunctions` now replaces every versioned nested type instead of mutating it, and `replaceNestedSimpleTypes` carries the custom names (`Nested`, `SimpleAggregateFunction`) over the rebuild. This branch is therefore resolved in favour of that implementation, and what it added on top of it - an `IDataType::transformChildren` override per container type, and the `unique_ptr` to `shared_ptr` switch of `DataTypeCustomNamePtr` - is dropped as duplicate machinery. What remains here is what `master` does not have, and it keeps this PR's intent - the race cannot come back, because the version can no longer be assigned in place at all: * `DataTypeAggregateFunction::setVersion` and `updateVersionFromRevision` are removed, and `version` is no longer `mutable`. Both mutators were left without callers by the rewrite on `master`; the version is now set only at construction (parsed from AST, decoded from the binary type encoding, or chosen by `setVersionToAggregateFunctions`, which builds a new type). * Unit and functional coverage of the behaviour, which `master` has only indirectly. ### Testing * `gtest_aggregate_function_version_race` (14 tests) pins the type-level behaviour: the shared type object is not mutated; a wrapper is rebuilt only when a leaf was actually replaced; the `Point`, `Nested` and `SimpleAggregateFunction` custom names survive, including a `Tuple`-backed `SimpleAggregateFunction`; a `Variant` keeps its discriminator order and throws when two alternatives would collapse; a `JSON` typed path keeps the version spelled in its own type name; and an 8-thread x 2000-iteration stress over one shared type object is race-free. * `04612_aggregate_function_version_custom_type_names` round-trips `Nested`, `SimpleAggregateFunction` and a wrapper-named type through `Native` (which assigns the version in the writer and again in the reader) and through `DETACH`/`ATTACH`, and checks that a deeply nested `Nested` stays linear in the nesting depth. * `04613_aggregate_function_version_not_sticky` asks for a `Native` response at a revision below the one that introduced versioning and then checks the column again, so a version pinned for that one response would be visible both in the values read back (`sumMap` over `Decimal32`) and in `system.columns`. The revision is pinned explicitly and the type name the response carries is asserted, so the test cannot pass without that path having run.

signal.title: Add server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread`
signal.text: Each thread accumulates up to `max_untracked_memory` (4 MiB by default) of allocations before reporting them to the server-wide `MemoryTracker`. With many threads, this unreported memory can sum to a large amount, causing the server's tracked memory usage to under-count actual consumption and leading to OOM. This PR introduces a server-level setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) and speculatively charges this amount to the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. The global tracked memory becomes a tighter upper bound on actual consumption when `max_untracked_memory` for those workers does not exceed this setting; operators that permit a larger per-query value must raise the server setting accordingly. The reservation is charged on the server-wide (total) tracker only — deliberately not through the query's tracker chain. Query-level accounting feeds heuristics that compare memory deltas against byte thresholds (conversion of aggregation hash tables to two-level via `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes`, spill-to-disk decisions), and phantom reservations of `num_threads * 4 MiB` trip those thresholds immediately: an earlier revision of this PR that charged the query tracker showed consistent slowdowns of GROUP BY queries in performance tests for exactly this reason. The reservation itself does not alter query-level or user-level accounting (`max_memory_usage`, `memory_usage` in `system.processes`); however, every pipeline worker flushes its pending real allocation reports before releasing its outermost reservation, so those counters and memory-based heuristics can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. The speculative reservation uses the throwing path of the memory tracker, so when it would exceed the server memory limit the corresponding job is treated as failed with `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — the same behavior as if the job itself had exceeded the limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) which speculatively reserves this amount on the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. When it is at least the workers' `max_untracked_memory`, it makes server-wide tracked memory a tighter upper bound on actual consumption and reduces the risk of OOM with many concurrent pipeline workers. The reservation does not alter query-level or user-level accounting, but workers flush pending real allocation reports before releasing their outermost reservation, so those counters can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - signal.title: Do not hold the DDL guard during TRUNCATE
signal.text: `TRUNCATE TABLE` held the table's DDL guard while removing data, and truncate can wait for running merges or for other replicas to process `DROP_RANGE`. Any DDL on that name — including background threads that need it — was blocked for that whole time. Release the guard before `IStorage::truncate` for databases with UUIDs, matching `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION`, which never took it. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `TRUNCATE TABLE` no longer blocks concurrent `DROP`, `RENAME` and other DDL queries on the same table while the data is being removed.

signal.title: Add mutation completion time `finish_time` to `system.mutations`
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/89216 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105255 Adds a `finish_time` column to `system.mutations` reporting when a mutation was completed; `0` means the mutation is not finished yet or its completion time is unknown. This is a rework of #105255 that avoids any new persistent state: no mutation-file format changes and no new Keeper znodes, so there is no upgrade path, no cleanup changes, and no retry/idempotency concerns. For non-replicated `MergeTree` tables the value is tracked in memory (like `latest_fail_time`) and stamped only when the completion is observed by the event that caused it: the commit of the last mutated part, or the creation of a mutation that has no parts to process. Mutations whose completion moment was not observed (entries loaded at startup, parts removed by `DROP PARTITION`) report `0` instead of a fabricated timestamp. For `ReplicatedMergeTree` tables the value is per-replica and equals the modification time of the replica's `mutation_pointer` znode — the write that marks mutations done on the replica. After the replica state is reloaded (e.g. server restart), the completion time of the mutation the pointer points at is restored from the znode `mtime`; older completed mutations report `0`. A cluster-wide completion time can be obtained with `max(finish_time)` grouped by `mutation_id` across replicas. Note for the CH Inc sync: `SharedMergeTree` constructs `MergeTreeMutationStatus` positionally and will need a follow-up to populate `finish_time`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a `finish_time` column to `system.mutations` that records when a mutation was completed. Unfinished mutations and mutations whose completion time is unknown report zero. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.text: `clickhouse-client` printed `Connecting to ...` twice whenever it had to ask for a password: ``` $ clickhouse client --host clickhouse.new --secure --user alexey-milovidov ClickHouse client version 26.8.1.1. Connecting to clickhouse.new:9440 as user alexey-milovidov. Password for user (alexey-milovidov): Connecting to clickhouse.new:9440 as user alexey-milovidov. Connected to ClickHouse server version 26.8.1. ``` Neither `--password` nor `--ask-password` was given, so the client did not know whether the user has a password at all and connected without one. signal.title: Require a join subquery alias only when it removes a real ambiguity
signal.text: `joined_subquery_requires_alias = 1` (the default) rejected every unaliased subquery, table function or union used in a multi-table join, even when the missing alias could not cause any ambiguity. That is stricter than necessary: an alias only serves to qualify a column, so it is only needed when the unaliased table expression exposes a column whose name also occurs in another table expression of the same join. `validateJoinTableExpressionWithoutAlias` now throws `ALIAS_REQUIRED` only on such a name collision (computed with the existing `getColumnsFromTableExpression` helper over the sibling table expressions), and otherwise allows the missing alias. Genuine ambiguities involving non-sibling table expressions are still caught later by the normal `AMBIGUOUS_IDENTIFIER` resolution, exactly as they are for ordinary tables. This lets standard queries such as TPC-DS q14 (whose `cross_items` derived table has no correlation name) run without setting `joined_subquery_requires_alias = 0`: ```sql SELECT i_item_sk FROM item, (SELECT iss.i_brand_id AS brand_id FROM store_sales, item AS iss ...) WHERE i_brand_id = brand_id; -- no shared column name -> no alias needed ``` Notes: - Validation in `resolveJoin`/`resolveCrossJoin` is moved to run after all table expressions of the join are resolved, so sibling columns are known when the collision is checked. - The change is purely permissive: it never turns a previously-succeeding query into an error. When the columns of any side cannot be determined it falls back to the old strict behavior. - Only the analyzer is affected; the deprecated non-analyzer path keeps the stricter behavior. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): With `joined_subquery_requires_alias = 1` (the default), the analyzer now rejects an unaliased subquery or table function in a join only when the missing alias would make one of its columns unreachable, for example because the name collides with another joined table expression or is shadowed by an in-scope alias; otherwise the query is allowed. If the analyzer cannot determine the exposed names up front, it keeps the old strict behavior. Unambiguous queries, such as some standard TPC-DS queries, no longer require adding an alias. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109368&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109368](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109368+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add a style check for the spelling of `ClickHouse`
signal.text: The product name is written `ClickHouse` - one word, with a capital `C` and a capital `H`. Two case variants are accepted, because a mixed case is unusable there: `clickhouse` for identifiers, package, binary and host names, and `CLICKHOUSE` for macros and environment variables. Everything else - `Clickhouse`, `clickHouse`, `click_house`, `CLICK_HOUSE`, `click-house`, `Click House` - is a misspelling, and until now nothing stopped it from being committed. ## The check The new `clickhouse_spelling` check of the style job searches every file tracked by git, and the file names themselves, in code as well as in comments, messages and documentation. A `git grep -P` prefilter finds the candidate lines (a provable superset of what is reported), so the check costs about a second on a warm page cache and a minute on a cold one. Only the space-separated form is anchored at word boundaries, so an unrelated phrase - "click Household" - is not taken for the product name. The other forms are left unanchored on purpose, so that a misspelling inside a longer identifier - `ClickhouseBuffer` - is reported too. Rather than a long list of excused files, the sources of false positives are handled structurally: * `contrib` - third-party sources. * The generated locale directories of the documentation, `docs/<locale>/` and `docs/snippets/<locale>/`, taken from `docs/gt.config.json`. They are a machine translation of the English pages, so a misspelling there is fixed by fixing the English page; the default locale is not excluded, and `docs/en/` stays enforced. * Release notes - a record of what was published, not edited after the fact. Same pattern as the "new analyzer" wording check in `various_checks.sh`, so the landing and status pages that live next to them stay enforced. * `docs/_specs` - API specifications pinned from their generator by `ci/jobs/cloud_api_docs_nightly.py`. * Regions between `AUTOGENERATED_START` and `AUTOGENERATED_END` markers. Their source of truth - a `FunctionDocumentation` string, for instance - is checked instead, which is what a contributor is supposed to edit. * URLs. A link whose path spells the name differently is not a mistake we can fix, and rewriting it would only break the link. `docs/resources/about/adopters.mdx` alone holds eleven of them. What is left goes into `ci/jobs/scripts/check_style/clickhouse_spelling_ignore.txt`, in the spirit of the existing `experimental_settings_ignore.txt`: a path alone exempts a file, a path followed by a literal exempts only the lines containing that literal. It has fifteen entries, each with the reason next to it, and every one of them is text that is not ours to spell: names defined by other projects (the `ClickhouseClientOptions` of our Azure SDK fork, the `clickHouse*` parameters of Google's Dataflow templates, a third-party client library), verbatim quotations (Stack Overflow post titles shown as query output), and the misspellings that tests feed to the server on purpose - `LIKE` / `ILIKE` case variants, `hasPhrase(message, 'Click House')`, `click_house:` as an unknown URI scheme. ## The fixes The check found 191 misspellings, all fixed here. Most are prose and comments. The renamed identifiers are `isClickhouseApp`, `getClickhouseAttemptNumber` / `setClickhouseAttemptNumber`, `getClickhouseTableSchemaById` / `hasClickhouseTableSchemaById`, the `Clickhouse*` classes of `clickhouse-diagnostics`, the `tabClickhouse` / `btnQueryClickhouse` element ids of the `utils` web tools, and `clickHousePartsInserter.js`, which is renamed. No stale reference to an old name survives - one would be a misspelling, and the check reports those. Three of the fixes are visible to tests, and the first two rely on the server being case-insensitive there, which I confirmed against a running server rather than assumed: * the `X-Clickhouse-Format` HTTP header of `02015_async_inserts_1` - Poco header collections compare names case-insensitively; * the `SOURCE(Clickhouse(...))` dictionary source of `03071_fix_short_circuit_logic` - the parser lowercases the source name (`ExpressionElementParsers.cpp`); * a directory named `Clickhouse` in `03600_disk_app_plain_rewritable_disks_list_cmd`, renamed in the command and in the reference. Its position in the listing is unchanged, since `ClickHouse` sorts before `Cloud` either way. The rule is also written down as item 18 of the `Names` section of the style guide, so a contributor can find it before CI tells them. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114926&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114926](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114926+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

The server did not die: no `<Fatal>` line, no sanitizer report, empty `dmesg`, clean shutdown. The `--hung-check` liveness probe failed and the run was aborted. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110479&sha=038667a9c024695126415fe5f37b76f7a06662fa&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%20flaky%20check%29 Root cause: `tests/clickhouse-test` collapses every in-band abort cause into `STOP_TESTING_EXIT_CODE = 2`, and the job side appends `Server died` for that code unconditionally. Master already carved two causes out of code 2 for this reason; this is the third. Code 2 is generic, and a worker seeing a `<Fatal>` line reaches the parent through `stop_tests()`, exiting 143 - correct there, but decided outside the carrier. signal.title: Do not kill a mutation whose transaction is past its commit point
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a server abort (`LOGICAL_ERROR: Cannot find mutation`) when `KILL MUTATION` raced the `COMMIT` of the transaction that had started the mutation. `KILL MUTATION` now reports `cant_cancel` for a mutation whose transaction has already passed its commit point, instead of destroying state the commit still needs. ### Description `StorageMergeTree::killMutation` erased the `current_mutations_by_version` entry and removed `mutation_*.txt` **before** resolving the owning transaction, calling `TransactionLog::rollbackTransaction` only afterwards. Past the commit point that rollback is a no-op: `rollback` CASes `csn` `UnknownCSN -> RolledBackCSN`, which fails once `beforeCommit` stored `CommittingCSN`, so `rollbackTransaction` early-returns. The erase, however, is permanent. The committing thread then reached `afterCommit` -> `setMutationCSN`, could not find the entry, and threw `LOGICAL_ERROR "Cannot find mutation"` from a `noexcept` function, aborting the server. The fix resolves the transaction first and claims the cancellation through `rollback`'s `csn` CAS before destroying anything. That CAS contends with `beforeCommit`'s `UnknownCSN -> CommittingCSN` CAS on the same atomic, so exactly one wins and the decision is atomic with respect to the commit point. When the commit wins, `killMutation` returns `CancelCannotBeSent` (`cant_cancel`) and changes nothing. Merely reading the CSN would not be enough: the commit does not take `currently_processing_in_background_mutex`, so read-then-erase is a TOCTOU that reproduces the same abort. Refusing loses no work, because `beforeCommit` waits for every mutation of the transaction before its CAS, and it matches how `executeRollback` and `KILL TRANSACTION` already treat a committing transaction. The non-transactional path is unchanged, and `setMutationCSN` is deliberately untouched: an early return there would silently drop a committed mutation's CSN. Reaching this requires `allow_experimental_transactions`, enabled by `tests/config` for every stateless and stress job. Validation: the new stateless test drives the race deterministically with three new pauseable failpoints; it aborts the server without the fix and passes with it. 50/50 randomized and 50/50 plain runs pass, and a scope over every `KILL MUTATION` test plus the transaction-isolation families shows no verdict change against the unmodified build. `afterCommit` remains `noexcept` with no internal guard, so any other future throw there is still fatal; that is the #45736 family, for a separate change. No related open issue found.

signal.title: Honour lock_acquire_timeout for the lightweight update lock in Keeper
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112380 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed lightweight `UPDATE` on `ReplicatedMergeTree` being rejected with `TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED` after a few seconds under concurrent updates, long before the configured `lock_acquire_timeout` elapsed. The Keeper lock acquisition loop was bounded by a fixed number of tries instead of by the timeout, so raising `lock_acquire_timeout` had no effect. ### Description A valid lightweight `UPDATE` was rejected with ``` Code: 159. Failed to get lock with 100 tries for lightwegiht update in auto mode. (TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED) ``` after about 3 seconds, with `lock_acquire_timeout` at 120 seconds and the cluster granting locks normally. `update_parallel_mode` defaults to `auto`, so this is the default path. Root cause: `getLockForAutoMode` watched the parent directory `.../lightweight_updates/in_progress`, whose child set changes on every concurrent update, and `Poco::Event` returns at once when already signalled: across 15228 waits requesting 120000 ms the longest was 0.086 s, so the loop spun to `max_tries = 100`. `getLockForSyncMode` had the same shape, at ~6 s. Elapsed time against `lock_acquire_timeout` is now the only failure condition, and the wait is on the conflicting update's own node: - Remaining time is a `Stopwatch` subtraction in the millisecond domain: the setting has no upper constraint and a `steady_clock` deadline overflows above ~9223372036 s. - `ZBADVERSION` from the parent-version CAS, which any unrelated update invalidates, has no node to wait on, so it backs off 50 ms instead of retrying at once, counted by a new `PatchesAcquireLockBadVersionRetries` profile event. - The wait is split into 3 s slices polling query cancellation, plus one poll on leaving the loop so a cancellation arriving in the last slice is not reported as the lock timing out. All four paths share this helper, including the plain `MergeTree` ones that waited in a single `try_lock_for`/`wait_for`: with a held lock and `max_execution_time = 2`, each now ends on its own limit. The first attempt stays unconditional, so an uncontended update still succeeds at `lock_acquire_timeout = 0`. Behaviour change: a query that failed after a few seconds may now wait up to `lock_acquire_timeout`, as the setting documents. Acquisition is still unfair (the `EphemeralSequential` node is created but not used for ordering); fair queueing needs a predecessor-watch protocol and a mixed-version story, out of scope. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Debug build, single node with embedded Keeper. 15 concurrent same-column updaters split into three arms by `lock_acquire_timeout`, in one concurrency window. Time-to-failure must track the timeout. | arm | `lock_acquire_timeout` | before | after | |---|---|---|---| | A | 120 s (default) | 13/237 rejected at 3.03/3.23/3.62 s | 0/205 rejected | | B | 600 s | 11/233 rejected at 3.03/3.26/3.48 s | 0/219 rejected | | C | 3 s | 19/242 rejected at 3.14/3.25/3.51 s | 11/269 rejected at 3.08/3.08/3.10 s | Before, every arm failed at the same ~3.2 s regardless of its timeout; after, only the 3 s arm fails, at its own. Same for `update_parallel_mode = 'sync'` (~6.2 s before). Each mechanism was checked against a build with only that mechanism removed, Build IDs asserted: - parent-directory watch restored: 19 lock tries against 2, passing the table above identically, i.e. the deadline alone turns a premature failure into a busy spin. - `ZBADVERSION` backoff removed: worst-case tries for one query 221/228/176 across three repeats, against 115/116/115 with it (measured directly, not asserted by the test). - unchunked wait: a waiter with `max_execution_time = 2` runs 17.2 s uninterrupted, against stopping at 3.03 s. With only the loop-exit poll removed, all four `lock_acquire_timeout = 2.5` arms report the lock timeout at ~2.52 s instead of their own 2 s limit. - watch re-registered per slice: a waiter parked across six slices registers 7 watches on the node, against 1. `03100_lwu_57_lock_acquire_timeout` covers the timeout arms, a large timeout, churn bounding the try count, a lost parent-version CAS, cancellation on both engines and in the single-slice case, and watch registration by one parked waiter. It fails on unpatched master. Every arm is fixed by construction rather than timed: holders and the CAS victim park at failpoints, so the watch arm's span is 12331-12345 ms against a 9000 ms bound over six randomized runs, and the CAS arm pins its one retry. Parked time falls inside `PatchesAcquireLockMicroseconds`, so that arm does not assert the backoff duration. `03100_lwu_35_lock_profile_events` still passes. </details>

signal.title: Support PostgreSQL regexp operators and make psql \d work over the PostgreSQL protocol
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/25757 Disclaimer: I do not like Postgres operators! I think they are ugly. It makes the language similar to Bash and Perl. They use operators instead of functions only because of some design drawbacks related to the index analysis. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support PostgreSQL-style regular expression match operators: `~` (an alias for the `match` function), `~*` (case-insensitive match), `!~` and `!~*` (negations). The `\d`, `\dt`, `\dv` commands of `psql` now work when connected to ClickHouse over the PostgreSQL compatibility protocol, and a failed query no longer terminates the connection. --- `psql` could not run its `\d` command against ClickHouse over the PostgreSQL wire protocol: ``` alexey-milovidov=> \d ERROR: Query execution failed. DB::Exception: Exclamation mark can only occur in != operator: Syntax error: failed at position 665 (!) (line 10, col 21): !~ '^pg_toast' ... SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly The connection to the server was lost. Attempting reset: Succeeded. ``` This fixes every layer of that incompatibility: - The lexer and the expression parser now understand the PostgreSQL regular expression match operators `~`, `~*`, `!~`, `!~*`, desugaring to `match` and the new functions `matchCaseInsensitive`, `notMatch`, `notMatchCaseInsensitive` (trivial `MatchImpl` variants). The KQL dialect, which previously consumed its own `!~` operator as two error tokens, is adjusted to accept the new single token. - The PostgreSQL wire protocol handler removes the `pg_catalog.` schema qualifier from incoming queries at the token level, mapping references such as `pg_catalog.pg_class` onto the emulated per-session catalog views. - The emulated `pg_class` view now contains the actual tables of the current database (with `relname`, `relnamespace`, `relowner`, `relam`, `relkind`), `pg_namespace` contains the real databases, and a `pg_am` view is added (newer `psql` versions join it). The previous fixed rows are preserved for driver compatibility. - New compatibility functions `pgGetUserById` (alias `pg_get_userbyid`) and `pgTableIsVisible` (alias `pg_table_is_visible`) support the catalog query psql sends. - A failed query now keeps the connection alive: the server sends `ErrorResponse` and returns to the `ReadyForQuery` state, like PostgreSQL. The connection is still closed if some result bytes were already sent for the failed statement, since the output stream could be cut in the middle of a protocol message. The result: ``` psql (18.4, server 26.7.1.1) db_psql_test=> \d List of relations Schema | Name | Type | Owner --------------+-------------+-------+-------- db_psql_test | t_described | table | pguser db_psql_test | t_mt | table | pguser db_psql_test | v_described | view | pguser (3 rows) ``` Known limitation: `\d <name>` (describing a specific table) sends follow-up queries using `OPERATOR(pg_catalog.~)` syntax, `COLLATE pg_catalog.default` and `format_type`, which are not supported yet; the error is now reported without dropping the connection.

signal.title: Perf: use compact presence masks for PromQL set operators
signal.text: ## Summary The PromQL `and`, `or`, and `unless` lowering only needs to know whether a value is present at each step. The compact presence mask is now built with: ```sql groupBitOrForEach(arrayMap(x -> isNotNull(x), values)) ``` Because `isNotNull()` produces a `UInt8` 0/1 value, bitwise OR is exactly the presence reduction needed by the set operators. The aggregate state is a zero-initialized `UInt8`, avoiding the generic `max(UInt8)` initialized-state bookkeeping. ## What changed - Use `Array(UInt8)` presence masks instead of `Array(UInt64)` counts. - Use `groupBitOrForEach` for the per-step presence reduction. - Share the mask expression between `and`, `or`, and `unless`. - Keep the existing NULL filtering and join behavior. - Cover all three operators in the plan-shape test. - Keep the original 8,000-series baseline workload. - Add a sparse fan-in workload with 1,000 matching groups and four physical replicas per group, with `replica` excluded by `on(instance)`. This targets the general set-operator path. The exact-group fast path is separate. ## Checks - Verified that `groupBitOr` is registered for integer inputs and that the `ForEach` combinator accepts array arguments. - Updated the plan-shape checks for `and`, `or`, and `unless` to require `groupBitOrForEach` and reject `countForEach`. - Existing end-to-end set-operator coverage continues to exercise mixed, NULL, and missing-step behavior. ## Benchmark The checked-in workload contains two variants, each using 300 query steps: - Baseline: 8,000 series with one series per matching group. - Sparse fan-in: 8,000 series with four replicas per matching group and staggered 50% sample presence. Queries match on `instance` while retaining `replica` in the physical labels. The second variant exercises the actual per-step presence reduction across multiple rows in each `on(...)` group. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Use compact presence masks for PromQL set operators.

signal.title: Add VALID FOR clause for users and credentials
signal.text: We support `VALID UNTIL` for users and credentials. This adds `VALID FOR <interval>` as a convenience shorthand. Instead of an absolute date and time, `VALID FOR` accepts an interval, and the expiration deadline is computed as the current time plus that interval at the moment the query is executed. The result is stored in the `VALID UNTIL` form, so `SHOW CREATE USER` always displays the resolved absolute deadline. It can be used everywhere `VALID UNTIL` can - at the user level and per authentication method, in both `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER`. Examples: ```sql CREATE USER u1 VALID FOR INTERVAL 1 DAY; CREATE USER u2 IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x' VALID FOR INTERVAL 3 MONTH; ALTER USER u1 VALID FOR INTERVAL 1 DAY + INTERVAL 12 HOUR; ``` Implementation notes: the current time is injected as a literal (rather than using `now`, which is non-deterministic and would not fold to a constant expression), and the deadline is computed with `toDateTime64` so that large intervals saturate at the `DateTime64` upper bound instead of overflowing the year-2106 boundary of `DateTime`. Note on the system table schema: to represent deadlines beyond the year 2106 exactly, the `valid_until` column of `system.users` changes from `Array(DateTime)` to `Array(DateTime64(0))`. This is a backward-incompatible change of a documented system table for tooling that introspects the column type; the values themselves keep second precision. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `VALID FOR <interval>` clause to `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER` as a shorthand for `VALID UNTIL`. The expiration deadline is computed as the current time plus the given interval at query execution time and stored in the `VALID UNTIL` form. The `valid_until` column of the `system.users` table now has the type `Array(DateTime64(0))` instead of `Array(DateTime)`, so that deadlines beyond the year 2106 are represented exactly; tooling that reads this column should handle the new type. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110171&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110171](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110171+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Cache the finalized cardinality in `uniq_v2` statistics
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113038 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up query planning when `uniq_v2` column statistics are used. The estimated number of distinct values is now cached instead of being recomputed on every request, which query planning issues many times per query. This is most visible on aarch64. Closes #113038. ### Description `IStatistics::estimateCardinality` is a pure function of the aggregate state, but it was recomputed on every call, and planning calls it many times per query: once per column with statistics in `ConditionSelectivityEstimator::estimateRelationProfileImpl`, which `MergeTreeWhereOptimizer` invokes once per condition group. For `uniq_v2` that recomputation is expensive. `uniq_v2` is `uniqCombined64` with `K = 12`, which selects the fully functional `Denominator` specialization whose `get` (`src/Common/HyperLogLogCounter.h:180-189`) walks all 54 rank buckets in `long double`. On aarch64 that is software binary128, so every step compiles to `__multf3` / `__floatunsitf` / `__addtf3` libcalls; on x86-64 it is native x87 arithmetic. That is why the regression is aarch64 only. Since 26.7 the default `auto_statistics_types` includes `uniq_v2`. The fix memoizes the finalized value in the object owning the state, as `cardinality + 1` so `0` means "not computed yet" without reserving a representable cardinality as a sentinel (0 distinct values is legal for an all NULL column). The member is a `mutable std::atomic<UInt64>` because the estimator is shared between concurrent queries; relaxed ordering suffices as all racers compute the identical value. On this PR's own arm_release Performance Comparison, `JoinOptimizeMicroseconds` drops 73% on TPC-DS Q14 and 63% on TPC-H Q20, the two queries in the report, with `server_time` -31% and -51%. Estimates and the chosen plan are unchanged (1206 `system.parts_columns` estimate rows and the `EXPLAIN indexes=1` output of a 6 way join are byte identical). The analysis, patch direction and aarch64 measurements are @ egor-click's.

signal.title: Wrong result: optimize_trivial_count_query makes count(arrayJoin(arr)) return the table's row count instead of the number of array elements
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe what's wrong - With the default `optimize_trivial_count_query = 1`, `SELECT count(arrayJoin(arr)) FROM t` returns the number of rows in the table instead of the number of array elements. - arrayJoin is a row-multiplying operator, so the aggregate must observe the post-expansion stream. The trivial-count optimization replaces the entire table read with a stored row counter and never evaluates count's argument, so the ARRAY JOIN expansion is silently dropped. No error, no warning. - The optimization rests on the premise "the number of rows the aggregate sees equals the number of rows stored in the table." That holds for `count()`, `count(1)` and `count(non_nullable_col)`, but arrayJoin breaks it, and nothing in the guard list checks for it. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce - https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/a93a2cb4-e0f1-450b-a97e-0acef509da3b ``` ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬──────────┐ │ Query │ Result │ Correct? │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(arrayJoin(A)) │ 2 │ ✗ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(arrayJoin(A)) SETTINGS optimize_trivial_count_query = 0 │ 5 │ ✓ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(*) FROM (SELECT arrayJoin(A) ...) │ 5 │ ✓ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ sum(length(A)) │ 5 │ ✓ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴──────────┘ ``` ### Expected behavior - The `count(arrayJoin(A))` should return the total number of array elements across all rows, equivalent to sum(length(A)). ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signal.title: Push subcolumn reads into subqueries
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/75538 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/92455 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Read only the requested subcolumns of columns exported by subqueries, CTEs and views instead of the whole columns. For example, `SELECT data.a FROM (SELECT * FROM table)` with a `JSON` column `data` now reads only the subcolumn `data.a` from the table. Controlled by the new setting `optimize_push_subcolumns_into_subqueries` (enabled by default). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) --- When a subcolumn of a column exported by a subquery is requested, it is resolved into the `getSubcolumn` function over the whole column: `SELECT data.a FROM (SELECT * FROM test)` reads the whole `data` column from the table and extracts the subcolumn afterwards. The new query tree pass `PushSubcolumnsIntoSubqueries` adds the subcolumn to the subquery projection and replaces the `getSubcolumn` function with a reference to it. If the whole column is not used anywhere else, it is then removed from the subquery projection by the subsequent `RemoveUnusedProjectionColumns` pass, so only the subcolumn is read from the table. The pushdown works through several levels of subqueries, CTEs and views, and also applies to `Tuple`, `Nullable`, `Array` and other types with subcolumns. `UNION ALL` subqueries are supported: the subcolumn is added to every branch at the same position, all-or-nothing, and only when the branch types match exactly (the subcolumn of the least supertype is not guaranteed to be the supertype of the branch subcolumns). The `DISTINCT`, `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` modes deduplicate or match rows over all projection columns, so such subqueries are not rewritten (nor are recursive CTEs). The pushdown is skipped when it could change the query result: - when the subquery uses `DISTINCT`, `GROUP BY`, aggregate functions, or `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL` (an added projection column would change the result or would not be valid); - when the subquery is on a side of a `JOIN` that can be filled with default values for non-matched rows (`getSubcolumn` of a default value is not always equal to the default value of the subcolumn type, e.g. for the `null` subcolumn of `Nullable` columns); a shared subquery node (an ordinary CTE referenced several times) found in any such position is ineligible for all of its occurrences; - in the outer query with aggregation, an occurrence of `getSubcolumn` is only replaced when it is evaluated before the aggregation step (`WHERE`, `JOIN ON`, arguments of aggregate functions) or when the whole expression is an aggregation key; - when the column types diverge, e.g. under `join_use_nulls` or `group_by_use_nulls`; - when the whole column is also read in the outer query, including uses by correlated subqueries and uses under a different exported name of the same physical column (`SELECT tup AS x, tup FROM t`, or a trivial `ALIAS` storage column next to its base column), and uses of an exported column the pushed subcolumn is a part of (`SELECT x.b, tup FROM (SELECT tup.a AS x, tup FROM t)`, where the live `tup` export already reads everything `tup.a.b` reads; an export of a sibling or of a deeper subcolumn does not block the pushdown, it reads less than the whole column): the subquery would then read both the whole column and the subcolumn from the table, while extracting the subcolumn from the already read column is cheaper. For a `UNION ALL` target the alias equivalence of exported names is detected in every branch (the pushdown is applied to all branches or to none), so a single branch exporting the same physical column under another name that stays alive blocks the rewrite. The decision counts only sibling subcolumns that are validated as actually pushable into the target (in a side-effect-free dry run): when two subcolumns of the same exported column are requested and only one of them can be pushed (e.g. the other is shadowed by a same-named storage column inside the subquery), nothing is pushed, since the unpushable sibling keeps the whole column alive. - for references of a reused `MATERIALIZED` CTE (`enable_materialized_cte`): the temporary table serves all references of the CTE, so pruning the parent column there would require proving that no reference needs the whole column. Single-use materialized CTEs are inlined by the analyzer and take the ordinary subquery path (subcolumn reads over materialized CTEs are currently broken on master independently of this change, see https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113623). Subqueries spelled with an alias list, e.g. `SELECT x.a FROM (SELECT json FROM t) AS s(x)`, are supported. Trivial `ALIAS` columns (an `ALIAS` whose body is just another column of the same table, possibly chained) exported by a subquery are followed down to the underlying storage column. A subquery can also export a derived subcolumn (e.g. `SELECT json.a AS x FROM ...` over a deeper subquery keeps a `getSubcolumn(json, 'a')` projection expression); reading a subcolumn of such an export composes the paths (`a` + `b` -> `a.b`), so the pushdown continues through derived exports down to the base table. Conversely, when no name of such an alias-equivalent class of exports remains referenced in the outer queries, the never-referenced sibling exports are dead together with the replaced ones (all of them are removed by `RemoveUnusedProjectionColumns`), so they do not block the pushdown through the deeper levels of subqueries; the alias-equivalent classes are taken from every branch of a `UNION ALL` target.

signal.title: Silk fibers integration
signal.text: Splits the silk runtime integration out of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111275, so that it can be reviewed on its own. This adds the plumbing that lets ClickHouse run work on [silk](https://github.com/ClickHouse/silk) fibers, without yet putting any subsystem on them. - `Silk::initializeFiberScheduler` / `Silk::destroyFiberScheduler`, called by the server when the `enable_silk_runtime` server setting is enabled. The fiber stack size is configurable through the `silk.fiber_stack_size` configuration key (320 KiB by default, which leaves enough room for OpenSSL handshakes). - `FiberLocal` - fiber-local storage. A fiber can migrate between operating-system threads, so it must not observe another fiber's `thread_local` state; the values of the registered slots are swapped in and out on every fiber switch instead. `current_thread` (`ThreadStatus`), the OpenTelemetry tracing context, and the memory-tracker and exception blockers are moved to it. - The silk thread-local-storage sanitizer: an LLVM pass in `utils/silk-thread-local-storage-sanitizer` that instruments every `thread_local` access and aborts when a fiber touches raw thread-local storage. Without it, a variable that was not migrated to `FiberLocal` produces silent corruption rather than a diagnostic. It is enabled in the debug and ASan CI builds. - `Silk::ConnectionPool` and `Silk::streamSocketFactory` - a `Connection` pool and a socket factory that suspend the calling fiber instead of blocking the operating-system thread. `PoolBase` and `ConnectionPool` are templated on the lock and the condition variable to make that possible, and `ConnectionPool` stays an alias of the `std::mutex` instantiation, so the existing call sites are unchanged. - Memory that the runtime maps outside the C++ heap - fiber stacks and `io_uring` rings - is charged to `total_memory_tracker` through silk's mmap accounting hooks. - The low-level silk runtime counters are exported to `system.asynchronous_metrics` under a `Silk` prefix. - `Common/Fiber.h` and `Common/FiberStack.h` are renamed to `Common/StackfulCoroutine.h` and `Common/CoroutineStack.h`. They implement the boost-context coroutines used by `AsyncTaskExecutor`, which are unrelated to silk fibers, and having two different things called "fiber" in the same codebase is confusing. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111275 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added experimental support for the [silk](https://github.com/ClickHouse/silk) fiber runtime, enabled with the `enable_silk_runtime` server setting. When it is enabled, the server initializes the silk fiber scheduler at startup, so that subsystems supporting it can run their jobs on fibers instead of occupying an operating-system thread while waiting for I/O. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112667&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112667](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112667+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Promote exponentialTimeDecayed window-functions to aggregate-functions
signal.text: ## Motivation `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` already exist and are documented as aggregate functions, but their current implementation is a special window-function implementation in `WindowTransform`. They do not provide mergeable aggregate states that can be persisted and combined with aggregate combinators such as `-State` and `-Merge`. This prevents incremental time-decayed aggregation in engines such as `AggregatingMergeTree`: data has to be evaluated through the window path instead of being aggregated independently in multiple batches and merged later. This PR adds regular, mergeable aggregate implementations for those three names while preserving the existing window implementation and its behavior. ## What changes For the regular aggregate form, each state keeps the weighted sum and sum of weights at the greatest timestamp observed by that state, plus that timestamp. When a row or another state has an older anchor, it is moved to the newer anchor with: `exp((older_time - newer_time) / decay_length)` The existing semantics are unchanged: `decay_length` is the interval after which a contribution has weight `1/e`. It is not a half-life. With the default `exponential_time_decay_aggregate_function_calculation_budget = 0`, the state representation makes independently built states mergeable with the same calculation. Input rows do not need to be timestamp ordered, and different row orders and batch distributions produce the same mathematical result subject to normal `Float64` rounding. A positive calculation budget opts into approximate aggregation: it is the maximum contribution age measured in decay lengths. Older rows or states are discarded before evaluating `exp`, improving performance when their remaining weight is not useful. Approximate results near the cutoff can depend on row order or merge grouping. The aggregate forms accept numeric timestamps, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64`. ### Finalized decaying values The sum and count aggregate forms return the experimental parameterized type: `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` The decay length is part of the type. Its tuple-compatible storage is canonicalized as `(sign, signed_unit_time, decay_length)`, where `unit_time = anchor_time + decay_length * ln(abs(value))` is the timestamp at which the curve has unit magnitude and `signed_unit_time = sign * unit_time`. Zero has the canonical form `(0, 0, decay_length)`. This representation makes native sorting and relative comparisons match the curve values at any common timestamp for values with the same decay length. Comparisons across different decay lengths are rejected. The redundant decay-length marker is checked against the type parameter when a value is evaluated or combined, preventing incompatible values from being silently mixed through layout-compatible custom-tuple paths. Values can be constructed/aggregated with: `exponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)(value, time)` A finalized decaying value can be aggregated again without repeating the decay length: `exponentialTimeDecayedSum(decaying_value)` When the input is `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)`, the decay length is inferred from its type and the result has the same parameterized type. This gives the closure property required by `SimpleAggregateFunction`, so it can be stored directly in `AggregatingMergeTree`: ```sql CREATE TABLE decaying ( key UInt64, value SimpleAggregateFunction( exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(60)) ) ENGINE = AggregatingMergeTree ORDER BY key; ``` The scalar helpers are: - `exponentialTimeDecayingValueAt(value, target_time)` — evaluate the same exponential curve before, at, or after its anchor, including at `now()` / `now64()`; - `exponentialTimeDecayingDecayLength(value)` — read the decay length encoded in the type; - `exponentialTimeDecayingAdd(a, b)` — combine two values at their greatest anchor. The `+` operator uses the same addition logic for two decaying values. Different decay lengths are rejected. `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg` continues to return `Float64`. All new regular-aggregate and decaying-value behavior is experimental and disabled by default behind `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. ## Effect on the existing window functions The existing window-function implementation remains in place. Window calls continue to use the previous frame-based implementation, retain their `Float64` result, and do not require `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. This PR also corrects the function documentation to consistently call the parameter `decay_length` and describe the existing `1/e` decay semantics. ## Correctness and tests Stateless tests cover: - regular aggregation and `-State` / `-Merge`; - direct aggregation of finalized `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` values; - direct `SimpleAggregateFunction(exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length))` storage and merging in `AggregatingMergeTree`; - different input orders and batch distributions, including reproducibly generated randomized inputs; - numeric, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64` time arguments; - the experimental setting in enabled and disabled forms; - forward and backward value evaluation, addition, decay-length lookup, and rejection of inconsistent/mixed decay lengths; - native sorting and all relative comparison operators, including negative, zero, and positive values; - exact-default, bounded-cutoff, and state-merge calculation-budget behavior; - signed values, empty input, nullable paths, canonical reconstruction, and large-time decay/underflow cases. The implementation uses `Float64` accumulation. As with other floating-point reductions, large signed values that nearly cancel can expose order/grouping-dependent rounding. Stronger reproducibility for that case is intentionally left for a separate improvement if feedback shows it is important in practice. ## Benchmark status There are no end-to-end ClickHouse benchmark results yet. The benchmark already posted in the PR discussion is a standalone C++ microbenchmark of the decay formulas. It showed the expected benefit from avoiding redundant `exp` evaluations in the merge/value paths, but it excludes ClickHouse aggregation, column access, serialization, scheduling, and `AggregatingMergeTree` overhead and therefore is not evidence of end-to-end query throughput. An end-to-end benchmark, preferably a ClickHouse performance test covering state creation and state merging, is still pending. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add experimental mergeable `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` aggregate forms, including a parameterized decaying-value type that can be stored directly with `SimpleAggregateFunction` in `AggregatingMergeTree`, while preserving the existing window-function behavior. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110934&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110934](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110934+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
