signal.title: Fix an infinite uncancellable loop in `hop` and `windowID` on an interval whose span wraps modulo 2^32
signal.text: <!-- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an infinite, uncancellable loop in functions `hop` and `windowID` when the span of an interval argument in seconds is a multiple of 2^32 (for example, `toIntervalDay(2147483648)`): the wrapped subtraction dodged the time-overflow check, and with constant arguments the loop ran at analysis time, where the query could not even be killed. The same interval could also spin a background thread of a `WINDOW VIEW` forever; such a window view is now rejected at creation. An interval like `toIntervalDay(2147483648)` spans `2^31 * 86400 = 43200 * 2^32` seconds, so subtracting it in the wrapping `UInt32` arithmetic of `AddTime` is a no-op: `wstart == wend`, which dodges the `wstart > wend` time-overflow guard added by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/61523. The window-searching loop of `executeHop` then decrements `wend` by one hop at a time past zero, where it wraps back to ~2^32 while staying congruent to its starting point modulo `gcd(86400, 2^32) = 128`, never hits a value `<= time`, and spins forever. With constant arguments the loop runs during constant folding in `QueryAnalyzer::resolveFunction`, at analysis time, where nothing checks the cancellation. The same loop shape exists in `executeHopSlice` (`windowID`). The fix makes the guard `wstart >= wend` - subtracting a whole positive interval must change the time, and equality only happens on a wrap - and adds a wrap check to the loop itself (the new `wend` coming out greater than the old one throws the same `Time overflow` error), which terminates every wrapping loop regardless of how the pre-loop values were corrupted. The new test `04891_time_window_functions_wrapped_interval_overflow` covers both functions with the fuzzed arguments (both hung before the fix) and checks that a sane `hop`/`windowID` is unaffected. The same "a positive interval must move the time" invariant is relied upon by the loops which advance the window bounds of a `WINDOW VIEW`: the two watermark loops of `updateMaxWatermark`, the window splitting of `getNewBlocks`, and the fire loop of `threadFuncFireProc`. A processing time window view such as `GROUP BY tumble(now(), toIntervalDay(2147483648))` spun in the fire loop forever - `slide_interval` is `0`, so `next_fire_signal` never advances - in a background thread, while holding `fire_signal_mutex`. All these loops now advance through `addTimeStrictly`, which requires the time to move and throws `Time overflow in the window view` otherwise. Since such a window is not representable at all, `innerQueryParser` also rejects the window, slide and slice intervals which cannot move the time, so the window view fails at creation. This is covered by the new test `04892_window_view_wrapped_interval_overflow`. Found by the AST fuzzer in the stress test of a CI run of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112930 (hung check): [Stress test (arm_debug) report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112930&sha=1c5bf0b613146bd6666b6d2bd2be55f539f6c0d8&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_debug%29). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114605 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/61521 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/61523

signal.title: `timeSeriesRange`/`timeSeriesFromGrid` silently truncate `Int64`/`UInt64` step to lower 32 bits for `DateTime`/`UInt32` timestamps
signal.text: _Found via ClickGap automated review. Please close or comment if this is incorrect or needs adjustment._ _Retrospective finding from a historical scan of [PR #85435](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/85435) (merged 2025-08-13). Confirmed on current codebase — close with a note if already fixed._ ### Describe what's wrong When timestamps are `DateTime` or `UInt32` and the user passes a step value larger than `INT32_MAX` (e.g. an `Int64`/`UInt64` step of 4294967297), the function silently keeps only the lower 32 bits of the step instead of either erroring out or honoring the user's request. `SELECT timeSeriesRange(toDateTime('2025-01-01 00:00:00'), toDateTime('2025-01-01 00:00:10'), CAST(4294967297 AS Int64))` returns 11 timestamps (as if step=1) instead of the correct 1-element array. **Root cause:** src/Functions/TimeSeries/timeSeriesRange.cpp:264 — `auto step = static_cast<IntervalType>(step_raw);` performs an unchecked narrowing cast from `Int64` to `Int32` (when `IntervalType=Int32`). The function accepts arbitrary `isNativeInteger` step types at parse-time but only protects the multiplication step at line 262, not this final narrowing cast. **Why we believe this is a bug:** `FunctionTimeSeriesRange::doExecute` (src/Functions/TimeSeries/timeSeriesRange.cpp:185) → row loop at :249 → step computation at :261-264. `common::mulOverflow` (line 262) only guards the `step_column.getInt(i) * step_multiplier` multiplication; the subsequent `auto step = static_cast<IntervalType>(step_raw);` at line 264 narrows `Int64 step_raw` to `Int32` for the `UInt32`/`DateTime` template instantiation (`doExecute<UInt32, Int32>` at :170) without any range check. When `step_raw` has high bits set but the lower 32 bits are a non-zero positive value, the truncated step quietly differs from what the user passed and the subsequent `step <= 0` check at :272 does not catch it. `checkDataTypes` at :97 explicitly admits `isNativeInteger(step_type)` — i.e. UInt64/Int64 — so users CAN pass these types. **Affected locations:** - `src/Functions/TimeSeries/timeSeriesRange.cpp:264` — `auto step = static_cast<IntervalType>(step_raw);` — silent truncation when IntervalType=Int32 - `src/Functions/TimeSeries/timeSeriesRange.cpp:170` — `doExecute<UInt32, Int32>` instantiation — the IntervalType=Int32 path that exhibits the truncation - `src/Functions/TimeSeries/timeSeriesRange.cpp:97` — type check accepts `isNativeInteger(step_type)` — admits UInt64/Int64 step values that can exceed Int32 range **Impact:** Silent wrong results from a publicly registered, non-experimental function. Both `timeSeriesRange` and `timeSeriesFromGrid` (which share this template) produce arrays of unexpected length for `DateTime`/`UInt32` timestamps when the step value's lower 32 bits are positive but the value itself exceeds `INT32_MAX`. For `timeSeriesFromGrid` with a `values` array, this can also turn a successful call into a `BAD_ARGUMENTS` 'Number of values doesn't match number of steps' error or vice versa, depending on the truncated step. ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `430a15348ad`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Test: timeSeriesRange/timeSeriesFromGrid silently truncate Int64 step values to Int32 for DateTime/UInt32 timestamps -- Covers: src/Functions/TimeSeries/timeSeriesRange.cpp:264 — `static_cast<IntervalType>(step_raw)` for IntervalType=Int32 silently truncates without overflow check -- For DateTime/UInt32 timestamps the IntervalType is Int32 — large steps that fit in Int64 step_raw -- get truncated to their lower 32 bits, producing wrong number of timestamps without any error. -- The mulOverflow check at line 262 only checks the multiplication, not the cast at line 264. -- Step = 4294967297 (= 2^32 + 1). Lower 32 bits = 1. Truncated to step=1. -- Expected: either error (DECIMAL_OVERFLOW) or 1-element array (since step >> end-start). -- Actual (buggy): 11 timestamps as if step=1. SELECT timeSeriesRange(toDateTime('2025-01-01 00:00:00'), toDateTime('2025-01-01 00:00:10'), CAST(4294967297 AS Int64)); -- Step = 8589934594 (= 2*2^32 + 2). Lower 32 bits = 2. Truncated to step=2. -- Expected: error or 1-element array. -- Actual (buggy): 6 timestamps as if step=2. SELECT timeSeriesRange(toDateTime('2025-01-01 00:00:00'), toDateTime('2025-01-01 00:00:10'), CAST(8589934594 AS Int64)); -- Step = 4294967296 (= 2^32). Lower 32 bits = 0. Truncated to step=0. -- Caught by `if (step <= 0)` check — but this is by accident, not by design. SELECT timeSeriesRange(toDateTime('2025-01-01 00:00:00'), toDateTime('2025-01-01 00:00:10'), CAST(4294967296 AS Int64)); -- {serverError BAD_ARGUMENTS} -- Compare: same query with DateTime64 timestamps (IntervalType=Decimal64=Int64) — no truncation, gives the correct result. SELECT timeSeriesRange(toDateTime64('2025-01-01 00:00:00', 0), toDateTime64('2025-01-01 00:00:10', 0), CAST(4294967297 AS Int64)); ``` [Try it on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/90602391-2bec-41e7-b4bc-5f155cd50b1f) ### Expected behavior ``` ['2025-01-01 00:00:00'] ['2025-01-01 00:00:00'] ['2025-01-01 00:00:00'] ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` ['2025-01-01 00:00:00','2025-01-01 00:00:01','2025-01-01 00:00:02','2025-01-01 00:00:03','2025-01-01 00:00:04','2025-01-01 00:00:05','2025-01-01 00:00:06','2025-01-01 00:00:07','2025-01-01 00:00:08','2025-01-01 00:00:09','2025-01-01 00:00:10'] ['2025-01-01 00:00:00','2025-01-01 00:00:02','2025-01-01 00:00:04','2025-01-01 00:00:06','2025-01-01 00:00:08','2025-01-01 00:00:10'] ['2025-01-01 00:00:00' ``` ### Additional context **Open risks:** - The same narrowing-cast pattern at lines 254 (`start_timestamp`) and 259 (`end_timestamp`) can theoretically truncate `Int64` raw values too; in practice the input column types are constrained so values fit, but this is fragile. - `timeSeriesFromGrid` can return mis-aligned (timestamp, value) pairs when steps are truncated, since `num_values != num_steps` might be true for the user's requested step but false for the truncated step — masking real input errors. **Suggested fix:** After the `mulOverflow` check at line 262 (and similarly for `start_timestamp_raw`/`end_timestamp_raw` at lines 252/257), add a range check before the narrowing cast: `if (step_raw > std::numeric_limits<IntervalType>::max() || step_raw < std::numeric_limits<IntervalType>::min()) throw Exception(ErrorCodes::DECIMAL_OVERFLOW, ...)`. Alternatively widen `IntervalType` to `Int64` for the UInt32-timestamp path or reject step values exceeding `INT32_MAX` upfront in `checkDataTypes`. **Analysis details:** Confidence HIGH | Severity P1 | Testability: `STATELESS_SQL` Found during automated review of [PR #85435](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/85435). --- _ClickGapAI · Confidence: HIGH · Severity: P1 · Finding: `h_pr85435_step_truncation`_

signal.title: Expression in SELECT evaluated on rows filtered out by WHERE when JOIN runtime filter fuses with Prewhere Actions (regression 26.1 → 26.2)
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe what's wrong Since 26.2, a SELECT expression that is only valid for rows matching a WHERE predicate can throw because the SELECT expression and its WHERE guard are fused into sibling nodes in a single Prewhere Actions step. The SELECT expression is evaluated on rows that the WHERE clause should have already eliminated. This is a regression introduced by #95838, which postpones PREWHERE optimization until after JOIN runtime filter construction, causing the runtime filter, WHERE predicates, and SELECT expressions to all be folded into the same ActionsDAG step. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Reproducer: https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/bfadcea1-3c93-4960-9d16-71db35056613 ``` CREATE TABLE t (a UInt8, s String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'x'); SELECT toUInt64(s) AS k FROM t INNER JOIN (SELECT toUInt64(1) AS wh) AS r2 ON toUInt64(s) = r2.wh WHERE a = 1 AND s LIKE '1%'; ``` Does not reproduce on 26.1. Reproducer on 26.2 can be mitigated by disabling the optimization: `SETTINGS enable_join_runtime_filters = 0` ### Expected behavior Queries should always follow the "filter before project" concept in the SQL standard ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Received exception from server (version 26.2.1): Code: 6. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:9000. DB::Exception: Cannot parse string 'x' as UInt64: syntax error at begin of string. Note: there are toUInt64OrZero and toUInt64OrNull functions, which returns zero/NULL instead of throwing exception: while executing 'FUNCTION toUInt64(s : 0) -> toUInt64(__table1.s) UInt64 : 4': While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder). (CANNOT_PARSE_TEXT) (query: SELECT toUInt64(s) AS k FROM t INNER JOIN (SELECT toUInt64(1) AS wh) AS r2 ON toUInt64(s) = r2.wh WHERE a = 1 AND s LIKE '1%';) ``` ### Related issues and pull requests Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/95838 ### Additional context #95838 (26.2) postponed PREWHERE optimisation to run after JOIN runtime filter construction so that runtime filters can also be pushed to PREWHERE. The side effect is that the runtime filter, the WHERE conditions, and the SELECT expressions are fused into a single Actions step as siblings at the table scan level: ``` FUNCTION like(s, '1%') -- WHERE guard FUNCTION toUInt64(s) -- SELECT expression — should only run on rows surviving the guard ``` Because they are siblings, toUInt64(s) runs on every row before the LIKE filter eliminates them.

signal.title: Add two-model mode to continue-all-prs script
signal.text: Adds an optional two-model workflow to `continue-all-prs.sh`. A cheaper triage model checks the pull request first and can update it to the latest base branch or perform a clean base-branch merge. Work requiring source, test, or documentation changes is described in a structured handoff and continued by a fresh session using the coding model in the same worktree. The existing single-model mode remains unchanged. The status bar reports triage and coding-model spending separately, and the per-PR timeout is shared between both models, and Codex usage is priced according to the model active for each turn. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not applicable.

signal.title: Wrong DISTINCT results (and debug abort) with partial_merge JOIN + optimize_distinct_in_order — Equal values are not contiguous
signal.text: # `Logical error: 'Equal values are not contiguous within the range assumed to be sorted'` — `DISTINCT` in order over `partial_merge` JOIN (wrong results in release) ## Summary With `join_algorithm = 'partial_merge'` (or `'prefer_partial_merge'`), the query plan assumes the join preserves the left stream's sort order and applies the pre-`DISTINCT` stage as `DistinctSortedStreamTransform` (`optimize_distinct_in_order`, default on). But `PartialMergeJoin` matches the left stream against the right side **per right block**: when the right table has more than one block/part, the left key ranges are re-emitted for each right block, so equal left-key values are no longer contiguous in the joined stream. - **Debug builds**: `chassert` in `findEqualRangeEndAssumeSorted.h:88` fires → `Logical error: 'Equal values are not contiguous within the range assumed to be sorted'` → abort. Stack: `DistinctSortedStreamTransform::transform → getEqualRangeEndAssumeSorted → checkEqualRangeEndAssumeSorted (ColumnVector<UInt32>)`. - **Release builds**: the check is compiled out, so `DistinctSortedStreamTransform` computes equal-ranges on a stream that violates its precondition — **`DISTINCT` can silently return duplicate rows** (wrong result). Found by the AST-fuzzer correctness-oracle campaign (PR #99980): two independent fleet hits (2026-06-29 `DISTINCT … FULL OUTER JOIN … QUALIFY`, 2026-06-30 `DISTINCT … INNER JOIN … ORDER BY`), minimized from the second snapshot. ## Minimal repro Flaky by nature (depends on chunk arrival order across the two right-side parts; `max_threads = 4` observed rate ≈ 40–50%, single attempt often enough on a debug build). Run a few times: ```sql CREATE TABLE t1 (x UInt32, y UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (x, y); CREATE TABLE t2 (x UInt32, y UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (x, y); INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (0,0),(1,10),(2,20),(3,30),(4,40); INSERT INTO t2 VALUES (2,21),(2,22),(4,41); INSERT INTO t2 VALUES (0,0),(4,42),(5,50); -- second part is load-bearing SET join_algorithm = 'prefer_partial_merge'; SELECT DISTINCT t1.*, t2.* FROM t1 INNER JOIN t2 ON intDiv(t2.y, 2147483647) = toUInt64(t1.x); ``` Also reproduces in `clickhouse-local` with the same script (abort, exit 134). The original fuzzed query had a baroque `ON and(if(...), key = key)` condition and an `ORDER BY … DESC NULLS LAST` — neither is needed (verified: pure-equality `ON` hits, no-`ORDER BY` hits). ## Mechanism (EXPLAIN PIPELINE) `prefer_partial_merge` (bug path): ``` DistinctTransform DistinctSortedStreamTransform × 2 <-- assumes sorted-by-left-prefix stream JoiningTransform × 2 2 → 1 <-- PartialMergeJoin MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder) × 2 <-- left read in order FillingRightJoinSide MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder) ``` `hash` (correct path): plain `DistinctTransform`, no in-order read, no sorted assumption. The left read is in `(x, y)` order and the plan carries that sort property through the join to justify `DistinctSortedStreamTransform`. `PartialMergeJoin` breaks the property: it processes the right side block-by-block and re-emits matching left ranges for each right block, so a left key that matches rows in two right blocks appears in two separate runs. Controls (each verified with a 10-attempt harness against the snapshot server): - `join_algorithm = 'hash'` → never reproduces (plain `DistinctTransform`). - `optimize_distinct_in_order = 0` → does not reproduce (MISS ×10). - `join_algorithm = 'partial_merge'` (strict) → reproduces, same as `prefer_partial_merge`. - `SELECT DISTINCT t1.*` only (no `t2` columns) → does not reproduce (MISS ×10); the `DISTINCT` set must include right-side columns. - Baroque original `ON and(if(...), key = key)` and the `ORDER BY … DESC NULLS LAST` → both unnecessary (pure-equality, no-`ORDER BY` variant reproduces). ## Environment - HEAD `01e08fd49182` (2026-06-28 master merge), debug build, aarch64. - Snapshot: `tmp/fuzz_lab/runs/merged7/crashes/inst-06-20260630-184002` (original), also `inst-12-20260629-115230` (same family, first sighting), `inst-05-20260701-012001` (`Sort order of blocks violated` — likely same root: a sort-order property claimed across `PartialMergeJoin` and violated downstream in a merge-sort transform instead of DISTINCT). ## Suggested fix direction `PartialMergeJoin` (and any join that rescans the left side per right block) must not report the left input's sort description as preserved on its output — the plan should either drop the sort property across it (forcing plain `DistinctTransform` / a re-sort before order-dependent consumers) or the join should be excluded from `optimize_distinct_in_order` / read-in-order propagation.

signal.title: Add a TOLERANCE clause to ASOF JOIN
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Use case `ASOF JOIN` currently matches each left row with the most recent right row at or before the left timestamp, with no way to cap how far back that match may reach. We would like an optional `TOLERANCE` clause that bounds the maximum time gap between the left key and the matched right key, so that only "recent enough" matches are returned and stale rows are excluded. This is a common requirement in time-series and financial analytics (for example transaction cost analysis, quote-to-trade enrichment, and sensor/state enrichment), where a match that is technically the latest available but minutes or hours old is misleading. **Current behavior** For a trade joined to the prevailing quote: ```sql SELECT t.time, t.symbol, t.price, q.bid, q.ask FROM trades AS t ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes AS q ON t.symbol = q.symbol AND t.time >= q.time ``` If the nearest preceding quote for a given trade is very old, `ASOF JOIN` still returns it. There is no built-in way to say "only match if the quote is within N units of the trade". ### Describe the solution you'd like An optional `TOLERANCE` clause on `ASOF JOIN` that accepts an interval (or numeric) value and restricts matches to those where the difference between the left and matched right key is within the given bound. Suggested syntax (open to alternatives): ```sql SELECT t.time, t.symbol, t.price, q.bid, q.ask FROM trades AS t ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes AS q ON t.symbol = q.symbol AND t.time >= q.time TOLERANCE INTERVAL 10 SECOND ``` **Semantics**: a left row at `t.time` matches a right row at `q.time` only if both hold: - `q.time <= t.time` (existing ASOF inequality) - `t.time - q.time <= tolerance` When no right row is within tolerance, the behavior should follow the join type: `ASOF LEFT JOIN` returns the left row with NULL/default right columns, `ASOF JOIN` (inner) drops the row. ### Describe alternatives you've considered The gap can be filtered after the join: ```sql SELECT t.time, t.symbol, t.price, q.bid, q.ask FROM trades AS t ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes AS q ON t.symbol = q.symbol AND t.time >= q.time WHERE t.time - q.time <= INTERVAL 1 SECOND ``` This is correct but can be slower than necessary. The join still scans backward to find a match that the `WHERE` clause then discards. With a native tolerance, the backward scan can stop as soon as a right row is older than the left row by more than the tolerance, since no earlier row can qualify. This early termination is both a **correctness** convenience and a **performance** win, especially on sparse or illiquid keys where the scan would otherwise reach far back. ### Additional context This capability is well established, which gives a clear reference for expected semantics.
signal.author: ayakovlev-clickhouse

signal.title: Mongo queries (wire protocol + dialect)
signal.text: Adds two ways to run MongoDB queries against ClickHouse: - a **wire protocol endpoint** (`mongo_port`), so MongoDB drivers and tools such as `pymongo` and `mongosh` can connect to ClickHouse as if it were a MongoDB server; - a **query dialect** (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`), so MongoDB shell syntax can be sent over the usual ClickHouse interfaces. A Mongo database maps onto a ClickHouse database, a collection onto a table, a document onto a row, and a nested field onto an `a.b` column. A collection created by the first `insert` gets one column per field of the first inserted document. The supported commands are `insert`, `find`, `count`, `update`, `delete`, `create`, `drop`, `createIndexes`, `listDatabases`, `listCollections`, `isMaster` and `saslStart`; only the `PLAIN` authentication mechanism is supported, because it is the only one that provides the cleartext password ClickHouse needs. Both are experimental and cover a subset of MongoDB. They are meant for pointing an existing MongoDB application at ClickHouse without rewriting its queries, not as a MongoDB replacement. The limitations are listed in `docs/en/interfaces/mongo.md`. Task: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58394 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol endpoint (the `mongo_port` server setting) and a MongoDB query dialect (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`) for basic collection operations.

signal.title: `rewrite_in_to_join` uses `equals` in WHERE losing IN's three-valued NULL logic
signal.text: _Found via ClickGap automated review. Please close or comment if this is incorrect or needs adjustment._ _Retrospective finding from a historical scan of [PR #83991](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/83991) (merged 2025-09-30). Confirmed on current codebase — close with a note if already fixed._ ### Describe what's wrong When `rewrite_in_to_join=1` and the LHS is a `Nullable` column, `NULL IN (subquery)` returns 0 instead of NULL, and `NULL NOT IN (subquery)` returns 1 instead of NULL. In a WHERE clause, `WHERE x NOT IN (subquery)` incorrectly includes rows where x IS NULL. **Root cause:** resolveFunction.cpp:613: the rewrite unconditionally uses `equals` for the WHERE comparison, but `equals` does not preserve IN's three-valued NULL logic. The `transform_null_in` setting is also not consulted. **Why we believe this is a bug:** `resolveFunction.cpp:613` → `FunctionNode("equals")` is used in the EXISTS WHERE clause. `equals(NULL, x)` returns NULL (falsy in WHERE), so EXISTS never matches NULL rows. But IN's semantics require `NULL IN (non-empty-set)` → NULL, not 0. **Affected locations:** - `src/Analyzer/Resolve/resolveFunction.cpp:613` — equals function used in EXISTS WHERE clause - `src/Analyzer/Resolve/resolveFunction.cpp:624` — equals result assigned to WHERE without NULL handling **Impact:** Wrong query results for anyone enabling the experimental `rewrite_in_to_join` setting with `Nullable` columns. `WHERE x NOT IN (subquery)` includes NULL rows that should be excluded. `transform_null_in=1` with NULLs in subquery returns 0 instead of 1. ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `513c9cc82b52`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Test: rewrite_in_to_join produces wrong results for Nullable columns -- Covers: src/Analyzer/Resolve/resolveFunction.cpp:613 (equals-based rewrite) SET enable_analyzer=1; SET rewrite_in_to_join=1; SET allow_experimental_correlated_subqueries=1; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_nullable_in; CREATE TABLE t_nullable_in (x Nullable(UInt64)) ENGINE=MergeTree() ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t_nullable_in VALUES (0), (1), (NULL), (5); -- IN as column expression: NULL should remain NULL, not become 0 SELECT x, x IN (SELECT number FROM numbers(3)) AS r FROM t_nullable_in ORDER BY x NULLS LAST; -- NOT IN in WHERE: NULL rows should NOT pass the filter SELECT x FROM t_nullable_in WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT number FROM numbers(3)) ORDER BY x NULLS LAST; -- NOT IN as column expression: NULL should remain NULL, not become 1 SELECT x, x NOT IN (SELECT number FROM numbers(3)) AS r FROM t_nullable_in ORDER BY x NULLS LAST; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_nullable_in; ``` [Try it on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/05e293f1-0bfd-45e6-969b-79caa58c759c) ### Expected behavior ``` 0 1 1 1 5 0 \N \N 5 0 0 1 0 5 1 \N \N ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 0 1 1 1 5 0 \N 0 5 \N 0 0 1 0 5 1 \N 1 ``` ### Additional context **Open risks:** - Same NULL issue likely affects multi-column Tuple IN with Nullable elements **Suggested fix:** Either skip the rewrite when the first argument's resolved type is `Nullable`, or replace `equals` with NULL-aware comparison logic (e.g., `isNotDistinctFrom` for the `transform_null_in=1` case, and preserving NULL result for `transform_null_in=0`). **Analysis details:** Confidence HIGH | Severity P1 | Testability: `STATELESS_SQL` Found during automated review of [PR #83991](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/83991). --- _ClickGapAI · Confidence: HIGH · Severity: P1 · Finding: `h_pr83991_001`_

signal.title: Fix LOGICAL_ERROR in DatabaseReplicatedDDLWorker with max_replication_lag_to_enqueue=0
signal.text: Reject `max_replication_lag_to_enqueue = 0` at parse time everywhere it can be supplied. `0` was never useful: it asks the post-recovery unsynced check `max_log_ptr + max_replication_lag_to_enqueue <= new_max_log_ptr` to be trivially true (the ZooKeeper counter is monotonically non-decreasing), which mis-flags a caught-up replica as unsynced and then trips `chassert(our_log_ptr < max_log_ptr)` in `DatabaseReplicatedDDLWorker::initAndCheckTask`, aborting the server on debug and sanitizer builds. Switching the setting type from `UInt64` to `NonZeroUInt64` lets the parser reject `0` from every source: `CREATE DATABASE ... SETTINGS`, the `<database_replicated>` server-config block, `ATTACH` replay, and upgrade-time replay of existing database metadata. The post-recovery comparison stays at the original `<=` because the bad value can no longer reach the worker. The smallest valid value is `1`. New regression test `04298_98823_replicated_zero_lag_assertion` checks both the rejection (`A setting's value has to be greater than 0`, BAD_ARGUMENTS) and the smallest valid value (`1`) going through the post-recovery DDL path that previously aborted. Adapted from the analysis in #100043. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reject `max_replication_lag_to_enqueue = 0` on `Replicated` databases. The value made the post-recovery unsynced check trivially true and aborted the server with `LOGICAL_ERROR` in debug and sanitizer builds. `0` is now rejected at parse time with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` from every source (`CREATE DATABASE ... SETTINGS`, `<database_replicated>` server-config block, `ATTACH` replay, and upgrade-time replay of existing metadata). The smallest valid value is `1`. Closes #98823. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Fix LOGICAL_ERROR in join order optimizer for duplicate column names via merged expression
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`Left and right columns have same names`) in the join order optimizer that could be triggered by a comma join over a multi-table view when `query_plan_merge_expression_into_join` is enabled. ### Description No related open issue found. Found by the SQLancerPP nightly on master (server abort in the sanitizer build): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=3d31d8f59df88ee56b9b739f2eedb1b7a6acc6a4&name_0=NightlySQLancer&name_1=SQLancerPP The pre-reorder guard `joinGraphHasOverlappingColumnNames` flattens the join graph to check for duplicate qualified column names and skips reordering when it finds any. It peeled only passthrough expression steps. The optimizer's `addChildQueryGraph` also peels a non-passthrough expression step and flattens the child join beneath it when `query_plan_merge_expression_into_join` is enabled. So the guard saw one relation fewer than the optimizer produced and missed a duplicated name (`__table3.c1`); reconstructing the reordered join with `JoinExpressionActions` then threw the error. Fix: make the guard peel expression steps the same way as `addChildQueryGraph`, so it inspects the same relation set the optimizer builds and correctly skips reordering when names overlap. Known residual, not addressed here: this guard is a read-only mirror of `buildQueryGraph`, and it does not replicate the `get_exposed_columns` side-clash suppression that keeps a join boundary collapsed. That predates this PR (the mirror landed in `2ddbf356499caa5`, the clash check a week later in `69f802454c23ee6`) and can only cost a reordering, never correctness. I have not found a query where the two disagree, so I have left it for a separate change rather than adding an unexercised check here.

signal.title: Bound submodule cache population so it cannot kill the Config Workflow job
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114811 `Config Workflow` computes the workflow matrix, so when it dies no build and no test job is ever scheduled. On a submodule cache miss it clones 141 submodules inside its own `timeout=600` budget, and when that does not finish praktika SIGTERMs the job, silently dropping the whole matrix: the public `26.5` run at `f724d2da9360` recorded 4 checks against 102-155 on healthy commits. 7 occurrences over 7 refs in 30 days, including a release branch and three backport PRs. The function's error path is already deliberately non-fatal (`Status.OK`, cache hash left unset, dependent jobs clone from GitHub). That handler is not new here: it arrived with the cache itself in April, and a job-level SIGTERM is the one route that bypasses it. So this bounds the clone with `timeout -s KILL`, letting an overrun land in that existing handler, and sizes the job cap for its actual work: - step budget 600s, above p99 494.5s and the slowest population that currently succeeds (517s) - job cap `SUBMODULE_CACHE_POPULATE_TIMEOUT_SEC + 600`, i.e. 1200s by default, above 600 + 44 (tar and upload) + 184 (rest of the job) = 828s Deriving the cap keeps it above the step bound when that bound is overridden per repository; if the two were equal the job watchdog would fire first and re-inflict the failure above, so a test in `ci/tests/test_config_job_no_cidb.py` pins that ordering. `retries` is dropped because `Shell.check` applies `timeout` per retry, not as a total. A transient failure now costs a cache population instead of a retry: a lost population is non-fatal by design, and no retry occurred in any failing run. Verified by driving the real function both ways: a below-clone budget leaves the job alive with the hash unset, a generous one still populates the cache. YAML regeneration is byte-identical.

signal.title: Add PCAP input format for reading packet captures
signal.text: # Add PCAP input format for reading packet captures ## (Human) Introduction As someone who works with ClickHouse but also occasionally opens a pcap in Wireshark, I've always had a wish to be able to do some quick stats on a pcap using ClickHouse SQL. Especially for large files, I always thought it would also be nice to be able to persist them in a MergeTree, so they don't have to be re-scanned every time. So this is my first draft at making this a reality: adding PCAP as an (experimental) input format which can be read by Clickhouse directly (and consequently be ingested, as well). It currently only parses very basic stuff (mostly L2-L4), but this could be extended in the future (imagine having all Wireshark dissectors 😍 ) I realize this may be considered "unfinished" (in the sense: lacking features), but I wanted to open a PR and get feedback on the idea early on, to see if it was worth pursuing. Full transparency: this is basically 100% vibe-coded -- ideas and some design decisions are mine, but I didn't really write any code. Thanks Claude. In that spirit, here's the Claude-generated description including some notes that may be relevant to reviewers: ## AI-generated Overview Adds a `PCAP` input format that reads packet capture files (classic `pcap` and `pcapng`) and produces one row per packet with decoded L2–L4 fields — timestamp, lengths, link type, the ordered protocol chain, Ethernet/IPv4/IPv6/TCP/UDP header fields, the L4 payload, and the raw frame. Modelled structurally on the `DWARF` format. Parsing uses `libtins` for dissection and `libpcap` for reading the capture container, added as contrib submodules behind a new `USE_PCAP` flag (`libpcap` built offline-only with pre-generated BPF grammar/scanner; WPA2/ACK-tracking disabled to avoid OpenSSL and Boost.ICL). Includes documentation and a stateless test with small Wireshark sample captures. > Transparency note: this PR was vibe-coded with Claude (Anthropic `claude-opus-4-8`) in an agentic workflow, with human review and direction. The AI co-authorship is recorded via `Co-authored-by` trailers on the commits. ### Notes for reviewers - **New contrib submodules:** `libtins` (v4.5) and `libpcap` (1.10.5), gated behind `ENABLE_PCAP`/`USE_PCAP` (on by default with `ENABLE_LIBRARIES`). They use the upstream repositories directly (not ClickHouse forks). - **libpcap build:** built offline-only using the `null` capture backend (no live capture / remote / optional backends). Its BPF grammar/scanner are pre-generated with bison/flex and checked in under `contrib/libpcap-cmake/generated/` so the build needs no flex/bison. A hand-written `config.h` targets Linux/glibc. - **libtins build:** hand-written `config.h`; WPA2 decryption and ACK tracking are disabled to avoid pulling in OpenSSL and Boost.ICL for now. Deeper protocol dissection can be layered on later. - **Disabled-build safety:** the format is wrapped in `#if USE_PCAP` with empty registration stubs, so linking succeeds when the feature is off (e.g. fasttest builds with `ENABLE_LIBRARIES=0`). The stateless test is tagged `no-fasttest` for the same reason. - **Test fixtures license:** the capture files under `tests/queries/0_stateless/data_pcap/` are sample captures from the Wireshark test suite (GPL-2.0); provenance is recorded in that directory's `README.md`. Happy to swap them for self-authored synthetic captures if the GPL-2.0 provenance is a concern. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New input format `PCAP` for reading network packet captures (`pcap` and `pcapng`), producing one row per packet with decoded Ethernet/IP/TCP/UDP fields, the protocol chain, payload, and raw frame.

signal.title: Support per-authentication-method GRANTS clause in CREATE USER and ALTER USER
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109117 Implements per-authentication-method grant limits, the first part of the linked issue: ```sql ALTER USER vasya ADD IDENTIFIED WITH password BY 'WYmdFyas8PftrHbHQQo8' VALID UNTIL '2026-12-31' GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table) ``` When a user logs in with such a method, the access rights of the session are the intersection of the user's access rights (including granted roles) with the listed elements. The clause never adds rights: a listed privilege that is not granted to the user stays unavailable. This provides a way to create tokens for applications: an additional credential with an expiration date and a limited set of grants, which is tied to the user — it is displayed in `query_log` and `processlist` as the user, stops working if the user is deleted, and is narrowed when the user loses grants. Details: - The clause is parsed after the per-method `VALID UNTIL`, works with `CREATE USER`, `ALTER USER [ADD] IDENTIFIED`, and `NOT IDENTIFIED`, is shown by `SHOW CREATE USER`, and persists through the SQL serialization of access entities (and therefore backups). Elements without a database name are bound to the current database when the query is interpreted. - The intersection erases all grant options (the clause cannot express them), so such sessions cannot `GRANT` anything. Role administration is denied entirely (fail-close), including per-role admin option. `EXECUTE AS`, `ALTER USER`, `CREATE USER` and similar escapes require the corresponding rights to be listed explicitly and granted to the user. - Reattaching to a named session (`session_id`) with a different credential re-applies the limit of the credential used by the new connection, so a limited credential cannot pick up the full rights of a session created by an unrestricted one. - The limit is captured at login: `ALTER USER` affects new sessions, not established ones (same as `VALID UNTIL`). - A new `auth_grants` column in `system.users` exposes the limit of each authentication method. - `ContextData`'s copy constructor now preserves `external_roles` and the new field: previously a recalculation of access rights on a copied context silently dropped external roles; for the new field that would mean silently widening the rights. - `EXECUTE AS <user> <statement>` now keeps the current database of the caller's session. `Context::setUser` sets the current database from the target user's `DEFAULT DATABASE`, so the wrapped statement used to be re-scoped and an unqualified table name resolved in a different database; the session form (`EXECUTE AS <user>` without a statement) already preserved it. Test `04907_execute_as_preserves_current_database` covers both forms. Known limitations (consistent with `VALID UNTIL` and external roles): the limit is not propagated to other nodes of a cluster in distributed queries or `ON CLUSTER` DDL (the query is checked on the initiator), and the clause is not available in `users.xml`. The `CREATE TOKEN` syntactic sugar and the separate grant for self-service `ADD IDENTIFIED` mentioned in the issue are left for a follow-up. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Authentication methods in `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER ... ADD IDENTIFIED` support a `GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table, ...)` clause which limits the access rights of sessions authenticated with that method to the intersection with the listed grants. This allows using additional credentials as tokens for applications: `ALTER USER vasya ADD IDENTIFIED WITH password BY '...' VALID UNTIL '2026-12-31' GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table)`. Closes [#109117](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109117). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Perf: Coalesce contiguous unmatched ranges in MergeJoin
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/12118 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid materializing a temporary filtered column for dense unmatched ranges in partial_merge RIGHT and FULL JOINs. ### What does this PR do? - Finds unmatched ranges once and keeps their start and length. - Appends dense unmatched ranges directly with insertRangeFrom. - Uses the existing filtered-column path when unmatched rows are too fragmented. - Reuses the range storage between output blocks. - Keeps the existing whole-block path when no right rows were matched. - Adds RIGHT and FULL correctness coverage with nullable and string right columns. - Adds dense and interleaved RIGHT cases to the partial_merge_join performance fixture. ### Why? - The old path calls filter for every right column. - Direct range insertion avoids temporary filtered columns for dense runs. - The range list avoids scanning the same mask again in the direct path. - One insertRangeFrom per range is not good for fragmented masks. - The fallback keeps fragmented cases on the existing path. - The result and row order stay unchanged. ### Performance - Dense unmatched runs use bulk range insertion. - Fragmented masks use the filtered-column path. - The benchmark now materializes right-side UInt64, String, and LowCardinality(String) columns in the outer join cases. - The interleaved case consumes the LowCardinality payload with sum(length(b.label)). - The fixture covers sparse, dense, and interleaved RIGHT and FULL JOIN shapes. ### Benchmark The completed CI comparison for commit 3b5eb1a was against master commit 0fc2db3. These are client_time values in seconds per query from the performance dashboard. The table shows the three new join shapes from that run. | Case | AMD before | AMD after | ARM before | ARM after | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Interleaved ALL RIGHT | 0.0860s | 0.0902s (+4.9%) | 0.0743s | 0.0766s (+3.1%) | | Dense ALL RIGHT | 0.0075s | 0.0079s (+5.3%) | 0.0058s | 0.0056s (-3.4%) | | Dense ALL FULL | 0.0080s | 0.0078s (-2.5%) | 0.0061s | 0.0061s (0.0%) | ### Crossover sweep A local sweep was run with partial_merge, a 1,000,000-row dense right table, and a LowCardinality(String) payload. The query consumes all right-side payload columns. | Average unmatched run | Elapsed | | ---: | ---: | | 1 | 0.928s | | 2 | 0.616s | | 4 | 0.387s | | 8 | 0.232s | | 16 | 0.143s | | 32 | 0.099s | The current cutoff is 8 rows per unmatched range. The 8, 16, and 32 row cases use the direct range path and continue to improve in this sweep. Fixture: partial_merge_join. - Interleaved case: pmj_u64_mult2 ALL RIGHT JOIN pmj_u64_mult3. - Dense cases: pmj_u64_sparse_right ALL RIGHT or ALL FULL JOIN test_u64_right_1000000. - Data: 10,000 sparse left keys and 1,000,000 dense right keys, plus multiples-of-2 and multiples-of-3 tables. - The right tables include payload UInt64, text String, and label LowCardinality(String). The queries aggregate count(), sum(b.k), sum(b.payload), sum(length(b.text)), and sum(length(b.label)). A follow-up run for commit 5da87de was started after the range reuse and fixture updates. It did not reach the performance jobs because Build (arm_tidy) failed in an untouched TableJoin test, so the performance jobs were skipped. Fast test and style check passed.

signal.title: Perf: Reuse consecutive HashJoin probe results for fixed-width keys
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reduce HashJoin probe overhead by reusing lookup results for repeated fixed-width join keys. ### What does this PR do? - Adds a **probe-only** consecutive-key cache for fixed-width HashJoin getters. - Reuses the previous **mapped pointer and hash-table offset** when the next probe key has the same raw bytes. - Keeps build-side insertion on the existing path. - Preserves duplicate right-side row handling through RowRef and RowRefList. - Covers **key32/key64**, packed keys32/64/128/256, and the corresponding two-level variants. - Leaves key8/key16, strings, nullable keys, range joins, and the build path unchanged. - Adds ALL INNER, RIGHT, and FULL correctness coverage. - Covers duplicate and unmatched rows. - Adds packed **keys256** correctness coverage with repeated probe keys. - Adds a run-length sweep, large build-map coverage, and packed keys128/keys256 benchmark cases. ### Why? - **Current path:** calculates the probe key and probes the hash table for every left-side row. - **Typical input:** primary-key ordered or clustered data often has long runs of the same join key. - **Repeated work:** the old path repeats the same key calculation and hash-table lookup for every row in a run. - **New path:** the first row does the normal lookup; later equal-key rows reuse its result. - **Unclustered input:** different keys still use the normal lookup path. - **Safety:** the generic consecutive-key cache is not used because HashJoin needs the real hash-table offset. - **Mapped values:** the cache stores the pointer from the real hash-table cell instead of copying RowRefList. - **Join behavior:** matched rows, duplicate right-side rows, and RIGHT/FULL join flags stay unchanged. ### Performance - **Clustered input:** avoids repeated key calculation and hash-table lookup for equal-key runs. - **Interleaved input:** adds only the key-equality check before the normal lookup. - **Expected benefit:** grows with the number of repeated rows per key. - **Regression control:** run length 1 and interleaved cases measure the no-hit cost. ### Benchmark - **Fixture:** `hashjoin_consecutive_keys`. - **Probe input:** 20M rows per measured query. - **Run lengths:** 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, and 10,000 rows per key. - **Small build map:** 2,000 keys. - **Large build map:** 2,000,000 keys. - **Packed keys:** clustered and interleaved cases for keys128 and keys256. - **Join settings:** hash algorithm with table swapping disabled. ### Benchmark results - **CI:** [AMD release performance comparison](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/PRs/115046/843550ba1e290f6f1a34058fb041055c034aa3cc/performance_comparison_amd_release_master_head_4_6/all-queries.html), master vs this PR. - **Input:** 20M probe rows per query. - **Unit:** seconds, lower is better. | Case | Master | PR | Change | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Run length 1 | 0.089 | 0.141 | +58.0% | | Run length 2 | 0.086 | 0.123 | +41.9% | | Run length 4 | 0.086 | 0.115 | +33.6% | | Run length 8 | 0.086 | 0.111 | +28.0% | | Run length 16 | 0.088 | 0.110 | +25.6% | | Run length 64 | 0.087 | 0.112 | +27.9% | | Run length 10,000 | 0.087 | 0.108 | +24.9% | | Large UInt64 map, unclustered | 0.324 | 0.366 | +12.7% | | keys128, unclustered | 0.172 | 0.253 | +47.5% | | keys256, unclustered | 0.367 | 0.397 | +8.0% | - **Note:** This shard includes the run-length sweep and unclustered controls. The clustered large-map and packed-key cases were not recorded in this report.

signal.title: Extract reusable `ActionsDAG` lineage computation into `actionsDAGUtils`
signal.text: The new `traceActionsDAGLineage` computes lineage for every `ActionsDAG` output using iterative traversal with memoization shared across all output roots. Each output is traced to at most one input through supported hops. Hops are classified as: - `Identity` - `ValuePreserving` - `DistinctValuesBound`, meaning output NDV is bounded by input NDV plus `ndv_delta` Inputs and outputs are identified by position rather than column name, so the reusable lineage result remains unambiguous when names are duplicated. `remapColumnStats` in the join-order optimizer now uses this API instead of its local `describeValueHop`/ `backTrackColumnsInDag` traversal. This changes the call site as follows: - Lineage is computed once per `ActionsDAG`, with memoization shared across all outputs, instead of running an independent DFS for every statistics entry. - Statistics names that do not match a DAG input no longer trigger additional per-name traversals. A nonempty statistics map causes at most one lineage computation. - An explicit mapped.empty() guard preserves the common case where absent statistics require no lineage traversal. - Remapping becomes a direct loop over output lineage results, using the traced input position and ndv_delta. The lineage-related complexity changes from approximately `O(#stats × DAG)` to `O(DAG + #outputs)`, with the remaining statistics-map handling linear in the number of entries. For outputs that can be represented unambiguously by the name-keyed statistics map, the computed statistics remain unchanged. The supported-hop and `ndv_delta` rules are equivalent to the previous implementation: nullable-to-non-nullable hops may add one distinct value, and the existing overflow guard remains in place. `remapColumnStats` does not currently distinguish between lineage kinds; it only uses `traceability`, `input_position`, and `ndv_delta`. The reusable API handles duplicate names positionally. `remapColumnStats` itself remains keyed by column name and therefore cannot represent separate statistics for conflicting duplicate output names. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): - Not for changelog

signal.title: Add JOIN observability columns to system.query_log
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111352 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111748 ## Motivation `system.query_log` says almost nothing about what the JOINs in a query actually did. Answering questions like "which queries ran a `CROSS` join we didn't expect", "which joins fell back to `grace_hash` and spilled to disk", or "which algorithm was really chosen when `join_algorithm = 'auto'`" currently requires re-running `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` (impossible post-mortem) or scraping `ProfileEvents` query by query. ## Changes Four columns are added to `system.query_log`, with the matching fields in `QueryLogElement`: - `used_number_of_joins` (`UInt64`) — the number of physical joins executed by the query. It is collected from the query pipeline, so it reflects the joins that really ran after all optimizations, not the number of `JOIN` clauses in the query text. - `used_join_algorithms` (`Array(LowCardinality(String))`) — the algorithms that were actually used, e.g. `hash`, `parallel_hash`, `grace_hash`, `direct`, `full_sorting_merge`, `partial_merge`. The `join_algorithm` setting only lists the allowed algorithms; the choice among them happens at runtime, and an algorithm can even be replaced mid-execution (a `hash` join switching to `grace_hash` under memory pressure). - `used_join_kinds` (`Array(LowCardinality(String))`) — Kind of the joins present in the query. - `used_join_strictness` (`Array(LowCardinality(String))`) — Strictness of the joins present in the query. - `join_spilled_to_disk` (`UInt8`) — whether any of the joins spilled to disk. This PR currently adds the schema only. The fields are declared but nothing populates them yet, so the columns read as `0` and `[]`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added four columns to `system.query_log` describing the JOINs a query executed: `used_number_of_joins` (the number of physical joins in the executed pipeline), `used_join_algorithms` (the algorithms actually used at runtime, which can differ from the `join_algorithm` setting), `used_join_kinds` (`INNER`, `LEFT`, `CROSS`, `ASOF` and so on), and `join_spilled_to_disk` (whether any join wrote temporary data to disk). This makes it possible to find problematic JOIN patterns across a fleet without reproducing each query.

signal.title: ASOF JOIN returns a different tied row depending on join_algorithm and on the number of rows on the right side
signal.text: ### Describe the unexpected behaviour When the right side of an `ASOF JOIN` has more than one row with the same value in the ASOF column, which of those rows comes back depends on the join algorithm. It also depends on how many rows are on the right side, which is the part that surprised me. `full_sorting_merge` consistently returns the last of the tied rows. `hash` returns different ones depending on row count. With 252 rows on the right it returns `B`, with 259 it returns `A`. Nothing else differs between those two runs. I think the cause is in `src/Interpreters/RowRefs.cpp`. Entries are radix sorted when there are more than 256 of them, and go through `::sort` otherwise: ```cpp if (likely(entries.size() > 256)) { ... RadixSort<RadixSortTraits>::executeLSDWithTrySort(entries.data(), entries.size(), is_descending); ... } ... ::sort(entries.begin(), entries.end(), GreaterEntryOperator()); ``` `::sort` is pdqsort, which is not stable, so below the threshold the relative order of equal keys is arbitrary. Above it the radix sort is stable and keeps insertion order. The 256 boundary in the code is exactly where the result flips. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Reproduced on `master` built locally, `SELECT version()` reports 26.8.1.1. I have not checked older releases. ### How to reproduce ```sql CREATE TABLE r (id UInt32, t UInt32, v String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (id, t, v); INSERT INTO r SELECT 1, 1, 'filler' FROM numbers(250); INSERT INTO r VALUES (1, 10, 'A'), (1, 10, 'B'); OPTIMIZE TABLE r FINAL; CREATE TABLE l (id UInt32, t UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY (id, t); INSERT INTO l VALUES (1, 20); SELECT r.v FROM l ASOF JOIN r ON l.id = r.id AND l.t >= r.t SETTINGS join_algorithm = 'hash'; ``` Both rows at `t = 10` are valid matches for the left row at `t = 20`, so the join has to pick one. Results: | rows on right | `join_algorithm = 'hash'` | `join_algorithm = 'full_sorting_merge'` | | --- | --- | --- | | 252 (`numbers(250)`) | `B` | `B` | | 259 (`numbers(257)`) | `A` | `B` | Change only the argument to `numbers()` between the two runs. ### Expected behavior I am not sure what the right answer is, which is why I am opening an issue instead of sending a patch. The docs for `ASOF JOIN` do not currently say anything about duplicate values in the ASOF column, so there is nothing to check the behaviour against. Two options I can see: - pick a tie break rule, first or last matching row, and make both algorithms follow it - leave it unspecified but state that in the documentation Either is fine by me. What bothers me is that the same query on the same data can start returning a different row once the table grows past a few hundred rows, with no settings changed and nothing in the output to indicate it. If you are joining trades to quotes and two quotes share a timestamp, the query stops being reproducible and there is no signal that anything happened. ### Additional context Tested on a single part after `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL`, one join key, `UInt32` timestamps. I have not checked multi part tables, multiple join keys, or `DateTime64`, so the behaviour there may differ.

signal.title: [WIP] Byte stream split Codec
signal.text: ### Changelog category Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry Added experimental ByteStreamSplit codec for fixed-width columns. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Motivation:** : Floating-point and integer columns often have bytes at the same positional offset that are nearly identical across rows (e.g. the exponent byte of Float32 values in a narrow range). Grouping those bytes together can sometimes increases the compressibility of the data for general-purpose compressors. In tests on public GeoIP IPv6 datasets, this approach improved compression ratios by 2.43x over standard Zstd and 3.85x over LZ4. Similar gains were observed in UUIDv7 data, where BSS-LZ4 outperformed standard LZ4 by 1.94x. I also reproduced the https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PARQUET-1716, and it saw similar gains in scientific floating point datasets. Because the ipv6 was my target use case, I added specialization for w=16 bytes so the performance is acceptable. **Enabling:**: The codec is gated behind the experimental codecs setting: ```sql SET allow_experimental_codecs = 1; ``` **Parameters:**: ByteStreamSplit accepts one optional integer argument — the element byte width. When omitted, the width is inferred from the column data type. - No argument (default) — element width inferred from column type (e.g. 4 for Float32, 8 for Float64, 16 for UUID/IPv6) - Explicit integer (e.g. ByteStreamSplit(4)) — override the element width; useful with FixedString Supported types: Any fixed-size type with element width ≥ 2: Float32, Float64, Int16/32/64/128, UInt16/32/64/128, Date, DateTime, DateTime64, IPv4, IPv6, UUID, FixedString(N) for N ≥ 2 and N<=255 (for now) Need to see if FixedString(N) is worth it. **Example use:** ```sql SET allow_experimental_codecs = 1; CREATE TABLE example ( val_f32 Float32 CODEC(ByteStreamSplit, LZ4), val_f64 Float64 CODEC(ByteStreamSplit, ZSTD(1)), val_u128 UInt128 CODEC(ByteStreamSplit(16), LZ4), val_fs FixedString(8) CODEC(ByteStreamSplit(8)) ) ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY val_f32; ``` ### Implementation - Registered under method byte 0x9d. - Maximum element width: 255 bytes. ### Testing - Tested using my Harness in the misc_script_folder and using in real dataset, need to run the clickhouse static test. - Benchmark Compression: [Google Sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1h-Rcg6oXKD6pdf_GzaEe0YUvP41-K32B0idnsNAy-GU/edit?gid=0#gid=0) - Benchmark Speed: #### Specs - CPU: Intel i7-12500H (Alder Lake) - Data: 256–500 MiB, multiple rounds with inner iterations - Compiler: Clang -O2 #### Results Median (GB/s) | W | Ours Encode | Ours Decode | Arrow Encode | Arrow Decode | Speedup Encode | Speedup Decode | |-----|------------|------------|--------------|--------------|----------------|----------------| | 1(memcopy) | **19.4** | **19.9** | **19.4** | **19.9** | **1.0×** | **1.0×** | | 2 | 10.5 | 10.8 | 9.7 | 10.7 | 1.08× | 1.01× | | 4 | 10.4 | 10.8 | 10.0 | 10.9 | 1.04× | 0.99× | | 8 | 9.1 | 10.3 | 10.5 | 10.9 | 0.87× | 0.94× | | 16 | 7.4 | 10.2 | 4.6 | 4.7 | 1.61× | 2.17× | | 20 | 5.1 | 5.5 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 1.13× | 1.20× | | 32 | 4.9 | 5.4 | 3.7 | 4.1 | 1.32× | 1.32× | | 64 | 4.5 | 5.2 | 2.5 | 2.6 | 1.80× | 2.00× | | 128 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 2.4 | 2.4 | 1.88× | 1.92× | ***Arrow supports W > 255; ours would need VLA or dynamic allocation.***

signal.title: MergeTree: rethrow retryable errors from checkDataPart instead of returning empty checksums
signal.text: > **Series**: #112871 -> **#112874** (this), #112872, #112873, #112875, #112876 **Problem.** `checkDataPart` swallows a retryable error and returns empty checksums, so `CHECK TABLE` and the fetch path treat a transient failure as "verified" and can persist an empty integrity baseline. Failure scenario: ``` checkDataPart(): catch retryable -> return {} CHECK TABLE : empty -> reports OK downloadPartToDisk: empty -> accepts an unverified packed part ``` **Fix.** Rethrow retryable errors so callers' retry/skip guards fire; remove the now-dead empty-checksums guard on the fetch path. **Changes.** - `Storages/MergeTree/checkDataPart`: `return {}` -> `throw` on a retryable error. - `Storages/MergeTree/DataPartsExchange`: delete the now-dead empty-checksums fetch guard. - `tests/integration/test_azure_403_handling`: CHECK-TABLE-surfaces-transient test. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `checkDataPart` swallowing a retryable error and returning empty checksums, so `CHECK TABLE` could report a part as OK and a fetch could accept an unverified part after a transient failure. Retryable errors are now rethrown so the check is retried later instead of masking a transient failure as verified.

signal.title: Support shipping window (partitioned) sorts with plan-based parallel replicas
signal.text: Plan-based parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_plan_based`) lifts the split marker through `SortingStep`: the sort is cloned into the fragment shipped to the replicas and the initiator keeps a `MergingSorted` step above the union, so each replica sorts its own rows and the initiator only merges. A window function's pre-sort is also a `SortingStep`, but a special one: it is built with the partitioning constructor (`Planner::addWindowSteps`), so `partition_by_description` is set. Its contract is *one stream per `PARTITION BY` group*, not one sorted stream - `SortingStep::fullSort` scatters by the partition keys and deliberately skips the final merge, and `WindowStep` then runs one `WindowTransform` per stream. That contract cannot be expressed by the `MergingSorted` step the pass puts on the initiator, so such a sort is currently rejected in `sortingCanBeShipped` (`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp`) and window queries keep the split below the sort, the same as with classic parallel replicas. Shipping it collapsed both the sort and the window to a single stream. With `max_threads = 4` and a three-replica cluster: ```sql SELECT p, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY a) FROM t_win; ``` `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 0` (sort stays on the initiator): ``` (Window) Resize 4 → 4 WindowTransform × 4 (Sorting) MergeSortingTransform × 4 LimitsCheckingTransform × 4 PartialSortingTransform × 4 Resize × 4 3 → 1 ScatterByPartitionTransform × 3 1 → 4 ``` `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 1` with the sort shipped: ``` (Window) Resize 1 → 4 WindowTransform (Sorting) MergingSortedTransform 3 → 1 ``` Results stayed correct, because `full_sort_description` is `PARTITION BY` followed by `ORDER BY`, so a single globally merged stream still holds each partition contiguously and in order. What is lost is the per-partition parallelism of both the sort and the window. Two ways to support shipping it: 1. Clone the sort into the fragment *without* `partition_by_description`. Each replica then returns one stream sorted by `full_sort_description` and the initiator's merge produces a valid input for a single `WindowTransform`. The sorting work is distributed; the window itself still runs on one stream (`query_plan_enable_multithreading_after_window_functions` restores parallelism after it). 2. Preserve the per-partition scope on the initiator - re-scatter above the merge, or rebuild the parent as a partitioned sort. Closer to the current pipeline, but the replica-side scatter produces mutually unordered streams, so the merge contract has to be reworked. Note that read-in-order gives no reason to prefer shipping today: `optimizeReadInOrder` early-returns on a partitioned sort unless `query_plan_reuse_storage_ordering_for_window_functions` is enabled, and that setting defaults to `false`. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114315

signal.title: `UNION DISTINCT` skips the preliminary parallel `DISTINCT` that the equivalent rewrite gets
signal.text: 🕵️ **Describe the situation** `A UNION DISTINCT B` and `SELECT DISTINCT * FROM (A UNION ALL B)` are the same query, but they get different pipelines. The rewrite gets a preliminary per-stream `DistinctTransform` before the streams are merged; `UNION DISTINCT` does not, so every row funnels into one thread for deduplication. The planner adds only the final, single-stream `DistinctStep` for the `UNION DISTINCT` case, while the ordinary `SELECT DISTINCT` path adds a `pre_distinct` step first. **How to reproduce** Version `26.8.1.1384`. ```sql CREATE TABLE t_setops (k UInt64, g String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; INSERT INTO t_setops SELECT number, concat('v_', toString(number % 2000)) FROM numbers(8000000); -- A: UNION DISTINCT EXPLAIN PIPELINE SELECT g FROM t_setops WHERE k % 3 = 0 UNION DISTINCT SELECT g FROM t_setops WHERE k % 5 = 0 SETTINGS max_threads = 16; -- B: identical semantics, written by hand EXPLAIN PIPELINE SELECT DISTINCT g FROM (SELECT g FROM t_setops WHERE k % 3 = 0 UNION ALL SELECT g FROM t_setops WHERE k % 5 = 0) SETTINGS max_threads = 16; ``` A - no preliminary phase, all 32 streams merged into one before any deduplication: ``` (Distinct) DistinctTransform Resize 32 → 1 (Union) ... ``` B - each stream deduplicates first, so the single-threaded stage sees far fewer rows: ``` (Distinct) DistinctTransform Resize 32 → 1 (Union) (Distinct) DistinctTransform × 16 ... ``` The two queries return the same result. **Expected performance / actual performance** Best of 5, 8M rows, 2000 distinct values, `FORMAT Null`: | query | `max_threads=1` | `max_threads=8` | `max_threads=16` | scaling | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `UNION DISTINCT` | 0.21 s | 0.05 s | 0.05 s | **4.4x** | | `SELECT DISTINCT` over `UNION ALL` | 0.21 s | 0.03 s | 0.02 s | 10.3x | Same work, same result, 2x apart at 16 threads. The gap widens with the number of duplicates, because that is exactly what a per-stream preliminary `DISTINCT` removes before the merge. With entirely distinct values the two forms converge, as expected - the preliminary phase has nothing to discard. **Additional context** The `UNION DISTINCT` branch of `Planner::buildQueryPlanForUnionNode` adds one step, with `pre_distinct` false: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/src/Planner/Planner.cpp#L2092 ```cpp auto distinct_step = std::make_unique<DistinctStep>( query_plan.getCurrentHeader(), limits, 0 /*limit hint*/, query_plan.getCurrentHeader()->getNames(), false /*pre distinct*/); ``` The ordinary `SELECT DISTINCT` path passes `true /*pre_distinct*/` instead. `pre_distinct` is what decides whether the step is allowed to keep the streams: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/src/Processors/QueryPlan/DistinctStep.cpp#L28 ```cpp static ITransformingStep::Traits getTraits(bool pre_distinct) { const bool preserves_number_of_streams = pre_distinct; return ITransformingStep::Traits { { .returns_single_stream = !pre_distinct, ``` So adding a `pre_distinct` step before the existing one in the `UNION DISTINCT` branch should be enough, and plan B above shows the machinery already works over a united pipeline. The one case to keep in mind is the `LIMIT` interaction the ordinary path documents at `Planner.cpp:1339` - a preliminary `DISTINCT` is skipped when a `LIMIT` makes it not worth it.
signal.author: PedroTadim

signal.title: Reimplement the KQL (Kusto) dialect on a lexer, an AST and AST translation
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/61742 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reimplemented the experimental KQL (Kusto) dialect. It now has its own lexer and parser and builds an AST directly, instead of translating a token stream into SQL text and reparsing it. This fixes an expression-injection hole in the string operators (`contains`, `has`, ...), several results that silently disagreed with Kusto (`7 / 2`, `substring` with a negative start, `bin`), and 28 functions that were registered but did nothing. The supported subset is smaller and documented; anything outside it is now rejected by name instead of being mistranslated. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes `docs/guides/clickhouse/kusto-query-language.mdx` --- ## Why The dialect was contributed in 2022 and abandoned by its authors; the rewrite they promised in #62668 was closed unmerged. Since then it has been emergency-disabled once (#59305) and gated behind `allow_experimental_kusto_dialect` (#74224), and #61742 ("Remove KQL support if this code will not be fixed") has stayed open. The implementation translated a KQL token stream directly into ClickHouse SQL **text** and reparsed it — 298 `fmt::format` sites, 41 places that re-lexed generated text, and no AST anywhere in the function layer. Everything below follows from that: | | before | after | |---|---|---| | `T \| where s contains "x') OR 1 = 1 OR ilike(s, 'y"` | injected the expression | needle is an `ASTLiteral`; no injection is representable | | `'50x' contains '50%'` | `true` — needle was pasted into a LIKE pattern | `false` | | `substring('abcdefg', -3, 2)` | `'ab'` | `'ef'` | | `7 / 2` | `3.5` | `3` | | `format_timespan(col, 'hh:mm')` | `stoi: no conversion` — `std::stoi` on generated SQL | rejected by name | | `series_fir(...)` | `Function series_fir does not exist` (one of 28 stubs) | rejected by name | | `search 'x'` | `Unknown table expression identifier 'search'` | `'search' is not a supported KQL operator` | | `let` bindings | `static thread_local`, leaked between queries | scoped to one parse | ## What is here Two commits: the removal, then the reimplementation. ``` src/Parsers/Kusto/ KQLLexer KQL's own tokens: !in, =~, .., timespans (2.5h), verbatim @'...', datetime(...). A bad literal is an Error token carrying a reason, so nothing downstream asks isValidKQLPos() — the core of #61742. KQLAST the tabular level only. Scalar expressions are ClickHouse AST directly; a parallel expression hierarchy would add only conversions. KQLParser recursive descent. `let` bindings are an ordinary member. KQLTranslator each operator fills a still-empty clause of the select being built, or wraps what exists so far in a subquery and starts a new one. KQLFunctions name -> builder returning an ASTPtr. src/Functions/Kusto/ kqlDivide `7 / 2` is 3 in KQL and 3.5 in SQL — the choice depends on operand kqlBin types, so it is made by an IFunctionOverloadResolver during analysis rather than guessed from how the argument was spelled. ``` KQL now has its own entry point (`parseKQLQuery`) and never touches the SQL tokenizer. Because `ClientBase` already catches, the parser can simply throw — so there is no `tryParseKQLQuery`, and no `catch` anywhere in the new code. **`src/Parsers/Kusto` no longer needs its carve-out from check 19** ("do not catch exceptions in src/Parsers"), and this PR deletes it. `src/Parsers/Kusto` goes from 13017 lines to 3967, plus 337 lines of runtime functions. ## Scope Deliberately smaller than before, and written down in the guide. A construct is either translated with the semantics Kusto documents, or rejected by name. Rejected in this PR: `search`, `parse`, `mv-apply`, `lookup`, `evaluate`, `invoke`, `facet`, `top-nested`, `make-series` and friends; the `series_*`, `bag_*`/`pack_*` and `ipv4_*` families; `parse_url`, `parse_csv`, `parse_json`, `toscalar`, `format_timespan`; and `dynamic` **objects** (arrays map onto ClickHouse `Array`). Three known divergences are documented rather than papered over: subtracting two datetimes yields seconds instead of a timespan, `project-rename` moves the renamed column to the end, and `union` needs compatible schemas. ## Testing `04670`–`04673` cover the pipeline, the string operators (including the injection cases), the scalar semantics that used to be wrong, and 47 constructs that must be rejected. A 2500-query random fuzz found no crashes or logical errors. The 302 conformance cases that were deleted with the old implementation are being reintroduced separately, on top of this branch.

signal.title: clean orphans from keeper snapshots
signal.text: This change makes ClickHouse Keeper able to recover from snapshots that contain orphaned nodes — nodes whose parent is absent from the snapshot. Before this change, such a snapshot made Keeper fail to start with an opaque internal error thrown by `updateValue` ("Could not find key"). This pull request replaces that with a clear, opt-in recovery path: - By default (`keeper_server.remove_orphaned_nodes_on_startup` = `false`), Keeper still refuses to load a snapshot with orphaned nodes, but now throws an actionable `CORRUPTED_DATA` exception that reports the number of orphaned nodes and how to enable recovery. - When `keeper_server.remove_orphaned_nodes_on_startup` = `true` and `keeper_server.digest_enabled` = `false`, the orphaned nodes and all of their descendants are removed during startup, ACL usage counters and ephemeral bookkeeping are updated, and stale `numChildren` counters on surviving nodes are corrected, so Keeper can load the snapshot. Cleanup is strictly a startup recovery operation. A snapshot deserialized while the server is already running — for example, a follower applying a leader snapshot in `KeeperStateMachine::apply_snapshot` — is applied as-is and is never modified, so a follower cannot diverge from the rest of the cluster. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ClickHouse Keeper now throws an actionable `CORRUPTED_DATA` error reporting the number of orphaned nodes (nodes whose parent is missing) when loading a snapshot that contains them, instead of failing with an opaque internal error. With the new setting `keeper_server.remove_orphaned_nodes_on_startup` set to `true` and `keeper_server.digest_enabled` set to `false`, such orphaned nodes (and their descendants) are removed during startup so Keeper can load the snapshot. The cleanup is performed only on startup, never while the server is running. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)
