signal.title: Fix logical error in getMinMaxTime() when Nullable DateTime column has all NULLs
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/92834 When a `MergeTree` table has a `Nullable(Date)` / `Nullable(DateTime)` / `Nullable(DateTime64)` column in its partition key and a part contains only `NULL` values in that column, querying `system.parts` threw: `Part minmax index by time is neither DateTime or DateTime64`. Root cause: for an all-`NULL` part, `ColumnNullable::getExtremesNullLast` returns `POSITIVE_INFINITY` (a `Field::Types::Null` sentinel) for the minmax bounds. `getMinMaxTime` only handled `UInt64` (`DateTime`) and `Decimal64` (`DateTime64`) field types, so the `Null` field fell through to the `throw`. Changes: - In `getMinMaxDate` and `getMinMaxTime`, short-circuit to an empty range when either hyperrectangle bound is `Null` (all-`NULL` parts, and mixed `NULL` / non-`NULL` NullLast parts where only the upper bound is `Null`). - In `getMinMaxTime`, require **both** bounds to have the expected `Field` type (`UInt64` for `DateTime`, `Decimal64` for `DateTime64`) before calling `safeGet`, and return an empty range for any other type instead of throwing `LOGICAL_ERROR` — mirroring the guard in `getMinMaxDate`. - In `checkPartitionKeyAndInitMinMax`, first select a non-`Nullable` `Date` / `DateTime` / `DateTime64` partition-key column exactly as before, and only when the key has no non-`Nullable` candidate at all (an all-`Nullable` date/time key) fall back to unwrapping `Nullable` and `LowCardinality(Nullable(...))` via `removeLowCardinalityAndNullable` (`allow_nullable_key` permits the `LowCardinality` wrapper too, and the minmax writer unwraps `LowCardinality` before taking extremes, so its index bounds look exactly like the plain `Nullable` case). This preserves the previous selection for mixed keys such as `(d Date, nd Nullable(Date))` (still chosen from the non-`Nullable` `d`), while populating `min_*` / `max_*` for all-`Nullable` keys instead of leaving them silently empty. The fallback is restricted to new-syntax tables, so old-syntax `ENGINE = MergeTree(date, ...)` tables keep rejecting a `Nullable(Date)` date column at creation. - Add a stateless test `04822_minmax_index_nullable_datetime_all_nulls` covering the `#92834` reproducer; all-`NULL` / mixed-`NULL` / non-`NULL` cases for `Nullable(Date)` / `Nullable(DateTime)` / `Nullable(DateTime64)` partition keys; the mixed non-`Nullable` `Date` + `Nullable(Date)` and `DateTime` + `Nullable(DateTime)` selection; and `LowCardinality(Nullable(Date))` / `LowCardinality(Nullable(DateTime))` partition keys (non-`NULL` and all-`NULL`). Scope / not covered here: this PR only removes the user-visible exception. It rescues `NULL` bounds and stale minmax slots whose `Field` storage is incompatible with the expected date/time kind. A stale minmax slot after `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN ... AFTER` that happens to point at a non-date column sharing the same `Field` storage (a reordered `UInt64` read as `DateTime`, or a plain `Decimal64` read as `DateTime64`) is still read as a date/time and can surface a misleading `min_*` / `max_*` value rather than an empty range. Fully refreshing the cached per-part `minmax_idx_*_column_pos` after a column reorder is the deeper fix; it needs per-part column-order persistence to stay concurrency-safe with concurrent `SELECT`s and is left for a follow-up. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an exception when querying `system.parts` `min_time` / `max_time` / `min_date` / `max_date` for `MergeTree` parts whose cached date/time minmax slot contains `NULL` bounds or a `Field` storage type incompatible with the expected date/time bound (for example, an all-`NULL` `Nullable(Date)` / `Nullable(DateTime)` / `Nullable(DateTime64)` partition-key column). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: `RESTORE` never fsyncs the restored part files: an acknowledged restore loses all data on power loss
signal.text: > You have to provide the following information whenever possible. **Describe what's wrong** `RESTORE TABLE ... FROM File(...)` returns `RESTORED` without fsyncing any of the part files it wrote. The restore copy goes through `BackupReaderDefault::copyFileToDisk` (`src/Backups/BackupIO_Default.cpp:21-37`): `copyData` + `finalize()` only — no sync, and `WriteSettings` has no sync flag to thread through. The restored part is then attached through the rename machinery, bypassing the `INSERT` write path, so the `MergeTree` fsync setting family (`fsync_after_insert`, `fsync_part_directory`, ...) does not apply **even when the restored table itself carries those settings**. If the host loses power shortly after `RESTORED` was returned, the restored parts are torn (under ext4 delayed allocation typically every file is 0 bytes) and the data is gone: the parts are detached as `broken-on-start` at the next startup and the table is empty. This composes badly with the natural disaster-recovery workflow: restore a backup, receive the acknowledgement, resume operation — a power loss shortly after leaves the table empty while the operator believes the restore succeeded. Combined with #111320 (the backup itself is also written without fsync), both directions of the backup/restore cycle are not power-loss durable. Same detection methodology as #111269 / #111318 / #111320: strace-based fsync-coverage audit of the acknowledged operation, then power-loss confirmation. **How to reproduce** * Version: master `26.7.1.1311` (aarch64 nightly). Deterministic (3/3) with a `dm-flakey` power-loss simulation (server `path` on a dm-flakey-backed ext4 mount; "cut power" = suspend without flush + `drop_writes` + remount). The backup itself is made durable with a filesystem `sync` before the `RESTORE`, so only the restore's own writes are exposed to the cut: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, key String, v UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id SETTINGS fsync_after_insert = 1, fsync_part_directory = 1, min_rows_to_fsync_after_merge = 1, min_compressed_bytes_to_fsync_after_merge = 1; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, concat('k', toString(number % 7)), number FROM numbers(50000); BACKUP TABLE t TO File('bk1'); DROP TABLE t SYNC; -- sync the filesystem here (backup + drop durable; only RESTORE's writes are exposed) RESTORE TABLE t FROM File('bk1'); -- returns RESTORED SELECT count() FROM t; -- 50000 -- cut power; restart the server SELECT count() FROM t; -- 0 ``` Result, 3/3: ``` [post count] 0 0 detached: broken-on-start_all_1_1_0 broken-on-start <Error> default.t (...): while loading part all_1_1_0 ...: Cannot parse input: expected 'columns format version: 1\n' at end of stream: Part contains files: key.bin (0 bytes), columns.txt (0 bytes), checksums.txt (0 bytes), ... : Part is empty. (CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED) ``` **Expected behavior** Restored parts are committed data the moment `RESTORED` is acknowledged. They should get at least the durability the table's fsync settings promise for inserted parts (fsync the files and the part directory before attaching), or a restore setting should exist to request it. Currently there is none. **Additional context** The write path is distinct from #111320 (restore writes through `IDisk` onto the server's own data disk, not through the backup writers), so fixing one does not fix the other. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #111378 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1548` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.4.49`, `26.6.3.48` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Push LIMIT down into FINAL merge algorithms for early termination
signal.text: ## Summary When a query uses `FINAL` with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` on `AggregatingMergeTree`, `SummingMergeTree`, or `CoalescingMergeTree`, the limit is pushed down into the FINAL merge algorithm so it can terminate early once enough output rows have been produced, avoiding scanning the entire dataset. This is controlled by the `optimize_final_limit_pushdown` setting (default: off). Additionally, a new `optimize_final_sequential_partitions` setting (Bool, default: off) enables sequential partition processing via `ConcatProcessor` when combined with `do_not_merge_across_partitions_select_final`, allowing early termination at the partition level. The algorithm uses minmax index values to automatically determine partition order and verify non-overlapping. ### When does limit pushdown activate? All of the following conditions must be met: 1. The query uses `FINAL` 2. The query has `ORDER BY ... LIMIT N` (with `N > 0`) 3. `optimize_read_in_order = true` (default) — otherwise the optimizer never runs 4. `optimize_final_limit_pushdown = true` 5. No `FilterStep` (WHERE) exists in the plan — WHERE runs after the merge, so pushing limit into the merge would truncate rows before filtering. PREWHERE is safe because it runs within each part before the merge 6. The sorting key covers all ORDER BY columns (with monotonic wrappers and fixed-point skipping allowed), and the effective read direction is forward (+1) Rule 6 in detail: the matching loop in `buildInputOrderFromSortDescription` walks ORDER BY columns and sorting key columns in parallel. Each ORDER BY column must match the current key column — either directly or via a monotonic function (e.g. `ORDER BY a, toFloat64(b)` with key `(a, b)`). The effective direction of each column (`ORDER BY direction × key reverse_flag × monotonic direction`) must be consistent across all columns and must equal +1, because FINAL does not support reverse read-in-order. If any ORDER BY column fails to match, the loop breaks and `sort_description_for_merging` has fewer entries than the full ORDER BY — the guard `sort_description_for_merging.size() == description.size()` blocks pushdown. Fixed-point skipping: when a PREWHERE or WHERE condition fixes a key column to a constant (e.g. `PREWHERE b = 0` with key `(a, b, c)`), that column is added to `fixed_key_columns`. The matching loop skips fixed key columns via `++next_sort_key` without consuming an ORDER BY column, allowing subsequent key columns to match subsequent ORDER BY columns. For example, with key `(a, b, c)` and `PREWHERE b = 0 ORDER BY a, c`: `a` matches key[0], key[1] (`b`) is skipped (fixed), `c` matches key[2] — all 2 ORDER BY columns are matched, pushdown activates. Note that this interacts with rule 5: the fixed-point itself may come from either PREWHERE or WHERE, but limit pushdown is only safe when no FilterStep exists (i.e. the filtering is done via PREWHERE, not WHERE). Examples: | Scenario | Key | ORDER BY | Pushdown | |---|---|---|---| | Exact match | `(a, b)` | `a, b` | ✅ | | Prefix of key | `(a, b, c)` | `a, b` | ✅ | | Monotonic wrapper | `(a, b)` | `a, toFloat64(b)` | ✅ | | Reverse key + reverse ORDER BY | `(a DESC, b DESC)` | `a DESC, b DESC` | ✅ (effective direction +1) | | PREWHERE fixes middle key column | `(a, b, c)` | `a, c` + `PREWHERE b=0` | ✅ (b skipped as fixed point) | | WHERE fixes middle key column | `(a, b, c)` | `a, c` + `WHERE b=0` | ❌ (blocked by rule 5: FilterStep exists) | | ORDER BY extends beyond key | `(a, b)` | `a, b, c` | ❌ | | ORDER BY diverges from key | `(a, b)` | `a, c` | ❌ | | Monotonic of already-consumed column | `(a, b)` | `a, intDiv(a,10)` | ❌ (loop doesn't backtrack) | | Inconsistent direction | `(a, b)` | `a ASC, b DESC` | ❌ | ### Applicable engines - `AggregatingMergeTree` — merge aggregates groups; once limit rows are emitted, remaining groups are unnecessary - `SummingMergeTree` — merge sums groups; same reasoning - `CoalescingMergeTree` — merge coalesces groups; same reasoning ### Not applicable - `ReplacingMergeTree` — merge must see all versions to determine which row survives - `CollapsingMergeTree` / `VersionedCollapsingMergeTree` — merge must see cancellation pairs - `GraphiteMergeTree` — merge applies rollup rules across the full dataset - `Merge` tables (and the `merge` table function) over eligible children — the limit is not propagated through `ReadFromMerge`; such queries stay correct but perform full FINAL merges in the children without early termination ### Sequential partition processing (`optimize_final_sequential_partitions`) When `do_not_merge_across_partitions_select_final` is enabled, each partition is merged independently into its own pipe. Normally these pipes are combined with a parallel `Union`. With `optimize_final_sequential_partitions = true` and `final_limit > 0`, the optimizer can replace `Union` with `ConcatProcessor`, which activates only one input at a time. Once the downstream `Limit` is satisfied, remaining partitions are never read at all. The algorithm determines partition order using **minmax index values**: 1. **Compute `num_leading_fixed_sort_key_columns`** in `buildInputOrderFromSortDescription`: counts consecutive leading sorting key columns that are constant (fixed by WHERE/PREWHERE). This is passed through `InputOrderInfo`. 2. **Collect per-partition minmax values**: during the `merging_pipes` loop in `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreamsFinal`, for each partition, aggregate the minmax index `hyperrectangle` across all parts to get `{min_value, max_value}` per partition key column. 3. **Find the partition-related sorting key column**: starting from `num_leading_fixed` (skipping fixed columns) up to `used_prefix_of_sorting_key_size`, find the first sorting key column that matches a partition key minmax column name. All sorting key columns before it must be fixed — guaranteed by the search starting at `num_leading_fixed`. 4. **Sort partitions by minmax values**: create a permutation array and sort by each partition's `min_value` on the matched column. Ascending by default; descending if the sorting key column has `reverse_flag = true`. 5. **Verify non-overlapping**: walk adjacent partitions in sorted order and confirm that `partition[i].max < partition[i+1].min` (ascending) or `partition[i].min > partition[i+1].max` (descending). If any overlap is found, fall back to parallel `Union`. 6. **Reorder and connect with `ConcatProcessor`**: apply the permutation to `merging_pipes`, unite them, and add a `ConcatProcessor`. Key behaviors: - **Uncorrelated keys**: partition key column not in sorting key → no match found → falls back to parallel `Union` - **Fixed prefix columns**: `ORDER BY (a, b, ts)` with `WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2` → `num_leading_fixed = 2`, search starts at key[2] (`ts`), which matches partition key `toYYYYMM(ts)` - **Reverse key direction**: `ORDER BY (ts DESC)` → `reverse_flag = true` → sort partitions descending so newest partition comes first **Changes:** - Add `optimize_final_limit_pushdown` (Bool) and `optimize_final_sequential_partitions` (Bool) settings - Pass limit to `AggregatingSortedAlgorithm`, `SummingSortedAlgorithm`, and `CoalescingSortedTransform`; add `reachedLimit` early termination check in merge loops - Add `setLimit`/`reachedLimit` to `MergedData` base class - Introduce `final_limit` field on `ReadFromMergeTree`, set by optimizer separately from `input_order_info->limit` (which is cleared by filters) - Add `has_filter_step` flag to `buildSortingDAG` to distinguish PREWHERE (safe for limit pushdown) from WHERE/FilterStep (unsafe) - Add `sorting_key_covers_order_by` guard — only push limit when the sorting key fully covers all ORDER BY columns - Show pushed-down limit in `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` output as `Description: limit N` - Add `num_leading_fixed_sort_key_columns` to `InputOrderInfo`, computed in `buildInputOrderFromSortDescription` - Minmax-index-based sequential partition ordering with `ConcatProcessor` — automatically determines partition order from minmax values and verifies non-overlapping ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `optimize_final_limit_pushdown` setting to push `LIMIT` into `FINAL` merge algorithms for `AggregatingMergeTree`, `SummingMergeTree`, and `CoalescingMergeTree`, enabling early termination. Add `optimize_final_sequential_partitions` setting for sequential partition processing with early termination at the partition level, using minmax index values to determine partition order. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is not required (bug fix, no new user-facing feature)

signal.title: Add `array_join_use_nulls` setting for `LEFT ARRAY JOIN`
signal.text: Added `array_join_use_nulls` setting: when enabled, `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` on empty arrays produces `NULL` instead of default values, and the result column type becomes `Nullable`. Regular `ARRAY JOIN` is unaffected. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/72215 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry: Added `array_join_use_nulls` setting: when enabled, `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` on empty arrays produces `NULL` placeholder values and converts the joined column type to `Nullable` for element types that can be placed inside `Nullable`; for other element types (such as `Array`, `Map` or `AggregateFunction`) it preserves the original type and default padding. This is analogous to `join_use_nulls` for `JOIN`, which has the same limitation. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes When using `LEFT ARRAY JOIN`, rows with empty arrays produce placeholder values. The setting `array_join_use_nulls` controls how ClickHouse fills these cells. If `array_join_use_nulls = 0` (default), empty arrays produce the default value of the element type (e.g. `0` for integers, `''` for strings). If `array_join_use_nulls = 1`, the joined column type is converted to [`Nullable`](/reference/data-types/nullable) and empty arrays produce [`NULL`](/reference/syntax#null). This is analogous to how [`join_use_nulls`](/reference/settings/session-settings/join#join_use_nulls) works for `JOIN`. ```sql SELECT s, arr FROM arrays_test LEFT ARRAY JOIN arr SETTINGS array_join_use_nulls = 1; ┌─s───────────┬──arr─┐ │ Hello │ 1 │ │ Hello │ 2 │ │ World │ 3 │ │ World │ 4 │ │ World │ 5 │ │ Goodbye │ ᴺᵁᴸᴸ │ └─────────────┴──────┘ ``` This setting only affects `LEFT ARRAY JOIN`. Regular `ARRAY JOIN` drops rows with empty arrays regardless of this setting. Just like `join_use_nulls`, the setting applies only to element types that can be placed inside `Nullable`. For an element type that cannot — such as `Array`, `Map` or `AggregateFunction` — the array-joined column keeps its original type, and rows with an empty array keep getting the default value of that type (`[]`, `{}`, ...) rather than `NULL`.

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions clamp(), clamp_min(), clamp_max() and round()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `clamp`, `clamp_min`, `clamp_max`, and `round`. ### Description Implements four PromQL functions previously reported as not implemented: - `clamp(v, min, max)`, `clamp_min(v, min)`, `clamp_max(v, max)` — new `applyClampFunction` converter mapping to `greatest`/`least` SQL with explicit guards, because vectorized `least`/`greatest` in ClickHouse treat NaN as the largest value and ignore NULLs, which would corrupt NaN sample values and missing points. Prometheus special cases are reproduced exactly: `min > max` returns an empty vector, and a NaN bound propagates NaN. - `round(v[, to_nearest])` — new `applyRoundFunction` converter; replicates Prometheus inverse arithmetic (`floor(v * (1/to_nearest) + 0.5) / (1/to_nearest)`), including ties rounding toward `+Inf` and NaN propagation for `to_nearest = 0` or NaN. Both drop the metric name from results, matching Prometheus. Non-constant scalar bounds (for example, `clamp(v, time()*0-1, 2)`) are supported. No parser changes were needed; arity is enforced by each converter. The embedded support matrices for `prometheusQuery` and `prometheusQueryRange` list the new math functions and retain the implemented range functions `increase`, `changes`, and `resets`. **Semantics verified against Prometheus 3.5.0** for bound combinations `(0, 1)`, `(0, 1e12)`, `(1e12, 0)`, `(1e12, 1e12)`, and fractional `to_nearest`. **Testing**: adds `test_clamp` and `test_round`, plus conversion and aggregation regressions for empty scalar handling and a runtime scalar `quantile` parameter outside `[0, 1]`. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1566` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Do not alias pre-aggregation states of a zero-size aggregate in arrayReduceInRanges
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108781 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108781 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `arrayReduceInRanges` over an array whose elements are all NULL aborts a debug or sanitizer build with `Logical error: 'IAggregateFunction::merge called with the same source and destination state'`: ```sql SELECT arrayReduceInRanges('groupArray', [(1, 64)], arrayMap(x -> (x + NULL), range(64))); ``` Found by the AST fuzzer: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114747&sha=95a67283e1b33c000dba21cddefcd4418c4a2c94&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%29 An all-NULL argument collapses the aggregate to `AggregateFunctionNothing`, whose `sizeOfData()` is 0. `Arena::alignedAlloc` advances the arena by `size`, so every zero-byte allocation returns the same address. The function allocates one pre-aggregation state per 64 rows plus one state per range from a single arena, so all of those states alias and both the pairwise level merge and the per-range merge become `merge(p, p)`. The fix allocates `max(sizeOfData(), 1)` bytes for the pre-aggregation states, so they are distinct and every merge still runs. The per-range state needs no padding: that merge only runs when the range spans a whole 64-row block, which is also the condition for a pre-aggregation state to exist, and its one-byte allocation has already advanced the arena. For an aggregate with a non-empty state the allocation is byte-identical to before. I deliberately did not suppress the merge for zero-size states. `sizeOfData() == 0` does not imply that merging is a no-op: `StatelessWindowFunction` is also zero-size and its `mergeImpl` throws. Since the aggregate is caller-supplied, a genuinely empty state cannot be told apart from one whose merge enforces a contract, so skipping the call could drop that enforcement. Two further places with the same allocation pattern are left alone. `ColumnAggregateFunction` can hold zero-size states (the test builds one via `nothingState`) but its `insertMergeFrom` merges across two different arenas. The `Aggregator` merge paths have one reported sighting of the sibling assertion (`mergeAndDestroyBatch`, on #111459) that 15 probes did not reproduce. Release behaviour is unchanged - the assertion compiles out and `Nothing::mergeImpl` is empty.

signal.title: Fix mixed-case PromQL aggregation operators
signal.text: ### Description PromQL keywords are case-insensitive, and the grammar already accepts mixed-case aggregation operators. However, the parser kept the original spelling in the query tree, so expressions such as `SuM(up)` reached lowercase-only lowering dispatch and failed as unsupported. This change normalizes aggregation operator names when building the query tree. The normalization is limited to aggregation expressions, so metric names such as bare `SUM` and case-sensitive function names keep their original spelling. Parser coverage includes mixed-case `sum`, mixed-case `topk` with grouping, and preservation of the bare `SUM` metric name. ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL aggregation operators now accept mixed letter casing, matching Prometheus.** <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1569` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Automatic parallel replicas on TPC-H: evaluation and fixes
signal.text: Record of an evaluation of `automatic_parallel_replicas_mode` (AutoPR) against TPC-H and the defects it exposed. ## Setup Three-replica staging cluster, remote storage. 44 queries: an adapted/optimized TPC-H set (`a01`–`a22`, rewritten to use `IN` subqueries, aggregation pushdown and similar) and the official set (`o01`–`o22`), at sf=100 and sf=1, with statistics defined on all 8 tables and `use_statistics=1`. Three modes per query — single-node, plain parallel replicas, AutoPR — three warm-ups then four measured runs, median per cell. Headline metric is the geomean of per-query ratios against single-node; the median is useless here because AutoPR declines on most queries by design. ## Result sf=100, after the fixes below: | | geomean vs single-node | improved ≥10% | regressed ≥10% | |---|---|---|---| | AutoPR | **−9.6%** | 9 / 44 | **1 / 44** | | plain parallel replicas | −9.7% | 16 / 44 | 4 / 44 | Changed queries: | query | single-node | plain PR | AutoPR | plain PR | AutoPR | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | `a01` | 2658 | 1072 | 1145 | −60% | **−57%** | | `a19` | 1954 | 850 | 862 | −56% | **−56%** | | `o19` | 2575 | 1146 | 1176 | −55% | **−54%** | | `o01` | 2390 | 1118 | 1154 | −53% | **−52%** | | `a06` | 193 | 114 | 108 | −41% | **−44%** | | `o06` | 194 | 120 | 128 | −38% | **−34%** | | `a17` | 1390 | 976 | 978 | −30% | **−30%** | | `a13` | 1324 | 940 | 976 | −29% | **−26%** | | `o12` | 534 | 388 | 400 | −27% | **−25%** | | `a16` | 289 | 988 | 290 | **+242%** | +0% | | `o16` | 308 | 464 | 327 | **+51%** | +6% | | `a20` | 367 | 404 | 350 | +10% | −5% | | `a10` | 1788 | 1374 | 1725 | −23% | −4% | | `o11` | 479 | 379 | 472 | −21% | −1% | | `o09` | 3892 | 3398 | 3832 | −13% | −2% | | `a11` | 280 | 247 | 288 | −12% | +3% | | `o15` | 276 | 244 | 302 | −12% | +9% | | `o14` | 165 | 147 | 164 | −11% | −1% | | `a15` | 272 | 244 | 287 | −10% | +6% | | `o03` | 3025 | 3302 | 3192 | +9% | +6% | | `a07` | 1720 | 1718 | 1824 | −0% | +6% | | `a14` | 236 | 236 | 250 | +0% | +6% | | `a02` | 568 | 738 | 690 | +30% | **+21%** | Progression as fixes landed (geomean, all 44): −8.2% → −10.0% → −9.6%. At sf=1 AutoPR is +11.4% and declines 39 of 43 queries — correctly, since plain PR is +11.1% there. The residual is the probe plan build, a fixed cost on queries running in 13–318 ms. Still open: - **`query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges` is inert under parallel replicas** (details below). q16 is +228% for plain PR; AutoPR declines it, so AutoPR numbers are unaffected. - **AutoPR never accepts with `parallel_replicas_plan_based=1`** — 0 replicas engaged on all 44 queries, geomean +1.1% (pure probe overhead) against AutoPR's −10.2%. Plain PR + plan-based is a different trade rather than a regression (−9.6% vs −8.7%): it wins where query-tree mode is flat (`o07` −47%, `o08` −49%, `o09` −46%, `a02` −3% vs +27%) and loses where query-tree mode wins (`a17`, `a19`). - Shipping `IN` sets to replicas as temporary tables was prototyped and dropped: it fixes `a02` (+28% → +3%) but costs the same elsewhere (`a03` +2% → +35%, `a12` +2% → +36%), geomean ≈ 0. ## Fixed 1. **Selectivity estimation builds the `IN` set it is measuring.** The estimator executed `IN (subquery)` during planning purely to measure it. → [#114389](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114389) 2. **Compact-part input-bytes estimate assumes LZ4.** `estimateCompressedColumnSize` sampled with LZ4 regardless of the column's codec, overshooting ZSTD compact parts 1.5–3.5×. → [#114535](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114535) 3. **The probe re-runs the query's `IN` subqueries.** Index analysis over the probe's reads builds the set on the spot (`KeyCondition::tryPrepareSetIndexForIn`), re-executing subqueries the single-node plan had already run. → [#114231](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114231) 4. **Index analysis transplanted to one read only.** The replicas plan is built without index analysis and only the matched read gets the single-node result; other reads scan everything. q03 selected 94,718 marks against plain PR's 60,963. q22 +96% → +14%, q12 +13% → −13%, q14 +23% → −15%. → [#115153](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115153) 5. **The probe materializes `GLOBAL IN` / `GLOBAL JOIN` subqueries by executing them.** Building the discardable probe runs the `GLOBAL` rewrite, which executes each subquery. q15 materialized the `revenue0` view twice — 8444 marks against single-node's 5670. q15 +33% → +3% (adapted), +46% → +2% (official). → [115154](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115154) 6. **Cancelling waits out an unannounced replica's planning.** `cancelBefore` drains the packet in flight before cancelling; for a replica that has not announced, that packet is `MergeTreeAllRangesAnnouncement`, sent only after the replica has built its own plan. So the initiator blocks for that replica's whole planning phase to receive a message it no longer needs. Sending `Cancel` costs 0.04 ms and the replica acts 0.3 ms later — none of the cost is the wire. q22 +53% → +1%, q20 +96% → +17%, q04 +46% → −1%; each slowdown equalled its read-request time (318 / 353 / 604 ms). → [#114862](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114862) ## Structural limits (not defects) - **The parallelized table is chosen by position, not size.** `findTableForParallelReplicas` picks the leftmost usable table: on q03 (`FROM orders, (subquery over lineitem)`) that coordinates `orders` while the expensive `lineitem` scan stays on the initiator. Coordinated share is 1834 of 23,815 marks on q22, 1200 of 27,236 on q02. - **Only one read step is coordinated** (`TODO(nickitat)` in `considerEnablingParallelReplicas.cpp`). - **Not all queries are supported to begin with**: ``` ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ outcome │ queries │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ reached the cost model │ 27 / 44 │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ BAIL: cannot find matching node │ 9 / 44 — a05 a07 a10 a13 a15 a21 o08 o09 o13 │ └─────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` As for the missing wins (achieved by PRs but not AutoPR): ``` signal.title: Reserve memory for merges up front
signal.text: Add proactive memory reservation for background merges, enhancing the existing `merges_mutations_memory_usage_soft_limit` mechanism. `background_memory_tracker` measures memory that background tasks have *already* allocated, so `canEnqueueBackgroundTask` is purely reactive: when many merges are scheduled at the same time — for example right after a mutation produces many parts — their IO buffers are not allocated yet, all of them pass the gate, and only then grow their memory usage and collide. Every merge now estimates the memory of its input and output IO buffers (`CompactionStatistics::estimateNeededMemoryForMerge`) as the number of input column streams (over all source parts) times the read IO buffer size, plus the number of output column streams (of the result part) times the write IO buffer size. Object storage (S3) write buffers are large and double-buffered, so they are accounted separately. Since IO buffers only ever hold data that flows through them, the estimate is capped by the data volume of the merge (beyond the eagerly allocated per-stream compressor and file buffers, which honor adaptive write buffers): without this cap, a merge of tiny parts in a many-column table on object storage would reserve gigabytes it can never touch, and concurrent merges would saturate the soft limit and starve each other. The merge reserves this amount at start (`MergeMemoryReservation`) and releases it when it finishes. A merge that will certainly run the vertical algorithm is priced by the streams that are alive at once (the merging columns, one gathering column at a time, and up to `max_merge_delayed_streams_for_parallel_write` delayed streams) rather than all output streams concurrently, and a stream whose data volume is not derivable from the source parts (a rebuilt projection, a `DEFAULT`-filled column of variable size) is priced at the buffers its writer allocates before any data flows through it (its compressor block and file buffer) plus a projected-volume bound, rather than at any multipart upload size - a multipart writer starts from the buffer size its caller passes and grows it only with the data written into it, leaving further growth to the reactive tracker — over-reservation starves all merges, while under-reservation merely degrades to the reactive behavior of the current code for that stream. `canEnqueueBackgroundTask` now consults both the actual usage and the reservation: - a non-replicated background merge reserves at selection and is not scheduled when the reservation would exceed the limit (it retries later); once `CurrentlyMergingPartsTagger` chooses the actual destination disk, the reservation is corrected if the pre-selection guess made from the source parts was wrong, and a merge that waited in the background queue re-prices its reservation at task start against the destination disk's live multipart upload settings (a config reload could have raised them), as the replicated path does. Whether a background merge runs as a `ReplacingMergeTree` cleanup merge is decided at selection and carried to the scheduler, so a row-reducing cleanup merge is priced as one; - a replicated merge, already committed to run locally, reserves unconditionally at execution so the reservation still throttles selection of further merges; - a user-initiated merge (`OPTIMIZE`) also reserves unconditionally, so it is throttled by the gate for other merges but can never be silently skipped by it. A single merge whose estimate exceeds the whole limit is always allowed to proceed alone, so progress is never blocked. Adds the `MergesMutationsMemoryReservation` metric for observability, a `gtest` for the reservation accounting, and stateless tests: a smoke test and a regression test that `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` merges everything down to a single part under a pathologically small soft limit instead of silently doing nothing. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Background merges now reserve the memory of their input/output IO buffers up front against `merges_mutations_memory_usage_soft_limit`, so that scheduling many merges at once (for example right after a mutation) can no longer oversubscribe memory as they all start. A user-initiated `OPTIMIZE` is never silently skipped by this mechanism.

signal.title: Fix undefined behavior in DateTime64 reservoir quantiles
signal.text: The reservoir-sampling implementation of `quantile` and `quantiles` previously interpolated decimal-backed values through `Float64`. `DateTime64` ticks close to the upper `Int64` boundary, as well as `Decimal128` and `Decimal256` values near their limits, can collapse to the same `Float64` value and make conversion back to the native representation undefined or return an incorrect endpoint. Interpolate decimal-backed samples in their exact native domain instead, and cover scalar/plural `DateTime64` plus wide-decimal boundary cases with stateless regression tests. Found by the `arm_asan_ubsan` stress test: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112573&sha=762fa93f05ca081011efec5fef767e3c36be6853&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114485 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107154 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed undefined behavior and incorrect boundary results in `quantile` and `quantiles` for `DateTime64` and wide `Decimal` values.

signal.title: Add replica_host configuration for DatabaseReplicated
signal.text: <!--- Disable AI PR formatting assistant: true --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `replica_host` configuration parameter for DatabaseReplicated to specify advertised hostname for replica communication, independent from server bind address. Resolves #88378 ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) ### Details Currently, DatabaseReplicated uses `interserver_http_host` or the system hostname, which may not be routable from other replicas. This PR adds a new `replica_host` configuration parameter that allows administrators to explicitly specify the advertised hostname for DatabaseReplicated communication. Resolves #88378 ## Changes 1. **New Configuration Parameter**: `replica_host` - Optional parameter in `config.xml` - Takes precedence over `interserver_http_host` and system hostname 2. **Fallback Chain**: ``` replica_host (highest priority) ↓ interserver_http_host ↓ getFQDNOrHostName() (lowest priority) ``` 3. **Automatic Migration**: - When configuration changes (e.g., adding `replica_host`), automatically updates ZooKeeper if UUID and TCP port match - Prevents startup failures when only the advertised hostname changes - Rejects changes if UUID or port differ (different instance/misconfiguration) 4. **Implementation**: - Added `Context::getReplicaHost()`, `setReplicaHost()`, `hasReplicaHost()` - Modified `DatabaseReplicated::getHostID()` to use fallback chain - Added `parseHostID()` helper for UUID and port validation - Server.cpp reads `replica_host` from config on startup ## Configuration Example ```xml public.example.com 0.0.0.0 9000 ``` ## Backward Compatibility Fully backward compatible: - Optional parameter (no behavior change if not configured) - Existing `interserver_http_host` continues to work - Automatic migration prevents startup failures during config updates

signal.title: Fix build flag with new detection mode.
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107399 --> Fixes a build failure on AArch64 CPUs that are advertised as ARMv8.2-A but lack an optional feature of ClickHouse's "modern" ARM profile — for example the HiSilicon Kunpeng 920, which has no `rcpc` and faults with `SIGILL` on the `ldapr` instruction. Such CPUs must be built with `-DNO_ARMV81_OR_HIGHER=1`, but that profile previously failed to compile the Rust components. Root cause: the compatibility profile passed `target_feature=+crc,-neon` to Rust. NEON (Advanced SIMD) is part of the AArch64 baseline and is enabled by default for the `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` target. The `ring` crate (pulled in by `chdig` and `delta-kernel-rs`) statically asserts that NEON is available on little-endian aarch64 and fails to compile when it is disabled. Dropping the `-neon` lets the compatibility profile build `ring`, so `chdig` and `delta-kernel-rs` no longer need to be force-disabled under `NO_ARMV81_OR_HIGHER`. An earlier revision of this pull request auto-detected CPU features from `/proc/cpuinfo` at build time. That approach was reverted following review: ClickHouse always builds for an explicitly specified target platform and must not depend on the host machine (one can build on a coffee machine while targeting an AVX-512 server and vice versa). The pre-existing build-time `/proc/cpuinfo` "best-effort" guard on the AArch64 path is removed for the same reason. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107399 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Build/Testing/Packaging Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed building with `-DNO_ARMV81_OR_HIGHER=1` on AArch64: the compatibility profile no longer disables NEON for Rust, so `ring`-based components (`chdig`, `delta-kernel-rs`) compile and stay enabled. This unblocks building for ARMv8.2-A CPUs that lack `rcpc` (e.g. HiSilicon Kunpeng 920). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Accept PromQL line comments at EOF
signal.text: ### Description PromQL line comments currently require a newline, so valid queries with a trailing comment at EOF, such as `up # trailing comment`, are rejected by ClickHouse. Prometheus consumes line comments through CR, LF, or EOF and skips comment tokens before parsing the expression. This change matches that behavior, regenerates the checked-in ANTLR lexer artifacts, and adds coverage for EOF, LF, CRLF, adjacent comments, and comment-only input. Upstream references: - [Prometheus lexer](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/lex.go#L874-L882) - [Prometheus line-ending handling](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/lex.go#L1123-L1125) - [Prometheus parser comment handling](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse.go#L2817-L2855) - [Prometheus comment-only query test](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse_test.go#L3206-L3220) ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Accept PromQL line comments that end at EOF.**

signal.title: Do not serve min/max from an unusable minmax_count projection bound
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111938 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `min` and `max` returning a wrong value when the implicit `_minmax_count_projection` answered them from a part-level bound that is not a real row value: a `NULL` in a `Nullable` sorting key, a `NaN` in a float key, or a `Tuple` bound assembled component-wise. Such a query now reads rows instead of using the projection. ### Description `getMinMaxCountProjectionBlock` answers `min(col)`/`max(col)` from part-level bounds, feeding each straight into an aggregate state. That is only correct when the bound is a real row value, ordered as the aggregate orders it. Three ways it is not: - **NULL** (as reported): keys sort NULLS LAST so the top index entry is a NULL while `max` skips NULLs, and the `POSITIVE_INFINITY` pruning sentinel materializes as a SQL NULL. - **NaN**, no `Nullable` involved: the writer sorts NaN above every number while `max` skips it, so `Float64 ORDER BY k` over `(1),(200),(nan)` gives `nan`. - **Component-wise synthesis**, no NULL or NaN: `getExtremes` runs per column, so a `Tuple` bound envelopes each component's extreme and need not be any row. This breaks `min` too. Worse than the reported `NULL` is the silent shape: when the true maximum shares a part with a NULL, `max` returns the largest of the other parts, `4` instead of `200`. The fix declines the implicit projection for such a query, reusing the escape hatch this function already has earlier (`return {}` when a part has no final mark). A part whose bound pair is one repeated degenerate value stays exempt, since skipping it is the right contribution; for an index bound that exemption also requires a final mark, without which the index samples granule starts only and a repeated pair proves nothing. I rejected skipping only the poisoned part, which is the silent shape above, and changing the write path, since the sentinel is needed for `IS NULL` pruning and existing parts would stay broken. The new test covers each class across nullable, low-cardinality, tuple and float keys, ASC and DESC, one and several parts, and a part with no final mark. Issue #104412 is a different defect here, verified unaffected.
signal.author: groeneai

signal.title: Accept LowCardinality(UInt64) as a dictionary simple primary key
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104539 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `CREATE DICTIONARY` failing with `Incorrect type of ID column: must be UInt64, but it is LowCardinality` when the simple primary key is declared as `LowCardinality(UInt64)` and `dictionary_validate_primary_key_type` is enabled. Closes #104539. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104539 With `dictionary_validate_primary_key_type = 1`, declaring a simple primary key as `LowCardinality(UInt64)` is rejected: ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: Incorrect type of ID column: must be UInt64, but it is LowCardinality. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` With the setting off (the default) the same dictionary is created, loads, and answers `dictGet`/`dictHas`/`SELECT *` correctly, with the key normalized to plain `UInt64`. So valid input is rejected. **Root cause.** `StorageDictionary::getNamesAndTypes` compared the raw outer `TypeIndex` of the declared key type against `TypeIndex::UInt64`. For `LowCardinality(UInt64)` that yields the wrapper's index, not the payload's. `LowCardinality` is a physical-representation wrapper, not a distinct logical type, so the validator answered a logical question with a physical predicate. **The change** unwraps one `LowCardinality` level before the comparison, for both the test and the message. The declared simple-key type is already advisory everywhere else: `getKeyTypes()` returns `{UInt64}` unconditionally and every other simple-key site constructs `DataTypeUInt64` directly, which is why the setting-off path already worked. This is the only site in `src/` that type-tests the declared key type. **Exactly one type changes behaviour:** `LowCardinality(UInt64)` becomes accepted. `Nullable(UInt64)` and `LowCardinality(Nullable(UInt64))` stay rejected, since a NULL key is meaningless for a lookup; one-level unwrap gives that for free, and the new test pins it so a later switch to `removeLowCardinalityAndNullable` cannot silently widen it. `LowCardinality(String)` also stays rejected, as a plain `String` key is rejected by design; its message now names the payload. The setting's default (`false`) is unchanged and nothing valid today becomes invalid, so no `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` entry applies. Noted, not addressed here: `LowCardinality` keys are only constructible on `LAYOUT(FLAT())`, because `DictionaryStructure::getAttributes` strips `Nullable` but not `LowCardinality` and `AttributeUnderlyingType` has no `LowCardinality` member, so other layouts fail earlier with `UNKNOWN_TYPE` regardless of this setting.

signal.title: Fix CI crash reporter naming logical errors after query-echoed text
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108735 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: #108735 The functional/stress crash reporter (`FuzzerLogParser` in `ci/jobs/scripts/log_parser.py`, invoked by `ClickHouseProc.check_fatal_messages_in_logs`) names a failure by running `rg -o 'Logical error.*'` over the whole `clickhouse-server.log` and taking the first match. `executeQuery` logs the full query text (SQL comments included) into the server log, and the signal handler embeds the crashing query inside a `<Fatal>` record. So when a job hits a real logical-error crash, the reporter can pick up a *different* test's comment that merely quotes `Logical error '...'` and use it as the failure name, while the STID and stack come from the actual crash. This mislabels unrelated crashes and pollutes failure tracking. Concrete example (MasterCI, `Stateless tests (amd_llvm_coverage, ParallelReplicas, s3 storage, parallel)`): the real crash was `<Fatal> : Logical error: 'Got read request from replica 1 for unknown stream ...'` (`ParallelReplicasReadingCoordinator`), but the reporter named it after a regression test's `!part.empty()` / `Bad cast ...` comment. This wrongly reopened an unrelated tracking task. Fix, in `log_parser.py`: - Match `Logical error` only as the message of a real formatted log record, anchored to the line prefix `^<date> <time> [ tid ] {query_id} <Fatal> [logger]: Logical error: ...`. A query echo, a comment continuation line, and query text embedded mid-line on a `<Fatal>` signal record all fail that anchor. The anchor also requires the `<Fatal>` level and the `Logical error:` colon, so a benign `<Warning> ...: Logical error. Not all polled messages ...` is not selected. Genuine logical errors are always emitted via `LOG_FATAL` (`abortOnFailedAssertion`), so nothing real is missed. The other patterns (sanitizer, assertion, segfault, signal, memory) are byte-for-byte unchanged. - `get_failed_query()` reuses the query id of the selected fatal record instead of re-grepping the log from the top, so the reported failing query matches the crash. An explicitly empty id (background exception with no query) reports no query rather than an unrelated one; the inline `Inconsistent AST formatting` query (which aborts before an `executeQuery` record is logged) is still extracted, scoped to the selected record; and the query id is matched inside its `{...}` delimiters and escaped, so `q2` no longer also matches `{q20}` and a metacharacter id is literal. Added regression tests in `ci/tests/test_log_parser.py`; existing tests unchanged.

signal.title: More settings to randomize
signal.text: Extends the stateless-test randomizers in `tests/clickhouse-test` with settings added since they were last swept, and pins the tests that were implicitly relying on the old defaults. `SettingsRandomizer`: * Broadens `query_plan_optimize_join_order_algorithm` to cover `dpsub` and `dphyp` (always with `greedy` kept in the fallback chain, since exhausting the chain throws `EXPERIMENTAL_FEATURE_ERROR`), and randomizes `query_plan_optimize_join_order_max_searched_plans`. * Adds ~35 further query-level settings (`LIMIT BY` / `FINAL` / lazy-`FINAL` / runtime-filter / text-index / statistics / regexp-compilation toggles and their numeric companions). * Adds `use_statistics_for_part_pruning` → `use_statistics` and `use_projection_index_in_read_pools` → `optimize_use_projection_filtering` to `conditional_settings`, so a child setting is not enabled while its parent is off. * Randomizes `function_implementation` over the values the server actually supports, probed at startup: it globally filters every `ImplementationSelector`-backed function and each has a different arch-tag set, so a forced value that some function lacks would raise `NO_SUITABLE_FUNCTION_IMPLEMENTATION`. * A few settings are deliberately left commented out with the reason recorded in place, e.g. `use_constant_folding_in_index_analysis` (unsafe per-part min-max prune, and the trigger for https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109893), `correlated_subqueries_use_in_memory_buffer`, `min_filtered_ratio_for_lazy_final` (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112332) and `max_streams_for_union_step`. `MergeTreeSettingsRandomizer`: * Randomizes `concurrent_part_removal_threshold_for_remote_disk`. * The implicit min-max index settings (`add_minmax_index_for_block_number_column`, `add_minmax_index_for_block_offset_column`, `part_minmax_index_columns`) are explicitly kept out: they are not transparent to queries. The first two add real `MINMAX` skipping indices named `auto_minmax_index__block_number` / `auto_minmax_index__block_offset`, which surface in `SHOW INDEXES`, `system.data_skipping_indices`, part checksums and the `Skip` section of `EXPLAIN indexes = 1`; `part_minmax_index_columns = with_block_number_offset` gives every table a part-level min-max index even with no partition key, so `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` grows an extra `Min-Max / Condition: true` block everywhere. This is the same reason their siblings `add_minmax_index_for_{numeric,string,temporal}_columns` were never randomized — all five are `isReadonlySetting`, i.e. part of the table schema. The rest of the diff pins the affected settings in the stateless tests whose output depends on them. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107586 (fixes the `Invalid binary search result in MergeTreeSetIndex` logical error this randomization made much more likely to be hit; merged, so it is pulled in by the branch update) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109893 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112332 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Running CI a few times before merging.

signal.title: Support PromQL timestamp() function on both vector selectors and general expressions
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: `timestamp()` is now implemented for both direct selectors and general expressions, matching Prometheus 3.5.0 semantics. ### Description `timestamp(<expression>)` previously threw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. This PR implements `timestamp()` support for both direct vector selectors and general instant vector expressions (e.g. `timestamp(test)`, `timestamp(test offset 1m)`, `timestamp(test * 1)`, `timestamp(-test)`, `timestamp(timestamp(test))`). Matching Prometheus 3.5.0 semantics: - For direct instant vector selectors (plus optional direct `offset`/`@` modifiers), extracts the raw sample timestamp from storage via `timeSeriesTimestampToGrid`. - For general instant vector expressions (binary math, unary operators, comparisons, nested `timestamp()` calls), evaluates the argument as an instant vector and returns the query step evaluation timestamp ($T_{\text{eval}}$) for each present sample. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0**, including the timestamp-unit conversion (seconds, not milliseconds). **Testing**: Added integration test cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering bare vector selectors, offset/@ modifiers, binary math, unary minus, and nested `timestamp()` calls.

signal.title: Ask for continuation in single-line mode when query is incomplete
signal.text: ### What this PR does In single-line interactive mode, pressing Enter on an incomplete query (one where the parser reaches the end of input still expecting more tokens) no longer sends it and shows a syntax error. Instead, a newline is inserted into the same edit buffer, exactly like pressing Alt+Enter, so the whole query stays under a single prompt and the arrow keys can navigate and edit across all of its lines. A trailing `;` still forces submission (for example, to deliberately submit an incomplete query and see its syntax error). This replaces the earlier approach that printed a separate `:-] ` continuation prompt and read additional lines, which prevented cross-line editing and could split pasted queries. The completeness check is now passed to `ReplxxLineReader` as a callback and consulted from the `commit_action` bound to Enter. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/64886 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): In single-line interactive mode, `clickhouse-client` now keeps an incomplete query under a single prompt and lets you continue it on the next line (like pressing Alt+Enter) instead of sending it immediately. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (not required for this change)

signal.title: Fix wrong count and wrong DELETE when a NULL expression sits under NOT
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112242 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112242 Requested by @ nihalzp in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112242#issuecomment-5312306258 (reported by @ zlareb1). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results when a `WHERE` clause contained a `NULL` expression under a `NOT`, for example `SELECT count() FROM t WHERE NOT (id >= 20 AND NULL)`. Index analysis treated such a condition as provably true for the whole range, so the filter was skipped: `count()` returned rows the query rejects, and `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE` with that condition removed rows it should have kept. ### Description ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t SELECT number FROM numbers(40); SELECT count() FROM t WHERE NOT (id >= 20 AND NULL); -- returned 40, correct is 20 ``` Reading the rows returned 20, so `count()` and the row set disagreed on one predicate. A mutation was worse: `ALTER TABLE t DELETE WHERE NOT (id >= 38 AND NULL)` deleted all 40 rows, although the predicate is `NULL` for `id` 38 and 39, so those two had to survive. **Root cause.** `cloneDAGWithInversionPushDown` pushes `NOT` to the leaves. For `NOT (id >= 20 AND NULL)`, De Morgan turns the `and` into an `or` and pushes the inversion into both children; the all-NULL leaf is not recognized, so the tail wraps it in a literal `not()`, which `RPNBuilder` complements classically into "provably true for every row". Both steps hold only in two-valued logic: `NOT NULL` is `NULL`, which `WHERE` must reject. **The change.** Before the node dispatch, an all-NULL node absorbs the inversion instead of receiving a `not()` wrapper, the same idiom the neighbouring `materialize` and trivial-cast branches use. It still folds to "never true" downstream, correct because `NULL` is not `TRUE`, and a non-negated `x AND NULL` keeps its exact fast path. Absorbing the inversion substitutes the operand's type for the `not()` result type, so the guard is confined to `boolean_context`, the existing flag for positions where the caller discards the value. In a value position a negation would otherwise change type and drop valid rows. The all-NULL test needs both a column and a type check: `toInt64OrNull('x')` is typed `Nullable(Int64)`, while `if(id % 2, NULL, NULL)` has no constant column. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Debug build of the base commit vs the same build with the change. | probe | base | with change | correct | |---|---|---|---| | `count() WHERE NOT (id >= 20 AND NULL)` | 40 | 20 | 20 | | same with `toInt64OrNull('x')` | 40 | 20 | 20 | | same with `CAST(NULL, 'Nullable(UInt8)')` | 40 | 20 | 20 | | same with `if(id % 2, NULL, NULL)` | 40 | 20 | 20 | | same with `materialize(NULL)` | 40 | 20 | 20 | | `numbers(100) WHERE NOT (number = 5 AND NULL) LIMIT 10` | 9 | 10 | 10 | | minmax skip index, same predicate | 40 | 20 | 20 | | `ALTER DELETE WHERE NOT (id >= 38 AND NULL)`, survivors | `[]` | `[38,39]` | `[38,39]` | | `count() WHERE id >= 20 AND NULL` | 0 | 0 | 0 | | `numbers() WHERE number > 0 AND NULL LIMIT 10` | 0 fast | 0 fast | 0 fast | | value position, `ifNull(NOT materialize(CAST(NULL, 'Nullable(Int64)')), 0)`, rows | 40 | 40 | 40 | | same with `Nullable(Float64)`, rows | 40 | 40 | 40 | The new test fails on the base build, passes with the change, and passed 50/50 randomized runs. Deleting any one of the three parts of the guard makes it fail again on exactly the arms that part covers: the column test covers `toInt64OrNull` and `CAST`, the type test covers `if(id % 2, NULL, NULL)`, the `boolean_context` test covers the two value-position arms. The unbounded `numbers()` lines pin the positive direction, which an earlier attempt at this fix turned into a hang. The projection, `KeyCondition` and minmax test families were run on both builds: the same 23 tests fail either way, all on ZooKeeper and distributed connections unavailable in this sandbox, none mentioning the exact-count projection or `KeyCondition`. </details>

signal.title: Reduce the per-arm work of 04895_parquet_dictionary_source_prefetch_lifetime
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114668 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114668 (the use-after-free this test guards). @ PedroTadim asked for the per-arm work of this test to be trimmed. `04895` runs at 93.5% of the flaky check's 180 s per-arm cap on `Stateless tests (amd_asan_ubsan, flaky check)`: p50 141.5 s, p99 165.9 s, max 168.3 s over 50 arms in 21 days of public CIDB, so about 12 s of headroom. No duration breach yet, so this is headroom rather than a live failure. The fixture is larger than the mechanism needs. The detector requires many concurrent queued read ranges alive at throw time, and what supplies them is the row group count plus `input_format_parquet_local_file_min_bytes_for_seek = 1` and the 32 download / 32 parsing threads. None of that depends on payload size. Scaling `numbers()` and `output_format_parquet_row_group_size` by the same factor of 10 keeps the row group count at exactly 397 while cutting the file from 19,785,515 to 2,356,314 bytes. I did not shrink `repeat('y', 400)`: it is a single distinct value, so it is RLE_DICTIONARY encoded to about 0.25 B/row. `key` is 97.5% of the file and `val` 2.5%, and cutting the string width from 400 to 40 moves total bytes by only 18%. Validation. Against a binary with the `resetReadBuffer` override removed, the trimmed test fails 20/20 with the pure-virtual abort at `Prefetcher.cpp:116` in `readSync`, and passes 20/20 with the fix. Because both the trimmed and the untrimmed fixture saturate at 20/20 there, I lowered the thread counts until redness became fractional to get resolution: at 8 threads the trimmed fixture reddens 30/40 versus 4/40 untrimmed, so the trim makes the detector more sensitive, not less. All three oracles are unchanged and were each shown able to redden, `.reference` is untouched, and 50 randomized runs pass. <details> <summary>Measured duration, ASAN, trimmed vs current</summary> `tests/clickhouse-test`, randomized settings, 12 arms each against the same server: | arm | min | p50 | p90 | max | |---|---|---|---|---| | trimmed | 20.03 s | 20.84 s | 21.34 s | 21.90 s | | current | 21.14 s | 22.90 s | 23.49 s | 23.65 s | The serial gain is about 9% because the roughly 2000 row group reads per arm are deliberately kept. The gain grows with concurrency, which is the regime the flaky check runs in, since `allow_oversubscription` is False there and every worker runs the same test: | concurrent copies | trimmed p50 | current p50 | saving | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 11.43 s | 12.51 s | 8.6% | | 8 | 12.31 s | 15.16 s | 18.8% | | 16 | 12.87 s | 19.44 s | 33.8% | | 20 | 13.66 s | 22.67 s | 39.7% | Server side, reload phase IO drops from 54.24 MiB to 13.99 MiB at an identical 1985 row group reads. These are local numbers on one box and do not predict a contended CI runner, so there is no timing assertion in the test. </details>

signal.title: Fix compiled `if`/`multiIf` on a negative `Time` value
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `if` and `multiIf` returning a large positive value instead of a negative one when a `Time` branch is combined with `Time64`, `DateTime` or `DateTime64` and the expression is JIT-compiled. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114168 (found there in review; a separate mechanism) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/103390 A negative `Time` value read through a JIT-compiled `if`/`multiIf` comes back as a huge positive number: ```sql SELECT if(number % 2 = 0, toTime('-01:00:00'), toTime64('00:00:00', 3)) FROM numbers(1); -- executions 1-3: -01:00:00.000 -- execution 4+: 999:59:59.000 ``` No `SETTINGS` clause is needed to hit this: `compile_expressions` defaults to `1` and `min_count_to_compile_expression` to `3`, so the 4th execution of the expression in a session silently changes the answer. `enable_time_time64_type` also defaults to `1`. The wrong value is ticks `4294963696` = `2^32 - 3600`, i.e. the negative `Int32` tick count zero-extended to 64 bits. Root cause: `typeIsSigned` in `src/DataTypes/Native.cpp` did not list the `Time` family, so the widening cast emitted by `FunctionIfBase::compileImpl` asked whether `Time` is signed, got `false`, and LLVM emitted `zext` where `sext` was required. `Time` is `DataTypeNumberBase<Int32>` and is the only member of the date/time family that widens on this path, which is why the defect is specific to it. `Time64` is included in the same predicate for correctness of the contract: `isDecimal()` matches only `TypeIndex::Decimal32..256` and so does not cover `TypeIndex::Time64` - the same reason `isDateTime64()` is listed separately. No wrong-result carrier reaches the `Time64` half today, so it is not given a test that could not fail. Validation: five wrong-result carriers plus a `Nullable(Time)` case are covered by the new test. The reference values were taken from the non-compiled path on an unpatched binary, so the oracle is independent of this change. With the predicate token removed the test fails on 7 of 13 lines; non-negative `Time`, large-negative `Time`, and `DateTime64` controls are unchanged. 50/50 runs under settings randomization pass.

signal.title: Add exclude_data_from_backup MergeTree setting
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111827 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added exclude_from_backup and exclude_data_from_backup MergeTree table settings so BACKUP can skip a table entirely or skip only its data while still restoring its DDL. ### Description Implements #111827: a table-level setting so that `BACKUP` can skip a table's data while still including its DDL, so the table is restorable (empty) later. Useful for tables whose data can be regenerated from a source table (e.g. materialized-view targets), to reduce backup size. - New `Bool` MergeTree setting `exclude_data_from_backup` (default `false`). - Hooked into `BackupEntriesCollector::shouldBackupTableData()`: when the setting is enabled on a `MergeTreeData`-derived table, data collection is skipped for that table; DDL collection is unaffected (existing code path already handles DDL/data independently). - Added `tests/integration/test_exclude_data_from_backup/test.py` covering both the default (`false`, data backed up) and enabled (`true`, data skipped) cases; both pass. **Not yet tested** (feedback welcome): behavior on `ReplicatedMergeTree` specifically, and `BACKUP DATABASE`/`BACKUP ... ALL TABLES` paths (the hook is in the shared per-table code path used by all backup forms, so it should behave the same, but I haven't added explicit coverage for these yet). The setting name/interface is intentionally not MergeTree-specific in wording, per @alexey-milovidov's suggestion on the issue, so it could be adopted by other engines later.

signal.title: Do not read the master-only system.parts.files column in 04550_restore_fsync_after_insert
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111378 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115088 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `04550_restore_fsync_after_insert.sh` (added by #111378) read the `files` column of `system.parts` to size the encrypted-incremental-restore fsync assertion. That column was added by 476e9fcb3bb3f26 in January, after 25.8 forked, so the automated 25.8 backport #115088 fails at runtime even though the cherry-pick applied cleanly and the script is byte-identical: ``` Code: 47. Unknown expression identifier `files` in scope SELECT files FROM system.parts WHERE ... AND (`table` = 't_restore_fsync_enc'). (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) Code: 32. Attempt to read after eof: value cannot be parsed as UInt64 for query parameter 'files'. ``` CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115088&sha=980e9739e2ff0687cec113ed6460d38af75034f6&name_0=BackportPR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_asan%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%20parallel%2C%201%2F2%29 The count the assertion wants is how many files RESTORE copies and must therefore fsync. The test already measures exactly that for its first table, with `SELECT path FROM system.parts` plus `find`. This drops the `system.parts.files` read and feeds the encrypted arm the same count. The two tables have identical schema, data and part-layout settings, so their parts hold the same file set; the assertion gets stronger, since the physical count also covers `checksums.txt`, `columns.txt` and the zero-byte `arr.bin` that the checksums map does not enumerate. `.reference` is unchanged. Validation: on the official 25.8 binary the old test reproduces both errors above and the new one runs to completion. On master the encrypted restore performs 20 `FileSync` events against a required 18, and the two arms' part file lists are identical on both branches (18 files on master, 15 on 25.8), so the reuse does not depend on a master-specific layout. Disabling `fsync_after_insert` on the encrypted table still fails the test, so the assertion is not vacuous. 50/50 runs green with randomized settings. Note that #115088 cannot pick this up by regeneration: the backport tree is built from #111378's merge commit, so a regenerated backport carries the same broken line.

signal.title: Fix flaky 04896_orfill_merge_group_by_overflow_any under randomized index_granularity_bytes
signal.text: `04896_orfill_merge_group_by_overflow_any` fails on master whenever the stateless-test runner randomizes `index_granularity_bytes` down to a small value: ``` Code: 117. DB::Exception: Projection p is specified in setting force_optimize_projection_name but not used. (INCORRECT_DATA) ``` The runner's own diagnosis isolated the culprit to `--index_granularity_bytes 21597` (182/182 runs failed with it, 249/249 passed without randomization). Projection `p` stores five aggregate states per row, so its parts are several times wider than the parent table's three `UInt64` columns. With adaptive granularity on and a small `index_granularity_bytes`, the parts of `p` get cut into more granules than the parent parts — 5 marks against 2 at `--index_granularity_bytes 21597` — so `optimizeUseAggregateProjections` discards `p` as "not better than the original table with 2 marks", selects `p2` instead, and `force_optimize_projection_name = 'p'` throws. This fix turns adaptive granularity off for the table so that `p` and the parent table are cut into the same number of granules and `p` stays selectable. The test does not depend on granularity in any other way, and `index_granularity` itself stays randomized. Verified locally on `aarch64`: the test reproduces the failure deterministically before the change under the CI settings, and matches its reference after the change under the full CI setting set as well as across a sweep of `index_granularity_bytes` / `index_granularity` / `min_bytes_for_wide_part` values. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=39e9002316ee472caf62fbb837832c776f10c06f&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28arm_binary%2C%20parallel%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114740 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signal.title: Fix arrayROCAUC and arrayAUCPR returning order-dependent results for NaN scores
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104763 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `arrayROCAUC` and `arrayAUCPR` (and their aliases `arrayAUC` and `arrayPRAUC`) returning a different result for the same data depending on the order of the array elements when a score was `NaN`. A `NaN` score now makes the result `NaN`. Closes [#104763](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104763). ### Description Closes: #104763. **The problem.** These are pure functions of a set of (score, label) pairs, so permuting the pairs must not change the result. With a `NaN` score it did: `arrayAUCPR([nan, 0.5], [1, 1])` returned `nan` while `arrayAUCPR([0.5, nan], [1, 1])` returned `1`. No error was raised, so the metric was silently wrong. **Root cause.** Two independent defects in `FunctionArrayAUC::apply`, both reachable from a single `NaN`: 1. The descending-score comparator passed to `std::sort` is not a strict weak ordering when a score is `NaN` (every comparison with `NaN` is false, so incomparability is not transitive), so the sorted order, and the traversal with it, follows the input order. 2. `threshold` is seeded from the first sorted element so the first iteration never increments the area, but `nan != nan` is true, so the guard fires with `tp = fp = 0`, and the Precision-Recall precision term becomes `0 / 0`. **The change.** `apply` returns `NaN` if any score is `NaN`, before sorting. That removes both defects at once, and `std::sort`'s precondition then holds for every input reaching it. `NaN` in, `NaN` out matches `sum`, `avg`, `arraySum` and `corr`, and `arrayROCAUC` already used `NaN` for its undefined cases. Beyond the reported `arrayAUCPR` case this also fixes `arrayROCAUC`, both aliases, the `scale` argument and the 3- and 4-argument `partial_offsets` forms, all affected the same way. The intentional value change: any `NaN`-containing input now returns `NaN` instead of an order-dependent number, including the all-`NaN` case, where `arrayROCAUC` returned `1` or `0` depending on the label order. Infinities are ordered normally, so they are unaffected and have regression tests. A `NaN` label was already order independent. Rejecting `NaN` with an exception would be backward incompatible, so I did not pick it unilaterally. If a hard error is preferred, I will switch. Requested in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104763#issuecomment-5312328708.
