signal.title: Implement FIFO admission queue with per-waiter wakeup for ProcessList
signal.text: ## Summary This PR adds a FIFO admission queue to `ProcessList` as an alternative to the existing `condvar`-based admission (`have_space` → `notify_all`) and the `QuerySlot` resource scheduler. When `enable_query_admission_queue` is enabled, queries that exceed `max_concurrent_queries` enter a per-waiter FIFO queue instead of thundering-herd `notify_all` wakeups or immediate rejection. Each waiter gets its own `std::condition_variable`, so exactly one query is woken when a slot becomes available — O(1) wakeup with strict FIFO ordering. The queue includes a periodic alive-check that detects disconnected clients via `MSG_DONTWAIT | MSG_PEEK` on the socket, preventing slot leaks from abandoned connections. As a secondary optimization, `ThreadPool::worker` replaces `sched_yield` spin in the `Preparing→Running` handshake with `std::atomic::wait/notify_one`, eliminating a context-switch amplification loop that degraded throughput under high concurrency. ### Why not just use `CREATE RESOURCE ... (QUERY)` / `CREATE WORKLOAD`? The resource scheduler's query slot mechanism achieves similar throughput and latency, but requires DDL setup (`CREATE RESOURCE`, `CREATE WORKLOAD`). This PR simply extends the existing `max_concurrent_queries` + `queue_max_wait_ms` behavior — one server setting to enable, no DDL needed. It also adds client disconnect detection and observable metrics (`QueryAdmissionQueueLength`, `QueryAdmissionQueueWaitMicroseconds`) out of the box. **Changes:** - New server settings `enable_query_admission_queue` (default false) and `admission_queue_alive_check_interval_ms` (default 5000, clamped to [500, 10000]) - FIFO admission queue in `ProcessList::insert` using `std::deque<AdmissionWaiter>` with per-waiter `std::condition_variable` and `notify_one` - `QueryStatus::holds_admission_slot` tracks whether a query holds an admission slot, released in `executeQuery` (same timing as `QuerySlot`) or `~ProcessListEntry` - `releaseAdmissionSlotLocked(Lock &)` follows ClickHouse's lock-proof pattern (like `MergeTreeData::Transaction::commit(DataPartsLock &)`) - Socket alive-check callback (`SocketAliveCheck.h`) registered per protocol handler (TCP, HTTP, MySQL, PostgreSQL, gRPC, Arrow Flight) - New metric `QueryAdmissionQueueLength` and profile event `QueryAdmissionQueueWaitMicroseconds` - `ThreadPool::worker` uses `std::atomic::wait/notify_one` instead of `sched_yield` for thread startup handshake - Condition variable `have_space` renamed to `query_finished` to reflect its actual semantics (not admission-specific) - Uses `LockAndOverCommitTrackerBlocker` in `QueryStatus::releaseAdmissionSlot` to prevent deadlock with `OvercommitTracker` - 7 integration tests covering: basic admission, `REPLACE RUNNING QUERY`, no slot leak on timeout, client disconnect detection, wait-time profile event, `max_execution_time` fallback, and no-timeout-when-both-zero ## Benchmark Results Tested on a 96-core machine with k6 HTTP load testing, 5 scenarios, 3 rounds each with rotation for fairness. All three variants (FIFO, QuerySlot, Legacy) use the same binary — only server config differs. **Throughput (total iterations in 20s, avg of 3 rounds):** | Scenario | FIFO | QuerySlot | Legacy | vs QS | vs Legacy | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 150 concurrent, 100 slots | 53020 | 52792 | 52124 | +0.4% | +1.7% | | 200 concurrent, 100 slots | 53140 | 52901 | 51770 | +0.5% | +2.6% | | 500 concurrent, 100 slots | 53173 | 53032 | 50542 | +0.3% | +5.2% | | 500 concurrent, 10 slots | 112285 | 112290 | 68088 | -0.0% | +64.9% | | 200 concurrent mixed, 100 slots | 38043 | 37999 | 37406 | +0.1% | +1.7% | **p95 Latency (avg of 3 rounds):** | Scenario | FIFO | QuerySlot | Legacy | vs QS | vs Legacy | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 150 concurrent, 100 slots | 67.0ms | 67.2ms | 107.0ms | -0.3% | -37.4% | | 200 concurrent, 100 slots | 85.5ms | 85.6ms | 174.7ms | -0.2% | -51.1% | | 500 concurrent, 100 slots | 200.1ms | 200.5ms | 552.3ms | -0.2% | -63.8% | | 500 concurrent, 10 slots | 94.6ms | 95.1ms | 434.8ms | -0.5% | -78.2% | | 200 concurrent mixed, 100 slots | 222.8ms | 222.6ms | 285.9ms | +0.1% | -22.1% | **Tail spread (p95 - median, avg of 3 rounds):** | Scenario | FIFO | QuerySlot | Legacy | |---|---:|---:|---:| | 150 concurrent, 100 slots | 11.1ms | 11.0ms | 57.5ms | | 200 concurrent, 100 slots | 10.8ms | 10.6ms | 113.8ms | | 500 concurrent, 100 slots | 11.2ms | 11.1ms | 409.5ms | | 500 concurrent, 10 slots | 5.8ms | 6.3ms | 331.9ms | | 200 concurrent mixed, 100 slots | 157.1ms | 156.5ms | 207.0ms | FIFO matches `QuerySlot` throughput and latency across all scenarios while being significantly simpler to configure. Both dramatically outperform Legacy under contention — up to 65% higher throughput and 78% lower p95 latency at extreme bottleneck (500 concurrent connections, 10 slots). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add FIFO admission queue for `ProcessList` with per-waiter wakeup, configurable via `enable_query_admission_queue` server setting. Provides strict FIFO ordering, automatic client disconnect detection, and eliminates thundering-herd wakeups under high concurrency. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) New server settings: - `enable_query_admission_queue` (Bool, default `false`): When enabled, queries exceeding `max_concurrent_queries` wait in a FIFO queue instead of being rejected. Requires `queue_max_wait_ms > 0` on the query side. - `admission_queue_alive_check_interval_ms` (UInt64, default `5000`): Interval in milliseconds for checking if queued clients are still connected. Clamped to [500, 10000]. New metric: `QueryAdmissionQueueLength` — current number of queries waiting in the admission queue. New profile event: `QueryAdmissionQueueWaitMicroseconds` — time spent waiting in the admission queue. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Changes core query admission/concurrency paths in `ProcessList` and adds early-release/disconnect checks across multiple protocol handlers, which could affect fairness, timeouts, or query lifecycle under load. Mitigated by being gated behind a new server setting and covered by new integration tests. > > **Overview** > Adds an optional **FIFO query admission queue** for `max_concurrent_queries` (gated by new server setting `enable_query_admission_queue`) so excess queries wait in a per-waiter queue with `notify_one` wakeups instead of the legacy broadcast `condvar` path. > > Introduces disconnect-aware waiting via a new per-query `Context` callback (`setConnectionAliveCheck`) with a tunable server setting `admission_queue_alive_check_interval_ms`, plus new observability (`CurrentMetrics::QueryAdmissionQueueLength` and `ProfileEvents::QueryAdmissionQueueWaitMicroseconds`) and early admission-slot release in `executeQuery`. > > Separately replaces a ThreadPool startup busy-yield with `std::atomic::wait/notify_one`, and adds integration tests/config to validate FIFO ordering, timeouts/fallback behavior, replace-running-query interaction, disconnect cleanup, and metric/event reporting. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit fc0a34660161b24c95747aa28dbd3d111492870c. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: Require a converted constant to be a semantic point for a rewrite
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111924 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes wrong results and a spurious `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE` error when a chain of comparisons is rewritten into `IN`/`NOT IN`, or a two-term `AND` is folded, using a constant whose converted value does not compare the same way `equals` does. Affected constants include a float `0.0`/`-0.0` or `NaN`, a `FixedString` compared against a `String` column, an `Enum` compared against a `String`/`FixedString` column, a `Variant`/`Dynamic`/`JSON` constant, a string wider than a `FixedString(N)` column, and a constant that has no common type with a string column at all. A comparison over a `JSON` column, and one between a string column and such a constant, that the rewrites previously answered silently now correctly report `NO_COMMON_TYPE`. ### Description `LogicalExpressionOptimizerPass` rewrites `x = c1 OR x = c2 OR x = c3` into `x IN (c1, c2, c3)` (`tryReplaceOrEqualsChainWithIn`), the `notEquals` counterpart into `x NOT IN (...)` (`convertNotEqualsChainToNotIn`), and folds a two-term `AND` in `addComparisonFilter`. All three consume the constant converted into the expression's type through `tryConvertToColumnType`, whose contract is only *"does this convert losslessly?"*. That is weaker than what the three consumers actually need, which is *"is the converted `Field` a faithful semantic point for this type - does exact equality on it agree with what `equals` computes?"*. `in` builds a `Set` keyed on the converted value and matches it exactly (`SetUtils.cpp` -> `convertFieldToType` with `strict`), while the comparison it replaces is evaluated semantically in the wider of the two types; `compareComparisonFilters` and `canonicalizeNotEqualsKey` likewise treat the converted value as an exact point. Everywhere the two disagree, an optimization changes the answer - and in one case it makes a working query fail, because inserting the converted value into the set's column can throw. Eleven divergence classes, all measured at default settings (both chain-length settings default to 3), one mechanism: * **Float `+0.0`/`-0.0`.** `equals` compares with `accurateEquals` where `-0.0 == 0.0`, while the set is keyed on the exact IEEE value: `SELECT -0.0 = 0.0, -0.0 IN (0.0)` is `1, 0`. A chain over a column holding `-0.0` loses that row. * **Float `NaN`.** No comparison matches a `NaN`, but `nan IN (nan)` is `1`, so the chain gains a row. * **`FixedString` padding against a `String` target.** `ColumnFixedString::operator[]` yields all `N` bytes including the `'\0'` padding, so the set holds `'ab\0\0\0'` while the column holds `'ab'`. A full-width constant is unsound too, because zero-padded comparison also matches the value with trailing NULs. * **A converted string wider than a `FixedString(M)` target.** `ColumnFixedString::insert` throws `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE`, so a query that answers correctly without the rewrite fails with it. Reachable from a `FixedString(N > M)` source and from a plain `String` source of size `S > M` alike. * **`Enum` against a string-family target.** `equals` casts both operands to the enum's label, while `convertFieldToType` stringifies the enum's raw integer, so the set key for `'a'::Enum8('a' = 1)` against a `String` column is `'1'`. * **A `Variant` expression.** `equals` runs independently per active alternative; the set holds one discriminator-bearing key, and a constant `Field` carries no discriminator at all. * **A `Variant`/`Dynamic` constant.** `ColumnVariant::operator[]` and `ColumnDynamic::operator[]` return the bare underlying `Field` while `FunctionVariantAdaptor`/`FunctionDynamicAdaptor` compare using the active alternative's real type, so a source-type check sees only `Variant` and permits the rewrite. One shape additionally failed with `TYPE_MISMATCH`. * **A nested `NaN` in the `AND` fold.** The existing bail-out there inspects only a top-level `Float64` `Field`, so `Tuple(Float64)` slips past it. * **Distinct `NaN` payloads below an `Array`/`Map`.** Container equality treats any two `NaN`s as equal, while a compound set key hashes the nested float's raw bytes. * **A dynamic-structure expression in the fold.** Both `IN` builders already decline these; the fold does not, and it answered `0` for a comparison over a `JSON` column whose own terms legitimately raise `NO_COMMON_TYPE`. * **A constant with no common type with a string-family expression.** `equals` on a string-family operand is accepted at analysis time but is only executable when the const-string path can cast the constant, which needs the constant to be the string side. So a `String` column against e.g. an `Int64` constant, or against a multi-element `Tuple` or an `Array` constant, legitimately raises `NO_COMMON_TYPE` while the converted value round-trips, and all three rewrites answered instead - and a contradiction on an unrelated column could collapse the whole `AND` and drop the throwing operand entirely. The fix adds one shared predicate next to `tryConvertToColumnType` - the function whose contract it strengthens - and calls it from all three consumers, keeping the genuinely set-specific checks in the two `IN` builders. The string-family rule is modelled on the equivalent guard in `KeyCondition`, which declines index analysis for the same padding reasons and with the same `M >= N` exemption. The `NaN` check has a deliberate per-consumer depth. The fold compares two `Field`s with each other, so below an `Array`/`Map` boundary both sides go through the same `compareAt`, which treats any two `NaN`s as equal - the semantics already match and recursing deeper would only lose valid folds. A set instead matches a `Field`'s hash against a column's raw bytes, so the deeper check is required there. Symmetrically, the float-zero rule is set-specific only: `addComparisonFilter` compares with `accurateEquals`, under which `+0.0 == -0.0`, so it already folds those cases correctly and sharing the rule would delete a correct fold. The no-common-type rule is instead type-based and gated on the target, because the divergence is directional: the reverse pairing - a string-family constant against another type - is cast by the const-string path and stays rewritable, which is why `Date`, `UUID`, `FixedString` and `Enum` expressions with string constants must keep firing and are asserted to. It is also placed before conversion, so the parked filter carries no converted value and the global contradiction fold can veto the collapse. The rule covers composite (`Tuple`/`Array`/`Map`) constants as well: a multi-element `tuple(...)` or an `Array` against a string-family expression survives analysis, then raises `NO_COMMON_TYPE` from `executeGeneric`, and all three rewrites answered it instead. Only the spellings whose `String` rendering does not parse back - a single-element `tuple(...)` and a `Map` - were already declined by the round-trip guard. Both directions are asserted in the test. The rules are value-based wherever the divergence is value-based, so the optimization keeps firing everywhere the converted value really is a semantic point: float constants that are neither zero nor `NaN` at any width or across widths, `inf`/`-inf`, columns containing `-0.0`/`NaN` when no constant is, `FixedString(N)` against a wider-or-equal `FixedString(M)`, a `String` constant of size `S <= M` including one with a trailing NUL, an `Enum` expression with label or integer constants, `Decimal` scale pairs, `Date` with string constants, `UUID`, mixed integer widths, and `LowCardinality` columns. A blanket type-level exclusion of floats would silently disable all of those. Disclosed trade-offs, each measured: * A `Variant`- or `Dynamic`-typed constant no longer participates, including the cases that agree today. A nested such constant can carry a different active alternative per element, so there is no single alternative to resolve from the constant; resolving one would be right for a scalar and silently wrong for a nested one. * The string-family rules are broader than the minimum needed for the reported symptoms: a full-width `FixedString` constant against a `String` column is also declined, and the size rule is keyed on the converted value's size rather than on the source type, so a plain `String` source is covered too. * Queries whose chain or fold is now correctly declined lose that optimization. Correct results beat the rewrite. #### One reference line of another PR's test changes `04628_logical_optimizer_in_rewrite_variant_type.reference` line 23 moves from `1` to `0`. That test belongs to #111924 (@groeneai, merged), whose guard keeps the `IN` rewrite from changing a node's result type when a `Variant` expression is compared under the variant adaptor. Its comment read *"the guard must key on the drift and not on the type"*, and that is still true of **that** guard: this change does not touch it, its `setting = 0` line above is unchanged at `0`, and with `use_variant_default_implementation_for_comparisons = 1` the type drift really is gone so it no longer skips. What changed is that the chain is now declined one step earlier, by the converted-constant check, because a constant `Field` carries no discriminator and therefore cannot be a semantic point for a `Variant` expression. The comment is rewritten to say exactly that. The shape that line asserted is not intrinsically safe either - its fixture is `Variant(UInt256)` with `'1'`/`'2'`/`'3'` constants, which happen to parse exactly; change only the constant and the same fixture diverges. #### Two narrowings were considered and both are measurably unsound The obvious objection is that a `Variant` with exactly one alternative has nothing to depend on per row, so the decline should apply only to multi-alternative `Variant`s. Six single-alternative carriers say otherwise, all at default settings - for a `Variant` **target** the shared semantic-point rule matches none of its string-family, `Tuple`, `Array` or `Map` branches and falls through to accepting the constant, so every divergence above is live with one alternative: | single-alternative shape | before | ground truth | |---|---|---| | `Variant(String)` expression, `toFixedString('ab', 5)`-family constants | `0` | `3` | | `Variant(String)` expression, `Enum8` label constants | `0` | `3` | | `Tuple(Variant(String))` expression, `tuple(toFixedString(...))` constants | `0` | `2` | | `Variant(FixedString(3))` expression, `'abcde'` constants | `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` | `0` | | `Variant(Tuple(Variant(Float64, UInt64)))` expression, `tuple(1)`-family constants | `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` | `3` | | `Variant(DateTime64(1, 'UTC'))` expression, **same-scale** `DateTime64(1, 'UTC')` constants | `ILLEGAL_COLUMN` | `3` | The second narrowing - unwrap the sole alternative and re-apply the existing leaf checks to it - fixes the first five and still fails the last. With constants of the identical type nothing is converted: `tryConvertToColumnType` returns at its equal-types fast path, the value round-trips trivially, and every leaf check passes. The failure is a property of the wrapper, not of the constant: the set column for a `Variant` expression is built nullable and `ColumnNullable` refuses a `ColumnVariant` nested column unconditionally. So no value-level or leaf-level predicate can be sound here, and the decline keys on the type. The cost of that is three measured rewrites that are correct today and are now forgone - `Variant(Float32)` against `Float64` constants, `Variant(Enum8)` against `String` labels, and `Variant(UInt256)` against `Int64` - versus six carriers, three of which are silent wrong results and three of which are query failures. All three are asserted in the test with their results and with the rewrite not firing, so the trade is visible rather than implicit. #### The dynamic-structure expression guard is not redundant with the constant-side check The two rules leave different state behind, which is why both are needed. The expression guard in `addComparisonFilter` parks the filter **before** conversion, so its converted value is empty; the constant-side rule runs after conversion succeeded and parks a populated one. The global contradiction fold may only collapse an `AND` to `false` when no parked filter is missing its converted value, so only the expression guard can veto it - which is what keeps the query's own `NO_COMMON_TYPE` visible when a contradiction on an unrelated column would otherwise have collapsed the whole `AND` and dropped the throwing term. Without it, such a query's success would depend on `optimize_redundant_comparisons`. Measured on `i Int32, c JSON(x String)`: `(i = 1) AND (i = 2) AND (c != '{"x":1}'::JSON(x Int64))` answered `0` before and raises `NO_COMMON_TYPE` now. The guard keys on the expression type rather than on the individual comparison, because to be able to veto at all it has to park before conversion with no converted value; so a safe comparison over the same `JSON` column is vetoed too and that `AND` is retained as well. Results are unchanged either way, the cost is a forgone fold, and the same contradiction without a dynamic-structure term still folds. The two-expression row, the safe row's result and both plan shapes are asserted; the single-expression `JSON` fold row is closed by the same guard. #### Recursion depth The three constant walkers, both recursive type walks and the `forEachChild` callback call `checkStackSize()` at each composite recursion boundary, following `FieldVisitorHash`, which places it on its `Tuple`/`Map`/`Array`/`Object` operators and on none of its scalar ones. The callback needs it for the same reason as the rest: every `forEachChild` implementation invokes the callback from inside its own recursive frame, so the callback observes the accumulated nesting depth rather than a constant one. The walkers need it because `tryConvertToColumnType` returns immediately for equal types, so a nested same-type constant can reach them without having passed the check `convertFieldToType` performs. This is hardening, not a fix for an observed failure: a deeply nested constant already fails with a controlled `TOO_DEEP_RECURSION` from an earlier pass at the same depth with and without these walkers, and at default settings `max_ast_depth` rejects the shape long before that. `IDataType::hasDynamicStructure()` itself is left alone - it recurses unguarded, and it is called from 16 places outside its own overrides across 10 files, including two pre-existing ones in this pass, so guarding it belongs in `IDataType` and benefits all of them. Not addressed here, knowingly: `tryConvertToColumnType`'s round-trip check is top-level only, because `convertFieldToType` passes no source-type hint when recursing into `Array`/`Tuple`/`Map` elements, so a nested lossy leaf conversion escapes it. That belongs in `convertFieldToType` and is already being fixed there by #111399. Only its `Variant`-source form is closed here, since that PR does not touch the `Variant` branch. Also left alone deliberately: both builders bypass the chain-length gate for a `LowCardinality` expression, so on such a column no setting turns the rewrite off. That is a separate optimization decision and only amplified the severity; this change makes those cases correct regardless of chain length, because the guard runs per constant on every rewrite attempt. New test `04632_logical_optimizer_chain_to_in_value_equivalence` asserts every affected shape against ground truth computed as one subquery column per comparison, so no equals-chain pattern is left for the pass to rewrite. It also asserts, via `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE`, that the optimization still fires on every shape where the converted value is a semantic point - that half is what a too-broad guard would break.

signal.title: Read and checksum the UNIQUE KEY dense-index SST through IDataPartStorage
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow the UNIQUE KEY to work on encrypted and remote disks by reading and writing its dense-index SST through the part storage abstraction; the SST is now recorded in `checksums.txt`. ### Description The per-part UNIQUE KEY dense index (`unique_key_index.sst`) was opened and written by local filesystem path, which only worked on local disks and left the sidecar outside the part's checksum accounting. This PR drives the SST through `IDataPartStorage` using a custom RocksDB `Env`(a read-only `FileSystem` over `IDataPartStorage::readFile` for the reader, a `WriteBuffer`-backed one for the writer), so encrypted and remote disks work as well. The SST is now recorded in `checksums.txt`, so it is transferred by backup/fetch like any other part file and validated by `checkConsistencyBase`: a missing or wrongly-sized SST fails the standard consistency check and the part is detached as broken, while size-preserving corruption is caught at load time by `ensureValidDenseIndex` (RocksDB block-checksum + entry-count validation), which removes and rebuilds the index. On readonly storage a corrupt or absent SST fails the load closed instead of activating an unprobeable part. The previous restriction that UNIQUE KEY tables must reside on local-only storage policies is removed.

signal.title: Auto-enable uncompressed cache for MergeTree reads
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add the setting `enable_automatic_use_uncompressed_cache` (disabled by default) that automatically enables the uncompressed cache for eligible local reads from tables in the `MergeTree` family when `use_uncompressed_cache` is not explicitly set. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) This change improves the `MergeTree` read path by allowing the uncompressed cache to be enabled automatically for small eligible local reads, while keeping the old behavior for remote storage and explicit user settings. The automatic mode is opt-in (`enable_automatic_use_uncompressed_cache = 1`). The automatic mode is not enabled by default because the server cannot distinguish an explicit `use_uncompressed_cache=0` passed as an HTTP query parameter or a command-line client option from an unset one (`SettingsConstraints::checkOrClamp` erases settings changes whose value equals the current value), so a default-on automatic mode would silently override an explicit user opt-out on those paths. Only `SETTINGS use_uncompressed_cache = 0` in the query text or a settings profile takes precedence reliably. Defaulting the automatic mode to on would additionally need performance evidence, since the uncompressed cache is not universally beneficial.

signal.title: Re-land aggregate function `gini` in the `sum` family
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113868 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112280 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New aggregate function `gini`, which calculates the [Gini coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient) of a column of finite, non-negative numeric values. The result ranges from `0` (all values equal) towards `1` as inequality grows; for a sample of `n` values the maximum is `(n - 1) / n`. `NaN` values are skipped and infinite values are rejected. The function returns `Float64` and consumes `O(n)` memory. ### Description Re-lands the `gini` function that #113868 reverted, following the option-2 spec @ Manerone gave in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763#issuecomment-5217284116 and confirmed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763#issuecomment-5279278069. It re-adds #112280's function with exactly three items removed, and touches no file under `src/AggregateFunctions/Combinators/`: - the `getArgumentsThatCanBeOnlyNull` override, - `.returns_default_when_only_null = true` on registration, - the `argument_type->onlyNull()` branch in the creator. The property was doing the work. It made `AggregateFunctionFactory::getImpl` skip its only-null guard and build a real `gini` instance over `Nullable(Nothing)`, so `gini(NULL)` returned `Float64` `nan` where every `sum`-family function folds to `Nullable(Nothing)`. Without it the fold happens in the `Null` combinator before any other combinator is applied, and the creator's only-null branch becomes unreachable, which is also why `createAggregateFunctionSum` has no equivalent. `gini` now registers exactly like `sum`. Runtime `Nullable` handling is a separate axis, via `getOwnNullAdapter`, and is unchanged: `gini` over `[1, NULL, 3]` still returns `0.25`. Validated on three binaries: post-revert master (`gini` absent), a build carrying #112280's version, and this branch. Every literal-`NULL` cell on this branch equals the `sum` value measured on the same binary, and all non-`NULL` results are unchanged from #112280. Docs: `gini.mdx` plus its slug-map, navigation and redirect entries are restored byte-identically to their merged state in #114314, which #113868's revert had removed as collateral. The page keeps the hand-written header above `{/*AUTOGENERATED_START*/}`; the body inside the markers is what the generator produces from the `FunctionDocumentation` block in `AggregateFunctionGini.cpp`. The three index entries are needed, not cosmetic: without the slug-map row the nightly generator resolves no Mintlify destination and fails for this page. Since the page carries the markers, this needs the `pr-autogenerated-docs` label to pass the generated-region guard, as the guard's own message asks for. cc @Manerone

signal.title: TTL CLEAR INDEX for MergeTree parts
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107804 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78714 TTL CLEAR INDEX lets a MergeTree table keep secondary indexes for recent parts while dropping the physical index files from old parts. I recommend reviewing commit-by-commit. The motivating case is Observability log storage. For log tables, the raw data is not always the dominant cost. Text indexes can be very large, and most queries only touch recent data. We want to keep the index where it helps and stop paying for it on old parts that are rarely searched. Example syntax: ```sql TTL timestamp + INTERVAL 7 DAY CLEAR INDEX message_text ``` This follows the existing meaning of `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR INDEX`: remove the per-part index files, but keep the index definition in table metadata. Queries remain correct. Parts without the index just fall back to scanning. ## What this changes The patch adds a new table TTL action, `CLEAR INDEX`, and stores its per-part min/max TTL info in `ttl.txt` as `index_clear_ttl`. When a part is fully past the TTL for a target index, future maintenance may remove that index’s files from the part. If the table later reads that part, the secondary index reader already handles missing index files and simply does not use that index for that part. The patch also adds system table visibility: ```text system.parts.index_clear_ttl_info.{index_name,expression,min,max} ``` ## Merge behavior There are two cases. First, normal merges apply the TTL policy to their output. If a merge output is fully past the `CLEAR INDEX` TTL, the merge should not retain the target index files. This is important for late-arriving data: a tiny old insert should not cause a merge that rebuilds a huge old text index. Second, there is a dedicated TTL maintenance merge type: `MergeType::TTLClearIndex`. This is used for the case where a single old part has expired index files and does not otherwise need a merge. The first implementation is intentionally conservative: it selects one source part and produces one replacement part. Dedicated `TTLClearIndex` selection obeys the normal full-part merge byte and row limits. This keeps cleanup conservative when preserving the part would require copying unchanged files rather than hardlinking them. For eligible full-storage parts, the implementation uses a fast path: hardlink or copy unchanged files, omit the expired index files, rewrite checksums and metadata, and publish the replacement part. Projection directories are copied wholesale because the row set is unchanged. This avoids reading and rewriting the raw data. If the fast path is not safe, the code falls back to the normal rewrite path. The fallback may rewrite the part, but it still must not retain expired index files in the final output. Parts with incomplete TTL metadata are not selected for dedicated cleanup; `MATERIALIZE TTL` or an ordinary merge must first recalculate the current TTL rules. The fast path currently opts out for cases like packed part storage, UUID parts, legacy parts without metadata-version files, metadata version mismatches, patch parts, part-format changes, and projection subdirectories it cannot copy as-is. On remote or zero-copy storage, it copies unchanged files instead of hardlinking them. It handles packed skip-index archives by excluding dirty `skp_idx.packed` files from the hardlink/copy set and rewriting the archive for surviving packed entries. ## Rollout safety `TTLClearIndex` is a new merge type, and merge types are serialized in replicated MergeTree log entries. Older replicas would not understand a new merge type. For that reason, generation is gated by a setting: ```sql enable_ttl_clear_index_merge_type_generation ``` The default is off. The binary can parse and execute `TTLClearIndex`, but a server will not write that merge type to the replicated log unless the setting is enabled. The intended rollout is: 1. deploy code everywhere; 2. once every replica that can read the log understands `TTLClearIndex`, enable generation; 3. later we can consider changing the default. With the gate off, replicas will not schedule dedicated `TTLClearIndex` maintenance work. Regular merges can still apply the clear-index TTL to their outputs, which is safe because missing per-part index files are already supported. ## Interaction with `SYSTEM STOP TTL MERGES` `CLEAR INDEX` is a TTL effect, so it respects the TTL merge blocker. If TTL merges are already stopped before a regular merge starts, the merge continues without applying clear-index TTL effects. If TTL merges are stopped after a merge has already decided to apply clear-index TTL effects, the merge is cancelled, matching existing TTL-delete behavior. ## Validation and edge cases covered The tests cover: - invalid target index names - per-part `index_clear_ttl_info` in `system.parts`, including the target index name - minmax index clearing - text index clearing - the late tiny insert case, where an old cleared part later merges with a small old part - adding `CLEAR INDEX` TTL to a table that already has old indexed data - TTL dependency recalculation after mutating a column used by the TTL expression - replicated execution with embedded Keeper - generation off vs generation on ## Things deliberately left conservative The fast path is narrow on purpose. Physically unsupported parts use the regular fallback, while parts with incomplete TTL metadata wait for recalculation. We can broaden the fast path later once we are comfortable with storage-specific details. The generation gate is also conservative. It is there to make rolling upgrades safe, not to disable all `CLEAR INDEX` TTL behavior. Possible follow-ups: - share more code with the existing `ALTER ... CLEAR INDEX` mutation path - add more schema-evolution tests around dropping or changing target indexes - add more direct instrumentation around which files were hardlinked vs copied in the fast path ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): MergeTree tables now support `TTL ... CLEAR INDEX index_name`, which clears secondary index files from parts once all rows in the part are past the TTL. This can help to manage the lifecycle of large indexes on older data, to conserve disk space.

signal.title: Use the vector similarity index for integer reference vectors
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112233 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114291 The reference vector of an ANN query is extracted only when its array type is `Float64`, `Float32` or `BFloat16` and every element is a `Float64` field. An integer literal such as `[1, 2]` is typed `Array(UInt8)`, so `tryUseVectorSearch` bails out and the query silently falls back to a brute-force scan over the whole table, although `[1, 2]` denotes the same point as `[1.0, 2.0]` and `L2Distance` accepts it. `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` shows no `vector_similarity` entry and gives no hint why, so a one-character difference in a literal becomes a sharp performance cliff on large tables. Native integer arrays are now accepted as reference vectors and their elements are converted to `Float64`, which is the type the reference vector is stored in anyway. Added `02354_vector_search_bug112233`, covering unsigned, signed, mixed integer/float, and not-exactly-representable reference vectors, plus an equality check between the integer and float spellings of the same query. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Vector search queries now use the `vector_similarity` index when the reference vector is written as an integer array literal, e.g. `ORDER BY L2Distance(vec, [1, 2])`. Previously such queries silently fell back to a brute-force scan.
signal.author: hamidr

signal.title: Support bearer-token authentication in BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP
signal.text: `BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP` had no way to authenticate with a bearer token: callers spliced an `Authorization: Bearer` entry into the header list themselves and had to remember not to pass HTTP Basic credentials at the same time, because both occupy the same header. `create` now takes the credential directly, in three overloads: Basic credentials, a bearer token, or both — with a non-empty token taking precedence, so the either/or rule lives in one place instead of in every caller. `create` also appends the bearer header to a local copy of the header list rather than mutating the builder, so a builder can be reused without carrying over a stale token. Every bearer-token call site of the class is migrated to the new overloads: - `HTTPBasedCatalogUtils` and `UnityCatalog`: built the header by hand and passed never-used HTTP Basic credentials alongside; now call `create` with the token. - `RestCatalog`, `OneLakeCatalog`, `BigLakeCatalog`: `getAuthHeaders` now returns an `AuthHeaders` (a bearer token plus extra headers). The bearer goes to `create`; only genuine extra headers (a user-supplied `auth_header`, `x-goog-user-project`, `User-Agent`) stay in the header list. `OneLakeCatalog`'s pre-obtained token also moved from a spliced header to the bearer. - `PaimonRestCatalog`: the `bearer` token provider (the `dlf` request-signing branch keeps its own signed headers). Out of scope — different transport (plain Poco requests or S3-client headers), not `BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP`: `OpenAIProvider`, `CloudJWTProvider`, ArrowFlight `AuthMiddleware`, GCS `diskSettings`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ...

signal.title: Enable CORS in clickhouse-local by default
signal.text: `clickhouse-local` can serve HTTP after `SYSTEM START LISTEN HTTP`, but it normally runs without a config file, so it had no `http_options_response` section and answered the CORS preflight with a bare `204` carrying no `Access-Control-*` headers. A browser therefore refuses every cross-origin request to it - including the Web UI opened from a `file://` URL, whose origin is `null`. Now `clickhouse-local` sets the same default `http_options_response` headers that the `clickhouse-server` configuration ships (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and friends). A configuration file with its own `http_options_response` section still replaces them entirely, and the headers are sent only for requests that carry an `Origin`, exactly as in `clickhouse-server`. Note the implication, which is now documented next to the existing security warning for the listeners: while an HTTP listener is open, any web page you visit can query the local instance over the loopback address and read the results. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `clickhouse-local` now answers CORS preflight requests with the same permissive headers as `clickhouse-server`, so the HTTP interface opened by `SYSTEM START LISTEN HTTP` can be used from a browser out of the box, including the Web UI opened from a `file://` URL. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1522` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Read all summed columns for SELECT FINAL from SummingMergeTree
signal.text: `SELECT ... FINAL` from a `SummingMergeTree` table returned wrong results when the query read only a subset of the columns of the summation. A merge removes a row when the values in **all** of the columns of the summation are zero after summing. The FINAL read applied the same rule, but only over the columns the query happened to read. Two ways to misbehave follow from that: - A query reading a subset of the summed columns removed every group whose visible columns summed to zero, even though an unread summed column made the row survive a real merge — rows silently disappeared. The most common victim is bare `count()`, which reads a single smallest column (plus the internally added sorting key): on a table `(c0 Int8, c1 Int32, c3 UInt64) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree ORDER BY c3` with two overlapping parts where `c0` sums to zero for some keys, `SELECT count() FROM t FINAL` returned 10 instead of 15, and `SELECT c0, c3 FROM t FINAL` lost the same 5 rows. - A query reading none of the summed columns (e.g. only the sorting key) never removed anything, keeping rows that a real merge deletes. The fix always includes all columns that a merge would aggregate into the FINAL read set (and into the set protected from plan-level column pruning), so the removal decision is taken over the same set of columns as in a real merge. This makes `SELECT ... FINAL` agree with `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` followed by a plain `SELECT`. Note that queries over `SummingMergeTree FINAL` that previously read a subset of the summed columns now read all of them, which is the price of the correct result. Found by the nightly SQLancer `FinalMerge` oracle (`SELECT count() FROM t0 FINAL` returned 9947 before `OPTIMIZE TABLE t0 FINAL` and 9999 after it on the same data): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=5c9f28ed5a2c585ad46bf74d6600cdcf3aa07a9e&name_0=NightlySQLancer&name_1=SQLancer%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29&name_1=SQLancer ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results of `SELECT ... FINAL` from `SummingMergeTree` when the query reads only a subset of the columns of the summation: the decision to remove a row whose sums are all zero is now taken over all columns of the summation, as in a real merge, instead of only the columns the query reads. Previously, rows could silently disappear from the result (for example, `SELECT count() FROM table FINAL`). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Support `UNIQUE` predicate that tests for no duplicate rows in a subquery
signal.text: Implement the SQL standard `UNIQUE` predicate that returns true when all rows in a subquery are distinct and false when duplicates exist. Empty subqueries return true (vacuously unique). The implementation follows the same pattern as `EXISTS`: - Parser: `UniqueLayer` class parses `UNIQUE(subquery)` syntax - Analyzer: rewrites to `SELECT count() = uniqExact(*) FROM (subquery)` - Analyzer: correlated subqueries are rejected with a clear `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` error; the old analyzer rejects `UNIQUE` with a clear error as well Closes #99609 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added `UNIQUE(subquery)` predicate that returns true when all rows in the subquery are distinct. It behaves according to the SQL standard: duplicates yield false, empty subqueries yield true. Closes #99609 ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions sort_by_label() and sort_by_label_desc()
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support the PromQL functions `sort_by_label()` and `sort_by_label_desc()` in the experimental PromQL dialect for `TimeSeries` tables. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes: `sort_by_label(v instant-vector, label string, ...)` and `sort_by_label_desc(v instant-vector, label string, ...)` sort the elements of an instant vector by the natural sort order of the given label values, in ascending and descending order respectively. Several label names may be provided; earlier labels take precedence and later ones break ties. A missing label is treated as an empty string (matching Prometheus). ### Description This adds the PromQL sorting-by-label functions to the experimental PromQL-to-SQL converter: - `sort_by_label(v, label, ...)` — sort ascending by the given label values. - `sort_by_label_desc(v, label, ...)` — sort descending by the given label values. Unlike `sort()` / `sort_desc()` (which order by sample value), these order by the *natural* sort order of the requested label values, so numeric segments compare numerically (e.g. `host1, host2, host10, host20`). Multiple labels are supported: earlier labels take precedence, later labels break ties, and the full label set is appended as a deterministic final tiebreaker. A missing label is treated as an empty string. Implementation notes: - Grammar: added `sort_by_label` / `sort_by_label_desc` to `PromQLLexer.g4` and regenerated the ANTLR lexer. - Lowering: `applySortFunction` records the sort direction and the list of labels on the result; `finalizeSQL` emits `ORDER BY naturalSortKey(tupleElement(arrayFirst(t -> t.1 = '<label>', tags), 2)) [, ...], tags` with the corresponding direction. - Errors: at least two arguments are required, and every label argument must be a string. Testing: - Parser unit tests in `gtest_PromQLParser.cpp`. - Stateless test `04556_promql_sort_by_label` covering single-label natural ordering, descending order, multi-label ordering with the missing-label/tiebreak behaviour, and the argument-count / argument-type errors. > [!NOTE] > This PR is stacked on top of #112826 (`sort()` / `sort_desc()`), which introduces the shared sort infrastructure. Until that PR merges, the diff here also shows its commit; review only the `sort_by_label` commit.
signal.author: valerypetrov

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions stddev_over_time() and stdvar_over_time()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `stddev_over_time()` and `stdvar_over_time()` (population standard deviation/variance). ### Description Implements `stddev_over_time(v range-vector)` and `stdvar_over_time(v range-vector)`, previously reported as not implemented. **Key Technical & Numerical Stability Highlights**: 1. **Welford's Algorithm & Chan's Parallel Merge**: Uses a running centered-moment `{count, mean, m2}` accumulator ($M_2 = \sum (x - \bar{x})^2$) in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesVarianceOverTime.h` updated per sample via Welford's formula and merged pairwise via Chan et al.'s parallel merge algorithm. This avoids catastrophic cancellation on large-magnitude counter series (e.g. byte counters $\sim 5 \times 10^8$, where raw $\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2 / N$ loses all precision and produces false zeroes or negative variances). 2. **Prometheus Staleness Handling**: Implements full Prometheus stale-marker (`0x7ff0000000000002`) semantics. Stale markers are flagged at ingestion (`is_stale_marker`), excluded from range-vector aggregations (`WHERE NOT is_stale_marker`) so target disappearance does not pollute range windows with NaNs, while remaining detectable by instant selectors to correctly report series absence. 3. **Non-Invertible Two-Stacks / Recompute Strategy**: Avoids floating-point `unmerge` subtraction on moments to prevent numerical cancellation and drift over long sliding windows. Registered `timeSeriesStddevToGrid`/`timeSeriesStdvarToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the two `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`. **Verified numerically against Prometheus 3.5.0**: verified bit-for-bit accuracy against Prometheus 3.5.0 live responses, including cross-architecture (ARM64 vs x86_64) ULP tolerance handling in CI. **Testing**: SQL-level test (`04628_variance_timeseries_functions.sql`) covering empty/single/multi-sample windows and `AggregatingMergeTree` round-trips, plus integration cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` (including stale-marker ingestion and instant/range evaluations). This flips 12 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.

signal.title: Add groupBloomFilter aggregate function and bloomFilterContains scalar function
signal.text: Adds the `groupBloomFilter` aggregate function and the `bloomFilterContains` scalar function for memory-efficient probabilistic set-membership testing. This can be used to detect new values, perform approximate deduplication checks, and compare large datasets without materializing exact sets. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/11700 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add the `groupBloomFilter` aggregate function for building Bloom filter states and the `bloomFilterContains` scalar function for testing whether values are probably present. The functions support configurable expected element counts, false-positive rates, and seeds, and work with the `-State` and `-MergeState` combinators and `AggregatingMergeTree`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Documentation is added in `docs/en/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/groupbloomfilter.md` and `docs/en/sql-reference/functions/bloom-filter-functions.md`.

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions sum_over_time(), avg_over_time() and count_over_time()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `sum_over_time()`, `avg_over_time()` and `count_over_time()`. ### Description Implements three PromQL range-vector functions previously reported as not implemented. `sum_over_time`, `avg_over_time` and `count_over_time` are three different projections of the same `(sum, count)` accumulator, so they share one new header (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSumCountAvg.h`) with a single invertible `Summary{sum, count}` monoid (merge adds both fields, unmerge subtracts them), plugged into the existing generic `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesSlidingSum` sliding-window fast path — the same infrastructure already proven by `rate`/`increase`/`delta`. No changes were needed to the generic grid/bucket machinery (`AggregateFunctionTimeseriesBase.h`) or to `checkArgumentTypes` (all three take a single range-vector argument, the existing default). Registered `timeSeriesSumToGrid`/`timeSeriesAvgToGrid`/`timeSeriesCountToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the three `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`, matching `rate`/`increase`/`delta`'s convention. **Verified against Prometheus 3.5.0.** **Testing**: new SQL-level test (`04628_timeseries_sum_avg_count_over_time.sql`) plus cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` covering all three functions, an empty-window case, a window narrower than the step (grid points with no sample must be absent/NULL, not zero), and a nested `avg_over_time(rate(...)[2m:10s])` case. This flips 19 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed.

signal.title: Show file sizes next to artifact links in CI reports
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114722 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114803 Reimplements #114722 (reverted in #114803 because it duplicated the existing size-tracking functionality). Every link to an uploaded file now shows its size, e.g. `clickhouse-common-static_26.8.1.1332_amd64.deb (1.2 GiB)`, in both places file links appear: the widget on a job page and the expanded info row of any result. Instead of recording a new per-link size map at upload time, the size is taken from the `StorageUsage` data already attached to each result's `ext`: `uploaded_details` is a `{basename: bytes}` map, and a link's last path component is exactly that basename, so `json.html` looks the size up directly. This makes the rendering change purely a `json.html` one — no `s3.py`, `result.py`, or private-proxy link-rewrite changes are needed. Links with no recorded size (a link to another report, or any report produced before this change) render exactly as before; `json.html` has to be deployed for existing report URLs to pick up the rendering change. This PR also slims down the workflow-level report: when a job's result is embedded as a sub-result of the workflow result, only the `ext` keys the report renders per row are kept (`labels`, `hlabels`, `storage_usage`). The rest — notably the heavy decimated host `metrics` timeline — is dropped, as it is only needed on the job's own report, which is uploaded separately with the full `ext`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signal.title: Parquet: map TIME logical type to Time64
signal.text: The native Parquet reader currently maps both `logical.TIMESTAMP` and `logical.TIME` (and the deprecated converted types `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS`/`TIMESTAMP_MICROS`/`TIME_MILLIS`/`TIME_MICROS`) to `DataTypeDateTime64`. That was fine before ClickHouse 25.6, when there was no time-of-day type, but it now produces the Parquet analogue of #104038: when the target column is `Time64` and `session_timezone` is non-UTC, the `DateTime64 -> Time64` cast (PR #90310) shifts the value by the timezone — silent data corruption for a value that has no date/timezone to begin with. This PR splits the schema-converter branch so that: - `logical.TIME` / `TIME_MILLIS` / `TIME_MICROS` → `DataTypeTime64(scale)` (timezone-unaware). - `logical.TIMESTAMP` → `DataTypeDateTime64(scale, timezone)` (unchanged). It also extends `is_output_type_decimal` to recognize `Time64` so min/max stats stay enabled when the output column is `Time64`, and removes the stale comment that claimed ClickHouse has no time-of-day type. While covering explicit type hints in the test (`SELECT * FROM file(..., 'Parquet', 't Time')`), I hit a second pre-existing gap from 25.6: `Time64 -> Time` was never registered as a cast — it threw `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` because `IsDataTypeNumber<DataTypeTime>` is `false` (it inherits `DataTypeNumberBase<Int32>`, not `DataTypeNumber<Int32>`). Before this PR the path went `DateTime64 -> Time` and returned a wrong, timezone-shifted value; after the Parquet fix it would have thrown. The second commit adds an inline `Time64 -> Time` branch in `ConvertImpl` that divides by the scale multiplier — no timezone offset, because both Time64 and Time are timezone-unaware seconds-of-day. A new stateless test `04277_parquet_time_of_day` covers: - Schema-less inference (Parquet `time32[ms]`/`time64[us]`/`time64[ns]` → `Nullable(Time64(3/6/9))`; `TIMESTAMP` stays `Nullable(DateTime64(6, 'UTC'))`). - Import into `Time64(scale)` columns under `session_timezone = 'Asia/Shanghai'` (values must not shift). - Explicit type hints under non-UTC session: `Time64(3)` / `Time` / `DateTime64(3, 'UTC')` / `Int64`. Review follow-up: making `Time64 -> DateTime` legal also exposed that `ToDateTimeMonotonicity` treated `Time64` sources as monotonic, while the cast wraps negative time-of-day values with the default `date_time_overflow_behavior = 'ignore'` (`-00:00:01` -> `2106-02-07 06:28:15`), i.e. it drops at zero. `toDateTime` now reports non-monotonic for `Time`/`Time64` sources; the regression test `04828_time64_to_datetime_not_monotonic` shows that without the guard the key condition prunes every granule and range/point queries over a `Time64` key silently return empty results. The Parquet docs (`docs/reference/formats/Parquet/Parquet.mdx`) are updated for the new `TIME` -> `Time64` mapping. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix Parquet `time32`/`time64` columns being read as `DateTime64` and then silently shifted by `session_timezone` when inserted into a `Time64` target column. Parquet `TIME` logical types now map directly to `Time64`, and a previously-missing `Time64 -> Time` cast is added. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)
